Graphium teredon.headline: Swift blue-banded swallowtail patrolling rivers and hill valleys
Graphium teredon.upperwing: Deep velvety black crossed diagonally from forewing apex to hindwing by a continuous, tapered turquoise-blue band.
Graphium teredon.underwing: Dusky brown repeating the turquoise band plus crimson spots near the hindwing margin.
Graphium teredon.similarSpecies: Formerly grouped under Graphium sarpedon; separated from Common Jay by its continuous central band and short tooth-like hindwing projection.
Graphium teredon.habitat: Forested hills, riverbanks, cinnamon-rich habitats, and shaded estates.
Graphium teredon.behavior: Glides rapidly along canopy gaps and congregates at damp sand patches in sunny forest clearings.
Graphium teredon.tnDistribution: Common across Western and Eastern Ghats including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Kovai Kutralam, and Yercaud.
Graphium teredon.notes: Southern Indian subspecies formerly grouped under Graphium sarpedon, now widely treated as a distinct peninsular and Sri Lankan species.

Graphium doson.headline: Tailless pale-cyan jay often mud-puddling along streams
Graphium doson.upperwing: Dark brown-black crossed by a central chain of semi-translucent pale aqua-blue spots and marginal spots.
Graphium doson.underwing: Silvery-brown with crisp crimson-edged black spots along the hindwing costal and discal region.
Graphium doson.similarSpecies: Separated from Southern Bluebottle (Graphium teredon) by the detached row of central spots and distinct red-centered dark spots on the hindwing underside.
Graphium doson.habitat: Forest streams, damp roads, foothills, parks, and woodlands.
Graphium doson.behavior: Rapid flyer that gathers in large mixed mud-puddling clusters along sunny stream beds.
Graphium doson.season: Common year-round, peaking in spring and post-monsoon.
Graphium doson.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills and wooded plains.
Graphium doson.notes: Often mud-puddles in dense clusters alongside Southern Bluebottles along sunlit wet hill-stream sandbanks.

Graphium agamemnon.headline: Fast-darting emerald-spotted swallowtail of gardens and hills
Graphium agamemnon.upperwing: Black wings spangled with dozens of bright apple-green rounded and bar-shaped spots; hindwing carries a short tail.
Graphium agamemnon.underwing: Warm purplish-brown mirroring the green spots, accented with tiny red marks along the hindwing base.
Graphium agamemnon.similarSpecies: Spot rows are broken into discrete emerald dots and short tails rather than the continuous pale turquoise band of Common Jay or Bluebottle.
Graphium agamemnon.habitat: Urban gardens, avenues with False Ashoka trees, foothills, and evergreen forests.
Graphium agamemnon.behavior: Restlessly vibrates its wings even while sipping nectar from Ixora and Lantana flowers.
Graphium agamemnon.season: Seen throughout the year across Tamil Nadu.
Graphium agamemnon.tnDistribution: Abundant statewide in both urban parks and hill forests.
Graphium agamemnon.notes: One of the easiest swallowtails to attract to urban gardens planted with custard apple or False Ashoka.

Graphium antiphates.headline: Gliding cream-and-black swallowtail with slender long hindwing tails
Graphium antiphates.upperwing: Creamy-white with five bold black transverse bars crossing the forewing cell and inner margin, smoky grey-black wing tips, and long slender black tails edged with white.
Graphium antiphates.underwing: Translucent pale green near the forewing base, bright ochre-yellow across the hindwing outer half banded in black, and black bars showing through from above.
Graphium antiphates.similarSpecies: Separated from the Spot Swordtail (Graphium nomius) by five thick wedge-shaped black costal bars that stop halfway across the forewing rather than crisp spotted bands and chained marginal dots.
Graphium antiphates.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, forest streams, damp gravel roads, and shaded valleys.
Graphium antiphates.behavior: Glides rapidly high among canopy crowns before circling down in numbers to mud-puddle on wet sand and mineral-rich stream edges during warm mornings.
Graphium antiphates.season: Most conspicuous during pre-monsoon showers (March-June) and post-monsoon sunshine (September-December).
Graphium antiphates.tnDistribution: Western Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Graphium antiphates.notes: Occasionally congregates in dozens alongside Lime Butterflies and Common Jays on wet hill-stream sandbanks.

Graphium nomius.headline: Deciduous-woodland swallowtail striped in black and powdery white
Graphium nomius.upperwing: Crisp white to very pale bluish-white crossed by five broad jet-black transverse bands on the forewing, a dark outer border bearing a row of white spots, and a long slender black tail.
Graphium nomius.underwing: Warm bronzy-brown markings replacing parts of the black bands, accented by a neat row of small red spots nestled between black bars on the hindwing.
Graphium nomius.similarSpecies: Lacks the Five-bar Swordtail's greenish-yellow hindwing underside and instead shows distinct bronzy-brown bands enclosing red hindwing spots.
Graphium nomius.habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forests, scrub-clad foothills, seasonal stream beds, and wooded campus edges.
Graphium nomius.behavior: Emerges synchronously after first rains, fluttering energetically over moist sandbanks and nectar-rich Lantana or Albizia blossoms.
Graphium nomius.season: Strong seasonal peak from February through June following dry-season heat and early showers.
Graphium nomius.tnDistribution: Recorded across Eastern Ghats (Kalvarayan, Shervarayan, Pachamalai), Kallar foothills, Mudumalai, and foothills bordering Coimbatore and Madurai.
Graphium nomius.notes: Caterpillars feed primarily on deciduous Annonaceae trees like Miliusa tomentosa, causing brief spring abundance bursts across foothill scrubs.

Pachliopta aristolochiae.headline: Red-bodied swallowtail with white-spotted hindwing centre
Pachliopta aristolochiae.upperwing: Black forewings with pale rayed veins and dark-tailed hindwings marked by a central cluster of white spots encircled by pinkish-red marginal lunules.
Pachliopta aristolochiae.underwing: Similar to upperwing; crimson thorax and abdomen clearly signal distastefulness to predators.
Pachliopta aristolochiae.similarSpecies: Lacks the bold white forewing stripes of Crimson Rose and displays a white discal patch on the hindwing; lacks the red body of Common Mormon mimics.
Pachliopta aristolochiae.habitat: Gardens, scrub, grasslands, agricultural edges, and forest clearings.
Pachliopta aristolochiae.behavior: Weak, unhurried flight close to nectar plants; rests with wings partly spread in morning sun.
Pachliopta aristolochiae.tnDistribution: Widespread across plains, wetlands, and hills up to mid-elevations.
Pachliopta aristolochiae.notes: Serves as the classic model mimicked by the 'stichius' form of the female Common Mormon (Papilio polytes).

Pachliopta pandiyana.headline: Black-and-white red-bodied swallowtail endemic to the Western Ghats
Pachliopta pandiyana.upperwing: Deep soot-black forewings pale-streaked between outer veins, paired with black hindwings bearing a large creamy-white central patch and deep crimson submarginal crescents; thorax and abdomen sides bright red.
Pachliopta pandiyana.underwing: Mirrors the upperwing pattern closely with sharper red marginal lunules and crimson abdominal warning markings.
Pachliopta pandiyana.similarSpecies: Much larger than the widespread Common Rose (Pachliopta aristolochiae), with an almost continuous pale white central hindwing band extending closer to the inner margin.
Pachliopta pandiyana.habitat: Heavy wet evergreen hill forests, riparian shola edges, and shaded forested ghats.
Pachliopta pandiyana.behavior: Floats majestically with slow, measured wingbeats along sunlit openings over forest streams and occasionally joins mixed swallowtail nectaring clusters on Mussaenda.
Pachliopta pandiyana.season: Active year-round in wet evergreen belts, peaking between July and December.
Pachliopta pandiyana.tnDistribution: Restricted to moist Western Ghats sections of Tamil Nadu: Anamalai (Valparai, Topslip), Siruvani, Nilgiri slopes, and Tirunelveli-Kanyakumari hills.
Pachliopta pandiyana.notes: Named after the historic Pandya region of southern India and prized by visitors to wet evergreen Western Ghats trails.

Pachliopta hector.headline: A bold red-bodied swallowtail common across plains and hills
Pachliopta hector.upperwing: Jet-black forewings crossed by two broken white bands and hindwings bearing two bright rows of crimson-red crescent spots; head and abdomen are bright crimson.
Pachliopta hector.underwing: Matches the crisp black, white-banded, and crimson-spotted dorsal pattern; red body acts as a warning signal of Aristolochia-derived toxins.
Pachliopta hector.similarSpecies: Separated from the Common Rose (Pachliopta aristolochiae) by the two distinct white bands across the black forewing and vivid crimson hindwing spots.
Pachliopta hector.habitat: Open scrublands, coastal plains, urban gardens, dry deciduous foothills, and cultivated landscapes.
Pachliopta hector.behavior: Flies slowly with effortless wingbeats just above vegetation and participates in local coastal and peninsular movements.
Pachliopta hector.season: Common throughout the year across Tamil Nadu.
Pachliopta hector.tnDistribution: Statewide from Chennai coast and interior plains to Western and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Pachliopta hector.wpaStatus: Protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Schedule II).
Pachliopta hector.notes: Acts as the distasteful Batesian model mimicked by the female Common Mormon (hector form).

Troides minos.headline: Largest butterfly of southern India and a Western Ghats endemic
Troides minos.upperwing: Vast velvety black forewings outlined with pale grey vein streaks paired with brilliant golden-yellow hindwings bordered in black scalloped patches.
Troides minos.underwing: Mirrors the dramatic black-and-gold upperwing pattern, with golden-yellow abdominal segments and scarlet-red hair tufts on the thorax.
Troides minos.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu by sheer wingspan and soaring canopy flight; females carry larger black triangular hindwing spots than males.
Troides minos.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, foothills, coffee and cardamom estates, and forested valleys.
Troides minos.behavior: Soars effortlessly high in the forest canopy and descends early in the morning to feed on Mussaenda, Ixora, and Lantana blooms.
Troides minos.season: Seen year-round in wet hill forests, peaking between June and December.
Troides minos.tnDistribution: Western Ghats stretches of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, Kodaikanal, and Kanyakumari.
Troides minos.notes: Also known as the Sahyadri Birdwing; Tamil Nadu’s largest butterfly species.

Papilio clytia.headline: Tailless swallowtail occurring in two distinct milkweed-mimicking forms
Papilio clytia.upperwing: Two dramatic forms in both sexes: 'clytia' form is dark velvety brown with marginal arrow-shaped cream spots (mimicking Crows), while 'dissimilis' is black heavily streaked with creamy-white cell stripes (mimicking Tigers).
Papilio clytia.underwing: Dark chocolate or streaked cream-and-black accented by a diagnostic row of bright golden-yellow submarginal spots along the hindwing outer edge.
Papilio clytia.similarSpecies: Separated instantly from true Euploea Crows and Tirumala Tigers by its six stout black swallowtail legs, rounded hindwing yellow marginal spots below, and slow fluttering swallowtail flight.
Papilio clytia.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, coastal scrub groves, and wooded campuses.
Papilio clytia.behavior: Glides leisurely at mid-canopy height and lowers to mud-puddle or feed at Ixora flowers with vibrating wings before snapping them upright.
Papilio clytia.season: Seen throughout the year in forested foothills and plains pockets, peaking August to January.
Papilio clytia.tnDistribution: Occurs in Coimbatore foothills (Kallar, Siruvani), Mudumalai, Pachamalai, Sirumalai, and coastal groves such as Chennai Guindy.
Papilio clytia.notes: One of India's finest Batesian mimics: when disturbed from foliage, its slow initial Danainae mimic flight abruptly switches into rapid swallowtail evasion.

Papilio polytes.headline: Classic garden swallowtail famous for female Batesian mimicry
Papilio polytes.upperwing: Males are black with a neat chain of white spots across the hindwing; females occur in three forms, male-like 'cyrus', Common Rose mimic 'stichius', and Crimson Rose mimic 'romulus'.
Papilio polytes.underwing: Dark brown-black with white discal spots and submarginal orange-red or white crescents depending on morph.
Papilio polytes.similarSpecies: Mimetic females have black bodies instead of the bright crimson body found in true Pachliopta rose swallowtails.
Papilio polytes.habitat: Home gardens, citrus groves, parks, scrub, and forest edges.
Papilio polytes.behavior: Active sun-lover weaving briskly through curry-leaf and lemon bushes while fluttering wings at flowers.
Papilio polytes.tnDistribution: Found in almost every district of Tamil Nadu from coastal cities to hill valleys.
Papilio polytes.notes: A textbook demonstration of polymorphic Batesian mimicry observable right in Tamil Nadu backyard curry-leaf plants.

Papilio dravidarum.headline: Dark white-spotted forest swallowtail endemic to peninsular Western Ghats
Papilio dravidarum.upperwing: Dark velvety brown-black, paler toward the outer forewing; forewing shows a neat row of apical white dots and marginal white spots, while the hindwing carries white discal arrow-spots and marginal crescents without a tail.
Papilio dravidarum.underwing: Warm sepia-brown with sharper white arrow-shaped post-discal spots on the hindwing and small white basal dots.
Papilio dravidarum.similarSpecies: Resembles the Common Mime ('clytia' form) or female Euploea crows, but carries pointed arrow-like white discal markings on the hindwing and lacks the Mime's golden-yellow underside spots.
Papilio dravidarum.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests from foothills to 1,200 m elevation.
Papilio dravidarum.behavior: Keeps to shaded forest clearings and shaded coffee estates, flying steadily near understorey shrubs and damp stream gravel.
Papilio dravidarum.season: Mostly July through January during southwest and northeast monsoon humid spells.
Papilio dravidarum.tnDistribution: Western Ghats belts of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai Tiger Reserve, Anamalai, Nilgiri slopes, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Papilio dravidarum.notes: First recorded in the TNBS Mudumalai June 2024 survey highlight list and strictly linked to shaded Western Ghats habitats.

Papilio daksha.headline: Large tailed black swallowtail carrying a broad creamy hindwing patch
Papilio daksha.upperwing: Jet-black forewings subtly dusted along outer veins, contrasted with large black-tailed hindwings dominated by a striking three-lobed creamy-white upper patch.
Papilio daksha.underwing: Softer charcoal-brown retaining the bright white hindwing patch alongside vivid brick-red submarginal crescents ringing the outer margin.
Papilio daksha.similarSpecies: Separated from the Blue Mormon by its prominent spatulate hindwing tails and confined white upper-hindwing patch rather than an expansive sky-blue outer area.
Papilio daksha.habitat: Wet evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, forested valleys, and shaded hill streams.
Papilio daksha.behavior: Patrols hill-stream corridors with strong swooping glides, frequently pausing to mud-puddle on sunny sandy banks alongside Banded Peacocks.
Papilio daksha.season: Year-round in wet hill forests, most numerous from June to December.
Papilio daksha.tnDistribution: Abundant in Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Valparai, Palani Hills, and Tirunelveli ranges.
Papilio daksha.notes: TNBS checklist adopts the southern Indian endemic-complex treatment Papilio daksha (formerly listed under Papilio helenus daksha).

Papilio polymnestor.headline: Tailless giant swallowtail with powdery pale blue hindwings
Papilio polymnestor.upperwing: Velvety black forewings streaked with pale blue post-discal bands and large pale sky-blue outer hindwings dotted with two rows of black spots.
Papilio polymnestor.underwing: Deep black with faint red basal patches and wide greyish-white outer hindwing area bearing black spots.
Papilio polymnestor.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in southern India, tailless, huge, and bright sky-blue on the outer half of the hindwing.
Papilio polymnestor.habitat: Wooded gardens, citrus orchards, moist deciduous foothills, and evergreen forests.
Papilio polymnestor.behavior: Glides powerfully through forest glades and feeds at Ixora, Mussaenda, and Lantana without settling still for long.
Papilio polymnestor.season: Year-round, with highest counts during monsoon and post-monsoon months.
Papilio polymnestor.tnDistribution: Common in the Western and Eastern Ghats (Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Pachamalai) and frequent in wooded plains and cities.
Papilio polymnestor.notes: TNBS checklist retains Papilio polymnestor for the Blue Mormon; Butterflies of India treats the taxon in the Papilio memnon/agenor complex.

Papilio liomedon.headline: Rare black-and-yellow swallowtail endemic to the Western Ghats
Papilio liomedon.upperwing: Dark chocolate-black crossed diagonally from forewing apex to inner hindwing by a continuous chain of bright creamy-yellow spots and long hindwing tails.
Papilio liomedon.underwing: Dark brown with matching pale yellow median band plus brick-red and blue submarginal rings on the hindwing.
Papilio liomedon.similarSpecies: Unique continuous straight yellow spot-band and pronounced spatulate tails distinguish it from all other Tamil Nadu swallowtails.
Papilio liomedon.habitat: Primary evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests of the Western Ghats.
Papilio liomedon.behavior: Strong canopy flier occasionally seen descending to hill-stream clearings and damp mud.
Papilio liomedon.season: Mostly July to November around monsoon showers.
Papilio liomedon.tnDistribution: Localized in Western Ghats pockets of Tamil Nadu (Anamalai, Nilgiris, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai; highlighted in Pattampoochi Q2 2022).
Papilio liomedon.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Papilio liomedon.notes: A prized Western Ghats endemic documented by TNBS surveys.

Papilio demoleus.headline: Tailless black-and-yellow swallowtail common in citrus gardens
Papilio demoleus.upperwing: Black wings densely patterned with pale yellow spots and bands, accented by a blue-edged eyespot near the foremargin and a brick-red spot at the inner hindwing angle.
Papilio demoleus.underwing: Similar yellow-and-black mosaic overlaid with rich tawny-orange washes in the hindwing cells.
Papilio demoleus.similarSpecies: Tailless unlike most other yellow-and-black Papilio species, and lacks iridescent blue bands.
Papilio demoleus.habitat: Gardens, orchards, scrub, urban avenues, and open agricultural landscapes.
Papilio demoleus.behavior: Restless, fast-darting flight; settles briefly to mud-puddle on wet sand and bask with spread wings.
Papilio demoleus.season: Year-round, occasionally forming local migratory bursts (documented in Pattampoochi Q3 2018).
Papilio demoleus.tnDistribution: Ubiquitous across plains, foothills, and open hills throughout Tamil Nadu.
Papilio demoleus.notes: Young caterpillars mimic bird droppings before turning velvety green with eye-like thorax markings.

Papilio paris.headline: Black-and-green swallowtail carrying a glowing sapphire hindwing patch
Papilio paris.upperwing: Black thickly dusted with metallic green scales, illuminated by a large iridescent peacock-blue patch on the upper hindwing and a narrow green forewing line.
Papilio paris.underwing: Dull charcoal-black with a white-edged row of reddish-orange submarginal lunules along the hindwing.
Papilio paris.similarSpecies: Easily separated from Papilio crino by the brilliant square-ish blue hindwing patch instead of a continuous narrow band.
Papilio paris.habitat: Evergreen hill forests, moist forest clearings, streams, and shaded trails.
Papilio paris.behavior: Strong, patrolling flight; fond of sunlit stream-bed pebbles and wet sand.
Papilio paris.season: Recorded mostly during monsoon and winter across Western Ghats hills.
Papilio paris.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Valparai, Palani Hills, and southern Western Ghats.
Papilio paris.notes: Recorded during the June 2024 Mudumalai Tiger Reserve Monsoon Butterfly Survey.

Papilio crino.headline: Emerald swallowtail & emblem of The Nature and Butterfly Society
Papilio crino.upperwing: Velvety black dusted uniformly with sparkling emerald-green scales and crossed by a bright metallic blue-green median band across both wings.
Papilio crino.underwing: Dark brown dusted with pale ochre scales and a series of orange-ringed blue lunules along the hindwing margin.
Papilio crino.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Paris Peacock (Papilio paris) by the continuous median blue-green band across forewing and hindwing rather than a single isolated blue hindwing patch.
Papilio crino.habitat: Deciduous and dry evergreen forests, wooded foothill gardens, scrub jungles, and hill streams.
Papilio crino.behavior: Strong, rapid flier that hovers briefly while nectaring at Lantana and Clerodendrum flowers, and frequently mud-puddles along damp forest paths.
Papilio crino.season: Active throughout the year with peaks during and after monsoon months.
Papilio crino.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills and plains, including Kallar, Siruvani, Coimbatore, Pachamalai, and Salem foothills.
Papilio crino.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Papilio crino.notes: Recommended by TNBS members during state butterfly discussions (Pattampoochi Q2 2019) and depicted at the heart of the official TNBS society emblem.

Papilio buddha.headline: Iridescent green-banded endemic swallowtail of the Western Ghats
Papilio buddha.upperwing: Velvety black outer wings with an exceptionally broad metallic blue-green basal and median sheen that shifts from emerald to turquoise in sunlight.
Papilio buddha.underwing: Dark brown dusted with fine scales and pale submarginal crescents on the hindwing.
Papilio buddha.similarSpecies: Differs from Common Banded Peacock by its much broader blue-green wing base and narrower black outer half on the forewing.
Papilio buddha.habitat: Dense evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, river valleys, and high canopy.
Papilio buddha.behavior: Canopy flyer that swoops down along forest streams and occasionally puddles on damp gravel in Mudumalai and Anamalai.
Papilio buddha.season: Mainly June to December, peaking during southwest and northeast monsoons.
Papilio buddha.tnDistribution: Western Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai Tiger Reserve, Anamalai, Nilgiris, and Tirunelveli hills.
Papilio buddha.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Papilio buddha.notes: Highlight sighting of the June 2024 TNBS Mudumalai Monsoon Butterfly Survey.

Eurema andersoni.headline: Forest grass yellow marked by a single spot inside the forewing cell
Eurema andersoni.upperwing: Bright sulphur-yellow with a broad jet-black forewing outer border excavated cleanly inside spaces 2 and 3 and rounded along the hindwing edge.
Eurema andersoni.underwing: Paler yellow speckled lightly with rusty markings; forewing underside cell holds just a single small comma or spot plus faint apical streaks in dry forms.
Eurema andersoni.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Grass Yellow (two cell spots) and Three-spot Grass Yellow (three cell spots) by having a single cell spot on the underside forewing and strictly forest habitat.
Eurema andersoni.habitat: Shaded wet evergreen and moist deciduous forests along damp tracks and stream banks.
Eurema andersoni.behavior: Flies close to shaded forest undergrowth and settles softly on sunlit stream banks to sip dissolved minerals.
Eurema andersoni.season: Recorded mainly between July and February in humid Western Ghats valleys.
Eurema andersoni.tnDistribution: Western Ghats districts of Tamil Nadu: Nilgiris, Siruvani, Anamalai, Kodaikanal slopes, and KMTR.
Eurema andersoni.notes: Unlike lawn-dwelling grass yellows, caterpillars feed on the woody rhamnaceous liana Ventilago rather than Cassia legumes.

Eurema blanda.headline: Widespread grass yellow distinguished by three forewing cell spots below
Eurema blanda.upperwing: Vibrant canary-yellow in males (paler in females) framed by an uneven black forewing margin and narrow black scalloped hindwing rim.
Eurema blanda.underwing: Yellow marked lightly with reddish-brown marginal speckles and three clear, separate dark spots inside the forewing cell (smallest near the base).
Eurema blanda.similarSpecies: Count the spots inside the underside forewing cell: Three-spot shows 3 distinct marks, Common Grass Yellow has 2, and One-spot has 1.
Eurema blanda.habitat: Gardens, wooded plains, moist deciduous foothills, forest glades, and avenue trees.
Eurema blanda.behavior: Flutters continuously near canopy saplings and dense roadside Cassia/Albizia avenues, gathering in loose mud-puddling groups.
Eurema blanda.season: Present year-round across Tamil Nadu with highest abundance post-monsoon.
Eurema blanda.tnDistribution: Statewide from Chennai, Salem, and Coimbatore plains up to 1,400 m in Eastern and Western Ghats hills.
Eurema blanda.notes: Females often lay tidy egg clutches side-by-side on young Albizia and Gulmohar leaflets, resulting in synchronous caterpillar broods.

Eurema brigitta.headline: Open-grassland grass yellow with smoothly curved forewing black border
Eurema brigitta.upperwing: Warm deep yellow with a broad black forewing tip and outer margin whose inner edge sweeps in an unbroken smooth arc (lacking the deep square notch of E. hecabe).
Eurema brigitta.underwing: Buff to pale ochre-yellow with tiny scattered grey-black cell dots and indistinct dusky marginal speckles in dry-season broods.
Eurema brigitta.similarSpecies: Immediately distinguished from Common and Three-spot Grass Yellows by the evenly curved black dorsal forewing border lacking an inward tooth in mid-wing.
Eurema brigitta.habitat: Dry grasslands, open hill meadows, scrub margins, roadsides, and fallow agricultural plots.
Eurema brigitta.behavior: Skims quickly just centimeters above short grasses, frequently visiting yellow Asteraceae blooms such as Tridax procumbens.
Eurema brigitta.season: Active throughout the year with clear wet-season (darker) and dry-season (paler reddish-fringed) morphs.
Eurema brigitta.tnDistribution: Common across Tamil Nadu plains and open hill slopes from Coimbatore and Tirunelveli up to Nilgiri and Palani grasslands.
Eurema brigitta.notes: Often tolerates drier, sun-baked rocky slopes better than other grass yellows thanks to prostrate Chamaecrista host herbs.

Eurema hecabe.headline: Abundant yellow pierid famous for mass movements in Mudumalai
Eurema hecabe.upperwing: Bright sulphur-yellow with deep black forewing borders sharply indented in the middle like the silhouette of an inverted '3'.
Eurema hecabe.underwing: Yellow speckled with variable brown smudges and exactly two small black spots inside the forewing cell.
Eurema hecabe.similarSpecies: Separated from Three-spot Grass Yellow (Eurema blanda) by having 2 (rather than 3) spots inside the underside forewing cell and a cleaner forewing tip.
Eurema hecabe.habitat: Grasslands, roadsides, gardens, agricultural fields, scrub, and forest edges.
Eurema hecabe.behavior: Weak fluttering flight close to the ground; gathers in bright yellow puddles on moist soil.
Eurema hecabe.season: Year-round statewide; thousands migrated together during the June 2024 Mudumalai survey.
Eurema hecabe.tnDistribution: Found across every habitat and elevation in Tamil Nadu.
Eurema hecabe.notes: During the June 2024 Mudumalai Tiger Reserve Monsoon Survey, TNBS recorded thousands of Common Grass Yellows moving together, a notable mass-movement event.
sources: New Indian Express, Mudumalai mass movement (2024)

Eurema laeta.headline: Pointed-winged grass yellow lacking any spots in the underside forewing cell
Eurema laeta.upperwing: Bright lemon-yellow with a conspicuously pointed forewing apex, black outer border ending cleanly near the lower angle, and reduced hindwing border in dry morphs.
Eurema laeta.underwing: Dry-season individuals show warm rusty-ochre hindwings crossed by two straight dark streaks; completely lacks distinct spots inside the forewing cell (at most one faint speck).
Eurema laeta.similarSpecies: Sharp forewing apex and straight oblique dark bars across the dusty underside hindwing distinguish it from Small Grass Yellow (E. brigitta).
Eurema laeta.habitat: Open dry scrub, hill savannas, forest clearings, and grassy hill footpaths.
Eurema laeta.behavior: Flies close to dry grass tufts during warm midday hours and settles completely closed with cryptic dry-leaf undersides tilted toward the sun.
Eurema laeta.season: Recorded throughout the year, with sharp dry-season morphs dominating from November to April.
Eurema laeta.tnDistribution: Widespread in foothill scrub, Eastern Ghats slopes, Nilgiri eastern slopes, Coimbatore, and Madurai.
Eurema laeta.notes: Remarkable seasonal polyphenism led early naturalists to treat wet and dry broods as separate species.

Eurema nilgiriensis.headline: Western Ghats forest grass yellow endemic to southern Indian hills
Eurema nilgiriensis.upperwing: Deep golden-yellow in males (paler creamy-yellow in females) bearing a broad dark brown-black forewing border stepped inwards and a crisp black hindwing outer line.
Eurema nilgiriensis.underwing: Bright yellow in males with two faint cell bars, rusty ring-spot on forewing cell end, and fine dark speckling across hindwing.
Eurema nilgiriensis.similarSpecies: Separated closely from One-spot Grass Yellow (E. andersoni) and Sari (E. sari) by subtly rounded hindwing margin, two small forewing cell markings, and strict hill-forest range.
Eurema nilgiriensis.habitat: Wet evergreen shola edges, shaded stream corridors, and mid-to-high elevation Western Ghats forests.
Eurema nilgiriensis.behavior: Weak, hurried flight along shaded forest streams; rarely ventures far into open urban gardens.
Eurema nilgiriensis.season: Seen mainly from August to February across humid montane valleys.
Eurema nilgiriensis.tnDistribution: Upper Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Anamalai, and Palani Hills of Tamil Nadu.
Eurema nilgiriensis.notes: Described from the Nilgiri plateau (Yata, 1990) and retained on the TNBS state checklist as a localized southern hill taxon.

Catopsilia pomona.headline: Strong-flying pale lemon-and-white emigrant with silver underside spots
Catopsilia pomona.upperwing: Creamy white with bright yellow wing bases (crocale/pomona forms) and black forewing outer margins.
Catopsilia pomona.underwing: Pearly greenish-white to pale yellow, plain or marked with silvery dark-ringed discal spots.
Catopsilia pomona.similarSpecies: Lacks the fine brown transverse wavy striations covering the underside of Mottled Emigrant (Catopsilia pyranthe).
Catopsilia pomona.habitat: Avenues, gardens, scrub, open plains, and hills.
Catopsilia pomona.behavior: Powerful, buoyant flight high over shrubs and trees; forms migratory streams alongside tigers and crows.
Catopsilia pomona.season: Common throughout the year; surges around pre-monsoon and northeast monsoon seasons.
Catopsilia pomona.tnDistribution: Statewide across plains, towns, and hill ranges.
Catopsilia pomona.notes: Participated alongside Danainae migrants during Tamil Nadu 2024 migration flights.

Catopsilia pyranthe.headline: Pale greenish-white migrant pierced by tiny black forewing cell dots
Catopsilia pyranthe.upperwing: Chalky greenish-white with narrow black outer margins on the forewing and a small black oval dot at the end of the forewing cell; females carry heavier borders and spotting.
Catopsilia pyranthe.underwing: Densely etched in fine greenish-brown wavy striae ('mottled') over a pale creamy-green ground with tiny silver-ringed pink-edged cell dots.
Catopsilia pyranthe.similarSpecies: Slightly smaller than Common Emigrant (Catopsilia pomona), showing a prominent dorsal black forewing cell spot and finely mottled underside hatching.
Catopsilia pyranthe.habitat: Urban lawns, roadside Senna patches, scrub plains, wetlands, and agricultural hedges.
Catopsilia pyranthe.behavior: Fast, bouncing daytime flyer that pauses frequently at bright red/pink flowers and forms mixed directional flights ahead of monsoons.
Catopsilia pyranthe.season: Abundant year-round across Tamil Nadu plains and foothills.
Catopsilia pyranthe.tnDistribution: Occurs in all 38 districts of Tamil Nadu, thriving wherever roadside Senna weeds grow.
Catopsilia pyranthe.notes: Easily studied in city gardens where females oviposit rapidly on young Senna occidentalis buds.

Colias nilagiriensis.headline: High-altitude clouded yellow endemic to Nilgiri and Palani shola-grasslands
Colias nilagiriensis.upperwing: Golden-yellow (pale greenish-white in some females) bordered by broad dark brown-black outer bands dotted with yellow spots.
Colias nilagiriensis.underwing: Ochre-yellow dusted greenish with a crisp silver-white centered pink-ringed hindwing spot.
Colias nilagiriensis.similarSpecies: The only Clouded Yellow occurring in Tamil Nadu, immediately separated from lowland grass yellows by its thick spotted borders and montane habitat.
Colias nilagiriensis.habitat: Montane grasslands, shola margins, and temperate hill gardens above 1,500 m.
Colias nilagiriensis.behavior: Flies briskly close to cold montane grassland turf, basking sideways with wings closed to absorb sun heat.
Colias nilagiriensis.season: Year-round in high hills, brightest between October and May.
Colias nilagiriensis.tnDistribution: Restricted to high-elevation Nilgiris (Ooty, Avalanche, Upper Bhavani) and Palani Hills (Kodaikanal).
Colias nilagiriensis.notes: A classic temperate relic restricted to high shola-grassland plateaus of the Nilgiris and Palani Hills.

Colotis amata.headline: Delicate salmon-pink pierid dancing over coastal and arid scrublands
Colotis amata.upperwing: Soft salmon-pink framed by wide black wing borders containing tiny pink marginal spots; forewing carries a prominent black dot at the cell end (females may be whitish or yellowish).
Colotis amata.underwing: Soft greenish-yellow suffused subtly at the forewing base with pale pink and bearing faint transverse dark dots.
Colotis amata.similarSpecies: Smaller and distinctly bordered in spotted black compared to the warmer orange Large Salmon Arab (Colotis fausta).
Colotis amata.habitat: Coastal sand dunes, thorny dry scrub plains, saltmarsh edges, and Salvadora thickets.
Colotis amata.behavior: Stays close to thorny Salvadora bushes, fluttering weakly in small colonies and hiding inside foliage during windy afternoons.
Colotis amata.season: Active throughout the year in coastal and rain-shadow scrub tracts, peaking October to March.
Colotis amata.tnDistribution: Dry plains and east coast belt of Tamil Nadu including Point Calimere, Thoothukudi, Ramanathapuram, Tirunelveli, and drier Coimbatore scrub.
Colotis amata.notes: Closely tied to Toothbrush Tree (Salvadora persica), making it a reliable bioindicator of healthy coastal and arid thorn scrub.

Colotis danae.headline: White dry-zone butterfly tipped in black-rimmed blood-crimson apex
Colotis danae.upperwing: Pure white with a bold carmine-crimson apical patch broadly edged inwardly and outwardly in jet-black on the forewing; hindwing carries marginal black spots.
Colotis danae.underwing: White to buff-tinged underside with a distinct row of black-spotted orange-red subapical streaks and a clean row of dark hindwing discal dots.
Colotis danae.similarSpecies: Unmistakable bright crimson forewing tip inside a dark border (Little Orange-tip is smaller with orange, not deep carmine, tips).
Colotis danae.habitat: Dry scrublands, thorny plains, fallow fields, and coastal grasslands.
Colotis danae.behavior: Brisk low flier patrolling caper shrubs in harsh midday sun, visiting Leucas, Tridax, and Capparis flowers.
Colotis danae.season: Year-round in dry interior and coastal districts, peaking from November to April.
Colotis danae.tnDistribution: Widespread across plains and rain-shadow foothills of Coimbatore, Madurai, Dindigul, Tirunelveli, Ramanathapuram, and Chennai.
Colotis danae.notes: Dorsal black borders shrink markedly in hot dry-season individuals while underside hindwings turn faintly rosy-ochre.

Colotis etrida.headline: Tiny dry-scrub white bearing a compact black-bordered orange tip
Colotis etrida.upperwing: Chalky white with a neat oval orange forewing apex entirely enclosed by a black rim and a small black spot at the cell end; hindwing shows marginal black dots.
Colotis etrida.underwing: Greenish-yellow hindwing speckled finely in grey with a faint discal row of brownish dots and dull orange showing softly through the forewing tip.
Colotis etrida.similarSpecies: Noticeably smaller and whiter than Yellow Orange-tip, and unlike Plain Orange-tip (Colotis aurora), its black-edged orange tip contains zero isolated white spots.
Colotis etrida.habitat: Arid thorn scrub, coastal dunes, wasteland paths, and dry plains.
Colotis etrida.behavior: Weak, low-skimming flight among dry bushes and low weeds like Tridax and Justicia.
Colotis etrida.season: Common year-round in dry plains, especially abundant post-northeast monsoon.
Colotis etrida.tnDistribution: Ubiquitous across dry Tamil Nadu lowlands, Vellalore wetlands, Madurai plains, and Coromandel Coast.
Colotis etrida.notes: One of the smallest members of Pieridae regularly seen in dry urban wastelands across Tamil Nadu.

Colotis aurora.headline: Scrubland orange-tip separated by warm peach apex and fine dark dots
Colotis aurora.upperwing: White wings in males with a bright orange forewing tip bordered thinly in dark brown without a strong thick black inner edge; females have wider brown-spotted orange tips.
Colotis aurora.underwing: Pale ochre-yellow to pinkish-buff washed warmly on the hindwing and dotted with a faint post-discal spot arc.
Colotis aurora.similarSpecies: Separated from Little Orange-tip (C. etrida) by larger size, warmer peach-orange tip lacking a heavy black inner margin, and buff dry-season underside.
Colotis aurora.habitat: Thorn scrub jungles, rocky foothills, dry deciduous margins, and caper thickets.
Colotis aurora.behavior: Swift, erratic flier weaving just above thorny caper shrubs under intense sunshine.
Colotis aurora.season: Most active during late monsoon through dry summer months (October-May).
Colotis aurora.tnDistribution: Recorded across dry plains and Eastern/Western Ghats rain-shadow belts (Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Virudhunagar, Tirunelveli).
Colotis aurora.notes: Often flies alongside C. etrida and C. danae on shared Cadaba fruticosa host stands.

Colotis fausta.headline: Unmistakable pale salmon-orange pierid cruising dry thorn forests
Colotis fausta.upperwing: Rich warm salmon-orange across all wings (brighter than any other Colotis) with a black cell spot, ragged black forewing outer margin enclosing salmon spots, and black marginal dots on hindwing.
Colotis fausta.underwing: Uniform pale pinkish-salmon with faint brownish speckling and tiny dark discal dots.
Colotis fausta.similarSpecies: Far larger and completely uniform salmon-orange above rather than pink-centered with thick black-framed inner borders (Small Salmon Arab).
Colotis fausta.habitat: Open dry scrub, rocky thorn hills, dry deciduous foothills, and coastal dunes.
Colotis fausta.behavior: Strong, sustained low flier crossing open dry scrub rapidly and pausing eagerly on Pavetta indica and Lantana flowers.
Colotis fausta.season: Chiefly August to March, dispersing locally after seasonal rains.
Colotis fausta.tnDistribution: Interior and southern dry districts including Madurai (Kolinjipati), Coimbatore, Dindigul foothills, Ramanathapuram, and Tirunelveli.
Colotis fausta.notes: Noted feeding abundantly on white Pavetta indica clusters during the TNBS/MNCF Kolinjipati walk documented in Pattampoochi Issue 25.

Ixias marianne.headline: Dry-zone white pierid with bright orange forewing patches framed in black
Ixias marianne.upperwing: Chalky white with a broad vivid orange patch occupying the outer half of the forewing, enclosed inside a wide black margin.
Ixias marianne.underwing: Rich sulphur-yellow speckled with brownish spots and small white-centered eyespots.
Ixias marianne.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Yellow Orange-tip (Ixias pyrene) by its white ground colour above (instead of bright yellow).
Ixias marianne.habitat: Dry scrub, thorny jungles, open plains, and dry deciduous foothills.
Ixias marianne.behavior: Quick, low erratic flight through thorny caper bushes.
Ixias marianne.season: Year-round, particularly numerous in dry eastern and interior plains.
Ixias marianne.tnDistribution: Common across dry lowlands, Salem, Madurai, Tirunelveli, and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Ixias marianne.notes: Shows dramatic dry-season polymorphism with rich reddish eyespot-like speckles beneath.

Ixias pyrene.headline: Lemon-yellow pierid flashing a black-framed orange forewing band
Ixias pyrene.upperwing: Bright sulphur-yellow males carry a large triangular orange patch framed sharply in black across the outer forewing; females may be white or yellow with broken cream-orange apical patches.
Ixias pyrene.underwing: Deeper mustard-yellow sprinkled evenly with tiny rust-brown spots and eye-like pale-centered submarginal marks in dry-season broods.
Ixias pyrene.similarSpecies: Yellow ground colour distinguishes males instantly from the chalk-white White Orange-tip (Ixias marianne).
Ixias pyrene.habitat: Scrub jungles, deciduous foothills, forest trails, and overgrown gardens.
Ixias pyrene.behavior: Rapid, bounding flier active in bright sun; males regularly puddle on damp riverbed sand and wet forest roads.
Ixias pyrene.season: Year-round statewide, peaking during monsoon and cooler winter months.
Ixias pyrene.tnDistribution: Abundant across Tamil Nadu plains, Eastern Ghats (Kalvarayan, Pachamalai), and Western Ghats foothills.
Ixias pyrene.notes: Exhibits vivid seasonal variation: dry-season individuals turn richly mottled with brick-red ocelli-like spots beneath.

Hebomoia glaucippe.headline: India’s largest pierid with blazing orange-tipped white forewings
Hebomoia glaucippe.upperwing: Chalky white with brilliant vermilion-orange apical patches edged in black at the forewing tips.
Hebomoia glaucippe.underwing: Mottled pale bark-brown underside camouflaging the butterfly cleanly against dry leaves when resting.
Hebomoia glaucippe.similarSpecies: Separated from smaller orange-tips (Ixias, Colotis) by its massive swallowtail-like wingspan and pointed forewing apex.
Hebomoia glaucippe.habitat: Forest streams, damp mud patches, deciduous hills, and shaded gardens.
Hebomoia glaucippe.behavior: Very fast, powerful flight above shrubs; congregates on wet sand alongside Graphium jays.
Hebomoia glaucippe.season: Seen throughout the year, peaking post-monsoon.
Hebomoia glaucippe.tnDistribution: Foothills and forests across Western and Eastern Ghats, including Kallar, Siruvani, Kovai Kutralam, and Pachamalai.
Hebomoia glaucippe.notes: Largest pierid butterfly in India; its cryptic dry-leaf underside makes it vanish when perched with folded wings.

Pareronia ceylanica.headline: Deep powder-blue forest wanderer whose female mimics Dark Blue Tiger
Pareronia ceylanica.upperwing: Males are richer azure powder-blue with wide jet-black wing margins and clean black veins; females are blackish marked with narrow pale bluish streaks mimicking Tirumala tigers.
Pareronia ceylanica.underwing: Pale silvery-blue in males with soft dusky outer shades; females repeat the tiger-like dark-and-pale pattern.
Pareronia ceylanica.similarSpecies: Males are distinctly darker, deeper sky-blue with wider black outer borders than the paler Common Wanderer (Pareronia hippia).
Pareronia ceylanica.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, shaded forest roads, and wooded ravines.
Pareronia ceylanica.behavior: Glides swiftly through shaded forest corridors; females fly noticeably slower when mimicking unpalatable milkweed butterflies.
Pareronia ceylanica.season: Present year-round in hill forests, with strong peaks from August to January.
Pareronia ceylanica.tnDistribution: Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Pachamalai, Sirumalai, and southern Western Ghats hills.
Pareronia ceylanica.notes: Recorded consistently in TNBS Pachamalai and Mudumalai surveys alongside Pareronia hippia.

Pareronia hippia.headline: Widespread pale-blue butterfly showcasing sex-limited tiger mimicry
Pareronia hippia.upperwing: Males are pale ice-blue crossed neatly by black veins and moderate black wing borders; females occur in dark tiger-mimicking forms (often showing pale yellow basal tinges).
Pareronia hippia.underwing: Silvery pearlescent blue with faint marginal duskiness in males and dark streaked tiger patterns in females.
Pareronia hippia.similarSpecies: Paler ice-blue males with narrower borders than Dark Wanderer (P. ceylanica); females mimic Glassy and Blue Tigers closely except for their pointed wings and 6 walking legs.
Pareronia hippia.habitat: Scrub woodlands, urban green belts, deciduous forests, and foothills.
Pareronia hippia.behavior: Males cruise tirelessly in bright sun checking nectar shrubs, while females weave deliberately through thorny bushes.
Pareronia hippia.season: Active all year, most numerous after northeast and southwest rains.
Pareronia hippia.tnDistribution: Found throughout Tamil Nadu plains, Chennai, Coimbatore, Salem, Eastern Ghats, and foothill scrubs.
Pareronia hippia.notes: One of Tamil Nadu's best garden examples of Batesian mimicry confined solely to females.

Appias libythea.headline: Low-flying white pierid whose heavily marked females mimic gulls and tigers
Appias libythea.upperwing: Males are snow-white with narrow black apical borders; females are boldly overlaid with broad dusky-black margins and dark forewing cell streaks leaving crisp white patches.
Appias libythea.underwing: Creamy-white with smoky dusky outer veins in wet morphs and pale ochre-washed apex in dry morphs.
Appias libythea.similarSpecies: Smaller and rounder-winged than Common Albatross; females have solid dark costal forewing borders separating them from Common Gull females.
Appias libythea.habitat: Open plains, dry scrub, urban avenues, wasteland Capparis/Cleome patches, and coastal scrub.
Appias libythea.behavior: Flies close to herbaceous weeds in sunny open spaces, unlike canopy-patrolling Chocolate and Common Albatrosses.
Appias libythea.season: Abundant year-round in lowlands and occasionally joins local pierid movements.
Appias libythea.tnDistribution: Widespread across Chennai, Tiruchirappalli, Madurai, Coimbatore, and coastal plains.
Appias libythea.notes: Notice the female's crisp black forewing costal stripe, which earned the species the name Striped Albatross.

Appias lyncida.headline: Forest albatross bordered underneath in rich chocolate-brown
Appias lyncida.upperwing: Pointed snow-white forewings and rounded white hindwings framed by ragged jet-black outer teeth; females are extensively smoky dark brown with pale cream streaks.
Appias lyncida.underwing: Diagnostic rich chocolate-brown broad border surrounding brilliant lemon-yellow hindwings and white forewing base in males.
Appias lyncida.similarSpecies: Instant underside giveaway: bright yellow hindwings completely framed by a smooth dark chocolate border lacking white spots.
Appias lyncida.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, stream valleys, and wooded hill estates.
Appias lyncida.behavior: Swift stream-side flyer that puddles heavily on damp river sand and occasionally migrates along foothill corridors.
Appias lyncida.season: Peaks during June to January around rainy months.
Appias lyncida.tnDistribution: Western Ghats stretches of Tamil Nadu: Mudumalai, Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, and KMTR.
Appias lyncida.notes: Often shares damp gravel puddling bars with Common Albatross and Graphium swallowtails.

Appias albina.headline: Clean white forest pierid famous for hill-foothill seasonal flights
Appias albina.upperwing: Pure white in males with faintly dusted black forewing tips; females may be white or yellow with broader dark margins carrying white spots.
Appias albina.underwing: Unmarked satiny white or pale butter-yellow lacking prominent dark submarginal bands.
Appias albina.similarSpecies: More pointed forewings than Common Gull and lacks the bold dark underside border of Chocolate Albatross.
Appias albina.habitat: Semi-evergreen and deciduous hill forests, stream corridors, and dry-to-moist slopes.
Appias albina.behavior: Swifts along forest trails and forms dense white puddles on wet sandy stream banks.
Appias albina.season: Year-round in hills; abundant across Pachamalai Hills and Western Ghats streams.
Appias albina.tnDistribution: Recorded across Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, and abundantly across Pachamalai Hills.
Appias albina.notes: Frequently joins large seasonal Albatross mud-puddling and foothills dispersal flights in western Tamil Nadu.

Appias wardii.headline: Endemic Western Ghats albatross bearing broad black dorsal wing tips
Appias wardii.upperwing: Males are bright white with a broad jet-black forewing outer border containing small white subapical spots and a toothed black hindwing edge; females are white with wide dusky borders.
Appias wardii.underwing: Pearly white with pale yellow hindwings and soft ochre-yellow washing along the forewing tip.
Appias wardii.similarSpecies: Males show much broader, white-spotted black forewing borders than Common Albatross (Appias albina) and lack Chocolate Albatross's dark brown underside rim.
Appias wardii.habitat: Higher-elevation wet evergreen forests, montane sholas, and bamboo hill streams.
Appias wardii.behavior: Fast canopy and stream-corridor flyer; males congregate densely at muddy forest seepages during sunny intervals.
Appias wardii.season: Recorded mostly from September through March across wet hill ranges.
Appias wardii.tnDistribution: Localized in Nilgiris, Mudumalai higher slopes, Anamalai hills, Palani Hills, and southern Western Ghats.
Appias wardii.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Appias wardii.notes: A Western Ghats endemic protected under Indian wildlife law and often misidentified as Lesser Albatross without careful border checks.

Appias indra.headline: Fast white puffin patterned with a solid black forewing tip containing white dots
Appias indra.upperwing: Pointed white forewings bearing a wide black triangular outer tip pierced by two small white apical spots; hindwings are white with tiny marginal black speckles in wet broods.
Appias indra.underwing: Hindwings pale yellow to heavily mottled greyish-brown in wet-season forms; forewing apex is marbled grey-ochre bordered inwardly by an angled black bar.
Appias indra.similarSpecies: Two distinct white spots enclosed inside an unbroken black forewing apex and a heavy black underside subapical bar distinguish it from Appias albatrosses.
Appias indra.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, forested ghats, and mountain streams.
Appias indra.behavior: Powerful hill flyer often joining mud-puddling congregations on wet gravel near Kallar and Mudumalai streams.
Appias indra.season: Seen primarily between July and February across wet hill forests.
Appias indra.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Valparai, and southern Western Ghats hills.
Appias indra.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Appias indra.notes: Documented as a survey highlight in the June 2024 Mudumalai Tiger Reserve Monsoon Butterfly Survey.

Appias lalage.headline: Montane puffin sporting a prominent black discal spot on the forewing
Appias lalage.upperwing: Chalky white with broadly blackened veins toward the forewing margin and a bold detached black spot at the end of the forewing cell; females show heavy black borders.
Appias lalage.underwing: Forewing apex and entire hindwing mottled pale purplish-buff to warm ochre with a conspicuous black forewing cell spot.
Appias lalage.similarSpecies: Separated instantly from Plain Puffin (Appias indra) by the conspicuous isolated black spot sitting at the upper forewing cell end.
Appias lalage.habitat: High-elevation evergreen shola edges, montane streams, and upper Western Ghats slopes.
Appias lalage.behavior: Swift mountain flyer seen spiralling quickly down ravines to drink from damp stream edges during bright sunshine.
Appias lalage.season: Rarely encountered in Tamil Nadu hills, chiefly October to March.
Appias lalage.tnDistribution: Restricted in Tamil Nadu to high Western Ghats ranges including Nilgiris and Anamalai hills.
Appias lalage.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Appias lalage.notes: The South Indian subspecies A. l. lagela is protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.

Pieris canidia.headline: Temperate white butterfly thriving in Nilgiri and Palani hill gardens
Pieris canidia.upperwing: Creamy-white with dusty charcoal forewing base and black apical patch plus one (male) or two (female) dark post-discal spots on the forewing and black marginal dots on the hindwing.
Pieris canidia.underwing: Forewings white with two bold black spots; hindwings soft sulphur-yellow lightly dusted with dark basal scales and clean golden costa.
Pieris canidia.similarSpecies: In Tamil Nadu's high hills (>1,500 m), distinguished from Appias/Cepora whites by the soft yellowish unmarked hindwing underside and black marginal dot row above.
Pieris canidia.habitat: High-elevation hill stations, vegetable terraces, montane grasslands, and shola clearings.
Pieris canidia.behavior: Easy, fluttering garden flier active from early morning around highland mustard and cabbage cultivation.
Pieris canidia.season: Common year-round in high hills above 1,400 m.
Pieris canidia.tnDistribution: Abundant across Udhagamandalam (Ooty), Coonoor, Kotagiri, and Kodaikanal Palani Hills plateau.
Pieris canidia.notes: Represents a classic Himalayan/Palearctic hill-station colonist flourishing in southern India's montane plateau.

Cepora nerissa.headline: Widespread gull displaying dark-veined yellowish undersides
Cepora nerissa.upperwing: White wings with black veins widening toward the outer edges, black white-spotted forewing apex, and a prominent black spot at vein 3 in females.
Cepora nerissa.underwing: Hindwings tinted greenish-yellow with every vein broadly outlined in dark olive-black scaling (heavier in wet-season forms, subdued in dry forms).
Cepora nerissa.similarSpecies: Separated cleanly from Lesser Gull (Cepora nadina) by having all hindwing underside veins starkly darkened in olive-black rather than plain mottled brownish-yellow.
Cepora nerissa.habitat: Gardens, dry scrub, deciduous forests, edges of agriculture, and coastal plains.
Cepora nerissa.behavior: Steady, weaving flight among caper bushes; puddles frequently on wet sand and damp roadsides.
Cepora nerissa.season: Year-round across Tamil Nadu plains and foothills.
Cepora nerissa.tnDistribution: Common statewide from Chennai, Salem, and Erode plains up into Eastern and Western Ghats foothills.
Cepora nerissa.notes: Sharp wet- and dry-season morphs display dramatic variation in the darkness of ventral hindwing veins.

Cepora nadina.headline: Hill-forest gull with soft greenish-ochre unstreaked underside hindwings
Cepora nadina.upperwing: Pure white in males (heavily dusted blackish-brown in females) with broad black outer forewing border indented gently on its inner edge.
Cepora nadina.underwing: Hindwings smoothly washed in pale brownish-yellow to olive-green without dark outlines tracing every vein.
Cepora nadina.similarSpecies: Lacks the bold dark-veined grid found beneath the Common Gull (Cepora nerissa), and lacks the crimson hindwing underside spots of Painted Sawtooth.
Cepora nadina.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, forest streams, and shola glades.
Cepora nadina.behavior: Glides tirelessly along forested streams, dropping quickly onto damp sand patches alongside Puffins and Albatrosses.
Cepora nadina.season: Mostly September to April in humid hill ranges.
Cepora nadina.tnDistribution: Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, Palani Hills) and localized in Eastern Ghats foothill streams.
Cepora nadina.notes: Highlighted as an uncommon forest sighting at Amaidhi Solai foothills of Palani Hills (Pattampoochi Issue 24).

Prioneris sita.headline: Striking Jezebel mimic bearing serrated forewings and vermilion underside spots
Prioneris sita.upperwing: Large stark-white wings with every vein crisply traced in velvety black along the outer half; forewing costa shows minute comb-like serrations on males.
Prioneris sita.underwing: Bright golden-yellow hindwings framed by thick black veins and a bold submarginal chain of brilliant vermilion-red spots.
Prioneris sita.similarSpecies: Spectacular Batesian mimic of Common Jezebel (Delias eucharis), separated by being larger, pure white above with black veins on the forewing, and having a fine inner-margin edge to the red spots.
Prioneris sita.habitat: Wet evergreen hill forests, canopy glades, and high-rainfall Western Ghats ridges.
Prioneris sita.behavior: Strong, rapid flier around high forest canopies and hilltops, occasionally dropping to stream seepages or flowers.
Prioneris sita.season: Peak sightings between October and April across evergreen hill ranges.
Prioneris sita.tnDistribution: Wet Western Ghats hills of Tamil Nadu: Nilgiris, Anamalai, Valparai, Siruvani, and KMTR.
Prioneris sita.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Prioneris sita.notes: True Common Jezebels feed on mistletoes (toxic) and fly slowly, whereas Painted Sawtooth feeds on non-toxic Capparis and mimics Jezebels for predator protection.

Delias eucharis.headline: Striking white butterfly with bright yellow and scarlet-spotted underside
Delias eucharis.upperwing: White wings crisply outlined with black veins and a black outer border framing white marginal spots.
Delias eucharis.underwing: Unmistakable bright saffron-yellow hindwing framed by bold brick-red heart-shaped spots inside a black border.
Delias eucharis.similarSpecies: Only Painted Sawtooth (Prioneris sita) approaches its red-and-yellow underside pattern, but Painted Sawtooth is restricted to wet hills and has red spots closer to the margin.
Delias eucharis.habitat: Avenues, gardens, orchards, dry and moist forests where mistletoe parasitizes host trees.
Delias eucharis.behavior: Flies slowly around tree canopies and glides gracefully down to Lantana and garden flowers.
Delias eucharis.season: Year-round, noticeably abundant in winter and dry months.
Delias eucharis.tnDistribution: Very common across Tamil Nadu plains, cities, and hills.
Delias eucharis.notes: Its bright red underside warns insectivorous birds of toxic compounds sequestered from mistletoe leaves.

Leptosia nina.headline: Feather-light white butterfly drifting low over shaded weeds
Leptosia nina.upperwing: Translucent pure white marked by a single bold round black spot on the forewing and tiny dark apex.
Leptosia nina.underwing: White finely marbled with delicate pale olive-green striations across the hindwing.
Leptosia nina.similarSpecies: Rounded wingtips, fragile bobbing flight, and the solitary black forewing spot make Psyche unmistakable.
Leptosia nina.habitat: Shaded gardens, woodland edges, scrub undergrowth, and village hedges.
Leptosia nina.behavior: Weak, drifting bobbing flight just centimetres above shady undergrowth; rarely rises above waist height.
Leptosia nina.tnDistribution: Abundant across plains, urban green spaces, and hill foothills.
Leptosia nina.notes: Weak, bobbing low flight keeps it weaving effortlessly beneath thorny Capparaceae bushes even in breezy gardens.

Belenois aurota.headline: Black-veined white pierid common in open scrub and plains
Belenois aurota.upperwing: Creamy white with broad black wingtips and margins punctured by clean white oval spots, plus a comma-shaped black forewing bar.
Belenois aurota.underwing: White veins starkly bordered in charcoal-black with yellow tinting on the hindwing and white marginal cells.
Belenois aurota.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Gull (Cepora nerissa) by the bold black hockey-stick cell bar on the forewing upper surface.
Belenois aurota.habitat: Dry scrublands, open plains, roadside weeds, and agricultural borders.
Belenois aurota.behavior: Brisk flight low over dry scrub; known for long-distance dry-season dispersal flights.
Belenois aurota.season: Most conspicuous during dry and post-monsoon months.
Belenois aurota.tnDistribution: Common in central, eastern, and foothill scrub regions of Tamil Nadu.
Belenois aurota.notes: Strong vagrant capabilities bring periodic winter breeding eruptions across dry Coromandel and interior scrublands.

Libythea myrrha.headline: Fast-darting snout butterfly marked by an unbroken club-shaped orange forewing streak
Libythea myrrha.upperwing: Dark chocolate-brown with long forward-pointing beak-like palpi and squared wing tips; forewing bears an uninterrupted club-shaped bright orange streak from base through cell plus two pale orange-white subapical spots, while hindwing carries an oblique discal orange band (subspecies L. m. rama in South India).
Libythea myrrha.underwing: Forewing repeats the continuous orange cell streak and pale apical markings; hindwing is cryptically marbled in mottled greyish-brown and lilac striations that conceal perched adults like dry bark.
Libythea myrrha.similarSpecies: Separated from Southern Beak (Libythea laius) by the continuous, unbroken orange streak running through the forewing cell rather than a streak split into basal and discal lobes.
Libythea myrrha.habitat: Hill streams, moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forest paths, and wooded valleys.
Libythea myrrha.behavior: Flies swiftly with erratic, jerky turns along sunny stream banks, puddles avidly on damp sand and mineral-rich mud, and rests with wings snapped shut on bare twigs.
Libythea myrrha.season: Seen nearly year-round in the hills, peaking after monsoon rains between September and January and again in March-May.
Libythea myrrha.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats hill tracts including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Shevaroys, and Kolli Hills.
Libythea myrrha.notes: Often gathers in small puddling groups beside forest streams; the elongated labial palpi mimic a dead leaf petiole when perched.

Libythea laius.headline: Cryptic snout butterfly of drier scrub and foothills with a divided orange forewing streak
Libythea laius.upperwing: Deep brown with notched outer margins and projecting snout-like palpi; forewing displays a fragmented orange cell streak split into a narrow basal bar and a detached discal lobe alongside whitish-orange subapical spots, and hindwing bears a wavy lower orange band (subspecies L. l. lepitoides).
Libythea laius.underwing: Forewing underside clearly retains the broken orange cell pattern; hindwing shifts from warm brown-grey to finely freckled ash-grey bark mottling, becoming more cryptic in dry months.
Libythea laius.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Club Beak (Libythea myrrha) by the cleanly separated basal streak and rectangular discal spot inside the forewing cell, and a more strongly scalloped outer forewing margin.
Libythea laius.habitat: Dry deciduous forests, scrub jungles, foothill riverbeds, and thorny woodland edges.
Libythea laius.behavior: Nervous, rapid flier that settles abruptly on dry twigs, rocks, or wet sand to puddle, holding its wings tightly folded to expose only its bark-patterned underside.
Libythea laius.season: Active throughout the year in drier zones, with noticeable surges during October-January and pre-monsoon dry spells.
Libythea laius.tnDistribution: Foothills and dry tracts across Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Kallar, Sathyamangalam, Salem, Pachamalai, Gingee, and Tirunelveli.
Libythea laius.notes: Tolerates noticeably drier and lower-elevation thorn-scrub habitats than the more moisture-loving Club Beak.

Parantica aglea.headline: Delicate translucent tiger with a broad black-lined glassy patch in the forewing cell
Parantica aglea.upperwing: Sooty black-brown boldly patterned with semi-transparent bluish-white glassy streaks and submarginal spots; forewing discal cell contains a wide club-shaped glassy patch traversed by two fine dark lines (subspecies P. a. aglea). Sexes look alike, though males bear a small dark grey scent patch near the hindwing tornus.
Parantica aglea.underwing: Paler dark brown with the same crisp translucent bluish-white streaks, narrow black veins, and clean white spotting on head and thorax.
Parantica aglea.similarSpecies: Separated from Blue Tiger (Tirumala limniace) and Dark Blue Tiger (Tirumala septentrionis) by pale translucent glassy-white markings instead of vivid turquoise-blue spots and by the wide black-veined glassy forewing cell.
Parantica aglea.habitat: Moist evergreen and deciduous hill forests, shaded valleys, wooded estates, and seasonal migration corridors.
Parantica aglea.behavior: Glides slowly and effortlessly in dappled shade and along forest paths, pausing frequently on Crotalaria, Chromolaena, and Heliotropium for nectar and pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
Parantica aglea.season: Present year-round in forested hills, peaking from September to December during post-monsoon dispersal.
Parantica aglea.tnDistribution: Widespread in Western and Eastern Ghats including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Shevaroys, Pachamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Parantica aglea.notes: Joins mixed Danainae assemblages in Tamil Nadu's seasonal Ghats flights and sequesters cardiac glycosides and alkaloids for chemical defense.

Parantica nilgiriensis.headline: Dusky highland tiger endemic to southern Western Ghats hills
Parantica nilgiriensis.upperwing: Smoky dark brown wings filled with narrow, muted bluish-grey streaks and tiny marginal dots.
Parantica nilgiriensis.underwing: Dull brownish-grey repeating the fine pale streaks, blending quietly in montane mist.
Parantica nilgiriensis.similarSpecies: Much darker, smokier brown ground colour and narrower dull streaks distinguish it from the pale lowland Glassy Tiger (Parantica aglea).
Parantica nilgiriensis.habitat: Shola forest margins, tea estates, and montane hill streams above 900 m.
Parantica nilgiriensis.behavior: Calm gliding flight around shola edges and Ageratina flowers in cool mountain sunshine.
Parantica nilgiriensis.season: Year-round in high Western Ghats hills.
Parantica nilgiriensis.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Coonoor, Kotagiri, Valparai/Anamalai, Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), and Meghamalai.
Parantica nilgiriensis.notes: Endemic to the southern Western Ghats and protected under Indian wildlife legislation.

Tirumala limniace.headline: Key long-distance migrant across Western and Eastern Ghats corridors
Tirumala limniace.upperwing: Deep black wings patterned with translucent pale turquoise-blue streaks, rounded spots, and paired basal forewing stripes.
Tirumala limniace.underwing: Golden-brown underside mirroring the pale blue markings; males bear a small scent pouch on the hindwing.
Tirumala limniace.similarSpecies: Wider, paler blue streaks and rounded forewing spots distinguish it from the darker, narrower-streaked Dark Blue Tiger (Tirumala septentrionis).
Tirumala limniace.habitat: Scrublands, parks, hill forests, wetlands, and seasonal migratory flyways.
Tirumala limniace.behavior: Glides tirelessly along fixed directional flyways between the Eastern and Western Ghats during April–May and September–November.
Tirumala limniace.season: Year-round; huge directional aggregations recorded by TNBS in Sep–Nov and Apr–May.
Tirumala limniace.tnDistribution: Statewide; flagship species of TNBS’s 12+ years of Tamil Nadu migration monitoring.
Tirumala limniace.notes: Tracked annually by TNBS from Yercaud/Salem across Tiruppur and Coimbatore toward the Nilgiris and Anamalais.

Tirumala septentrionis.headline: Deep-blue forest tiger forming the backbone of September migrations
Tirumala septentrionis.upperwing: Velvety black wings etched with narrower, deeper sky-blue streaks and elongated spots.
Tirumala septentrionis.underwing: Dark chestnut-brown underside preserving crisp narrow pale-blue streaks.
Tirumala septentrionis.similarSpecies: Darker wing ground and much narrower, unbroken forewing basal blue streaks separate it from Blue Tiger (Tirumala limniace).
Tirumala septentrionis.habitat: Moist hill forests, wooded foothills, and seasonal migratory corridors across western plains.
Tirumala septentrionis.behavior: Gathers in dense overnight roosts in hill forests and surges across plains in steady migratory streams.
Tirumala septentrionis.season: Peaks dramatically from late September through November; documented at 10–200 butterflies/min over Coimbatore skies in Sep 2024.
Tirumala septentrionis.tnDistribution: Eastern Ghats (Yercaud, Pachamalai), Salem, Erode, Tiruppur, Coimbatore, and Western Ghats reserves.
Tirumala septentrionis.notes: Made up the majority of the 95% tiger share observed during TNBS September 2024 Coimbatore migration counts.

Danaus genutia.headline: Black-veined orange tiger common across wetlands, plains, and hills
Danaus genutia.upperwing: Rich orange-tawny etched with thick black veins on every wing, black outer margins dotted with double rows of white spots, and white-barred black forewing apex.
Danaus genutia.underwing: Paler orange-brown repeating the bold black-veined pattern.
Danaus genutia.similarSpecies: Heavy black stripes tracing every wing vein cleanly separate it from Plain Tiger.
Danaus genutia.habitat: Wetlands, scrub, foothills, forest clearings, and gardens.
Danaus genutia.behavior: Unconcerned slow flight; gathers in small groups around Crotalaria plants to harvest pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
Danaus genutia.season: Year-round, peaking between September and February.
Danaus genutia.tnDistribution: Widespread across coastal, interior, and hill landscapes of Tamil Nadu.
Danaus genutia.notes: Monitored alongside Blue Tigers and Crows in Tamil Nadu seasonal Danainae migration studies.

Danaus chrysippus.headline: Iconic orange-and-black monarch butterfly of open plains and gardens
Danaus chrysippus.upperwing: Warm tawny-orange with jet-black forewing tips slashed by a crisp row of white spots and a black-spotted hindwing centre.
Danaus chrysippus.underwing: Paler golden-orange with matching black borders and bright white spots.
Danaus chrysippus.similarSpecies: Unmarked tawny veins distinguish it from the boldly black-veined Striped Tiger (Danaus genutia) and the female Danaid Eggfly mimic (which lacks small black central hindwing spots).
Danaus chrysippus.habitat: Gardens, roadside milkweeds, dry plains, coastal dunes, and open hills.
Danaus chrysippus.behavior: Slow, buoyant flight; frequently visits Tridax, Lantana, and Calotropis blooms.
Danaus chrysippus.tnDistribution: Found in virtually all 38 districts of Tamil Nadu.
Danaus chrysippus.notes: Serves as the model mimicked by females of the Danaid Eggfly (Hypolimnas misippus).

Euploea sylvester.headline: Deep-brown migratory crow with iridescent blue forewing sheen
Euploea sylvester.upperwing: Dark chocolate-brown bathed in deep violet-blue gloss on the forewing, bordered by white spots; males carry two prominent parallel velvety brands on the forewing.
Euploea sylvester.underwing: Dark brown with crisp white marginal and submarginal spot rows.
Euploea sylvester.similarSpecies: Two parallel forewing scent brands (in males) and rich blue sheen separate it from Common Crow.
Euploea sylvester.habitat: Moist foothills, hill forests, and cross-state migration corridors.
Euploea sylvester.behavior: Glides powerfully alongside Dark Blue and Blue Tigers during seasonal Western–Eastern Ghats migrations.
Euploea sylvester.season: Peaks during April–May and September–December migration waves.
Euploea sylvester.tnDistribution: Western & Eastern Ghats foothills, Mudumalai, Coimbatore, Salem, and Erode corridors.
Euploea sylvester.notes: Clean pair of pale silky brands on the male forewing reliably confirms field identification against Common Crow.

Euploea klugii.headline: Glossy olive-brown plains crow bearing a short broad scent brand in males
Euploea klugii.upperwing: Peninsular subspecies E. k. kollari is rich dark olive-brown paling toward the outer margins, bordered by crisp white marginal dots and larger elongated white submarginal spots on the hindwing without metallic blue gloss; males carry a single short, broad velvety scent brand on the forewing.
Euploea klugii.underwing: Uniform paler olive-brown displaying the twin marginal and submarginal white spot rows plus 2-3 tiny bluish-white discal dots near the forewing cell.
Euploea klugii.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Crow (Euploea core) by its shorter, wider forewing male scent brand and elongated tornal hindwing streaks, and from Double-branded Crow (Euploea sylvester) by lacking deep blue sheen and having only one forewing brand.
Euploea klugii.habitat: Plains scrublands, urban avenues, riverine groves, agricultural hedges, and dry deciduous foothills.
Euploea klugii.behavior: Sails unhurriedly above shrubs and garden trees, gathering on drying Crotalaria and Heliotropium stems to harvest alkaloids and occasionally joining Danainae migrations.
Euploea klugii.season: Recorded throughout the year across Tamil Nadu, peaking during September-December monsoon and post-monsoon months.
Euploea klugii.tnDistribution: Plains and foothills statewide including Chennai, Chengalpattu, Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Salem, Tiruchirappalli, and Eastern Ghats margins.
Euploea klugii.notes: Historically treated as a separate species, the peninsular Indian Brown King Crow (subspecies kollari) lacks the iridescent blue sheen typical of northeastern E. k. klugii.

Euploea core.headline: Velvety dark-brown crow butterfly common in cities and migration flights
Euploea core.upperwing: Rich glossy dark brown bordered by two neat submarginal and marginal rows of clean white spots across both wings.
Euploea core.underwing: Warm dark brown with clear white discal spots in addition to the twin marginal spot rows; males show a single short brand on the forewing.
Euploea core.similarSpecies: Separated from Double-branded Crow (Euploea sylvester) by having one (rather than two) parallel forewing scent brands in males and simpler white inner-forewing spotting.
Euploea core.habitat: Urban gardens, avenues, scrub, hill forests, and seasonal migratory flyways.
Euploea core.behavior: Slow gliding flight; males often visit dry Crotalaria or Heliotropium stems.
Euploea core.season: Abundant year-round; participates prominently in TNBS pre- and post-monsoon migration flights.
Euploea core.tnDistribution: Statewide across plains, towns, and hills.
Euploea core.notes: Mimicked by the Common Mime (Papilio clytia) and the female Great Eggfly (Hypolimnas bolina).

Idea malabarica.headline: Giant translucent white-and-black glider endemic to Western Ghats wet forests
Idea malabarica.upperwing: Broad papery white wings veiled with charcoal-black veins and bold irregular black blotches and spots.
Idea malabarica.underwing: Identical translucent white-and-black pattern visible cleanly from below as it floats through the canopy.
Idea malabarica.similarSpecies: Unmistakable by size, papery slow flight, and translucent black-spotted white wings.
Idea malabarica.habitat: High-rainfall evergreen forests, shaded ravines, and undisturbed Western Ghats river valleys.
Idea malabarica.behavior: Floats gently like drifting tissue paper high among canopy lianas, occasionally descending to nectar at Ixora or Clerodendrum.
Idea malabarica.season: Seen throughout the year in wet evergreen pockets.
Idea malabarica.tnDistribution: Wet Western Ghats enclaves in Tamil Nadu: Nilgiris, Anamalai/Valparai, Silent Valley borders, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Idea malabarica.notes: Listed as Near Threatened globally and relies strictly on intact, unlogged wet evergreen valley forests.

Charaxes bharata.headline: Fast-flying black-and-lime nawab adorned with twin hindwing tails
Charaxes bharata.upperwing: Velvety black wings bisected by a wide pale creamy-green median band and sporting two sharp hindwing tails.
Charaxes bharata.underwing: Pale satiny cream bordered by warm olive-brown margins and dark spots.
Charaxes bharata.similarSpecies: Previously known as Polyura athamas; separated from Anomalous Nawab (Charaxes agrarius) by subtly narrower median band and habitat overlap.
Charaxes bharata.habitat: Forest streams, damp gravel roads, foothills, and wooded clearings.
Charaxes bharata.behavior: Exceptionally fast flight; males puddle intently on wet sand, animal dung, and tree sap.
Charaxes bharata.season: Common year-round in hills and wooded districts.
Charaxes bharata.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Pachamalai, and Salem hills.
Charaxes bharata.notes: Highlighted in TNBS field photography from moist Tamil Nadu hill tracts.

Charaxes agrarius.headline: Twin-tailed creamy-banded nawab diagnosed by two pale spots near the forewing tip
Charaxes agrarius.upperwing: Velvety black-brown wings bisected by a moderately broad pale greenish-cream median band and sporting two sharp hindwing tails; forewing carries two distinct pale subapical spots near the costa (a larger inner spot and smaller outer dot). Females are larger with a slightly wider pale band.
Charaxes agrarius.underwing: Satiny cream-white framed by warm olive-brown outer borders, fine dark hairlines, rust-red discal spots along the band edge, and twin pale spots mirroring the forewing apex.
Charaxes agrarius.similarSpecies: Closely resembles Indian Nawab (Charaxes bharata), but separated reliably by having two pale costal/subapical spots on the forewing rather than a single prominent spot.
Charaxes agrarius.habitat: Dry and moist deciduous foothills, scrub jungles, stony riverbeds, and open wooded clearings.
Charaxes agrarius.behavior: Powerful, bullet-fast flier that perches high on thorny canopies and drops rapidly to damp sand, animal scat, and tree sap.
Charaxes agrarius.season: Active year-round in suitable dry-to-moist tracts, with peaks in June-August and October-January.
Charaxes agrarius.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western and Eastern Ghats foothills and dry hills including Kallar, Coimbatore, Sathyamangalam, Mudumalai, Salem, Yercaud, Pachamalai, and Madurai.
Charaxes agrarius.notes: Formerly placed in genus Polyura; prefers slightly drier foothill and scrub landscapes alongside the widespread Indian Nawab.

Charaxes schreiber.headline: Striking sky-blue-edged white-banded nawab of dense evergreen forest canopies
