Charaxes schreiber.upperwing: Deep velvety black subtly glossed with dark indigo at the wing bases and crossed by a wide pure white median band sharply rimmed on both sides with luminous sky-blue, plus two small white apical dots and two stout hindwing tails (subspecies C. s. wardii). Females are larger with a broader white band.
Charaxes schreiber.underwing: Pearly silvery-white crossed by olive-brown bands, dark fine lines, and a vivid submarginal chain of brick-red and black crescent lunules along the hindwing.
Charaxes schreiber.similarSpecies: Unmistakable among Tamil Nadu nawabs by the vivid sky-blue borders framing the bright white median band across black wings and the gleaming pearly underside.
Charaxes schreiber.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forest canopies, shaded mountain streams, and tall riparian corridors.
Charaxes schreiber.behavior: Flies powerfully high in the canopy and descends swiftly to sunlit gravel beds, carnivore droppings, rotting fruit, or tree sap along forest streams.
Charaxes schreiber.season: Scarce and seasonal, recorded mostly during March-May and August-December.
Charaxes schreiber.tnDistribution: Western Ghats wet forests including Mudumalai, Gudalur, Nilgiri slopes, Siruvani, Anamalais, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kanyakumari.
Charaxes schreiber.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Charaxes schreiber.notes: A prized canopy species of intact South Indian wet forests whose swift, wary flight makes close observation away from mineral puddles rare.

Charaxes psaphon.headline: Bold orange-and-black forest rajah showing striking sexual dimorphism
Charaxes psaphon.upperwing: Males are rich fiery tawny-orange with a broad glossy black outer half on the forewing and wide black hindwing border enclosing two white-centered tornal dots; females are paler tawny-ochre crossed by a broad cream-white discal band edged inwardly in black, and bear longer twin hindwing tails than males.
Charaxes psaphon.underwing: Purplish-brown to warm rufous-ochre glossed with satiny sheen and crisscrossed by fine white-edged zigzag black basal and discal lines.
Charaxes psaphon.similarSpecies: Separated from Black Rajah (Charaxes solon) by bright tawny-orange wing bases (rather than dark black-brown with narrow pale bands) and from Common Nawab by rich rufous-purple cryptic undersides.
Charaxes psaphon.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous hill forests, evergreen margins, shaded forest roads, and wooded valleys.
Charaxes psaphon.behavior: Territorial, fast-flying canopy dweller; males perch watchfully on sun-dappled branch tips and descend to feed on sap fluxes, rotting fruit, carrion, and wet mud.
Charaxes psaphon.season: Seen throughout the year in forested tracts, most frequent from July to January and March-May.
Charaxes psaphon.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats hills and foothills including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Sathyamangalam, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, Sirumalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Charaxes psaphon.notes: South Indian populations belong to subspecies C. p. imna, long known to patrol high forest crowns before dropping rapidly onto decaying matter.

Charaxes solon.headline: Agile black-and-lime rajah bred widely on roadside tamarind trees
Charaxes solon.upperwing: Velvety brownish-black wings crossed by a crisp narrow pale greenish-white median band breaking into discrete spots toward the forewing apex, accompanied by a neat submarginal row of pale dots; hindwing carries two pointed tails that are noticeably longer in females.
Charaxes solon.underwing: Silvery grey-brown finely etched with dark reddish-brown hairlines, repeating the pale discal band alongside orange-ochre touches near the hindwing tornus.
Charaxes solon.similarSpecies: Darker ground color and much narrower, macular greenish-white median band easily distinguish it from Indian Tawny Rajah (Charaxes psaphon) and Indian Nawab (Charaxes bharata).
Charaxes solon.habitat: Tamarind-lined plains avenues, urban parks, dry scrublands, village groves, and deciduous foothills.
Charaxes solon.behavior: Darts rapidly around tall tree crowns and returns repeatedly to favoured exposed twigs; feeds eagerly on fermenting tree sap, overripe fruit, and damp mud rather than flowers.
Charaxes solon.season: Active year-round across Tamil Nadu plains and foothills, peaking during August-January.
Charaxes solon.tnDistribution: Statewide across plains and lower hills including Chennai, Chengalpattu, Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Salem, Tiruchirappalli, and Ghats foothills.
Charaxes solon.notes: One of the few large Charaxinae thriving in Tamil Nadu towns and farmlands thanks to widespread planted Tamarindus indica avenues.

Discophora lepida.headline: Elusive crepuscular bamboo specialist with violet-spotted males and gold-banded females
Discophora lepida.upperwing: Stout-bodied deep velvety brown butterfly; males carry three curved rows of pale bluish-violet spots toward the forewing outer half and a dark velvety discal scent brand on the hindwing, while larger females show an oblique bright ochre-yellow forewing band and pale marginal spots.
Discophora lepida.underwing: Warm buff-brown intricately striated like a dry bamboo leaf, bisected by a straight dark discal line and carrying two small muted ocelli on the hindwing.
Discophora lepida.similarSpecies: Unlike Palmking (Amathusia phidippus), lacks huge concentric hindwing eyespots below and tornal tails, and shows brightly spotted or banded upperwings.
Discophora lepida.habitat: Dense bamboo brakes and reed thickets inside evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests.
Discophora lepida.behavior: Skulks deep inside shaded bamboo clumps by day and flies swiftly at dawn and dusk, feeding on rotting fruit, tree sap, and animal droppings.
Discophora lepida.season: Most often encountered between July and January following monsoon flush of bamboo shoots.
Discophora lepida.tnDistribution: Moist Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Gudalur, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Discophora lepida.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Discophora lepida.notes: South Indian and Sri Lankan populations represent a distinct Western Ghats lineage tightly dependent on healthy native bamboo and Ochlandra reed stands.

Amathusia phidippus.headline: Giant dusk-flying palm specialist bearing dual bullseye eyespots underneath
Amathusia phidippus.upperwing: Massive warm chocolate-brown wings; males have a subtle hair tuft along the hindwing anal fold and short spatulate tornal lobes marked by two small black spots, while larger females are paler brown with an indistinct ochreous subapical band.
Amathusia phidippus.underwing: Pale fawn-grey neatly striped with parallel straight brown and creamy bands, featuring two large concentric black-and-ochre eyespots on each hindwing (one near costa, one near tornus).
Amathusia phidippus.similarSpecies: Separated from Southern Duffer (Discophora lepida) by larger wingspan, parallel straight underside bands, spatulate tornal lobes, and giant dual hindwing ocelli.
Amathusia phidippus.habitat: Humid coconut and palmyra groves, shaded palm understories, and lowland evergreen edges.
Amathusia phidippus.behavior: Strictly crepuscular and shade-bound, resting immobile on palm trunks by day and flying low with heavy wingbeats at twilight to feed on fallen fruit and sap.
Amathusia phidippus.season: Sporadic and very rare, with records mostly around monsoon and post-monsoon months (August-December).
Amathusia phidippus.tnDistribution: Extremely localized in humid southern Western Ghats foothills and palm tracts of Kanyakumari and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai along the Tamil Nadu-Kerala border.
Amathusia phidippus.notes: Peninsular Indian populations are extraordinarily rare and fragmented compared to Southeast Asian colonies, drawing recent taxonomic scrutiny.

Elymnias hypermnestra.headline: Distinctive palmfly addition mimicking tigers along palm edges
Elymnias hypermnestra.upperwing: Mainland subspecies (E. h. undularis): males are velvety black-brown with pale blue marginal spots and reddish hindwing borders; females closely mimic Striped Tiger with black-veined orange wings.
Elymnias hypermnestra.underwing: Mottled bark-brown and cream cryptic striations camouflaging the butterfly against palm bark.
Elymnias hypermnestra.similarSpecies: Separated from Tailed Palmfly (Elymnias caudata) by rounded hindwings lacking a prominent tail projection.
Elymnias hypermnestra.habitat: Coconut groves, ornamental palm gardens, coastal parks, and humid hill orchards.
Elymnias hypermnestra.behavior: Shade-loving skulker around palm fronds; adults feed on tree sap and fermenting fruit juices.
Elymnias hypermnestra.tnDistribution: Added recently to the Tamil Nadu Checklist following validated records around Chennai, Puducherry surroundings, and Sirumalai (Dindigul district).
Elymnias hypermnestra.notes: One of the newest additions to the Tamil Nadu butterfly list, updating historical assumptions that restricted it north of coastal Andhra.
sources: Pattampoochi Issue 27, A Note on Common Palmfly (pp. 9–11)

Elymnias caudata.headline: Tailed Western Ghats endemic palmfly mimicking milkweed tigers in flight
Elymnias caudata.upperwing: Dark brownish-black forewings patterned with a bold cream-white subapical band and pale bluish-grey marginal spots, paired with bright chestnut-orange hindwings bearing white-centered black borders and a sharp narrow tail at vein 4. Females are larger with a broader white forewing band.
Elymnias caudata.underwing: Cryptically marbled in intricate dark brown, cream-white, and rufous striations that camouflage the resting butterfly against dry palm fronds and bark.
Elymnias caudata.similarSpecies: Separated cleanly from Common Palmfly (Elymnias hypermnestra) by the prominent tail projection on the hindwing and the pale subapical band present in both sexes.
Elymnias caudata.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen foothills, shaded forest gardens, and areca-coconut estates.
Elymnias caudata.behavior: Flies weakly and lazily in dappled shade around palm crowns, mimicking unpalatable Striped and Plain Tigers until settling suddenly with closed wings.
Elymnias caudata.season: Recorded throughout the year across wet Western Ghats slopes, peaking between July and January.
Elymnias caudata.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills and hills of Tamil Nadu including Gudalur, Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Palani foothills, and Kanyakumari.
Elymnias caudata.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Elymnias caudata.notes: Endemic to the Western Ghats and southern peninsular India, serving as a classic Batesian mimic of toxic Danainae butterflies.

Melanitis leda.headline: Crepuscular brown butterfly masters of seasonal dry-leaf camouflage
Melanitis leda.upperwing: Dark earthy brown bearing a prominent black eyespot with two crisp white pupils and bright orange halos near the forewing tip.
Melanitis leda.underwing: Shows dramatic seasonal polyphenism: wet-season butterflies carry crisp concentric eyespots, while dry-season morphs turn into intricately mottled dead leaves.
Melanitis leda.similarSpecies: Common Evening Brown has larger orange halos around the white forewing spots than Dark Evening Brown (Melanitis phedima).
Melanitis leda.habitat: Shaded gardens, bamboo clumps, coconut groves, paddy bunds, and forest understorey.
Melanitis leda.behavior: Rests camouflaged among fallen leaf litter by day and becomes briskly active at dusk and dawn, feeding on ripe fruit and sap.
Melanitis leda.season: Year-round statewide; dry-season form dominates December–May.
Melanitis leda.tnDistribution: Very common across plains, farms, urban gardens, and forests throughout Tamil Nadu.
Melanitis leda.notes: Famous for extreme dry-season leaf polymorphism, where no two dry-season individuals look identically patterned underneath.

Melanitis phedima.headline: Velvety-dark crepuscular evening brown lacking bright orange halos on the forewing
Melanitis phedima.upperwing: Deep dark fuliginous-brown with a subtly angled forewing apex; males appear nearly unmarked dark brown with faint pale apical dots, while females show a dull ochreous-brown subapical smudge enclosing two blurred dark spots.
Melanitis phedima.underwing: Wet-season morph is dark purplish-brown dusted with fine ochre striae, bearing 4 small forewing ocelli and 6 white-pupilled hindwing ocelli (anal spot double); dry-season morph turns wildly variable dead-leaf brown with sharply hooked forewings and reduced ocelli.
Melanitis phedima.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Evening Brown (Melanitis leda) by its darker, unspotted male upperwing and absence of bright orange halos around the forewing spots; smaller and less strongly orange-patched than Great Evening Brown (Melanitis zitenius).
Melanitis phedima.habitat: Shaded forest understorey, bamboo thickets, moist foothills, and wooded plantation edges.
Melanitis phedima.behavior: Remains motionless on forest floor leaf litter through bright daylight hours and emerges at dawn and dusk to feed on tree sap and fallen fruit.
Melanitis phedima.season: Present year-round in forested districts; wet-season ocellated form flies June-November while cryptic dry-season morph dominates December-May.
Melanitis phedima.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats forests including Nilgiris, Gudalur, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Sirumalai.
Melanitis phedima.notes: Exhibits classic seasonal polyphenism in Tamil Nadu hills, switching from eyespot-deflected wet-season adults to dead-leaf mimicry in dry months.

Melanitis zitenius.headline: Largest Indian evening brown with hooked forewing tips and a broad ochre subapical patch
Melanitis zitenius.upperwing: Rich warm brown bearing a sharply produced, sickle-like forewing apex; displays two dark subapical spots bordered broadly on the inner side by a bright orange-ochre patch that is especially wide and vivid in females.
Melanitis zitenius.underwing: Wet-season morph shows pale striated brown wings with small neat white-pupilled submarginal ocelli (3-4 on forewing, 6 on hindwing); dry-season morph resembles a blotched, fungus-spotted dead leaf with obsolete eyespots.
Melanitis zitenius.similarSpecies: Substantially larger and more strongly falcate than Common Evening Brown (Melanitis leda) and Dark Evening Brown (Melanitis phedima), with a broader ochre-yellow patch extending well toward the forewing costa.
Melanitis zitenius.habitat: Dense evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, tall bamboo stands, and shaded ravines.
Melanitis zitenius.behavior: Flushes explosively from leaf litter when disturbed and settles quickly with wings tightly shut, flying purposefully in deep shade and twilight.
Melanitis zitenius.season: Scarcer than other evening browns; encountered mostly during July-January with dry-season morphs lingering into April.
Melanitis zitenius.tnDistribution: Moist Western Ghats hill forests of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Gudalur, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Melanitis zitenius.notes: Restricted to healthier forest interiors in Tamil Nadu compared to the garden-tolerant Common Evening Brown.

Parantirrhoea marshalli.headline: Unmistakable Western Ghats reed-bamboo specialist flushed with violet-mauve bands
Parantirrhoea marshalli.upperwing: Deep dusky fuscous-brown glossed with subtle violet; uniquely rounded forewing carries a curved crescentic pale violet-mauve band enclosing three small oblique white dots, and the hindwing extends into a sharp tail-like angle at vein 4. Females are slightly broader-winged with a softer mauve band.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.underwing: Warm pale ochreous-brown densely etched with fine dark brown striae and tiny obsolete submarginal ocelli, resembling dry reed foliage when perched.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu by its convex forewing margin, mauve white-spotted forewing crescent, and pointed hindwing projection.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.habitat: Undisturbed wild Ochlandra reed brakes inside wet evergreen hill forests of the southern Western Ghats.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.behavior: Weak, bouncing shade-dweller that flits rapidly between dense Ochlandra reed stems and rests hidden low near damp forest floors.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.season: Localized and seasonal, peaking after southwest and northeast monsoon rains from August to December.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.tnDistribution: Strictly southern Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kanyakumari hills, Meghamalai, and southern Anamalais.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Parantirrhoea marshalli.notes: A monotypic genus endemic strictly to the southern Western Ghats; survival depends directly on conserving native Ochlandra reed habitats.

Lethe europa.headline: Bamboo-dwelling treebrown with confluent forewing eyespots below and white-banded females
Lethe europa.upperwing: Rich dark olive-brown with a pointed forewing and short angular hindwing projection; females display a crisp oblique white band across the forewing and dark marginal hindwing spots, whereas males lack the white band and show only faint pale apical dots.
Lethe europa.underwing: Warm olive-brown crossed by a straight silvery-white inner line and lilac marginal edging; forewing bears 4-6 large, tightly packed confluent black ocelli, while hindwing carries 6 irregular black ocelli with speckled silvery centers.
Lethe europa.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Treebrown (Lethe rohria) by the continuous (rather than broken three-spot) white band on the female forewing and the large fused forewing ocelli on the underside.
Lethe europa.habitat: Bamboo groves, moist deciduous foothills, shaded riverbanks, and forested parks.
Lethe europa.behavior: Crepuscular and shade-loving; rests head-down or sideways on bamboo culms and feeds avidly on sap exudates and fallen fruit.
Lethe europa.season: Active throughout the year around bamboo stands, peaking from August to January.
Lethe europa.tnDistribution: Widely distributed across wooded foothills and bamboo patches in Tamil Nadu including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Anamalais, Shevaroys, Pachamalai, and Chennai tree parks.
Lethe europa.notes: Closely bound to wild and planted bamboo clumps; South Indian populations represent the nominate subspecies L. e. europa (or southern peninsular L. e. ragalva).

Lethe rohria.headline: Hill-forest treebrown with a spotted white female band and an enlarged apical hindwing ocellus
Lethe rohria.upperwing: Dark greyish-brown (subspecies L. r. neelgheriensis); females show a disjointed oblique forewing band composed of three separated white spots plus two white apical dots, whereas males lack the discal spots and carry only two small white subapical spots.
Lethe rohria.underwing: Dark grey-brown crossed by a straight pale lilac-white inner discal line; hindwing bears an arched series of 6 ringed ocelli in which the uppermost apical eyespot is noticeably larger than the remaining five.
Lethe rohria.similarSpecies: Separated from Bamboo Treebrown (Lethe europa) by the broken three-spot white band in females and smaller separated forewing ocelli underneath, and from Tamil Treebrown (Lethe drypetis) by having one enlarged apical hindwing ocellus rather than two large eyespots.
Lethe rohria.habitat: Montane evergreen edges, shola borders, shaded forest clearings, and mid-to-high hill slopes.
Lethe rohria.behavior: Bobs briskly along sunlit shola edges and shaded paths, settling abruptly on tree trunks, wet boulders, or damp earth.
Lethe rohria.season: Common in the hills throughout the year, peaking during June-December.
Lethe rohria.tnDistribution: Higher hill ranges across Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Kodaikanal, Siruvani, Anamalais, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Lethe rohria.notes: Unlike the bamboo-obligate Lethe europa, the South Indian Common Treebrown feeds broadly on woodland grasses, letting it thrive up to high montane elevations.

Lethe drypetis.headline: Shaded forest treebrown distinguished beneath by two oversized hindwing eyespots
Lethe drypetis.upperwing: Males are uniform rich glossy brown with slight golden-olive sheen and two tiny pale apical dots; females are warm brown with a broken oblique white forewing band, an isolated white bar in space 2, and dark submarginal hindwing spots.
Lethe drypetis.underwing: Warm brown suffused with pale lilac lines; forewing shows an incurved row of 4-5 blind dark spots, while the hindwing carries 6 yellow-ringed black ocelli in which the apical (space 6) and subtornal (space 2) eyespots are markedly larger than the others.
Lethe drypetis.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Treebrown (Lethe rohria) by having two enlarged hindwing underside ocelli (apical and subtornal) rather than a single oversized apical ocellus, plus lilac-bordered discal lines.
Lethe drypetis.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded bamboo ravines, and humid estate edges.
Lethe drypetis.behavior: Elusive shade-hugger that flits low through undergrowth and rests on tree trunks or fallen twigs, occasionally feeding on fermenting sap and dung.
Lethe drypetis.season: Recorded mainly between July and January, with scattered records in March-May.
Lethe drypetis.tnDistribution: Western and southern hill ranges including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, Sirumalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Lethe drypetis.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Lethe drypetis.notes: Often called the Two-eyed Treebrown in South India and represented across Peninsular India by subspecies L. d. todara.

Mycalesis anaxias.headline: Evergreen-forest bushbrown instantly tagged by an oblique white forewing tip bar
Mycalesis anaxias.upperwing: Deep blackish-brown on both wings crossed cleanly by an oblique snow-white preapical bar near the forewing tip (wider in females); males possess a pale yellow hair-tuft over a hindwing scent brand.
Mycalesis anaxias.underwing: Dark smoky brown across the basal half contrasting sharply with a pale ochre-buff outer marginal border; carries submarginal ringed ocelli (2-3 on forewing, 7 on hindwing) that diminish in dry-season adults while keeping the crisp white forewing bar.
Mycalesis anaxias.similarSpecies: Unmistakable among Tamil Nadu Mycalesis species by the pure white oblique preapical bar on the dark forewing upperwing.
Mycalesis anaxias.habitat: Shaded mid-to-high elevation evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests and damp forest trails.
Mycalesis anaxias.behavior: Hugs dark undergrowth and damp mossy banks, flying short distances low to the ground and feeding on rotting forest fruit and tree sap.
Mycalesis anaxias.season: Active throughout the year in wet Western Ghats forests, peaking from August to January.
Mycalesis anaxias.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Gudalur, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Mycalesis anaxias.notes: A reliable indicator of shaded, intact evergreen forest floor cover in Tamil Nadu hills.

Mycalesis perseus.headline: Widespread grass-feeding bushbrown with an inward-shifted hindwing eyespot beneath
Mycalesis perseus.upperwing: Dull dark grey-brown with faint pale marginal lines and a single prominent white-pupilled lower forewing ocellus in space 2 (larger in females); males carry a small dark forewing brand and a pale yellow hindwing hair-tuft.
Mycalesis perseus.underwing: Wet-season morph shows a straight pale violet-white discal line and ringed ocelli (2-4 on forewing, 7 on hindwing) where the hindwing ocellus in space 2 sits distinctly shifted inward out of line with its neighbors; dry-season morph turns mottled bark-brown with ocelli shrunk to white specks.
Mycalesis perseus.similarSpecies: Separated in the wet season from Dark-brand Bushbrown (Mycalesis mineus) by the inward-displaced hindwing ocellus in space 2 (leaving only the three lowest ocelli aligned, versus four aligned in M. mineus).
Mycalesis perseus.habitat: Grassy meadows, paddy bunds, scrub edges, urban parks, and Ghats foothills.
Mycalesis perseus.behavior: Bobs low through tall grass, basking diagonally in morning sun and resting sideways among dry grass stalks during midday heat.
Mycalesis perseus.season: Abundant year-round across Tamil Nadu; wet-season morphs fly July-December and dry-season forms dominate January-May.
Mycalesis perseus.tnDistribution: Statewide across plains, wetlands, farms, and Western and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Mycalesis perseus.notes: Dry-season adults are nearly impossible to separate by wing pattern alone from dry-season M. mineus without examining male scent brands.

Mycalesis mineus.headline: Common bushbrown carrying a short dark male brand and four straight-lined hindwing ocelli
Mycalesis mineus.upperwing: Dark earthy brown with pale marginal hairlines and one prominent yellow-ringed lower ocellus in space 2 on the forewing (occasionally a faint apical dot); males have a short, small dark brown scent brand on the forewing underside and a pale hindwing hair-tuft.
Mycalesis mineus.underwing: Wet-season form features a crisp whitish postdiscal band bordered inwardly by a dark line toothed near vein 1b, plus ringed ocelli (2 on forewing, 7 on hindwing) with the lower four hindwing ocelli arranged in a straight row; dry-season morph turns buff-brown with pinpoint dots.
Mycalesis mineus.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Bushbrown (Mycalesis perseus) by having the four posterior hindwing ocelli in a straight line and from Long-brand Bushbrown (Mycalesis visala) by the male's short dark brown forewing brand rather than a long yellow-ochre brand.
Mycalesis mineus.habitat: Shaded gardens, damp grass banks, scrub borders, plantations, and moist-to-dry forest edges.
Mycalesis mineus.behavior: Flies weakly through shaded grass tufts and feeds on rotting fruit, wet soil, and sap rather than nectar flowers.
Mycalesis mineus.season: Common throughout the year across Tamil Nadu, peaking in August-December.
Mycalesis mineus.tnDistribution: Widespread statewide from Chennai and coastal plains to Coimbatore, Madurai, Salem, and Western and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Mycalesis mineus.notes: South Indian populations correspond to subspecies M. m. polydecta and show sharp seasonal contrast between ocellated wet broods and cryptic dry broods.

Mycalesis igilia.headline: Compact Western Ghats endemic bushbrown with a slender pale-brown forewing brand
Mycalesis igilia.upperwing: Smaller and slightly rounder-winged than M. visala; dark greyish-brown bearing a distinct yellow-ringed black ocellus in space 2 of the forewing and 1-2 faint small ocelli on the hindwing.
Mycalesis igilia.underwing: Paler warm brown crossed by a slender whitish-violet discal fascia and a complete submarginal arc of ringed ocelli (2-4 on forewing, 7 on hindwing); males bear a narrow, moderately long pale ochre-brown scent brand in space 1b alongside a small hindwing costal brand.
Mycalesis igilia.similarSpecies: Smaller wingspan, rounder forewing apex, and narrower pale brown male brand separate it from Long-brand Bushbrown (Mycalesis visala), while its longer brand separates it from Dark-brand Bushbrown (Mycalesis mineus).
Mycalesis igilia.habitat: Shaded grassy understorey of moist deciduous and semi-evergreen Western Ghats foothills.
Mycalesis igilia.behavior: Shade-tolerant low flier that stays close to damp forest trails and tangled grass clumps, visiting fermenting fruit and moist soil.
Mycalesis igilia.season: Most frequently recorded between July and January following monsoon grass growth.
Mycalesis igilia.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills and slopes of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Gudalur, Siruvani, Anamalais, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Mycalesis igilia.notes: Endemic to southern India and often overlooked among lookalike Mycalesis species unless the male forewing brand and wing shape are examined closely.

Mycalesis visala.headline: Pointed-winged bushbrown diagnosed by a long bright ochre male scent brand beneath
Mycalesis visala.upperwing: Slightly produced, angular forewing tip; uniform dark brown with one large yellow-ringed ocellus in space 2 (rarely a minute apical dot); males possess a pale hair-tuft overlapping a dark brand near the hindwing costa.
Mycalesis visala.underwing: Wet-season morph is pale brown crossed by a narrow whitish discal line and ringed submarginal ocelli (2 on forewing, 7 on hindwing), with males displaying a very long, bright ochreous-yellow brand reaching or crossing the discal line; dry-season morph turns sharply angular and striated like a dry leaf.
Mycalesis visala.similarSpecies: Separated from Dark-brand Bushbrown (Mycalesis mineus) by its sharply angled forewing apex and very long bright ochre male forewing brand, and from Tamil Bushbrown (Mycalesis subdita) by its more acute forewing tip and narrower ochre brand.
Mycalesis visala.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous hill forests, bamboo-shaded foothills, and grassy stream edges.
Mycalesis visala.behavior: Skulks in shaded bamboo and grass undergrowth, flying short bouncing hops and feeding on ripe fallen fruit and damp earth.
Mycalesis visala.season: Seen throughout the year in hills and wooded foothills, with angular dry-season morphs common December-May.
Mycalesis visala.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats hills and foothills including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Mycalesis visala.notes: Dry-season adults show an exaggerated falcate forewing profile and intricate leaf striations that render them nearly invisible on dead foliage.

Mycalesis subdita.headline: Lowland southern bushbrown carrying a long broad nacreous-edged forewing brand
Mycalesis subdita.upperwing: Dark earthy brown with rounder forewing apex than M. visala and one crisp yellow-ringed lower ocellus in space 2 (occasionally 1-2 faint spots on the hindwing).
Mycalesis subdita.underwing: Wet-season form bears a distinct narrow whitish discal band and submarginal ringed ocelli (2 on forewing, 7 on hindwing) with the posterior four aligned straight; males carry a notably long, broad pale brown scent brand set inside a pearly nacreous patch reaching (but not passing) the discal line, while dry-season morphs show cryptic striae and pinpoint spots.
Mycalesis subdita.similarSpecies: Separated from Long-brand Bushbrown (Mycalesis visala) by its rounder forewing apex and broader, nacreous-enclosed male brand stopping at the discal line, and from Mycalesis mineus by the much longer male brand.
Mycalesis subdita.habitat: Coastal scrublands, dry evergreen patches, lowland grassy groves, and lower foothills.
Mycalesis subdita.behavior: Low, fluttering grass-dweller active along shaded hedgerows, scrub borders, and fallen leaf litter, feeding on ripe fruit and damp patches.
Mycalesis subdita.season: Recorded nearly year-round in lowland southern tracts, peaking between September and January.
Mycalesis subdita.tnDistribution: Plains, coast, and low foothills of Tamil Nadu including Chennai, Vandalur, Chengalpattu, Madurai, Coimbatore, Salem, and Tirunelveli.
Mycalesis subdita.notes: Restricted to southern India and Sri Lanka; sometimes treated historically as a southern subspecies of Mycalesis visala before detailed brand and genital comparisons separated it.

Mycalesis junonia.headline: Jewel-like Western Ghats bushbrown ringed beneath in metallic silvery-blue and gold
Mycalesis junonia.upperwing: Dark umber-brown framed by twin bright ochre-yellow marginal lines; forewing features a large lower black ocellus topped by a broad orange-yellow iris and triangular orange discal patch plus a small apical spot, while hindwing carries two tiny tawny-ringed ocelli.
Mycalesis junonia.underwing: Deep rich ochre-yellow crossed by a gleaming silvery-blue discal line; 2 forewing and 7 hindwing ocelli are encircled in outer metallic silvery-blue rings, with the apical and paired median hindwing spots glowing on bright yellow patches (subdued in dry season).
Mycalesis junonia.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu by its bright orange-ochre forewing patch above and rich golden underside adorned with metallic silvery-blue ocelli rings.
Mycalesis junonia.habitat: Shaded evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, mossy forest trails, and humid understorey.
Mycalesis junonia.behavior: Flies close to shaded forest floors and rests with closed wings on damp rocks or ferns, briefly flashing bright yellow undersides during short hops.
Mycalesis junonia.season: Active throughout the year in moist Western Ghats slopes, peaking between July and December.
Mycalesis junonia.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Gudalur, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Mycalesis junonia.notes: Often regarded as the Western Ghats counterpart of Sri Lanka's Mycalesis patnia and sometimes treated as a full southern Indian endemic species.

Telinga adolphei.headline: Montane Western Ghats bushbrown with fiery orange-ringed eyespots on dark umber wings
Telinga adolphei.upperwing: Dark umber-brown; forewing carries a prominent white-pupilled lower black ocellus ringed with bright reddish-orange and a tiny subapical spot, while the hindwing bears a tidy row of 2-4 small orange-ringed submarginal ocelli.
Telinga adolphei.underwing: Dark umber-brown sprinkled with fine transverse striae, with the basal half sharply demarcated by a dark brown discal line and broadly paler outer margins; bears 2 forewing and 7 curved small orange-ringed hindwing ocelli.
Telinga adolphei.similarSpecies: Separated from Red-disc Bushbrown (Telinga oculus) by having only a narrow orange ring around the forewing ocellus rather than a huge bright orange-red patch, and from Palni Bushbrown (Telinga davisoni) by brighter orange eye rings and 2 (not 4) forewing ocelli below.
Telinga adolphei.habitat: High-elevation shola-grassland margins, montane evergreen understorey, and shaded hill streams.
Telinga adolphei.behavior: Flies low along sunlit shola edges and bracken slopes, basking with half-open wings in chilly mountain sunshine before diving into dense grass.
Telinga adolphei.season: Active across mountain habitats most of the year, peaking in March-May and September-December.
Telinga adolphei.tnDistribution: High-elevation Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris (Coonoor, Ooty, Kotagiri), Mudumalai upper slopes, Siruvani, Anamalais, and Palani Hills.
Telinga adolphei.notes: Strictly endemic to the southern Western Ghats and formerly placed under Mycalesis or Heteropsis before recent molecular studies restored Telinga.

Telinga oculus.headline: Striking southern Western Ghats bushbrown flaunting a broad crimson-orange discal eye patch
Telinga oculus.upperwing: Rich rusty ferruginous-brown; forewing features a huge white-centered black lower ocellus broadly encircled by a luminous orange-red patch extending upward toward the costa plus a tiny subapical dot, while hindwing carries 3-4 small reddish-ringed ocelli.
Telinga oculus.underwing: Warm ferruginous-brown turning paler ochre outwardly, crossed by a distinct dark straight discal line and bearing 2 forewing and 7 well-formed white-centered hindwing ocelli that are larger than in T. adolphei.
Telinga oculus.similarSpecies: Easily separated from Red-eye Bushbrown (Telinga adolphei) and Palni Bushbrown (Telinga davisoni) by its larger wingspan and the vivid, wide orange-red halo flaring across the forewing upperwing.
Telinga oculus.habitat: Montane shola forests, high-elevation evergreen edges, and shaded grassland borders south of the Palghat Gap.
Telinga oculus.behavior: Glides smoothly through shaded shola understorey and sunlit fern clearings, perching on low foliage and feeding on forest floor organic matter.
Telinga oculus.season: Recorded year-round in high southern hills, peaking in February-May and August-December.
Telinga oculus.tnDistribution: High-altitude Western Ghats south of the Palghat Gap in Tamil Nadu including Anamalais, Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Telinga oculus.notes: One of the signature montane endemics of the southern Western Ghats, closely tied to undisturbed shola-grassland ecotones.

Telinga davisoni.headline: Dusky montane bushbrown of southern hills with shifted tornal eyespots underneath
Telinga davisoni.upperwing: Uniform dark dusky brown with faint pale submarginal lines; forewing shows a modest lower dark ocellus (and occasional tiny apical dot) framed by a narrow dull ochre-brown ring, lacking bright orange-red patches.
Telinga davisoni.underwing: Warm earthy brown crossed by a very fine thread-like whitish-edged postdiscal line that fades toward the forewing costa; forewing carries up to 4 small ocelli and hindwing bears 7 ocelli with the two posterior tornal ocelli shifted noticeably outward toward the margin.
Telinga davisoni.similarSpecies: Separated from Red-eye Bushbrown (Telinga adolphei) by duller upperwing eye rings, a finer postdiscal thread fading near the forewing costa, and outward-shifted tornal hindwing ocelli.
Telinga davisoni.habitat: Montane evergreen understorey, shola borders, and shaded grassy hill paths.
Telinga davisoni.behavior: Low-flying shade specialist that stays close to mossy trails and forest bamboo-grass margins, settling quickly on dry twigs or damp ground.
Telinga davisoni.season: Encountered mainly from March to May and September to December in higher hills.
Telinga davisoni.tnDistribution: Southern Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Palani Hills, Anamalais, Meghamalai, Nilgiris, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Telinga davisoni.notes: Named after naturalist William Davison from specimens collected in the Palani Hills; endemic to the southern Western Ghats.

Zipaetis saitis.headline: Velvety white-banded Western Ghats endemic enclosing five eyespots in a silver ribbon
Zipaetis saitis.upperwing: Jet-black (slightly browner in females) boldly crossed by a crisp broad oblique snow-white band on the forewing and a matching broad white postdiscal band across the hindwing.
Zipaetis saitis.underwing: Dark brown with wavy pale marginal lines and a dramatic hindwing row of 5 black, ochre-ringed white-pupilled ocelli enclosed together inside a single gleaming silvery band just inward of the white band (the second ocellus from apex is huge and bi-pupilled).
Zipaetis saitis.similarSpecies: Superficially mimics white-banded forest nymphalids in flight, but instantly diagnosed at rest by the five hindwing eyespots bundled inside one silvery ribbon.
Zipaetis saitis.habitat: Dense evergreen hill forests, shaded stream ravines, and wild Ochlandra reed thickets.
Zipaetis saitis.behavior: Flies slowly with floppy, gliding wingbeats through gloomy forest understories and reed stands, resting low on wet leaves and ferns.
Zipaetis saitis.season: Uncommon and localized; most records span July-December with scattered sightings in March-May.
Zipaetis saitis.tnDistribution: Western Ghats evergreen tracts of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris (Gudalur, Nadugani), Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Zipaetis saitis.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Zipaetis saitis.notes: A Western Ghats endemic and sole peninsular representative of genus Zipaetis, tightly coupled to undisturbed montane reed-bamboo ecosystems.

Orsotrioena medus.headline: Grass-dwelling dark brown marked underneath by a straight white bar and metallic-ringed eyespots
Orsotrioena medus.upperwing: Plain dark velvety brown devoid of upperwing eyespots and edged only by thin pale marginal and submarginal hairlines; males carry a black hair-tufted scent fold near the forewing dorsum.
Orsotrioena medus.underwing: Crossed cleanly across both wings by a straight pure white discal bar (narrower in dry season); wet-season adults show 2 forewing and 3 hindwing ocelli (two apical, one isolated tornal) ringed in gleaming silvery-violet, while dry-season morphs turn pale buff with tiny specks.
Orsotrioena medus.similarSpecies: Separated from all Mycalesis bushbrowns by having zero eyespots on the upperwing, a straight stark-white underside band, and exactly 2 forewing plus 3 hindwing ocelli.
Orsotrioena medus.habitat: Damp grassy clearings, paddy margins, marsh edges, and humid forest trails.
Orsotrioena medus.behavior: Flies slowly just above wet grass blades and settles quickly low in vegetation, visiting damp soil and fermenting fruit rather than flowers.
Orsotrioena medus.season: Active year-round in humid habitats, with strongly ocellated wet-season forms peaking June-December.
Orsotrioena medus.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills, humid valleys, and wet coastal or agricultural pockets including Gudalur, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Kanyakumari, and irrigated plains.
Orsotrioena medus.notes: Southern Indian populations represent the nominate subspecies O. m. medus and can thrive around wet rice paddies bordering forests.

Ypthima asterope.headline: Sun-loving dryland ringlet sporting three underside hindwing eyespots and a ringed forewing loop
Ypthima asterope.upperwing: Pale greyish-brown; forewing features a prominent bi-pupilled black subapical ocellus enclosed inside a broad pale-bordered brown ring-loop, while hindwing carries 1-2 small dark postdiscal spots.
Ypthima asterope.underwing: Pale whitish-grey densely dusted with fine brown striae; forewing ocellus sits inside a sharp circular brown loop, and hindwing displays 3 small yellow-ringed ocelli (one apical, two near the tornus) that shrink to tiny dots in dry weather.
Ypthima asterope.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Four-ring (Ypthima huebneri) by having only 3 (not 4) hindwing underside ocelli and a distinct dark circular loop bordering the forewing ocellus underneath.
Ypthima asterope.habitat: Dry open scrublands, fallow fields, rocky grasslands, and sunny foothill paths.
Ypthima asterope.behavior: Weak, jerky flier hugging bare ground and sparse grass tufts, basking flat in hot sun and visiting tiny Tridax and weed blossoms.
Ypthima asterope.season: Found year-round in dry plains and foothills, peaking during October-February.
Ypthima asterope.tnDistribution: Widespread across dry plains and rain-shadow foothills of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Ramanathapuram, Salem, and Chengalpattu.
Ypthima asterope.notes: One of the widest-ranging ringlets globally, extending from Africa across West Asia into India's driest Tamil Nadu thorn scrub.

Ypthima baldus.headline: Woodland ringlet bearing six paired eyespots below and a broad dark brand in males
Ypthima baldus.upperwing: Dark earthy brown; males carry a broad velvety dark scent brand across the forewing disc, while both sexes show a large bi-pupilled yellow-ringed forewing ocellus and 2-4 smaller yellow-ringed hindwing ocelli.
Ypthima baldus.underwing: Pale ochreous-white heavily etched with coarse brown striae and faint discal-submarginal bands; hindwing bears 6 yellow-ringed ocelli arranged in three distinct pairs (two apical, two median, and a fused tornal pair often counted as five rings), shrinking to pinpoint dots in dry season.
Ypthima baldus.similarSpecies: Separated from Southern Baby Five-ring (Ypthima tabella) by slightly larger size and the prominent dark forewing scent brand in males, and from four-ring species by having 6 paired hindwing underside ocelli.
Ypthima baldus.habitat: Moist-to-dry hill forest clearings, grassy trail edges, foothills, and wooded estates.
Ypthima baldus.behavior: Flits with quick hopping wingbeats along sunlit forest verges, nectaring on Tridax, Bidens, and Chromolaena and basking diagonally on low leaves.
Ypthima baldus.season: Common year-round in wooded hills and foothills, with wet-season ocellated broods peaking June-December.
Ypthima baldus.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats hills and foothills of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Palani foothills, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Ypthima baldus.notes: Called the Five-ring despite having six underside hindwing eyespots because the conjoined tornal pair appears as a single bi-pupilled ring.

Ypthima ceylonica.headline: Ubiquitous lawn and scrub ringlet flashing a bright white hindwing patch in flight
Ypthima ceylonica.upperwing: Dark brown forewing bearing one large bi-pupilled yellow-ringed subapical ocellus, paired with a striking pure white posterior half on the hindwing marked by 1-3 small dark submarginal spots. Sexes look closely alike, with females slightly paler.
Ypthima ceylonica.underwing: White finely striated with pale rufous-brown lines; forewing repeats the large bi-pupilled ocellus, while hindwing carries 4 yellow-ringed ocelli (one larger apical and three smaller linear postdiscal-tornal spots, the anal spot often bi-pupilled), reduced in dry forms.
Ypthima ceylonica.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu by the stark white lower half of the hindwing upperwing, separating it immediately from Common Four-ring (Ypthima huebneri) and Common Five-ring (Ypthima baldus).
Ypthima ceylonica.habitat: Urban lawns, road verges, coastal scrub, wetland bunds, cultivated fields, and Ghats foothills.
Ypthima ceylonica.behavior: Low, fluttering grass-dweller active even on overcast days; visits small ground herbs like Tridax procumbens and Phyla nodiflora and rests near turf roots.
Ypthima ceylonica.season: Abundant throughout the year across Tamil Nadu plains and lower hills.
Ypthima ceylonica.tnDistribution: Statewide from Chennai urban parks and coastal scrub to Coimbatore, Madurai, Trichy, Erode, Salem, and Western and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Ypthima ceylonica.notes: TNBS authors Hari Theivaprakasham, Hari Ramanasaran & Appavu Pavendhan documented its first complete immature stages from India and recorded Cynodon dactylon as a larval host plant in the Journal of Threatened Taxa (2021).
sources: Journal of Threatened Taxa #6656 (Ypthima ceylonica life stages)

Ypthima ypthimoides.headline: Dusky dark-undersided endemic ringlet of high southern Western Ghats grasslands
Ypthima ypthimoides.upperwing: Uniform dark smoky brown across both wings; forewing displays a large yellow-ringed bi-pupilled subapical ocellus, while hindwing carries 2-3 small dark yellow-ringed postdiscal ocelli.
Ypthima ypthimoides.underwing: Uniformly dark olive-brown to dusky grey-brown finely speckled with short greyish striae (lacking any stark white background); forewing repeats the bi-pupilled ocellus and hindwing carries 4-5 small neat yellow-ringed ocelli in an even curve, shrinking in dry-season adults.
Ypthima ypthimoides.similarSpecies: Separated cleanly from Nilgiri Four-ring (Ypthima chenu) by its uniformly dark striated brown hindwing underside rather than a bright white hindwing crossed by bold dark bands.
Ypthima ypthimoides.habitat: High-altitude montane grasslands, shola margins, bracken slopes, and marsh edges above 1,400 m.
Ypthima ypthimoides.behavior: Flies slowly over damp mountain tussocks during sunny breaks in mist, basking with open dark wings on grass stalks and visiting alpine wildflowers.
Ypthima ypthimoides.season: Active mostly during March-June and September-December across upper mountain plateaus.
Ypthima ypthimoides.tnDistribution: High-elevation southern Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Palani Hills (Kodaikanal grasslands), Anamalais (Grass Hills), Meghamalai, and upper Nilgiris.
Ypthima ypthimoides.notes: Originally described from the Palani Hills by Frederic Moore in 1881 and strictly endemic to the highest montane grasslands of the southern Western Ghats.

Ypthima chenu.headline: Montane Nilgiri endemic featuring a stark white, bold-banded underside with elongated eyespots
Ypthima chenu.upperwing: Dark sepia-brown; forewing features a prominent bi-pupilled yellow-ringed subapical ocellus and faint subterminal band, while the hindwing carries two small unipupilled submedian ocelli without a tornal spot.
Ypthima chenu.underwing: Forewing dusky grey-brown with posteriorly converging discal and subterminal dark fasciae (the outer band edged white on both sides); hindwing has a stark white ground heavily striated with brown, bold subbasal, discal, and subterminal brown bands, and 4 curved ocelli (one apical, three laterally elongated postdiscal).
Ypthima chenu.similarSpecies: Separated from Palni Four-ring (Ypthima ypthimoides) by the stark white, heavily dark-banded hindwing underside and laterally stretched postdiscal eyespots, and from Nilgiri Jewel Four-ring (Ypthima striata) by larger size and elongated single postdiscal spots.
Ypthima chenu.habitat: High-elevation montane grasslands, shola edges, and grassy road cuts above 1,200 m.
Ypthima chenu.behavior: Bounces low across hillside tussocks when mountain sun breaks through cloud cover, basking flat on bare turf and resting with boldly striped undersides hidden in grass.
Ypthima chenu.season: Peaks during March-May and September-December in upper hill stations.
Ypthima chenu.tnDistribution: High-altitude Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris (Ooty, Avalanche, Mukurthi, Kotagiri) and upper Anamalais.
Ypthima chenu.notes: First described from the Nilgiri Hills in 1843; dry-season individuals show even bolder dark hindwing bands alongside reduced ocelli.

Ypthima huebneri.headline: Plain brown grass ringlet with four curved underside hindwing eyespots and no white dorsal patch
Ypthima huebneri.upperwing: Uniform dull greyish-brown on both wings; forewing displays a large oval yellow-ringed bi-pupilled subapical ocellus and hindwing carries 2-3 small submarginal ocelli, completely lacking any white upperwing patch.
Ypthima huebneri.underwing: Greyish-white finely covered with dense brown striae and a weak pale brown discal shading; forewing repeats the large bi-pupilled ocellus, while hindwing carries 4 yellow-ringed ocelli in a gentle curve (one apical, three postdiscal-tornal with the anal one often bi-pupilled), reduced to dots in dry season.
Ypthima huebneri.similarSpecies: Separated from White Four-ring (Ypthima ceylonica) by lacking the white hindwing patch above, and from Common Three-ring (Ypthima asterope) by having 4 (not 3) hindwing ocelli and no circular brown loop around the forewing ocellus underneath.
Ypthima huebneri.habitat: Open grasslands, scrub edges, wetland margins, gardens, and foothill clearings.
Ypthima huebneri.behavior: Weak, hopping grass flier that stays within half a meter of the ground, visiting small herbaceous flowers and basking on sun-warmed grass blades.
Ypthima huebneri.season: Common year-round across Tamil Nadu, peaking during August-January.
Ypthima huebneri.tnDistribution: Statewide in plains, wetlands, and Western and Eastern Ghats foothills including Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Salem, Erode, and Sirumalai.
Ypthima huebneri.notes: Often flies side-by-side with White Four-ring in Tamil Nadu scrub and grassy margins, making upperwing checks decisive.

Ypthima singala.headline: Delicate foothill ringlet carrying finely striated white hindwings and neat yellow-ringed spots
Ypthima singala.upperwing: Dark greyish-brown; males are plain brown above with a faint or small forewing ocellus and 1-3 tiny hindwing dots, while females show a paler whitish-dusted hindwing submarginal zone framing small dark eyespots.
Ypthima singala.underwing: White cleanly overlaid with fine, even rufous-brown striations lacking heavy dark transverse bands; forewing carries a large oval bi-pupilled yellow-ringed ocellus, while hindwing bears 4-6 small yellow-ringed ocelli (typically a double or paired apical unit and 3-4 neat postdiscal spots in a shallow arc).
Ypthima singala.similarSpecies: Separated from Nilgiri Jewel Four-ring (Ypthima striata) by finer, more uniform underside striations lacking bold dark brown transverse bands anchoring the hindwing spots, and from White Four-ring by lacking a solid stark white hindwing patch above in males.
Ypthima singala.habitat: Dry-to-moist foothill grasslands, open hill savannas, and scrubby forest clearings.
Ypthima singala.behavior: Weak, low-skimming grass flier that weaves neatly among rocky hillside grass tufts and feeds on small composite blooms.
Ypthima singala.season: Uncommon and localized; most records fall between July and January.
Ypthima singala.tnDistribution: Foothills and mid-elevation slopes across southern Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Amaravathi-Chinnar slopes, Palani foothills, Sirumalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kolli Hills.
Ypthima singala.notes: Shared between Sri Lanka and peninsular southern India; historically confused with Y. striata and Y. avanta complexes until genital and striation characters clarified regional records.

Ypthima striata.headline: Endemic montane ringlet marked beneath by sharp dark striations and banded hindwing eyespots
Ypthima striata.upperwing: Dark brown on both wings; forewing displays a distinct bright yellow-ringed bi-pupilled subapical ocellus and hindwing carries 2-3 small yellow-ringed ocelli. Males have an indistinct scent patch on the forewing disc.
Ypthima striata.underwing: Stark white boldly etched with coarse dark brown striae and three prominent brown transverse fasciae (subbasal, discal, subterminal); hindwing displays a double apical ocellus on a short dark bar and three linear postdiscal-tornal ocelli (the innermost bi-pupilled) seated neatly atop a shared brown band.
Ypthima striata.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Small Jewel Four-ring (Ypthima singala) by coarser dark striations and distinct brown bands running directly across the hindwing eyespots, and from Nilgiri Four-ring (Ypthima chenu) by smaller size and rounded linear tornal ocelli.
Ypthima striata.habitat: Mid-to-high elevation Western Ghats grasslands, grassy hill slopes, and open forest borders.
Ypthima striata.behavior: Hops briskly low over open hillside grass in bright sun, pausing briefly on dry stalks and rocks with closed striated undersides.
Ypthima striata.season: Localized and seasonal, recorded primarily from August to December and March-May.
Ypthima striata.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Agasthyamalai-Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Ypthima striata.notes: Endemic to the southern Western Ghats and originally described from the Nilgiris; also called the Striated Five-ring in classical Indian literature.

Ypthima tabella.headline: Tiny Western Ghats grass ringlet separated from Common Five-ring by lacking a male brand
Ypthima tabella.upperwing: Small, delicate greyish-brown butterfly; forewing carries one crisp yellow-ringed bi-pupilled subapical ocellus and hindwing shows 2-3 small submarginal ocelli. Crucially, males lack the dark velvety forewing scent brand.
Ypthima tabella.underwing: Pale ochreous-grey finely covered in brown striations and faint discal shading; forewing has one large subapical ocellus and hindwing carries 6 small ocelli arranged cleanly in three pairs (two apical, two median, and a fused tornal pair), reduced to tiny dots in dry-season forms.
Ypthima tabella.similarSpecies: Closely mimics Common Five-ring (Ypthima baldus), but reliably separated by its noticeably smaller wingspan, paler ground tone, and complete absence of a male forewing scent brand.
Ypthima tabella.habitat: Shaded grassy forest clearings, bamboo-edge turf, and moist Western Ghats stream banks.
Ypthima tabella.behavior: Flutters weakly inches above damp forest grass and weed borders, disappearing quickly into low herb tangles when disturbed.
Ypthima tabella.season: Recorded mainly during June-December monsoon and post-monsoon months, with dry forms lingering to March.
Ypthima tabella.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forests and foothills of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Gudalur, Siruvani, Anamalais, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Ypthima tabella.notes: Endemic to the Western Ghats and long treated as a southern subspecies of Ypthima philomela before being recognized as a distinct species.

Acraea terpsicore.headline: Slender brick-orange butterfly of sunlit lawns and grasslands
Acraea terpsicore.upperwing: Narrow brick-orange wings dotted with neat black spots and bordered by a black hindwing margin spotted in white.
Acraea terpsicore.underwing: Paler orange-pink with glossy white marginal spots inside a black border on the hindwing.
Acraea terpsicore.similarSpecies: Elongated wings, black-and-white spotted hindwing margin, and long narrow abdomen distinguish it from leopards and fritillaries.
Acraea terpsicore.habitat: Sunny lawns, open fields, dry scrub, roadsides, and fallow gardens.
Acraea terpsicore.behavior: Weak, low leisurely flight; settles openly on grass blades and Tridax flowers.
Acraea terpsicore.tnDistribution: Common across Tamil Nadu plains, coasts, and open hills.
Acraea terpsicore.notes: Oozes bitter yellow defensive fluid when disturbed; females carry a leathery mating plug (sphragis) after pairing.

Cethosia mahratta.headline: Endemic serrated-wing beauty of Western Ghats wet forests
Cethosia mahratta.upperwing: Vivid fiery orange-red enclosed by heavily scalloped black borders and white subapical bands; females are duskier.
Cethosia mahratta.underwing: Spectacular mosaic of brick-red, white, black, and pale blue bands edged with delicate zigzags.
Cethosia mahratta.similarSpecies: Deeply scalloped wing edges and intricate multi-coloured lace-like underside make Tamil Lacewing unmistakable.
Cethosia mahratta.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, bamboo brakes, and hill streams.
Cethosia mahratta.behavior: Flutters gracefully through forest clearings and visits Mussaenda and Lantana blossoms.
Cethosia mahratta.season: Peak sightings from July to January.
Cethosia mahratta.tnDistribution: Western Ghats stretches of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Tirunelveli hills.
Cethosia mahratta.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Cethosia mahratta.notes: Endemic peninsular subspecies whose gregarious black-and-red spiny caterpillars sequester distasteful compounds from Adenia vines.

Argynnis hybrida.headline: High-elevation Nilgiri fritillary with dimorphic Plain Tiger-mimicking females
Argynnis hybrida.upperwing: Males are rich golden-orange patterned with rounded black discal spots, black cell bars, checkered dark outer borders, and slightly thickened dark veins along the forewing; females are paler golden-yellow washed olive-green at the base with a darkened forewing apex crossed by an oblique white band mimicking Plain Tiger.
Argynnis hybrida.underwing: Forewings are soft pinkish-orange spotted in black with greenish-ochre tips; hindwings are mottled olive-green and pale buff adorned with crisp black-edged silvery-white spots and silvery marginal crescents.
Argynnis hybrida.similarSpecies: Separated from Palni Fritillary (Argynnis castetsi) by the female's distinct black-and-white mimetic forewing apex (usually reduced or absent in castetsi) and its range north of the Palghat Gap; much larger with silver-spotted hindwing undersides than Phalanta leopards.
Argynnis hybrida.habitat: High-elevation montane shola edges, grassy downs, stream valleys, and hill gardens above 1,400 m.
Argynnis hybrida.behavior: Strong, sweeping flier across open grassy hilltops; males patrol sunlit downs while females visit Asteraceae and Lantana blooms low to the ground.
Argynnis hybrida.season: Recorded year-round in the Nilgiris with peaks during warmer post-monsoon and pre-monsoon clear spells (March-May and October-December).
Argynnis hybrida.tnDistribution: Restricted to higher Nilgiri elevations in Tamil Nadu, including Ooty, Mukurthi National Park, Doddabetta, Avalanche, and Upper Bhavani.
Argynnis hybrida.notes: Named by Evans (1912) from the Nilgiris for its intermediate female mimicry traits; females retain Batesian mimicry of the Plain Tiger (Danaus chrysippus) across open montane grasslands.

Argynnis castetsi.headline: Endemic Palni Hills shola fritillary with non-mimetic orange females
Argynnis castetsi.upperwing: Rich tawny-orange thickly marked with rounded black spots, sinuous submarginal lines, and dark borders; unlike northern Indian Fritillary populations, females lack a darkened white-banded forewing apex and look nearly identical to males, occasionally showing only a faint pale subapical trace.
Argynnis castetsi.underwing: Pale pinkish-amber across the forewing disc shading into olive-ochre at the tip, paired with a mossy olive-buff hindwing marbled with bold silvery-white dark-rimmed spots and silvery marginal lunules.
Argynnis castetsi.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Indian/Nilgiri Fritillary (Argynnis hybrida) by non-mimetic orange-toned females lacking a stark black-and-white forewing tip and its strict distribution south of the Palghat Gap; far larger with silvery hindwing spots underneath than Phalanta leopards.
Argynnis castetsi.habitat: Montane shola-grassland mosaics, grassy hill slopes, and damp forest clearings above 1,500 m.
Argynnis castetsi.behavior: Flies rapidly and low over montane grasses, pausing on wild bramble, Strobilanthes, and daisy-like shola flowers in bright sun.
Argynnis castetsi.season: Most frequently seen during dry sunny intervals from February to May and September to December.
Argynnis castetsi.tnDistribution: Endemic to Western Ghats ranges south of the Palghat Gap, notably Kodaikanal and the Palni Hills, Anamalai Grass Hills, and Meghamalai.
Argynnis castetsi.notes: Described by Oberthur (1891) from the Palni Hills; its loss of female Plain Tiger mimicry south of the Palghat Gap makes it a classic study species in Western Ghats biogeography.

Phalanta alcippe.headline: Shaded evergreen stream leopard smaller and darker-bordered than Common Leopard
Phalanta alcippe.upperwing: Warm golden-tawny with black wavy cell bars, scattered dark discal spots, and noticeably broader black outer margins on the forewing than Common Leopard; sexes are alike though females tend to be slightly paler.
Phalanta alcippe.underwing: Glossy warm yellow-ochre washed in delicate lilac sheen with a paler postdiscal band and clear dark-ringed marginal spots across both wings.
Phalanta alcippe.similarSpecies: Smaller and more compact-winged than Common Leopard (Phalanta phalantha), with heavier black outer forewing borders, brighter yellowish underside, and strict restriction to wet evergreen forests rather than dry scrub.
Phalanta alcippe.habitat: Shaded wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, stream corridors, and damp jungle clearings.
Phalanta alcippe.behavior: Agile, darting flier that stays close to shaded forest streams; males mud-puddle persistently on wet gravel and sandbars while both sexes sun briefly on streamside foliage.
Phalanta alcippe.season: Peak activity post-monsoon from September to January, with smaller numbers year-round in wet ghats.
Phalanta alcippe.tnDistribution: Localized in wet Western Ghats tracts of Tamil Nadu, including Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kanyakumari, Anamalai, and Siruvani hills.
Phalanta alcippe.notes: Represented in South India by the Sahyadri subspecies Phalanta alcippe mercea; far more forest-dependent and localized than the ubiquitous Common Leopard.

Phalanta phalantha.headline: Bright orange leopard-spotted butterfly common in gardens and foothills
Phalanta phalantha.upperwing: Bright golden-orange thickly scattered with neat rows of rounded black spots and wavy marginal lines.
Phalanta phalantha.underwing: Glossy tawny-yellow washed with lilac sheen and delicate dark rings.
Phalanta phalantha.similarSpecies: More elongated forewings and crisp violet-tinted underside sheen separate it from Small Leopard (Phalanta alcippe) and Rustic.
Phalanta phalantha.habitat: Gardens, dry deciduous foothills, scrub, forest roads, and parks.
Phalanta phalantha.behavior: Brisk, darting flight; suns briefly on shrubs with flatly spread wings and sips flower nectar constantly.
Phalanta phalantha.tnDistribution: Widespread statewide from urban parks to hills.
Phalanta phalantha.notes: Thrives around both urban willow/Flacourtia hedges and forest paths, often joining mud-puddling assemblages.

Vindula erota.headline: Large tailed orange-and-olive brush-footed butterfly of hill streams
Vindula erota.upperwing: Males are bright golden-orange; females are dramatically larger, dark olive-brown crossed by a wide white median band.
Vindula erota.underwing: Ochre-orange in males or brownish-white in females with subtle violet wash and twin hindwing eyespots.
Vindula erota.similarSpecies: Short pointed hindwing tails and larger size cleanly separate Cruiser males from Tamil Yeoman.
Vindula erota.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen hill forests, especially along sunlit forest streams.
Vindula erota.behavior: Males puddle eagerly along damp forest tracks and stream pebbles; females patrol canopy clearings.
Vindula erota.season: Year-round in Western Ghats hills, peaking post-monsoon.
Vindula erota.tnDistribution: Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Palani Hills, and southern Western Ghats.
Vindula erota.notes: Sexual dimorphism is so pronounced that early collectors described bright orange males and olive-green females separately.

Cirrochroa thais.headline: Tamil Nadu’s official State Butterfly (தமிழ் மறவன்)
Cirrochroa thais.upperwing: Warm bright orange crossed by fine dark wavy lines, dark forewing apex, and narrow black wing borders.
Cirrochroa thais.underwing: Paler ochre-orange with a prominent silvery-white median band (more pronounced in dry-season forms) bordered by dark brown lines.
Cirrochroa thais.similarSpecies: Looks superficially like the Cruiser (Vindula erota) male or Rustic (Cupha erymanthis), but lacks prominent yellow patches or hindwing tails and shows the crisp pale underside band.
Cirrochroa thais.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded streams, and shaded forest trails.
Cirrochroa thais.behavior: Strong, rapid flight along forest paths; puddles on damp sand and nectar-feeds in sunny clearings.
Cirrochroa thais.season: Recorded throughout the year, especially abundant post-monsoon across Western Ghats slopes.
Cirrochroa thais.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Palani Hills.
Cirrochroa thais.notes: Officially declared the State Butterfly of Tamil Nadu in June 2019, Tamil Nadu became the fifth state in India to name a state butterfly.

Cupha erymanthis.headline: Bright yellow-banded woodland nymphalid common along forested hill streams
Cupha erymanthis.upperwing: Warm ochre-brown crossed by a broad curved pale golden-yellow forewing median band enclosing black spots, set off by a broad black forewing apex and fine wavy marginal lines; sexes look similar.
Cupha erymanthis.underwing: Pale tawny-buff with a cream-yellow forewing median band, narrow dark transverse discal lines, and a continuous row of small dark-centered postdiscal spots.
Cupha erymanthis.similarSpecies: Immediately told apart from Tamil Yeoman (Cirrochroa thais) and Common Leopard (Phalanta phalantha) by its broad pale yellow forewing band enclosed by a bold black wingtip.
Cupha erymanthis.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forests, wooded hill streams, coffee estates, and Eastern Ghats shola-fringe valleys.
Cupha erymanthis.behavior: Active, jerky flyer patrolling sunlit forest edges and stream trails; feeds eagerly at Lantana, Chromolaena, and wild Ixora, and males gather at damp sand.
Cupha erymanthis.season: Recorded year-round in hill ranges, surging strongly from August to December.
Cupha erymanthis.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western Ghats (Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, KMTR) and Eastern Ghats hill complexes including Pachamalai, Kolli, and Shervarayan hills.
Cupha erymanthis.notes: Represented in peninsular India by Cupha erymanthis maja; its bright yellow forewing band flashes distinctly during rapid zig-zag flights along forest paths.

Moduza procris.headline: Rusty-orange woodland butterfly with a bold white cross-band
Moduza procris.upperwing: Rich brick-red and dark brown wings bisected across both wings by a striking clean white macular band.
Moduza procris.underwing: Pale greenish-grey base shading into warm rusty orange beyond the crisp white central band.
Moduza procris.similarSpecies: Bright brick-red upperwing ground combined with the bold white diagonal band makes Commander unmistakable.
Moduza procris.habitat: Forest stream banks, wooded foothills, damp trails, and riparian gardens.
Moduza procris.behavior: Glides smoothly over bushes, perches with wings spread flat on sunlit leaves, and paddles at damp sand.
Moduza procris.season: Common year-round in forested districts and foothills.
Moduza procris.tnDistribution: Western & Eastern Ghats foothills, Mudumalai, Pachamalai, Kovai Kutralam, and riverine green belts.
Moduza procris.notes: Caterpillars tie leaf frass chains onto midribs of Mitragyna saplings to deter crawling predators.

Athyma perius.headline: Boldly black-and-white sergeant marked by black dots inside hindwing spots
Athyma perius.upperwing: Velvety blackish-brown with crisp snow-white bands; the forewing white cell streak is cleanly divided into four segments ending in an arrowhead-shaped outer piece, and the hindwing postdiscal white spots each enclose a neat black inner dot; sexes share the same pattern.
Athyma perius.underwing: Rich golden-ochre ground colour bearing the dorsal white bands boldly outlined in crisp black, retaining the diagnostic black dots inside each white hindwing postdiscal spot.
Athyma perius.similarSpecies: Separated from all other Tamil Nadu sergeants and sailers by the four-part forewing cell streak, black-dotted white postdiscal hindwing spots, and bright golden-ochre black-outlined underside.
Athyma perius.habitat: Open forest clearings, scrub-bordered hills, woodland trails, and foothill gardens.
Athyma perius.behavior: Alternates brisk stiff-winged glides with quick flaps; perches conspicuously with flat-spread wings on exposed sunlit twigs and visits damp soil.
Athyma perius.season: Common year-round in hill forests and foothills, peaking October to February.
Athyma perius.tnDistribution: Widespread in Western and Eastern Ghats foothills and mid-elevations across Mudumalai, Nilgiris, Anamalai, Pachamalai, Yercaud, and Kolli Hills.
Athyma perius.notes: Unlike strongly dimorphic sergeants such as Staff and Colour Sergeants, both sexes share virtually the same crisp black-and-white livery, females showing a double row of lateral black dots on the abdomen.

Athyma ranga.headline: Uncommon wet-forest sergeant with white discal bands cut by black veins
Athyma ranga.upperwing: Smoky black-brown (glossed faintly metallic blue in fresh males) lacking a solid white forewing cell streak, instead showing faint greyish cell smudges and broad white discal bands conspicuously divided by thick black veins; females carry broader white patches.
Athyma ranga.underwing: Smoky olive-brown with diffuse greyish-white discal patches crossed by dark veins, bluish-grey cell streaks, and narrow pale submarginal lunules.
Athyma ranga.similarSpecies: Distinct from Common Sergeant (Athyma perius) and Staff Sergeant (Athyma selenophora) by lacking a clean white or red-tinged forewing cell streak and having broad white discal patches heavily veined in black.
Athyma ranga.habitat: Wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded ravines, and shaded stream corridors.
Athyma ranga.behavior: Fast canopy and mid-story glider that descends to wet forest tracks for mineral puddling and rests flat on overhanging tree leaves.
Athyma ranga.season: Scarce and seasonal, encountered mainly from September to January and April to June.
Athyma ranga.tnDistribution: Uncommon resident of Western Ghats hill forests in Tamil Nadu, recorded from Nilgiris, Anamalai, Valparai, Siruvani, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Athyma ranga.notes: Represented in southern India by the scarce Western Ghats race Athyma ranga karwara; closely tied to intact Oleaceae host trees in moist forest tracts.

Athyma selenophora.headline: Velvet-black and chestnut-underwinged sergeant with sailer-mimicking females
Athyma selenophora.upperwing: Strongly dimorphic: males are velvety jet-black with a divided reddish-ochre to dull white forewing cell streak and a crisp white postdiscal band across both wings; females are larger dark brown with a clean white cell streak and double white bands mimicking Neptis sailers.
Athyma selenophora.underwing: Males show a vivid bright chestnut-red ground crossed by wide white bands and a pale bluish-grey inner hindwing margin; females are duller ferruginous-brown with crisp double white bands.
Athyma selenophora.similarSpecies: Males are unmistakable for their deep chestnut-red underside and jet-black upperside with divided forewing cell streak; females mimic large Neptis sailers but have a heavier body and the divided cell streak characteristic of Athyma.
Athyma selenophora.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, bamboo-lined stream valleys, and forest clearings.
Athyma selenophora.behavior: Rapid, powerful flyer patrolling sunlit stream openings; males puddle eagerly on wet sand and animal droppings while females keep closer to canopy foliage.
Athyma selenophora.season: Recorded most reliably post-monsoon (September to February) with scattered summer sightings.
Athyma selenophora.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill forests of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Palani foothills, and Tirunelveli hills.
Athyma selenophora.notes: South Indian populations belong to Athyma selenophora kanara; females exhibit classic mimicry of distasteful Neptis sailers in flight.

Athyma inara.headline: Dramatically dimorphic sergeant pairing black-and-white males with orange females
Athyma inara.upperwing: Strikingly dimorphic: males are velvety black with a crisp white central band across both wings, bright orange forewing apical patches, and broken ochre-white cell spots; females are blackish-brown crossed by broad vivid golden-orange bands.
Athyma inara.underwing: Males are rich rufous-brown repeating the white central band and orange apical flush; females are warm ochre-yellow with paler creamy-orange bands framed by dark brown discal blotches.
Athyma inara.similarSpecies: Males differ from all other Tamil Nadu sergeants by pairing a white central band with bright orange forewing tips; orange-banded females could be confused with lascars (Pantoporia) or Yellow Jack Sailer (Lasippa viraja), but are larger with stout Athyma bodies and divided cell markings.
Athyma inara.habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous hill forests along shaded streams and forest edges.
Athyma inara.behavior: Strong, swift flier that perches high on sunny canopy leaves with open wings and visits wet sandbanks and flower clusters along streams.
Athyma inara.season: Most regular between August and January, especially along hill streams after rains.
Athyma inara.tnDistribution: Localized in Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu, including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Athyma inara.notes: Often treated historically as Athyma nefte inara; its extreme sexual dichromatism makes male and female appear like two unrelated butterfly species in the field.

Pantoporia hordonia.headline: Dainty orange-banded forest-edge lascar with continuous grey marginal lines
Pantoporia hordonia.upperwing: Dark brownish-black crossed by bright orange bands; the indented orange forewing cell streak merges smoothly into the upper discal band, and the outer margin bears a continuous pale grey submarginal line broader than the fine orange line outside it.
Pantoporia hordonia.underwing: Pale creamy-yellow with fine dark brown band edges and pearly sheen in wet-season morphs, shifting to clouded ochre-brown with blurred markings in dry-season broods.
Pantoporia hordonia.similarSpecies: Very close to Extra Lascar (Pantoporia sandaka), from which it is separated by the continuous, broader grey forewing submarginal line (versus broken grey dots in sandaka), unnotched upper cell-bar edge, and absence of a shiny pale hindwing speculum in males.
Pantoporia hordonia.habitat: Forest clearings, scrubby foothills, secondary growth, bamboo thickets, and garden fringes.
Pantoporia hordonia.behavior: Flutters swiftly near scrub canopies with short sailing glides, basking flat on sunlit bushes and probing Lantana and Chromolaena blossoms.
Pantoporia hordonia.season: Common year-round, with peak numbers from August to January and drier seasonal morphs emerging January to April.
Pantoporia hordonia.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western and Eastern Ghats foothills and wooded plains, including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Pachamalai, Kolli, and Javadi hills.
Pantoporia hordonia.notes: Dry-season P. hordonia morphs develop expanded orange upperwing bands and clouded undersides that can closely resemble wet-season P. sandaka.

Pantoporia sandaka.headline: Elusive wet-forest lascar separated by beaded grey submarginal spots
Pantoporia sandaka.upperwing: Deep blackish-brown patterned in rich golden-orange; the forewing cell streak carries a distinct upper notch, and the outer orange submarginal line is bolder than the inner grey line, which breaks into bead-like pale dots; males bear a glossy whitish hindwing costal speculum.
Pantoporia sandaka.underwing: Warm pale ochre-yellow with crisp dark-outlined bands and fine submarginal lines, darkening subtly with softer edges in dry-season individuals.
Pantoporia sandaka.similarSpecies: Very similar to Common Lascar (Pantoporia hordonia), but distinguished by the narrower, bead-broken grey forewing submarginal line, notched cell streak, and the male's pearly costal speculum on the dorsal hindwing.
Pantoporia sandaka.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded forest streams, and bamboo-rich valleys.
Pantoporia sandaka.behavior: Patrols mid-height sunlit openings along forest trails with rapid wingbeats and stiff glides; males occasionally settle on damp sandbars and wet stones.
Pantoporia sandaka.season: Seen mainly between September and March, overlapping with Common Lascar after monsoon rains.
Pantoporia sandaka.tnDistribution: Uncommon resident of Tamil Nadu's Western Ghats forests, recorded from Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Tirunelveli hills.
Pantoporia sandaka.notes: Represented in peninsular India by Pantoporia sandaka davidsoni; frequently overlooked in field surveys due to its close similarity to Common Lascar.

Lasippa viraja.headline: Golden-banded forest glider sailing over Western Ghats stream canopies
Lasippa viraja.upperwing: Velvety dark brown boldly banded in bright golden-orange; features an unbroken broad forewing cell streak extending well beyond the cell, wide oblique forewing spots, and two broad orange-yellow bands across the hindwing (wider in females).
Lasippa viraja.underwing: Paler warm orange-yellow with soft cream-tinted bands lightly edged in dusky brown, lacking heavy black borders.
Lasippa viraja.similarSpecies: Much larger with brighter, broader golden-orange bands and an unbroken elongated cell streak than Pantoporia lascars; separated from female Colour Sergeant (Athyma inara) by its slender sailer body and single continuous cell streak.
