Lasippa viraja.habitat: Wet evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous hill forests with cane and bamboo understory.
Lasippa viraja.behavior: Sails effortlessly at mid-canopy height over forest paths and hilltops; males perch territorially on sunny projecting leaves and visit damp creek edges.
Lasippa viraja.season: Most frequently recorded from October to February and May to July across Western Ghats slopes.
Lasippa viraja.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai Tiger Reserve, Siruvani, Anamalai, Valparai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Lasippa viraja.notes: South Indian race Lasippa viraja kanara; highlighted among forest canopy species during Mudumalai Tiger Reserve butterfly census surveys.

Neptis hylas.headline: Graceful black-and-white glider of scrub, gardens, and forest trails
Neptis hylas.upperwing: Velvety black boldly striped with clean white bands and a distinct white hockey-stick streak inside the forewing cell.
Neptis hylas.underwing: Warm golden-ochre underside with white bands sharply outlined in crisp fine black lines.
Neptis hylas.similarSpecies: Golden-ochre underside with crisp black outlines around the white bands distinguishes Common Sailer from Sullied and Short-banded Sailers.
Neptis hylas.habitat: Forest paths, village hedges, gardens, foothills, and open scrub.
Neptis hylas.behavior: Characteristic stiff-winged sailing glide alternated with quick shallow wingbeats.
Neptis hylas.tnDistribution: Found across every district in Tamil Nadu from coast to hills.
Neptis hylas.notes: Glides effortlessly on flat wings with intermittent shallow flicks, thriving across cities and hill forests alike.

Neptis jumbah.headline: Large woodland sailer distinguished by chestnut streaks and spots beneath
Neptis jumbah.upperwing: Deep velvety black marked with bluish-white bands; the narrow forewing cell streak is separated from a short triangular spot beyond the cell, while the hindwing bears a crisp white discal band and narrow pale submarginal crescents.
Neptis jumbah.underwing: Warm pale buff streaked boldly with rich chestnut-brown and marked by a prominent curved row of large dark chestnut discal spots on the hindwing.
Neptis jumbah.similarSpecies: Larger than Common Sailer (Neptis hylas) and separated from Short-banded Sailer (Phaedyma columella) by its narrower hindwing white band reaching closer to the margin, separated forewing cell streak and outer spot, and bold dark chestnut spots on the underside.
Neptis jumbah.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forest edges, wooded stream valleys, cashew groves, and shady rural gardens.
Neptis jumbah.behavior: Sails higher and more strongly than Common Sailer, circling tree crowns and gliding down to sunlit shrubs, damp paths, and flowering trees.
Neptis jumbah.season: Active throughout much of the year, peaking from September to January.
Neptis jumbah.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western Ghats foothills and moist hills (Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, KMTR) as well as Eastern Ghats hills like Pachamalai and Kolli Hills.
Neptis jumbah.notes: Peninsular race Neptis jumbah nalanda; named for the rich chestnut streaks and spots adorning its underwings.

Neptis clinia.headline: Rare evergreen-forest sailer with rufous underwings and tight cell spots
Neptis clinia.upperwing: Dark black-brown with narrow, slightly dusky white markings; the forewing cell streak and the triangular spot just beyond it sit closely together or nearly touch, and the hindwing white discal band is broken into well-separated spots along the veins.
Neptis clinia.underwing: Deep warm rufous-brown to dark ferruginous with clean white bands lacking black outlines, the forewing cell streak and adjacent spot often conjoined beneath.
Neptis clinia.similarSpecies: Closely resembles Common Sailer (Neptis hylas) and Clear Sailer (Neptis nata hampsoni), but lacks N. hylas's crisp black-outlined golden-ochre underside and shows darker ferruginous underwings with narrowly separated hindwing discal spots.
Neptis clinia.habitat: Shaded wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, stream ravines, and dense canopy openings.
Neptis clinia.behavior: Flies and glides low along shaded forest trails and stream gullies, resting briefly with outstretched wings on damp rocks and understory shrubs.
Neptis clinia.season: Scarce and localized, recorded mainly from September to January and during light summer showers.
Neptis clinia.tnDistribution: Rare Western Ghats forest specialist in Tamil Nadu, recorded from Nilgiris, Anamalai, and Tirunelveli-Kanyakumari wet hill tracts.
Neptis clinia.notes: Represented in southern India by the endemic Sahyadri race Neptis clinia kallaura; careful inspection of the forewing cell streak and underside vein spacing separates it from N. nata.

Neptis nata hampsoni.headline: Montane evergreen sailer with a sharply pointed spot beyond the forewing cell
Neptis nata hampsoni.upperwing: Deep purpurescent-black marked with crisp, sharply edged white bands; the forewing cell streak is bluntly truncate at its tip and cleanly separated from a conspicuously elongated, sharply pointed spot beyond the cell.
Neptis nata hampsoni.underwing: Dusky olive-purplish brown in dry-season morphs to warm reddish-brown in wet-season broods, with bright white bands edged gently in darker brown rather than crisp black lines.
Neptis nata hampsoni.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Common Sailer (Neptis hylas) by the sharply elongated pointed spot beyond the forewing cell and darker purplish-olive underside without black outlines; separated from Sullied Sailer (Neptis clinia) by the cleanly separated, pointed post-cell spot.
Neptis nata hampsoni.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation evergreen and shola forests, shaded hill streams, and moist bamboo clearings.
Neptis nata hampsoni.behavior: Glides steadily along sunny forest corridors and stream clearings, pausing to bask with flat wings on Trema and Strobilanthes foliage.
Neptis nata hampsoni.season: Recorded mostly from October to March and May to August in wet hill ranges.
Neptis nata hampsoni.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including the Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Palani Hills.
Neptis nata hampsoni.notes: Neptis nata hampsoni is the South Indian subspecies described from the Nilgiris; field identification requires close views of the elongated post-cellular spot and underside tone.
sources: Butterflies of India, Neptis nata hampsoni

Neptis palnica.headline: Endemic Western Ghats sailer awaiting validated Tamil Nadu sightings
Neptis palnica.upperwing: Black with creamy-white bands; forewing cell streak is broken into basal streak and detached triangular spot.
Neptis palnica.underwing: Deep warm chestnut-brown marked with creamy white bands.
Neptis palnica.similarSpecies: Separated from Sullied Sailer by creamier underside bands and warm reddish-brown underside ground.
Neptis palnica.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation evergreen and shola forests in the Western Ghats.
Neptis palnica.behavior: Glides smoothly along sunlit shola clearings.
Neptis palnica.season: Recorded seasonally in Palani and high Western Ghats ranges.
Neptis palnica.tnDistribution: Listed among the 4 checklist species awaiting validated TNBS photographic confirmation in Tamil Nadu.
Neptis palnica.notes: TNBS encourages field naturalists in the Palani and Western Ghats hills to submit dated photographic records for state validation.

Phaedyma columella.headline: Heavy-bodied woodland sailer marked by a short broad hindwing white band
Phaedyma columella.upperwing: Charcoal-black with broad pure white markings; the forewing carries a short narrow cell streak followed by a large detached spot, an elongated basal white streak in space 1a, and a broad hindwing white band stopping short of the costal border.
Phaedyma columella.underwing: Rich golden-ferruginous brown echoing the broad white dorsal bands, bordered outwardly by diffuse pale submarginal lunules and dark marginal dots.
Phaedyma columella.similarSpecies: Larger and heavier-winged than Common Sailer (Neptis hylas), and told from Chestnut-streaked Sailer (Neptis jumbah) by the broad, abruptly shortened white hindwing band, very narrow forewing cell streak, and absence of dark chestnut discal spots underneath.
Phaedyma columella.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded foothills, shaded streams, and orchard edges.
Phaedyma columella.behavior: Powerful, deliberate glider sailing along canopy margins and descending to mud-puddle on wet paths or feed on Lantana and sap drips.
Phaedyma columella.season: Recorded across most months in hill forests, peaking post-monsoon from October to January.
Phaedyma columella.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills and hills (Kovai Kutralam, Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, KMTR) plus wooded Eastern Ghats hills.
Phaedyma columella.notes: Documented on Coimbatore nature walks at Kovai Kutralam; structurally separated from Neptis by hindwing vein 8 ending on the outer margin below the apex.

Parthenos sylvia.headline: Magnificent large emerald-and-pearl glider of Tamil Nadu hill forests
Parthenos sylvia.upperwing: Velvety olive-emerald wings crossed by translucent pearly-white forewing spots and bold dark tiger-like stripes.
Parthenos sylvia.underwing: Paler bluish-green echoing the translucent forewing window spots.
Parthenos sylvia.similarSpecies: Huge wingspan, translucent pearly forewing squares, and sweeping gliding flight make Clipper unique.
Parthenos sylvia.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, wooded waterfalls, and hill streams.
Parthenos sylvia.behavior: Powerful, soaring glider that perches high with wings spread flat and visits Mussaenda and Lantana.
Parthenos sylvia.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Kovai Kutralam, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Valparai, and Tirunelveli.
Parthenos sylvia.notes: Subspecies Parthenos sylvia virens patrols riparian corridors and roosts beneath high riverside branches at dusk.

Euthalia aconthea.headline: Mango-feeding woodland butterfly with cryptic olive-brown upperwings
Euthalia aconthea.upperwing: Muted olive-brown wings etched with fine black cell loops and pale white spots (larger in females).
Euthalia aconthea.underwing: Warm ochre-brown matching dry mango bark and soil when settled.
Euthalia aconthea.similarSpecies: Separated from Baronet by dull olive-brown ground colour and from Redspot Duke by lacking bright crimson base spots.
Euthalia aconthea.habitat: Mango groves, home gardens, deciduous forests, and urban parks.
Euthalia aconthea.behavior: Fast buzzing flight close to the ground; basks with wings spread flat on sunlit paths and feeds eagerly on fallen mangoes.
Euthalia aconthea.season: Abundant year-round, especially during mango fruiting season.
Euthalia aconthea.tnDistribution: Common statewide wherever mango or cashew trees grow.
Euthalia aconthea.notes: Cryptic spiny green caterpillars blend almost invisibly along the central vein of mango leaves.

Euthalia lubentina.headline: Iridescent olive-green canopy baron spotted in vivid crimson and white
Euthalia lubentina.upperwing: Dark iridescent olive-green; males show crimson forewing cell bars, small white discal spots, and black-rimmed crimson spots on the hindwing; females are larger and duller with a bold oblique black-edged white forewing band and a bluish-green outer flush on the hindwing.
Euthalia lubentina.underwing: Dark purplish-ochre brown with bright crimson basal costal streaks and crisp red spots in both sexes, females displaying a broad pale greenish-blue wash across the hindwing tornus.
Euthalia lubentina.similarSpecies: Crimson cell bars and red hindwing spots distinguish it immediately from Common Baron (Euthalia aconthea) and Grey Count (Tanaecia lepidea); far smaller than Redspot Duke (Dophla evelina) and with crimson postdiscal hindwing spots instead of basal rings.
Euthalia lubentina.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forests, wooded hill gardens, orchard edges, and tree canopies hosting parasitic mistletoes.
Euthalia lubentina.behavior: Rapid, powerful flight high around tree canopies; drops down to feed on overripe fruits, tree sap, and damp tracks, basking flat on sunlit leaves.
Euthalia lubentina.season: Most noticeable from August to January, though present year-round near mistletoe-laden trees.
Euthalia lubentina.tnDistribution: Scattered across Western Ghats foothills and hills (Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, KMTR) as well as wooded Eastern Ghats hills and green corridors.
Euthalia lubentina.notes: South Indian race Euthalia lubentina arasada; caterpillars feed exclusively on woody Loranthaceae mistletoes growing on forest and orchard trees, camouflaged with long feathery lateral spines.

Symphaedra nais.headline: Tawny-orange dry-forest nymphalid flashing a brick-red white-banded underside
Symphaedra nais.upperwing: Bright tawny-orange framed by heavy black borders and crossed by bold black cell bars, black discal blotches, and a curved row of rounded black spots on the hindwing; sexes share similar patterns with slightly larger paler females.
Symphaedra nais.underwing: Rich brick-red to dark ochraceous-red, starkly patterned on the forewing with black-outlined crimson cell spots and a broad oblique creamy-white discal band edged in black.
Symphaedra nais.similarSpecies: Unmistakable among Tamil Nadu Limenitidinae by its vivid tawny-orange and black-spotted upperside paired with a brick-red, white-banded underside; unlike dull brown Common Baron (Euthalia aconthea).
Symphaedra nais.habitat: Dry deciduous forests, thorny scrub jungles, open woodlands, savannah foothills, and forest roads.
Symphaedra nais.behavior: Skims briskly just above bare soil and dry leaf litter, settling flat with wings pressed wide to bask on sunlit dirt tracks and fallen fruits.
Symphaedra nais.season: Active throughout the year, especially abundant from October to March in dry hill tracts.
Symphaedra nais.tnDistribution: Widespread in drier foothills and Eastern Ghats ranges including Kalvarayan, Shervarayan, Pachamalai, Sathyamangalam, and Mudumalai dry deciduous belts.
Symphaedra nais.notes: Recorded at 700-800 m elevation in Kalvarayan and Shervarayan Eastern Ghats surveys; its bright dorsal wings quickly snap shut to expose red-brown camouflage matching laterite forest soil.

Tanaecia lepidea.headline: Velvet-brown forest-floor glider bordered with a broad ash-grey band
Tanaecia lepidea.upperwing: Velvety dark brown patterned with obscure dark cell loops and bordered along both outer margins by a wide, continuous pale ash-grey terminal band that broadens toward the hindwing tornus; females are larger and slightly paler.
Tanaecia lepidea.underwing: Warm cinnamon-ochre to brown (paler on the hindwing) broadly suffused with lilac-grey along the outer borders and marked with wavy dark discal lines.
Tanaecia lepidea.similarSpecies: Broad ash-grey outer border running continuously across dark brown wings easily separates Grey Count from Common Baron (Euthalia aconthea) and female Gaudy Baron (Euthalia lubentina).
Tanaecia lepidea.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forests, bamboo brakes, shaded forest paths, and wooded foothills.
Tanaecia lepidea.behavior: Flies low with rapid wingbeats and short flat glides close to the forest floor; feeds eagerly on fallen fermenting fruits, wet soil, and sap.
Tanaecia lepidea.season: Recorded mainly from August to February, peaking post-monsoon along damp paths.
Tanaecia lepidea.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forest belts of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Gudalur, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Tanaecia lepidea.notes: Peninsular subspecies Tanaecia lepidea miyana; prefers shaded forest undergrowth where its broad pale grey wing border acts as disruptive camouflage on dappled leaf litter.

Dophla evelina.headline: Large mossy-green forest duke bearing crimson cell and basal wing spots
Dophla evelina.upperwing: Massive dark metallic olive-green butterfly etched with sinuous black cell loops enclosing a single vivid crimson spot inside the forewing cell; females are larger and paler green with a broad greyish-white forewing costal patch.
Dophla evelina.underwing: Muted sap-green densely dusted in leaden-grey, carrying the crimson forewing cell spot and three vivid black-ringed crimson spots near the base of the hindwing.
Dophla evelina.similarSpecies: Far larger than Common Baron (Euthalia aconthea) and Grey Count (Tanaecia lepidea), and uniquely identified by the single red forewing cell spot above and three black-ringed crimson basal spots on the hindwing underside.
Dophla evelina.habitat: Shaded wet evergreen and moist semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded ravines, and rubber or cardamom estate edges.
Dophla evelina.behavior: Powerful, fast flier keeping close to shaded understory tracks and low tree trunks; strongly attracted to rotting forest fruits, fallen jackfruit, and toddy-palm sap.
Dophla evelina.season: Seen year-round in dense wet hill forests, peaking between September and February.
Dophla evelina.tnDistribution: Restricted to wet Western Ghats tracts in Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kovai Kutralam, Anamalai, Valparai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kanyakumari.
Dophla evelina.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Dophla evelina.notes: South Indian race Dophla evelina laudabilis; despite its large wingspan, its mossy green upperwings blend rapidly into dappled jungle shade once settled.

Cyrestis thyodamas.headline: Fragile translucent white butterfly etched with dark cartographic map lines
Cyrestis thyodamas.upperwing: Semi-translucent creamy-white wings (pale yellow-tinted in dry-season forms) laced with delicate dark brown map-like veins and wavy transverse lines, dusky brown forewing tips, short pointed hindwing tails, and a bright orange-ochre tornal patch dotted with black.
Cyrestis thyodamas.underwing: Mirrors the crisp cartographic line network of the upperwing through thin translucent scales, showing paler outer marginal lines and the orange tornal patch.
Cyrestis thyodamas.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu for its translucent paper-like wings covered in fine dark contour-like lines and a small hindwing tail.
Cyrestis thyodamas.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen hill forests, shaded mountain streams, waterfalls, and riparian fig groves.
Cyrestis thyodamas.behavior: Glides gracefully with flatly held wings across forest streams, often resting upside-down on the underside of leaves and gathering in tight clusters on wet stream sand.
Cyrestis thyodamas.season: Year-round in wet hill forests, with conspicuous puddling congregations during dry sunny spells from November to April.
Cyrestis thyodamas.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western Ghats slopes (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, Palani Hills, KMTR) and higher Eastern Ghats ranges such as Kolli and Shervarayan hills.
Cyrestis thyodamas.notes: Southern Indian subspecies Cyrestis thyodamas indica; its fragile semi-transparent wings resemble tattered leaves or spiderwebs when motionless beneath foliage.

Byblia ilithyia.headline: Orange scrubland butterfly displaying bold black-edged white bands underneath
Byblia ilithyia.upperwing: Bright rich orange overlaid with bold black costal bars, irregular black cell streaks, wavy discal bands, and a black-spotted orange margin; females are slightly paler with heavier black submarginal bands.
Byblia ilithyia.underwing: Warm ochre-orange crossed prominently on the hindwing by three creamy-white transverse bands boldly edged by rows of black spots and lines, bordered by checkered black-and-white fringes.
Byblia ilithyia.similarSpecies: Separated from Common and Angled Castors (Ariadne spp.) by its smooth rounded wing margins and bold black-edged creamy-white bands across the hindwing underside; lacks the elongated abdomen and white-spotted black hindwing margin of Tawny Coster (Acraea terpsicore).
Byblia ilithyia.habitat: Dry thorny scrub, arid grasslands, coastal plains, fallow agricultural edges, and open savanna foothills.
Byblia ilithyia.behavior: Weak, fluttering flight close to dry grasses and stinging Tragia vines; settles frequently on bare earth, low herbs, and Tridax blooms with wings half-open.
Byblia ilithyia.season: Most abundant from September to March following northeast and southwest monsoon showers.
Byblia ilithyia.tnDistribution: Common in dry plains and scrub belts across Coimbatore, Tiruchirappalli, Madurai, Ramanathapuram, Tirunelveli, and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Byblia ilithyia.notes: One of the few butterflies in Tamil Nadu thriving on stinging Tragia creepers; the dry-season brood shows expanded creamy bands underneath for resting camouflage on dry grass stems.

Ariadne ariadne.headline: Tawny-russet castor with sharply angled margins and single wavy lines
Ariadne ariadne.upperwing: Warm tawny-russet crossed by fine, widely spaced single dark brown wavy lines, a tiny white subapical forewing spot, and distinctly truncated, sharply angled outer margins; males carry a glossy dark scent-patch underneath the forewing overlap.
Ariadne ariadne.underwing: Deep chestnut-brown to mottled purplish-rufous (darker in dry-season morphs) crossed by darker brown bands and fine pale outer lines.
Ariadne ariadne.similarSpecies: Separated reliably from Common Castor (Ariadne merione) by the acutely angled, concave forewing outer margin and single, finer dark discal lines across the upperwing (versus rounded margins and paired wavy lines in A. merione).
Ariadne ariadne.habitat: Scrub jungles, dry deciduous foothills, village hedges, neglected gardens, and forest clearings where stinging nettle-vines grow.
Ariadne ariadne.behavior: Flies slowly with jerky, gliding wingbeats close to low shrubs, basking with wings held flat and frequently circling patches of stinging Tragia vines.
Ariadne ariadne.season: Present throughout the year statewide, peaking during post-monsoon months (October to January).
Ariadne ariadne.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains, coastal scrub, Coimbatore, Chennai greenways, Eastern Ghats, and Western Ghats foothills.
Ariadne ariadne.notes: Represented in peninsular India by Ariadne ariadne indica; the deeply angular wing silhouette makes it look like a crinkled dry leaf when settled on twigs.

Ariadne merione.headline: Ubiquitous reddish-ochre castor fluttering around wild and roadside castor bushes
Ariadne merione.upperwing: Rich reddish-ochre patterned with close-set, paired wavy dark brown transverse lines and a crisp white subapical spot on the forewing (stronger in wet-season morphs), with gently scalloped rather than sharply angled outer margins; females have slightly heavier bands.
Ariadne merione.underwing: Warm rufous-brown crossed by alternating pale and dark purplish-brown wavy bands, showing stronger contrast in dry-season individuals.
Ariadne merione.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Angled Castor (Ariadne ariadne) by its smoother, less deeply indented forewing margin and closely paired, denser wavy dark lines across the upperside.
Ariadne merione.habitat: Roadway edges, agricultural fields, fallow plots, urban gardens, and open scrublands wherever castor grows.
Ariadne merione.behavior: Weak, low gliding flight around roadside castor bushes; settles flat on upper leaves in morning sun and visits small weeds like Tridax and Lantana.
Ariadne merione.season: Abundant year-round across plains and lower hills, increasing sharply after rains.
Ariadne merione.tnDistribution: Very common statewide across all Tamil Nadu districts from Chennai and coastal deltas to interior agricultural plains and ghat foothills.
Ariadne merione.notes: Peninsular race Ariadne merione merione; often breeds abundantly on wild and cultivated castor (Ricinus communis), making it one of Tamil Nadu's most familiar roadside butterflies.

Rohana parisatis.headline: Swift stream-side prince contrasting jet-black males with tawny-brown females
Rohana parisatis.upperwing: Extreme sexual dimorphism: males are velvety jet-black with a single tiny snow-white subapical forewing speck; females are warm ochre-brown crossed by dark brown discal bands, wavy submarginal lines, and three small white subapical dots.
Rohana parisatis.underwing: Males are dark purplish-mahogany with subtle black cell spots and faint pale postdiscal shading; females are duller ochre-brown echoing dorsal bands and a minute tornal eyespot.
Rohana parisatis.similarSpecies: Males are unmistakable for their small size and pure velvety-black upperside marked by a single white forewing speck; tawny females resemble Common Castor (Ariadne merione) in flight but have smoother dark-bordered wings and a stout apaturine thorax.
Rohana parisatis.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded ravines, shaded stream banks, and coffee plantations.
Rohana parisatis.behavior: Males dart swiftly from sunlit stream rocks and overhanging branches to chase rivals, returning to the same perch or puddling on damp soil; females fly quietly around Celtis trees.
Rohana parisatis.season: Most frequently encountered from September to March and May to July across wet hill slopes.
Rohana parisatis.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Palani Hills, and KMTR.
Rohana parisatis.notes: South Indian race Rohana parisatis atacinus; males hold tight sunlit territories along jungle streams, aggressively intercepting passing butterflies.

Euripus consimilis.headline: Scarce canopy courser with crimson-spotted males and crow-mimicking females
Euripus consimilis.upperwing: Strongly dimorphic: males have black forewings streaked with cream-white discal spots and snowy-white hindwings bordered in black with crimson tornal spots; females are larger and dark brown with pale blue-white streaks mimicking toxic Euploea crows or tigers.
Euripus consimilis.underwing: Males are creamy-white veined in dark brown with bright crimson-red spots along the hindwing margin; mimetic females have dark brown undersides with pale streaks and basal dots matching danaid models.
Euripus consimilis.similarSpecies: Males are unique among Tamil Nadu butterflies with white-streaked black forewings, white hindwings, and crimson hindwing spots; females closely mimic Common Crow (Euploea core) or tigers in flight but show pointed forewings and yellow-tipped proboscis of Apaturinae.
Euripus consimilis.habitat: Dense wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded river valleys, and high forest canopies.
Euripus consimilis.behavior: Males fly rapidly high in forest canopies and descend occasionally to puddle on wet gravel or animal scat; mimetic females adopt a slow, floating glide resembling Euploea crows.
Euripus consimilis.season: Rare and seasonal, sighted primarily from September to January and March to May.
Euripus consimilis.tnDistribution: Rare Western Ghats forest resident in Tamil Nadu, recorded from Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Euripus consimilis.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Euripus consimilis.notes: Represented by the South Indian endemic subspecies Euripus consimilis meridionalis; a textbook Western Ghats example of female-limited Batesian mimicry targeting unpalatable Euploea butterflies.

Vanessa indica.headline: Montane velvety-black admiral slashed with vivid scarlet-orange bands
Vanessa indica.upperwing: Deep velvety black-brown slashed diagonally across the forewing by a vivid scarlet-orange band bearing black blotches, crisp white subapical spots, and a matching scarlet-orange hindwing border dotted with black; sexes look alike.
Vanessa indica.underwing: Forewing repeats the scarlet band and white spots with a metallic blue ring in the cell; hindwing shows an intricate dark camouflage mosaic of smoky brown, grey, white, and fine black marbling.
Vanessa indica.similarSpecies: Easily separated from Painted Lady (Vanessa cardui) by its dark velvety ground colour and vivid scarlet-orange forewing band and hindwing border.
Vanessa indica.habitat: High-elevation montane shola edges, hill-station gardens, grassy ridges, and rocky summit clearings above 1,200 m.
Vanessa indica.behavior: Fast, powerful flier patrolling sunny hill ridges and Lantana or garden borders; perches aggressively on sunlit paths and rocky outcrops with open wings.
Vanessa indica.season: Active throughout the year on upper plateaus, peaking between February and May and September to December.
Vanessa indica.tnDistribution: Confined to high hills of Tamil Nadu, chiefly the Nilgiris (Ooty, Coonoor, Kotagiri, Mukurthi), Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), and high Anamalai-Meghamalai ridges.
Vanessa indica.notes: Peninsular India holds the endemic southern subspecies Vanessa indica pholoe; caterpillars construct folded leaf shelters out of stinging Girardinia nettles.

Vanessa cardui.headline: Cosmopolitan migrant recorded across hills and interior plains
Vanessa cardui.upperwing: Warm pinkish-orange wings patterned with black blotches and dark forewing tips dotted with bright white spots.
Vanessa cardui.underwing: Intricate marbled buff, rose-pink, and olive pattern bearing four neat submarginal eyespots on the hindwing.
Vanessa cardui.similarSpecies: Lacks the bright crimson-red forewing band of the Indian Red Admiral (Vanessa indica).
Vanessa cardui.habitat: Open grasslands, hills, dry scrub, fallow farmland, and urban gardens.
Vanessa cardui.behavior: Swift erratic flyer known for eruptive long-distance movements across Tamil Nadu.
Vanessa cardui.season: Irregular year-round; notable invasions documented in Pattampoochi (Q4 2019) and June 2026 Sivaganga press coverage.
Vanessa cardui.tnDistribution: Recorded from high Nilgiri/Palani peaks down to Sivaganga, Coimbatore, and coastal plains.
sources: Times of India, Painted Lady in Sivaganga (2026)
Vanessa cardui.notes: Holds one of the longest known insect migration circuits globally, reaching Tamil Nadu hills and plains irregularly in winter.

Kaniska canace.headline: Hill-forest bark mimic flashing an electric turquoise band across dark wings
Kaniska canace.upperwing: Deep indigo-black crossed across both wings by a broad gleaming turquoise-blue postdiscal band, with a crisp white subapical forewing bar and jagged, scalloped margins; females are slightly larger with a broader blue band.
Kaniska canace.underwing: Dark charcoal-brown densely covered in fine wavy black bark-like striations and a paler median band, with strongly hooked forewing tips in dry-season morphs.
Kaniska canace.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu: far darker indigo ground and broader continuous turquoise band across both wings than Blue Pansy (Junonia orithya), and lacks the brown leaf-tail of Blue Oakleaf (Kallima horsfieldi).
Kaniska canace.habitat: Shaded evergreen and shola forests, mossy stream banks, wooded ghats roads, and hill-station gardens above 800 m.
Kaniska canace.behavior: Darting territorial flyer that rests head-downward on tree trunks, wet rocks, and damp paths, snapping wings shut to vanish against dark bark and feeding on tree sap and overripe fruit.
Kaniska canace.season: Recorded year-round in cool hill forests, most numerous from September to January.
Kaniska canace.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges (Nilgiris, Coonoor, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Valparai, Kodaikanal, KMTR) and high Eastern Ghats hills like Shervarayan and Kolli Hills.
Kaniska canace.notes: Southern Indian subspecies Kaniska canace viridis; its bark-textured underwing and angular wing outline make perched individuals virtually invisible on wet tree trunks.

Junonia orithya.headline: Sun-loving grassland pansy with electric-blue male hindwings
Junonia orithya.upperwing: Males show velvety black forewings with cream bands and dazzling metallic sky-blue hindwings ringed by twin orange-edged eyespots; females are duller brown with larger eyespots.
Junonia orithya.underwing: Cryptic sandy-grey and brown dry-grass camouflage.
Junonia orithya.similarSpecies: Electric blue hindwing contrasting against dark forewings cleanly separates it from all other Tamil Nadu Junonia pansies.
Junonia orithya.habitat: Dry grasslands, open lawns, bare rocky paths, scrub, and hill meadows.
Junonia orithya.behavior: Perches flat on bare sunlit earth or short grass to defend small sunny territories.
Junonia orithya.season: Common year-round, especially in sunny dry weather.
Junonia orithya.tnDistribution: Widespread across plains, grasslands, and open hills in Tamil Nadu.
Junonia orithya.notes: Territorial males fan iridescent azure hindwings repeatedly toward passing insects from bare ground perches.

Junonia hierta.headline: Sun-loving lemon-yellow pansy stamped with an iridescent blue hindwing patch
Junonia hierta.upperwing: Males are brilliant lemon-yellow framed by a jet-black forewing costa and apex holding a pale yellow bar, plus a black hindwing costal patch enclosing a bright metallic sky-blue spot; females are duller ochre-yellow with broader dark borders and twin small ringed eyespots.
Junonia hierta.underwing: Pale sandy-buff to greyish-yellow etched with fine dusky striations and faint eyespots, turning warmer ochre-brown with dead-grass camouflage in dry-season morphs.
Junonia hierta.similarSpecies: Bright lemon-yellow colouration and black-and-blue hindwing patch separate it cleanly from Blue Pansy (Junonia orithya) and orange Peacock Pansy (Junonia almana).
Junonia hierta.habitat: Dry open scrublands, fallow fields, sunny lawns, sandy riverbeds, and bare rocky hill slopes.
Junonia hierta.behavior: Low, brisk territorial flier that basks with flatly open wings on warm bare earth, rocks, and Tridax flowers, darting out at passing insects.
Junonia hierta.season: Common year-round across sunny habitats, peaking in dry bright months from November to May.
Junonia hierta.tnDistribution: Widespread statewide from Chennai coastal scrub and dry southern plains (Madurai, Ramanathapuram, Tirunelveli) to Coimbatore and open hill slopes.
Junonia hierta.notes: Males show stark black-yellow-blue contrast to signal territory holders, while females rely on duller patterns and eyespots when ovipositing near ground level.

Junonia iphita.headline: Chocolate-brown pansy common along shaded trails and wet forests
Junonia iphita.upperwing: Rich dark chocolate-brown crossed by darker wavy bands and subtle pale marginal lines.
Junonia iphita.underwing: Resembles a veined dead leaf with a faint pale central line and small indistinct eyespots.
Junonia iphita.similarSpecies: Uniform deep chocolate-brown tones and lack of lemon spots or conspicuous large upperwing eyespots distinguish it from other pansies.
Junonia iphita.habitat: Wooded paths, shaded parks, hill forests, wetlands, and bamboo thickets.
Junonia iphita.behavior: Flies low along forest paths and sits flat on sunlit leaves in dappled shade.
Junonia iphita.season: Abundant year-round, especially in monsoon and winter.
Junonia iphita.tnDistribution: Common in both plains greenways and Western/Eastern Ghats forests.
Junonia iphita.notes: Shady forest roads and damp riverbanks often host multiple territorial males chasing each other in tight spirals.

Junonia atlites.headline: Pale silvery-grey marsh pansy ringed with delicate orange-centered eyespots
Junonia atlites.upperwing: Pale lavender-grey to silvery-buff crossed by delicate dark wavy lines across the cells and discs, featuring a curved row of orange-and-black centered eyespots across the outer half of both wings; females are slightly darker and larger.
Junonia atlites.underwing: Very pale silvery-white to soft buff-grey with faint wavy lines and reduced eyespots in dry-season forms, sharpening to crisp dark-edged eyespots in wet-season individuals.
Junonia atlites.similarSpecies: Pale silvery-grey ground colour with delicate wavy lines and a row of small orange-rimmed eyespots easily distinguishes it from Lemon (Junonia lemonias) and Chocolate (Junonia iphita) Pansies.
Junonia atlites.habitat: Paddy bunds, marsh edges, wet grassy ditches, canal banks, and humid coastal gardens.
Junonia atlites.behavior: Flutters gently low over damp marsh herbs and rice-field margins, basking openly on grass blades and nectaring on Phyla nodiflora and Tridax.
Junonia atlites.season: Year-round near water bodies, becoming especially abundant from August to February after rains.
Junonia atlites.tnDistribution: Common across irrigated lowlands, Cauvery delta, coastal marshes (Chennai, Chengalpattu, Vedanthangal, Point Calimere), and foothill wetlands statewide.
Junonia atlites.notes: Strongly associated with humid wetlands and irrigated paddy landscapes, often sharing Hygrophila host beds with Peacock Pansy (Junonia almana).

Junonia almana.headline: Rich orange wetland pansy with large concentric eyespots
Junonia almana.upperwing: Bright golden-orange marked with bold ringed eyespots, especially a huge multi-coloured peacock eyespot on each hindwing.
Junonia almana.underwing: Shows dramatic seasonal forms: wet-season butterflies carry crisp underside eyespots, while dry-season morphs have angular falcate wingtips and plain brown leaf-like undersides.
Junonia almana.similarSpecies: Bright orange ground colour and prominent giant peacock eyespots separate it cleanly from Lemon and Chocolate Pansies.
Junonia almana.habitat: Wetlands, marsh borders, paddy fields, garden lawns, and canal banks.
Junonia almana.behavior: Basks openly on low wetland plants and feeds eagerly on Tridax and Phyla blooms.
Junonia almana.tnDistribution: Abundant in wetlands and irrigated tracts across Tamil Nadu.
Junonia almana.notes: Wet-season individuals bear crisp marginal rings underneath, whereas dry-season adults mimic dead brown leaves.

Junonia lemonias.headline: Olive-brown garden pansy spotted in pale lemon with bright eyespots
Junonia lemonias.upperwing: Olive-brown dotted with creamy lemon-yellow spots and bright blue-centered orange-ringed eyespots.
Junonia lemonias.underwing: Warm ochre-brown to dark reddish leaf-brown in dry-season forms.
Junonia lemonias.similarSpecies: Lemon-yellow forewing spots separate it from the uniformly dark Chocolate Pansy and grey-white Grey Pansy.
Junonia lemonias.habitat: Gardens, roadside weeds, agricultural edges, scrub, and forest trails.
Junonia lemonias.behavior: Low, brisk territorial flight; perches frequently on bare ground or low foliage with wings fully open.
Junonia lemonias.season: Very common all year across Tamil Nadu.
Junonia lemonias.tnDistribution: Occurs statewide from urban gardens to hills.
Junonia lemonias.notes: Uses its cryptic brownish underside to blend seamlessly onto gravelly soil while basking flat in morning sun.

Hypolimnas bolina.headline: Large eggfly of wooded gardens and forests with iridescent egg spots
Hypolimnas bolina.upperwing: Males are velvety black with glowing violet-rimmed white oval spots on all wings; females vary from dark Common Crow mimics to orange-patched morphs.
Hypolimnas bolina.underwing: Dark brown crossed by a crisp pale scalloped submarginal chain.
Hypolimnas bolina.similarSpecies: Larger than Danaid Eggfly and bears white oval patches on all four wings in males (including small subapical forewing spots).
Hypolimnas bolina.habitat: Wooded parks, forest edges, gardens, and foothills.
Hypolimnas bolina.behavior: Males perch conspicuously high on sunlit shrubs and swoop after intruders.
Hypolimnas bolina.season: Year-round, peaking during monsoon and winter months.
Hypolimnas bolina.tnDistribution: Common across plains and hill forests throughout Tamil Nadu.
Hypolimnas bolina.notes: Females exhibit remarkable regional polymorphism across India, unlike uniform white-patched iridescent males.

Hypolimnas misippus.headline: Sexual-dimorphic eggfly whose female closely mimics Plain Tiger
Hypolimnas misippus.upperwing: Males are velvety jet-black with three brilliant violet-rimmed white ovals; females mimic the orange, black, and white Plain Tiger.
Hypolimnas misippus.underwing: Males show bold white bands on golden-brown; females show tawny-orange with a single large black spot at mid-hindwing costa.
Hypolimnas misippus.similarSpecies: Females lack the cluster of small black central dots inside the hindwing cell found in true Plain Tigers (Danaus chrysippus).
Hypolimnas misippus.habitat: Open scrub, lawns, gardens, roadsides, and fallow plains.
Hypolimnas misippus.behavior: Males defend sunlit perches and chase passing butterflies aggressively; females drift calmly like Plain Tigers.
Hypolimnas misippus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains, coasts, and foothills.
Hypolimnas misippus.wpaStatus: Protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Schedule II).
Hypolimnas misippus.notes: Classic textbook Batesian mimicry where orange-and-black females mimic the toxic Plain Tiger (Danaus chrysippus).

Kallima horsfieldi.headline: Famous Western Ghats leaf mimic flashing iridescent blue in flight
Kallima horsfieldi.upperwing: Deep indigo-blue crossed diagonally by a broad pale azure-white forewing band.
Kallima horsfieldi.underwing: Astonishingly realistic dry-leaf disguise complete with a central leaf midrib, fungal specks, and leaf-petiole hindwing tail.
Kallima horsfieldi.similarSpecies: Unmistakable: brilliant blue above, indistinguishable from a dead leaf when wings are snapped shut on tree bark.
Kallima horsfieldi.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, stream banks, and shaded plantations.
Kallima horsfieldi.behavior: Darts swiftly between tree trunks and vanishes abruptly upon landing with folded wings to sip sap.
Kallima horsfieldi.tnDistribution: Western Ghats stretches of Tamil Nadu (Mudumalai, Anamalai, Nilgiris, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai).
Kallima horsfieldi.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Kallima horsfieldi.notes: Protected endemic-complex leaf butterfly revered as one of nature finest examples of dead-leaf camouflage.

Doleschallia bisaltide.headline: Swift golden-tawny forest flyer disguised as a crisp dry leaf at rest
Doleschallia bisaltide.upperwing: Rich golden-tawny shading into a broad jet-black forewing apex dotted with small white subapical spots, a pointed falcate forewing tip, and a short hindwing tail; females are slightly paler tawny with a broader pale subapical band.
Doleschallia bisaltide.underwing: Remarkable dead-leaf camouflage ranging from warm autumn-ochre to deep purplish-brown, marked with a dark central midrib line from forewing tip to hindwing tail and scattered silvery or fungal-like spots that vary across seasons and individuals.
Doleschallia bisaltide.similarSpecies: Dorsal orange-and-black wings might briefly suggest Cruiser (Vindula erota) or Rustic (Cupha erymanthis) in flight, but the pointed falcate forewing apex, short hindwing tail, and dead-leaf midrib underside set Autumn Leaf completely apart (and Blue Oakleaf Kallima horsfieldi is indigo-blue above).
Doleschallia bisaltide.habitat: Evergreen and moist semi-evergreen forests, shaded stream banks, shaded hill gardens, and humid forest clearings.
Doleschallia bisaltide.behavior: Flies swiftly along shaded jungle trails before snapping down vertically onto twigs or undersides of leaves with closed wings, vanishing instantly as a dead leaf; males also visit damp sand and tree sap.
Doleschallia bisaltide.season: Recorded most consistently from August to February across humid hill forests.
Doleschallia bisaltide.tnDistribution: Western Ghats wet forest belt of Tamil Nadu, including Mudumalai, Nilgiri slopes, Siruvani, Kovai Kutralam, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Doleschallia bisaltide.notes: Peninsular India hosts the endemic race Doleschallia bisaltide malabarica; exhibits both seasonal polyphenism and individual underside variation so no two perched leaves look identical.

Curetis thetis.headline: Coppery-orange and silver-white sunbeam of wooded edges and scrub
Curetis thetis.upperwing: Males flash brilliant fiery coppery-orange framed in black; females are dark brown with crisp white central patches.
Curetis thetis.underwing: Gleaming unmarked satiny silver-white on both sexes, making resting butterflies look like silvery leaves.
Curetis thetis.similarSpecies: Cleaner straighter underside post-discal dot row and slightly rounded forewing tip help separate it from Angled Sunbeam (Curetis acuta).
Curetis thetis.habitat: Forest streams, coastal scrub, wooded parks, and riverbanks.
Curetis thetis.behavior: Strong, rapid flight; basks with partially opened copper wings on sunlit foliage.
Curetis thetis.season: Year-round, common in winter and post-monsoon.
Curetis thetis.tnDistribution: Widespread across coastal, plains, and hill forests of Tamil Nadu.
Curetis thetis.notes: Dazzling silvery-white underside reflects light starkly while its orange upperwing flashes in rapid flight.

Curetis acuta.headline: Angled copper-and-silver sunbeam of deciduous canopies and hill streams
Curetis acuta.upperwing: Males are bright coppery-orange with wide black margins, an acutely pointed forewing apex, and a prominent black tooth jutting across the forewing cell-end; females are dark brown with large clean white central patches on both wings.
Curetis acuta.underwing: Satiny silver-white on both sexes, lightly traced with faint grey-brown postdiscal dashes and marginal dots where the hindwing stria in space 6 is shifted inward out of line with space 5; tailless with a subtly angled hindwing termen.
Curetis acuta.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Sunbeam (Curetis thetis) by the sharper forewing apex, broad black hindwing borders, and strong black cell-end tooth; differs from Siva Sunbeam (Curetis siva) by the inward-dislocated hindwing underside dash in space 6.
Curetis acuta.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous hill forests, riparian corridors, bamboo brakes, and shaded forest edges.
Curetis acuta.behavior: Flies swiftly along sunlit forest canopies and stream corridors; males descend eagerly to mud-puddle on wet sand and rest with wings tightly clamped shut like pale leaves, opening briefly to bask.
Curetis acuta.season: Recorded almost year-round in hill forests, peaking from August to January after rains.
Curetis acuta.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kolli Hills, Shevaroys, and Pachamalai.
Curetis acuta.notes: Unlike Polyommatinae blues, Curetis caterpillars lack ant-appeasing dorsal nectary organs and instead deter predators using twin tall cylindrical tubercles on segment 11 that evert rapidly when disturbed.

Curetis siva.headline: Wet-forest sunbeam distinguished by aligned hindwing underside dashes
Curetis siva.upperwing: Males glow deep fiery orange-red framed by wide dark brown borders along outer and inner margins and a smaller cell-end tooth than Curetis acuta, with rounded wing outlines; females are dark brown with bold white discal patches.
Curetis siva.underwing: Gleaming silvery-white patterned with fine greyish-brown postdiscal dashes and marginal specks, lacking tails; diagnostic hindwing dash in space 6 stands closely aligned with the dash in space 5.
Curetis siva.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Angled Sunbeam (Curetis acuta) by its blunter forewing apex, rounded hindwing margin, and aligned space 5 and space 6 underside striae; separates from Indian Sunbeam (Curetis thetis) by broad dark borders on the male hindwing.
Curetis siva.habitat: Evergreen and moist semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded valleys, and shaded stream banks.
Curetis siva.behavior: Darts rapidly across mid-story foliage and settles upside down beneath leaves or on damp stream boulders during midday puddling.
Curetis siva.season: Most frequently recorded between June and December across wet Western Ghats slopes.
Curetis siva.tnDistribution: Humid Western Ghats tracts of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Nadugani, Valparai, Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kanyakumari.
Curetis siva.notes: Described by W. H. Evans in 1954 and historically overlooked as a form of Curetis thetis; larvae bear whipping tentacular defensive organs rather than ant-tended honey glands.

Spalgis epius.headline: Unique carnivorous lycaenid whose caterpillars prey on plant mealybugs
Spalgis epius.upperwing: Dark smoky brown bearing a small pale white square patch near the middle of the forewing.
Spalgis epius.underwing: Silvery grey-white intricately scribbled with dozens of fine, wavy dark-brown lines.
Spalgis epius.similarSpecies: Fine scribbled grey-white underside lacks distinct black dots, bands, or tails, completely distinct from all grass blues.
Spalgis epius.habitat: Home gardens, orchards, coffee/guava farms, and forest edges hosting mealybug colonies.
hostPlants: Predatory caterpillar feeding on mealybugs (Planococcus / Ferrisia species) rather than plant foliage
Spalgis epius.behavior: Hovers briskly around mealybug-infested hibiscus, citrus, or guava shoots; its pupa remarkably resembles a tiny rhesus-monkey face.
Spalgis epius.tnDistribution: Found quietly across Tamil Nadu gardens, farms, and forests.
Spalgis epius.notes: Purely entomophagous caterpillars prey directly on scale insects and citrus mealybugs instead of eating plants.

Cigaritis lohita.headline: Richly ochreous silverline whose hindwing subbasal band runs along vein 1b
Cigaritis lohita.upperwing: Males are dark brown glossed richly with deep violet-blue across the basal two-thirds of both wings, paired with an orange-ochreous hindwing tornal lobe bearing two silver-speckled black spots; females are plain brown without blue gloss and show faint orange-red forewing streaks.
Cigaritis lohita.underwing: Pale ochreous-yellow crossed by dark red-brown to chestnut bars centered with bright metallic silver streaks; on the forewing a club-shaped basal streak runs into the cell, and on the hindwing the subbasal band extends along vein 1b nearly to the discal band, ending in two white-tipped black tails.
Cigaritis lohita.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Silverline (Cigaritis vulcanus) and Plumbeous Silverline (Cigaritis schistacea) by its deep crimson-brown ventral bands on a warm yellow ground and the long hindwing subbasal band running down vein 1b.
Cigaritis lohita.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forest edges, wooded stream banks, bamboo brakes, and shaded hill clearings.
Cigaritis lohita.behavior: Flies briskly around mid-storey bushes and bamboo clumps, perches on sunlit leaf tips, feeds eagerly at flowering shrubs, and twists its hindwings slowly after landing.
Cigaritis lohita.season: Recorded across most months in wet hill tracts, peaking between August and January.
Cigaritis lohita.tnDistribution: Western Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, as well as moist Eastern Ghats hills like Shervaroys.
Cigaritis lohita.notes: Subspecies Cigaritis lohita lazularia is strongly myrmecophilous; caterpillars live inside silken shelters on host stems tended by Crematogaster ants such as Crematogaster rothneyi.

Cigaritis vulcanus.headline: Widespread orange-banded silverline of sunny scrub, gardens, and dry hills
Cigaritis vulcanus.upperwing: Dark brown with a faint violet sheen in fresh males, marked on the forewing with three to four bright orange-red transverse bands descending from the costa; females are slightly larger and rounder with paler, broader orange bands and an orange-red tornal patch on the hindwing.
Cigaritis vulcanus.underwing: Pale greyish-buff to cream-yellow crossed by clean, evenly spaced rusty-red to ochreous bars edged finely in black and centered with crisp metallic silver lines; bears two white-tipped black tails and a double black-spotted orange tornal lobe.
Cigaritis vulcanus.similarSpecies: Unlike Plumbeous Silverline (Cigaritis schistacea), lacks the bright blue male hindwing gloss and shows wider pale gaps between its cleaner ventral silver bars; Common Shot Silverline (Cigaritis ictis) shows a single fused triangular orange forewing patch rather than three separate orange bands.
Cigaritis vulcanus.habitat: Dry scrub jungles, thorny hedges, urban parks, open plains, roadside Lantana patches, and deciduous foothills.
Cigaritis vulcanus.behavior: Low, darting flier that basks with half-open wings on sunny twigs, visits Tridax and Chromolaena blooms, and oscillates its hindwings to animate the orange tornal false head.
Cigaritis vulcanus.season: Active year-round across Tamil Nadu, most abundant after northeast monsoon showers from October to February.
Cigaritis vulcanus.tnDistribution: Statewide from Chennai coastal scrub, Guindy, and Point Calimere across Coimbatore, Madurai, Salem, Pachamalai, and Western Ghats foothills.
Cigaritis vulcanus.notes: By far Tamil Nadu's commonest silverline; females lay eggs only near Crematogaster ant trails, and caterpillars feed on tender shoots while guarded inside ant-attended leaf shelters.

Cigaritis schistacea.headline: Steel-blue glossed silverline with tightly packed ventral silver bars
Cigaritis schistacea.upperwing: Males are pale brown with variable orange-red forewing markings and a striking bright plumbeous-blue gloss over the disc of the hindwing; females are larger and plain dark brown without blue sheen, showing a muted orange-red forewing patch and pale orange anal area.
Cigaritis schistacea.underwing: Dull greyish-ochreous to leaden buff crossed by closely set, densely packed reddish-brown bands heavily edged in black and lined with metallic silver; the tight band spacing leaves narrow pale interspaces, ending in two tails and an orange tornal spot.
Cigaritis schistacea.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Silverline (Cigaritis vulcanus) by the male's bright leaden-blue hindwing disc rather than faint violet gloss and by much closer, denser underside bands on a duller greyish ground.
Cigaritis schistacea.habitat: Moist deciduous woodlands, riverine scrub, bamboo margins, and mid-elevation forest clearings.
Cigaritis schistacea.behavior: Darting low-strata flyer that perches alertly on sunlit grass blades and forest-edge shrubs, occasionally mud-puddling along damp forest tracks.
Cigaritis schistacea.season: Mainly post-monsoon and winter (September to March), with scattered records in summer months.
Cigaritis schistacea.tnDistribution: Mid-elevation Western Ghats foothills and Eastern Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris lower slopes, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Shervaroys.
Cigaritis schistacea.notes: Often shares sunny forest clearings with Cigaritis vulcanus and Cigaritis lohita; larvae shelter beneath bark crevices tended by arboreal Crematogaster ants.

Cigaritis ictis.headline: Sun-loving dry-zone silverline flashing an angled orange forewing patch
Cigaritis ictis.upperwing: Dark brown glossed with purple-blue at wing bases in males, featuring a prominent roughly triangular bright orange discal patch on the upper forewing enclosing two short dark bars; females show a broader, brighter orange patch and lack the purplish gloss.
Cigaritis ictis.underwing: Pale ochreous-yellow to greyish-buff crossed by pale tawny-brown bands lined with narrow metallic silver and fine dark edges; on the forewing a subbasal band reaches below the median vein and the hindwing carries two white-tipped black tails at a dull orange anal lobe.
Cigaritis ictis.similarSpecies: Readily distinguished from Common Silverline (Cigaritis vulcanus) by the broad triangular orange forewing patch instead of discrete transverse bars, and separated from Scarce Shot Silverline (Cigaritis elima) by having a forewing subbasal spot below the cell and duller orange-brown ventral bands.
Cigaritis ictis.habitat: Dry deciduous scrub, thorny plains, rocky hillocks, open grasslands, and dry eastern foothills.
Cigaritis ictis.behavior: Extremely fast, erratic flight low over rocky ground and thorny bushes; males aggressively defend sunlit gravel perches and damp patches.
Cigaritis ictis.season: Flies throughout the year in dry plains and foothills, peaking during September to March.
Cigaritis ictis.tnDistribution: Widespread across dry interior Tamil Nadu and foothills, including Coimbatore, Sathyamangalam, Madurai, Virudhunagar, Tirunelveli, Pachamalai, and Kallar.
Cigaritis ictis.notes: Exhibits marked seasonal variation between darker wet-season and paler dry-season broods; caterpillars associate closely with Crematogaster ants inside stem shelters.

Cigaritis abnormis.headline: Rare Western Ghats silverline with broken, thread-thin ventral bands
Cigaritis abnormis.upperwing: Males are dull smoky greyish-violet with a subdued violet gloss, broad blackish-brown forewing costal and outer borders, a pale whitish-grey hindwing inner margin, and a muted greyish-orange anal patch lacking distinct black spots; females are darker brown with broader rounded wings and pale basal shading.
Cigaritis abnormis.underwing: Pale greyish-ochreous crossed by unusually narrow, broken, faint ochreous-brown lines carrying fine silvery central streaks, a small cell dot and end-bar on the forewing, and short white-tipped dull orange tails.
Cigaritis abnormis.similarSpecies: Unmistakable among Tamil Nadu Cigaritis by its washed-out, fragmented, thread-narrow underside silver bands and lack of bright dorsal orange forewing patches or crisp black tornal spots.
Cigaritis abnormis.habitat: Localized dry-to-moist deciduous hill forests and bamboo-rich eastern slopes of the southern Western Ghats.
Cigaritis abnormis.behavior: Elusive and low-flying; perches briefly on dry grass stems and sunlit forest-floor saplings, rubbing its short-tailed hindwings gently.
Cigaritis abnormis.season: Scarce and seasonal, recorded primarily between October and March and during early summer.
Cigaritis abnormis.tnDistribution: Localized along eastern Western Ghats slopes of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiri foothills, Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Anamalais, and KMTR.
Cigaritis abnormis.notes: An endemic Indian silverline restricted mainly to the Western Ghats; its reduced silver markings make it the oddest member of the genus, earning the name abnormis.

Cigaritis elima.headline: Acute-winged dry-scrub silverline with pale red-edged ventral bands
Cigaritis elima.upperwing: Forewings are distinctly pointed at the apex; males are brown glossed with steely smalt-blue over the lower forewing and central hindwing with a small subapical reddish patch enclosing two dark spots, while females are browner without blue and display a large triangular orange-red forewing patch.
Cigaritis elima.underwing: Pale sandy testaceous to straw-buff with very pale, delicate reddish-edged transverse bands traversed by thin silver lines; the forewing lacks a separate basal spot below the cell, and the hindwing anal lobe projects prominently ahead of two fine tails.
Cigaritis elima.similarSpecies: Differs from the closely similar Common Shot Silverline (Cigaritis ictis) by its sharper forewing tip, bright smalt-blue sheen on the male upperside, and paler sandy underside lacking the extra subbasal forewing spot.
Cigaritis elima.habitat: Dry thorn scrub, rain-shadow foothill savannahs, rocky dry hill slopes, and open deciduous woodland.
Cigaritis elima.behavior: Swifter and warier than Cigaritis vulcanus; settles briefly on bare twigs, dry soil patches, and small flowering Acacia herbs in hot midday sun.
Cigaritis elima.season: Observed mainly during post-monsoon and dry winter months from October to April.
Cigaritis elima.tnDistribution: Rain-shadow plains and eastern foothill tracts of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Sathyamangalam, Nilgiri eastern slopes, Dharmapuri, and Madurai.
Cigaritis elima.notes: Far scarcer in Tamil Nadu than Cigaritis ictis; early stages remain poorly documented in the southern hills, though larvae depend strictly on Crematogaster ants.

Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.headline: Recently described Western Ghats silverline from Meghamalai hills
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.upperwing: Dark brown wings extensively marked with iridescent metallic blue across both forewing and hindwing.
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.underwing: Buff-yellow crossed by metallic silver-centered dark bands: forewing discal and post-discal bands lie parallel from the costa, and the hindwing post-basal band is unbroken.
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.similarSpecies: Diagnosed from all other Western Ghats Cigaritis (Spindasis) silverlines by the parallel conjoined forewing bands and continuous hindwing post-basal band ending at vein 1b.
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.habitat: Montane cloud forest clearings and edges in the southern Western Ghats.
hostPlants: Myrmecophilous associations (documented with Crematogaster ants in original description)
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.behavior: Observed basking briefly on low vegetation along cloud-forest hill slopes.
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.season: Documented around monsoon and post-monsoon months in high hills.
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.tnDistribution: Meghamalai Hills (Theni district, Tamil Nadu), the type locality of this newly described species.
Cigaritis meghamalaiensis.notes: Described by S.R.K. Naicker, K. Sadasivan & colleagues in ENTOMON (2023) and formally added to the Tamil Nadu Butterfly Checklist.
sources: Pattampoochi Issue 27, Cloud Forest Silverline Note (p. 11)

Anthene emolus.headline: Tailless forest blue whose caterpillars live under weaver-ant protection
Anthene emolus.upperwing: Males are uniform deep violet-purple with slender dark margins and rounded forewing tips; females are dull brown with faint dull blue basal scales and indistinct dark hindwing marginal dots.
Anthene emolus.underwing: Pale grey-brown crossed by regular, unbroken white-edged dark discal bands without a sub-basal spot in space 7 near the hindwing base; bears an orange-capped black tornal spot in space 2 and three tiny hair-like marginal ciliary tufts instead of a true tail.
Anthene emolus.similarSpecies: Separated from Pointed Ciliate Blue (Anthene lycaenina) by its rounded forewing apex, unbroken forewing discal band, and absence of the dark white-ringed spot near the base of hindwing space 7.
Anthene emolus.habitat: Low- to mid-elevation moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, wooded stream edges, and dense canopy clearings.
Anthene emolus.behavior: Males fly swiftly around tree canopies and puddle along shaded forest streams; females inspect trees colonized by weaver ants before laying eggs on tender flush.
Anthene emolus.season: Recorded mainly during pre-monsoon and post-monsoon forest surveys from April to November.
Anthene emolus.tnDistribution: Restricted and scarce in moist southern and western Tamil Nadu hill forests, notably Kanyakumari Wildlife Sanctuary (Kizhviyar), Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Siruvani, and Anamalais.
Anthene emolus.notes: Obligate myrmecophile closely tended by Asian Weaver Ants (Oecophylla smaragdina); Pattampoochi Issue 26 documented the May 2023 Kizhviyar record in Kanyakumari WLS as a landmark Tamil Nadu photographic confirmation.

Anthene lycaenina.headline: Sharp-winged blue marked by a dark basal spot on the hindwing underside
Anthene lycaenina.upperwing: Males shine brighter, paler lilac-blue with a hairline dark margin, pointed forewing apex, and acutely angled hindwing tornus; females are greyish-brown with pale blue basal suffusion and faint hindwing marginal spots.
Anthene lycaenina.underwing: Buff-grey to pale brown with broken, staggered white-edged discal bands forming a Y-like fork at forewing vein 3, a diagnostic dark white-ringed basal spot in hindwing space 7, an orange-crowned black spot in space 2, and fine ciliary tufts rather than a tail.
Anthene lycaenina.similarSpecies: Readily told from Common Ciliate Blue (Anthene emolus) by the acute forewing tip, broken forewing discal band, and prominent dark basal spot touching vein 7 on the hindwing underside.
Anthene lycaenina.habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forests, foothills, scrub edges, and wooded riverbanks.
Anthene lycaenina.behavior: Darts energetically around flowering forest canopies and settles rapidly on wet gravel or bird droppings along sunny forest trails.
Anthene lycaenina.season: Active throughout much of the year, peaking during dry-to-wet transition months from March to November.
Anthene lycaenina.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills and wooded foothills including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, Pachamalai, and Gingee.
Anthene lycaenina.notes: Larvae secrete honeydew from a dorsal nectary organ and are fiercely guarded by Weaver Ants (Oecophylla smaragdina) and Camponotus ants on tender shoots.

Petrelaea dana.headline: Muted tailless lineblue carrying twin black tornal eyespots without orange
Petrelaea dana.upperwing: Males are dull frosted violet-blue with a narrow dark outer margin and rounded hindwings; females are dark brown with pale dull blue limited to the wing bases.
Petrelaea dana.underwing: Uniform dingy brownish-grey crossed by weak, blurred whitish lines enclosing pale four-lineblue bands without sub-basal cell lines; bears two equal-sized jet-black subtornal spots in spaces 1b and 2 dusted faintly with metallic scales and lacking orange caps, completely tailless.
Petrelaea dana.similarSpecies: Separated from Tailless Lineblue (Prosotas dubiosa) and White-tipped Lineblue (Prosotas noreia) by its twin subequal black tornal spots without orange crowns and faded greyish underside striae.
Petrelaea dana.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen hill forests, riparian corridors, and damp sandy stream beds.
Petrelaea dana.behavior: Males congregate densely on damp sand and animal dung along shaded forest streams; flight is low, fluttering, and easily overlooked.
Petrelaea dana.season: Commonest from October to March and during post-monsoon months in hill forests.
Petrelaea dana.tnDistribution: Recorded in Western and Eastern Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Pachamalai.
Petrelaea dana.notes: Its larvae feed on Terminalia flowers and buds rather than legumes, setting this single-species genus apart ecologically from true Nacaduba and Prosotas lineblues.

Nacaduba pactolus.headline: Largest of the Tamil Nadu lineblues with broad crisp white bands
Nacaduba pactolus.upperwing: Males are rich deep purple-blue framed by distinctly broad dark brown outer margins; females are dark brown with a vivid iridescent blue discal patch on the forewing and pale blue hindwing base.
Nacaduba pactolus.underwing: Warm greyish-brown lacking sub-basal white lines inside the forewing cell (4-lineblue pattern), crossed by broad, stark white transverse lines defining wide darker bands, a prominent orange-crowned black subtornal spot in space 2, and a delicate white-tipped tail.
Nacaduba pactolus.similarSpecies: Much larger and darker above with broader borders and wider white ventral lines than Pale 4-lineblue (Nacaduba hermus), and separated from all 6-lineblues by lacking sub-basal lines across the forewing cell.
Nacaduba pactolus.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, forest canopies, and shaded riverine glades.
Nacaduba pactolus.behavior: Stronger flier than smaller lineblues, patrolling upper-canopy climbers and descending to wet mud along sunlit stream crossings.
Nacaduba pactolus.season: Seen mainly from July to February across humid hill tracts.
Nacaduba pactolus.tnDistribution: Localized in moist Western and Eastern Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu, including Siruvani, Kallar, Nadugani, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kanyakumari, and Kolli Hills.
Nacaduba pactolus.notes: Caterpillars bore into tender shoots and floral buds of giant forest lianas like Entada rheedii and are facultatively visited by foraging ants.

Nacaduba hermus.headline: Paler four-lineblue distinguished by hoary grey-brown underside bands
Nacaduba hermus.upperwing: Males are dark purplish-brown overlaid with a pale silvery-violet gloss in side light and two white-edged dark hindwing spots in spaces 1b and 2; females are brown with a soft pale blue central forewing patch.
Nacaduba hermus.underwing: Pale hoary grey-brown lacking sub-basal lines in the forewing cell (4-lineblue pattern), marked with finer, cleaner white transverse lines, a compact orange-ringed black spot in space 2, and a slender white-tipped tail at vein 2.
Nacaduba hermus.similarSpecies: Smaller and noticeably paler hoary grey beneath with narrower white bands than Large 4-lineblue (Nacaduba pactolus), and lacks the forewing cell sub-basal line pair present in Nacaduba kurava and other 6-lineblues.
Nacaduba hermus.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, stream banks, and shaded jungle clearings.
Nacaduba hermus.behavior: Hovers briskly around shaded forest foliage and joins mixed lineblue mud-puddling groups along damp gravel tracks.
Nacaduba hermus.season: Mostly recorded from August to February during humid hill seasons.
Nacaduba hermus.tnDistribution: Occurs across Western Ghats slopes of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kanyakumari, with occasional records from wetter Eastern Ghats hills.
Nacaduba hermus.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Nacaduba hermus sidoma; males often blend silently into large puddling aggregations of 6-lineblues.

Nacaduba kurava.headline: Frosted six-lineblue whose underside stripes show faintly through the wings
Nacaduba kurava.upperwing: Males are bright pale frosted violet-blue with thin dark borders, translucent enough that the underside bands show subtly from above; females are dark brown with a pale iridescent blue discal patch turning whitish on the outer forewing.
Nacaduba kurava.underwing: Pale greyish-brown with a full six-lineblue pattern including a pair of sub-basal white lines across the forewing cell, crisp white-edged postdiscal bands, weak dark internal striae in males, broad lunulate submarginal spots, an orange-capped black tornal spot in space 2, and a thin tail.
Nacaduba kurava.similarSpecies: Separated from Opaque 6-lineblue (Nacaduba beroe) by paler, semi-translucent wings and complete sub-basal costal spots; differs from 4-lineblues by possessing sub-basal white lines inside the forewing cell.
Nacaduba kurava.habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous hill forests, forest gardens, and stream edges.
Nacaduba kurava.behavior: Flies rapidly in bright clearings around flowering shrubs and puddles abundantly on wet soil alongside Ceruleans and Prosotas lineblues.
Nacaduba kurava.season: Common year-round in wet hill forests, peaking post-monsoon from September to March.
Nacaduba kurava.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Pachamalai.
Nacaduba kurava.notes: Females in southern India (subspecies canaraica) frequently display a striking whitish blur across the forewing blue disc, helping field separation from darker female congeners.

Nacaduba beroe.headline: Richly scaled six-lineblue with darkened wing bases and cloudy lines
Nacaduba beroe.upperwing: Males are rich dark opaque violet-blue with narrow dark borders and noticeably darkened wing bases that hide ventral bands from above; females are brown with shiny blue confined to the basal half of the forewing.
Nacaduba beroe.underwing: Darker warm brown with six-lineblue sub-basal lines inside the forewing cell (the lowest sub-basal costal spot in space 11 frequently absent), softer pale bands, weak internal dark striae in males, an orange-crowned black spot in space 2, and a fine white-tipped tail.
Nacaduba beroe.similarSpecies: More opaque and darker purple above than Transparent 6-lineblue (Nacaduba kurava), and differs from Rounded 6-lineblue (Nacaduba berenice) by weaker dark internal striae inside the ventral bands.
Nacaduba beroe.habitat: Evergreen, moist deciduous, and riparian hill forests from foothills to mid-elevations.
Nacaduba beroe.behavior: Darts along shaded forest paths and gathers in tight clusters on damp sand banks, salt-licks, and wet rocks.
Nacaduba beroe.season: Active most of the year in forested tracts, most numerous between September and March.
Nacaduba beroe.tnDistribution: Found across Western and Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kanyakumari, Shevaroys, and Kolli Hills.
Nacaduba beroe.notes: Southern Indian populations belong to subspecies Nacaduba beroe gythion, whose caterpillars feed on tender shoots and flower buds of woody forest climbers.

Nacaduba berenice.headline: Compact rounded six-lineblue with bold dark striae inside ventral bands
Nacaduba berenice.upperwing: Noticeably rounded forewing apex and convex outer margins; males are dull dark violet-blue with fine black borders and darkened veins, while females are dark brown with restricted leaden-blue discal scaling and pale-ringed hindwing spots.
Nacaduba berenice.underwing: Warm buff-brown showing a full six-lineblue pattern with forewing cell sub-basal lines, strongly etched dark internal striae within the white-bordered bands in both sexes, broad chevron-shaped submarginal spots, a bright orange-crowned black spot in space 2, and a short tail.
Nacaduba berenice.similarSpecies: Separated from Opaque 6-lineblue (Nacaduba beroe) and Transparent 6-lineblue (Nacaduba kurava) by its rounder wing profile, strong dark internal band striae in both sexes, and chevron-shaped submarginal lunules.
Nacaduba berenice.habitat: Dense evergreen and semi-evergreen foothill and mid-elevation rainforests.
hostPlants: Sapindaceae trees and climbers (local South Indian larval host unconfirmed; feeds on Sapindaceae and Connaraceae shoots across its range)
Nacaduba berenice.behavior: Flies close to understory foliage and settles quietly on damp mud or sunny leaves along narrow forest trails.
Nacaduba berenice.season: Scarce; recorded mainly during humid months from July to February.
Nacaduba berenice.tnDistribution: Rarely documented in humid Western Ghats pockets of Tamil Nadu including Kanyakumari, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Anamalais, Siruvani, and Nilgiri foothills.
Nacaduba berenice.notes: Peninsular Indian and Sri Lankan populations represent subspecies Nacaduba berenice ormistoni; field records often require sharp ventral photos to separate from Nacaduba calauria.

Nacaduba calauria.headline: High-contrast dark six-lineblue of southern evergreen rainforests
Nacaduba calauria.upperwing: Males are deep dark violet-purple with narrow dark borders and dense opaque scales; females are dark brown with bright blue restricted to the forewing base and disc and crisp black submarginal hindwing lunules.
Nacaduba calauria.underwing: Deep chocolate-brown crossed by crisp stark white six-lineblue striae (including forewing cell sub-basal lines) with strong dark internal band lines, a straight forewing postdiscal band, sharply pointed submarginal spots in spaces 4 and 5, an orange-capped black spot in space 2, and a delicate tail.
Nacaduba calauria.similarSpecies: Darker beneath with sharper white bands and sagittate submarginal spots in spaces 4 and 5 than Rounded 6-lineblue (Nacaduba berenice), and much darker and higher contrast than Nacaduba kurava.
Nacaduba calauria.habitat: Undisturbed wet evergreen rainforests, shaded streamsides, and mid-elevation hill valleys.
hostPlants: Forest Sapindaceae and Fabaceae climbers (confirmed Indian larval host plant awaiting documentation)
Nacaduba calauria.behavior: Swift understory flier; males visit wet gravel bars near forest streams while females remain higher among canopy vines.
Nacaduba calauria.season: Recorded intermittently between May and January in heavy-rainfall tracts.
Nacaduba calauria.tnDistribution: Uncommon specialist of southern and central Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu, recorded from Kanyakumari, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Anamalai, Siruvani, and Nilgiris.
Nacaduba calauria.notes: Indian and Sri Lankan populations correspond to subspecies Nacaduba calauria evansi; its larval ecology in the Western Ghats remains an active field gap.

Nacaduba sinhala.headline: Pale translucent six-lineblue rediscovered in the Agasthyamalai hills
Nacaduba sinhala.upperwing: Rounded wing outline with thin, semi-translucent scaling; males are pale bright violet-blue showing faint hints of ventral bands from above, while females are dark brown with shiny blue restricted to the basal halves and a pale whitish outer forewing patch.
Nacaduba sinhala.underwing: Pale ashy-grey to greyish-brown patterned with six-lineblue sub-basal cell lines and broad crisp white bands formed of unusually wide ribbon scales, an orange-ringed black subtornal spot in space 2, and a slender hindwing tail.
Nacaduba sinhala.similarSpecies: Smaller and paler ashy-grey beneath with wider ribbon-scale white bands than Transparent 6-lineblue (Nacaduba kurava); reliable separation in the Agasthyamalai complex often rests on male genitalia and life-history traits.
Nacaduba sinhala.habitat: Low- to mid-elevation wet evergreen and moist deciduous forests along southern mountain streams.
Nacaduba sinhala.behavior: Flies swiftly along forest openings and damp tracks; males puddle beside streams in loose company with other lineblues.
Nacaduba sinhala.season: Recorded mainly during post-monsoon and summer-shower windows from October to May.
Nacaduba sinhala.tnDistribution: Restricted in Tamil Nadu to the southern Western Ghats, particularly the Agasthyamalai landscape across Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Tenkasi foothills, and Kanyakumari.
Nacaduba sinhala.notes: Mainland Indian population was described in 2021 as endemic subspecies Nacaduba sinhala ramaswamii (Ramaswami's Six-lineblue), bridging a historic biogeographic link with Sri Lanka.

Prosotas nora.headline: Ubiquitous tailed lineblue flashing bright ochre beneath in dry months
Prosotas nora.upperwing: Males are shining purple-blue with narrow dark brown borders; females are dull dark brown with pale blue scaling confined near the wing bases.
Prosotas nora.underwing: Pale buff-brown to warm yellow-ochre (brightest in dry-season broods) crossed by pairs of crisp white lines enclosing darker sub-basal, cell-end, and postdiscal bands extending below the forewing cell, an orange-crowned black subtornal spot in space 2, and a short white-tipped tail.
Prosotas nora.similarSpecies: Separated instantly from Tailless Lineblue (Prosotas dubiosa) and White-tipped Lineblue (Prosotas noreia) by its distinct hindwing tail, and from Pointed Lineblue (Ionolyce helicon) by its rounded forewing apex.
Prosotas nora.habitat: Scrub jungles, deciduous foothills, forest trails, riverbanks, and wooded rural edges.
Prosotas nora.behavior: Weak erratic flight close to thorny shrubs and stream edges; dozens of males pack tightly onto wet mud patches during hot midday hours.
Prosotas nora.season: Abundant year-round across Tamil Nadu hills and plains, peaking after monsoons.
Prosotas nora.tnDistribution: Statewide across Tamil Nadu from coastal scrub and interior plains to high Western and Eastern Ghats valleys.
Prosotas nora.notes: Shows marked seasonal polyphenism in Tamil Nadu, shifting from grey-brown in wet monsoon months to warm yellowish-ochre in dry summer broods; larvae are tended by Camponotus and Technomyrmex ants.

Prosotas dubiosa.headline: Tiny tailless lineblue easily overlooked in mixed stream-puddling swarms
