Prosotas dubiosa.upperwing: Males are dark purplish-blue with narrow dark borders and rounded hindwings; females are dark brown with restricted dull violet-blue basal dusting.
Prosotas dubiosa.underwing: Warmer, darker chocolate-brown than Prosotas nora, crossed by closely paired crisp white lines framing dark cell and discal bands, a bold black subtornal spot in space 2 crowned with bright orange, and completely tailless.
Prosotas dubiosa.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Lineblue (Prosotas nora) by lacking a hindwing tail and showing darker brown ground color; distinguished from Dingy Lineblue (Petrelaea dana) by crisp white-edged bands and a single orange-crowned tornal spot.
Prosotas dubiosa.habitat: Forest clearings, dry and moist deciduous scrub, thorny Acacia groves, and damp riverbeds.
Prosotas dubiosa.behavior: Flutters rapidly around flowering leguminous climbers and joins dense mixed-species puddling clusters on damp soil.
Prosotas dubiosa.season: Common year-round statewide with highest numbers from September to April.
Prosotas dubiosa.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains, foothills, and hills including Coimbatore, Chennai, Madurai, Erode, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Pachamalai, and Shevaroys.
Prosotas dubiosa.notes: Often flies side-by-side with tailed Prosotas nora; caterpillars feed on tender flower buds of climbing acacias and are attended by small ants.

Prosotas noreia.headline: Tailless hill lineblue bordered with crisp white-frosted marginal markings
Prosotas noreia.upperwing: Males are pale brown flushed with shining violet-purple across the inner disc, leaving noticeably wider dark brown margins than Prosotas nora; females are plain brown with faint basal blue sheen.
Prosotas noreia.underwing: Dull brown patterned with sharp white-edged discal bands, prominent white-tipped submarginal and marginal lunules giving the hindwing border a frosted edge, a distinct orange-ringed black subtornal spot in space 2, and no tail.
Prosotas noreia.similarSpecies: Differs from Tailless Lineblue (Prosotas dubiosa) by broader brown male upperwing margins and crisper white-frosted hindwing terminal markings; separated from Common Lineblue (Prosotas nora) by lacking a tail.
Prosotas noreia.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation moist deciduous and evergreen hill forests, forest edges, and damp trails.
Prosotas noreia.behavior: Weak, low flight around forest margins and leguminous canopy trees; males regularly visit wet soil and stream margins.
Prosotas noreia.season: Recorded intermittently between July and March, mainly in hill tracts.
Prosotas noreia.tnDistribution: Scarce and localized in Tamil Nadu hills, notably the Nilgiris (type locality of subspecies hampsoni at Ootacamund), Anamalais, Siruvani, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Shevaroys.
Prosotas noreia.notes: Indian subspecies Prosotas noreia hampsoni was described from Ootacamund in the Nilgiris by Lionel de Niceville in 1885.

Ionolyce helicon.headline: Sharp-tipped forest lineblue with a yellow-orange ring at the tornus
Ionolyce helicon.upperwing: Forewing apex distinctly acute and outer margin straight; males are deep dark violet-blue with a slender black border, whereas females are dark brown with brilliant metallic blue restricted strictly to the wing bases.
Ionolyce helicon.underwing: Pale greyish-brown marked with fine, broken white transverse lines enclosing slightly darker bands, a prominent black subtornal spot in space 2 encircled by a bright yellow-orange ring, and a delicate white-tipped tail.
Ionolyce helicon.similarSpecies: Readily told from Common Lineblue (Prosotas nora) and Nacaduba species by its sharply pointed forewing silhouette, restricted basal blue on the female upperwing, and bright yellow-orange ring around the tornal eyespot.
Ionolyce helicon.habitat: Evergreen and moist semi-evergreen forest understories, shaded nullahs, and bamboo valleys.
Ionolyce helicon.behavior: Keeps to shaded forest clearings and stream edges, fluttering swiftly around Allophylus shrubs and puddling singly or in small numbers on wet rocks.
Ionolyce helicon.season: Active throughout moist months, peaking from August to February.
Ionolyce helicon.tnDistribution: Occurs in humid Western and Eastern Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kanyakumari, and Shevaroys.
Ionolyce helicon.notes: In contrast to legume-feeding Prosotas lineblues, Pointed Lineblue caterpillars specialize on tender shoots and flower buds of Allophylus cobbe.

Caleta decidia.headline: Bold black-and-white forest pierrot marked by an angled white band
Caleta decidia.upperwing: Dark brownish-black in both sexes crossed by a broad pure white median band angled sharply inward near the forewing costa like an elbow and extending smoothly onto the hindwing.
Caleta decidia.underwing: Chalky white with stark dark brown to black patterns: a thick diagonal sub-basal bar from forewing base to mid-costa, an irregular broken discal band, and black submarginal spots lacking metallic blue scales, plus a fine white-tipped tail.
Caleta decidia.similarSpecies: Separated from Banded Blue Pierrot (Discolampa ethion) by lacking blue sheen on the male upperwing and metallic blue tornal scales below, and from Common Pierrot (Castalius rosimon) by solid bold bands rather than scattered discrete dots.
Caleta decidia.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous hill forests, scrub-forest edges, shaded trails, and stream crossings.
Caleta decidia.behavior: Flutters weakly through dappled forest undergrowth and congregates prominently in large mud-puddling groups on wet sand and animal scat.
Caleta decidia.season: Common year-round in forested belts, surging after northeast and southwest monsoons.
Caleta decidia.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu foothills and hill ranges including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, Pachamalai, and Gingee.
Caleta decidia.notes: Larvae feed on young Ziziphus foliage and are occasionally attended by ants; dry-season broods exhibit noticeably broader white dorsal bands.

Discolampa ethion.headline: Jewelled white-banded pierrot flashing iridescent blue in sunbeams
Discolampa ethion.upperwing: Males glow deep dark blue-purple overlaid by a broad shared white median band across both wings and wide black borders; females are black-brown with the crisp white median band and no dorsal blue iridescence.
Discolampa ethion.underwing: Snowy white neatly banded with two curved black sub-basal bars, broken black postdiscal bars, submarginal black spots dusted near the hindwing tornus with faint metallic bluish-green scales, and a fine white-tipped tail.
Discolampa ethion.similarSpecies: Males are unmistakable with their dark iridescent blue gloss over a crisp white median band; females differ from Angled Pierrot (Caleta decidia) by parallel curved sub-basal underside bars and metallic bluish tornal speckling.
Discolampa ethion.habitat: Shaded evergreen and moist deciduous forest streams, foothill trails, and bamboo corridors.
Discolampa ethion.behavior: Weak fluttering flight inside shaded canopy gaps; males puddle eagerly beside forest streams and flash violet-blue when wings tilt to sunlight.
Discolampa ethion.season: Recorded throughout the year in moist hill forests, peaking from August to January.
Discolampa ethion.tnDistribution: Well distributed in Tamil Nadu hill forests including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kanyakumari, Sirumalai, Shevaroys, and Kolli Hills.
Discolampa ethion.notes: Closely tied to Ziziphus climbers along shaded stream banks; caterpillars chew characteristic troughs on young jujube leaves and are visited by ants.

Jamides bochus.headline: Blazing metallic sapphire cerulean common from urban parks to hill ridges
Jamides bochus.upperwing: Males flash dazzling deep metallic sapphire-blue across the basal and discal wings framed by a broad black forewing apex and outer margin; females are dull pale frosty blue with wide dark brown borders.
Jamides bochus.underwing: Dark greyish-brown crossed by narrow crisp white wavy transverse lines (with a regular, nearly straight forewing postdiscal band), a bold orange-crowned black tornal eyespot in space 2, twin metallic-scaled marginal specks, and a slender white-tipped tail.
Jamides bochus.similarSpecies: Male is instantly separated from Common Cerulean (Jamides celeno) and Metallic Cerulean (Jamides alecto) by its intense dark sapphire sheen and broad black forewing apex; females show darker brownish-grey undersides than J. celeno.
Jamides bochus.habitat: Urban gardens, agricultural edges, scrublands, and deciduous to evergreen hill forests.
Jamides bochus.behavior: Fast, erratic flight around flowering legume trees and shrubs; males perch aggressively on sunlit tips and puddle along wet paths.
Jamides bochus.season: Common year-round across Tamil Nadu, increasing noticeably from September to March.
Jamides bochus.tnDistribution: Statewide from Chennai coastal parks and Coimbatore wetlands to Mudumalai, Siruvani, Pachamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Jamides bochus.notes: Caterpillars bore inside flower buds and pods of cultivated pulses and Pongam trees and are tended by Camponotus and Crematogaster ants.

Jamides celeno.headline: Abundant milky-blue cerulean showing strong wet and dry seasonal forms
Jamides celeno.upperwing: Males are pale milky whitish-blue with a narrow black border (widening sharply in wet-season broods); females are pale greyish-blue framed by broad dark brown borders and dark hindwing submarginal lunules.
Jamides celeno.underwing: Pale buff-grey to grey-brown crossed by crisp white pairs of lines where the forewing postdiscal band runs evenly from vein 3 to vein 7 without extra basal costal dashes, a bright orange-capped black tornal eyespot in space 2, and a fine white-tipped tail.
Jamides celeno.similarSpecies: Separated from Metallic Cerulean (Jamides alecto) by its milky whitish-blue male colour and continuous forewing postdiscal band (not stepped at vein 3); differs from Forget-me-not (Catochrysops strabo) by lacking an isolated forewing costal dot.
Jamides celeno.habitat: Gardens, roadside weeds, fallow fields, scrub jungles, and forest clearings.
Jamides celeno.behavior: Weak fluttering flight at shrub height, pausing frequently on Tridax, Chromolaena, and Lantana flowers and basking with half-spread wings.
Jamides celeno.tnDistribution: Ubiquitous across every district of Tamil Nadu from coastal dunes and urban campuses to Western and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Jamides celeno.notes: Demonstrates textbook seasonal polyphenism in Tamil Nadu: dry-season individuals are pale chalky buff beneath with broad white stripes, whereas monsoon individuals have darker brown undersides and wider black dorsal borders.

Jamides alecto.headline: Large glistening sky-blue cerulean breeding inside wild gingers and cardamom
Jamides alecto.upperwing: Males are bright gleaming metallic sky-blue with a very thin black outer margin and fine dark tornal dots on the hindwing; females are paler frosted blue with broad black borders and bold blue-ringed dark hindwing marginal spots.
Jamides alecto.underwing: Warm pinkish-grey to pale buff-grey with bold white parallel stripes where the forewing postdiscal band is clearly dislocated at vein 3 and extra white costal dashes appear near the forewing base, plus a large orange-crowned black eyespot in space 2 and a long slender tail.
Jamides alecto.similarSpecies: Larger and much brighter metallic sky-blue than Common Cerulean (Jamides celeno), with the forewing underside postdiscal band broken at vein 3 and extra basal costal dashes.
Jamides alecto.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded cardamom estates, and stream valleys.
Jamides alecto.behavior: Strong swift flight through shaded mid-story clearings around ginger clumps; males descend regularly to mud-puddle on damp gravel.
Jamides alecto.season: Active year-round in humid hill forests, peaking between July and January.
Jamides alecto.tnDistribution: Humid Western Ghats hill tracts of Tamil Nadu including Valparai, Siruvani, Kallar, Nadugani, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kanyakumari.
Jamides alecto.notes: Unlike legume-feeding relatives, subspecies Jamides alecto alocina caterpillars bore directly inside flower spikes and capsules of Zingiberaceae gingers and cardamom, often tended by ants.

Catochrysops strabo.headline: Lilac-blue open-country regular carrying a midway forewing costal dot
Catochrysops strabo.upperwing: Males are soft pale lilac-blue with a hairline dark margin and a small black spot near the hindwing tornus; females are dark brown with bright blue basal dusting, pale discal shading, and an orange-crowned black hindwing spot.
Catochrysops strabo.underwing: Pale greyish-buff patterned with white-edged darker bands, a diagnostic small black costal dot situated midway between the forewing cell-end bar and the postdiscal band, two black costal spots on the hindwing, a large orange-crowned black eyespot in space 2, and a thin tail.
Catochrysops strabo.similarSpecies: Separated from Silver Forget-me-not (Catochrysops panormus) by the forewing costal dot placed midway between cell-end bar and postdiscal band rather than touching the band; differs from Ceruleans by discrete costal dots and buff tone.
Catochrysops strabo.habitat: Open grasslands, agricultural fields, fallow scrub, home gardens, and forest edges.
Catochrysops strabo.behavior: Brisk low flight over sunny weeds and pulse crops; frequently visits Tridax and legume blossoms and puddles on damp soil.
Catochrysops strabo.tnDistribution: Abundant across plains, agricultural belts, urban wetlands, and foothills throughout all districts of Tamil Nadu.
Catochrysops strabo.notes: Caterpillars feed inside flowers and green pods of legumes and secrete sugary nectar collected by Camponotus and Oecophylla ants.

Catochrysops panormus.headline: Scarcer silvery-white relative with the costal dot shifted to the band
Catochrysops panormus.upperwing: Males are bright silvery lilac-blue (slightly frostier and paler than Catochrysops strabo) with a fine dark marginal thread; females are brown with pale bluish-white central areas and dark hindwing submarginal spots.
Catochrysops panormus.underwing: Pale silvery-grey to off-white with crisp white-bordered buff bands where the small forewing costal spot sits adjacent to (or touching) the upper end of the postdiscal band, sharper chevron-shaped submarginal lunules, an orange-capped black eyespot in space 2, and a fine tail.
Catochrysops panormus.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Forget-me-not (Catochrysops strabo) by its silvery-white ventral ground colour and the forewing costal spot lying close against the postdiscal band rather than midway to the cell-end bar.
Catochrysops panormus.habitat: Moist and dry forest edges, wooded foothills, coastal scrub-forests, and grassy clearings.
Catochrysops panormus.behavior: Swift erratic flight close to woodland herbs and flowering shrubs; settles sharply on sunlit grass blades and damp soil.
Catochrysops panormus.season: Uncommon and patchy, mostly noted from August to February.
Catochrysops panormus.tnDistribution: Localized across Tamil Nadu in scattered Western Ghats foothills and wooded coastal pockets including Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Mudumalai, and Chennai-Chengalpattu scrub.
Catochrysops panormus.notes: Mainland Indian populations belong to subspecies Catochrysops panormus exiguus; often passes unnoticed among swarms of common Catochrysops strabo unless underside spots are checked closely.

Lampides boeticus.headline: Long-distance migratory blue tailed with twin black eyespots
Lampides boeticus.upperwing: Males are soft frosted violet-blue; females are brown with blue wing bases; both carry two conspicuous black dots near the delicate hindwing tails.
Lampides boeticus.underwing: Pale buff-brown neatly rippled with white wavy stripes, a crisp white submarginal band on the hindwing, and twin orange-crowned black eyespots.
Lampides boeticus.similarSpecies: Rippled brown-and-white underside with a clean pale hindwing band separates it from Zebra Blue (which has stronger zebra-stripe contrast) and Ciliate Blues (which lack tails).
Lampides boeticus.habitat: Gardens, agricultural fields, fallow scrub, open hills, and Crotalaria patches.
Lampides boeticus.behavior: Brisk erratic flight around flowering legumes; famous global migrant.
Lampides boeticus.tnDistribution: Statewide from coastal plains to Nilgiri peaks.
Lampides boeticus.notes: Cosmopolitan legume-pod feeder whose larvae develop inside rattlepod (Crotalaria) and cultivated bean pods.

Leptotes plinius.headline: Tiger-striped garden blue breeding on Plumbago shrubs statewide
Leptotes plinius.upperwing: Males are rich violet-blue with a hairline black margin and subtle dark spots showing near the hindwing tornus; females are dark brown with bright blue basal scales and checkered white-and-brown central patches.
Leptotes plinius.underwing: Creamy white tightly rippled from base to outer margin with crisp brown zebra-like bands, twin jet-black hindwing tornal eyespots flecked with metallic green and edged in pale orange, and a short thread-like tail.
Leptotes plinius.similarSpecies: Separated from Pea Blue (Lampides boeticus) by continuous bold brown-and-white zebra stripes covering the entire underside rather than a broad pale white submarginal hindwing band.
Leptotes plinius.habitat: Home gardens, urban hedges, scrublands, riparian weeds, and hill station roadsides.
Leptotes plinius.behavior: Quick, fluttering flight right around flowering leadwort bushes; mud-puddles frequently and rotates hindwings gently while perched to draw attention to tornal false-head eyespots.
Leptotes plinius.tnDistribution: Found throughout every district of Tamil Nadu from coastal Chennai parks to Nilgiri and Palani hill gardens.
Leptotes plinius.notes: Caterpillars consume Plumbago flower buds and young pods and are regularly tended by Camponotus and Crematogaster ants.

Castalius rosimon.headline: Dainty white-and-black spotted pierrot common in gardens and scrub
Castalius rosimon.upperwing: White wings with metallic pale-blue iridescent bases, dark margins, and bold scattered black spots.
Castalius rosimon.underwing: Pure white neatly spotted and streaked with jet-black marks and a delicate hair-like tail.
Castalius rosimon.similarSpecies: Differs from Angled Pierrot (Caleta decidia) and Banded Blue Pierrot (Discolampa ethion) by discrete scattered underside spots rather than solid dark diagonal bands.
Castalius rosimon.habitat: Scrublands, roadside Ziziphus shrubs, gardens, wetlands, and dry foothills.
Castalius rosimon.behavior: Weak fluttering flight close to thorny jujube bushes; mud-puddles at damp patches.
Castalius rosimon.tnDistribution: Common across plains, cities, and hills of Tamil Nadu.
Castalius rosimon.wpaStatus: Protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Schedule I/II history).
Castalius rosimon.notes: Flutters just above Ziziphus jujube bushes; caterpillars graze characteristic translucent windows on young leaves.

Tarucus balkanicus.headline: Rare dark-spotted thorn-scrub pierrot recorded in Coimbatore wetlands
Tarucus balkanicus.upperwing: Males are glossy dark violet-blue (often suffused dusky smoky-brown in Indian subspecies nigra) with a bold black cell-end spot and distinct black discal spots in forewing spaces 1b to 4; females are dark brown mottled with pale bluish-white central spots.
Tarucus balkanicus.underwing: Chalk-white heavily marked in jet-black: a solid streak along the forewing subcostal-cell zone, an oblique black discal bar below vein 4, separated upper postdiscal spots, broken submarginal dots, metallic green-flecked tornal spots, and a fine tail.
Tarucus balkanicus.similarSpecies: Separated from Rounded Pierrot (Tarucus nara) by clear black postdiscal spots on the male upperwing and broken submarginal dots beneath rather than a continuous black submarginal line.
Tarucus balkanicus.habitat: Arid and semi-arid thorn scrub, wetland bunds, and dry Ziziphus thickets.
Tarucus balkanicus.behavior: Flies briskly around low thorny Ziziphus bushes in harsh midday heat and pauses briefly on dry twigs or damp mud edges.
Tarucus balkanicus.season: Scarce and seasonal, chiefly noted during dry and post-monsoon periods from October to March.
Tarucus balkanicus.tnDistribution: Rare in Tamil Nadu with verified dry-zone and wetland records from Coimbatore (documented in Pattampoochi Issue 5), Erode, Sathyamangalam, and rainshadow plains.
Tarucus balkanicus.notes: Indian subspecies Tarucus balkanicus nigra was spotlighted in Pattampoochi Issue 5 (Jan-Mar 2018) as a rare Tamil Nadu find; larvae are tended by ants on Ziziphus.

Tarucus nara.headline: Common thorn-scrub pierrot marked by an unbroken submarginal line below
Tarucus nara.upperwing: Males are bright pale violet-blue with a slender black margin and a fine black cell-end dash without discal black spotting; females are dark brown mottled with white and pale blue central blotches.
Tarucus nara.underwing: Crisp pure white patterned with elongated black basal and discal streaks, a diagnostic continuous unbroken black submarginal line running parallel to both outer margins, tiny metallic green-speckled hindwing tornal dots, and a slender white-tipped tail.
Tarucus nara.similarSpecies: Separated from Spotted Pierrot (Tarucus callinara) and Pointed Pierrot (Tarucus indica) by its continuous unbroken black submarginal stripe on both wings rather than a row of separate dots.
Tarucus nara.habitat: Dry thorn scrub, roadside jujube thickets, wetland edges, dry deciduous foothills, and open fallow plots.
Tarucus nara.behavior: Weak, busy flight looping closely around spiny Ziziphus bushes; regularly visits small ground flowers like Tridax and puddles on damp soil.
Tarucus nara.season: Common year-round in dry regions, peaking from September to March.
Tarucus nara.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains, wetlands, and dry foothills including Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli, Salem, Tirunelveli, Sathyamangalam, and Chengalpattu.
Tarucus nara.notes: Obligately tended on Ziziphus foliage by Crematogaster and Camponotus ants, which shelter larvae inside leaf-curls in exchange for sweet secretions.

Tarucus callinara.headline: White-and-black pierrot displaying clean separated underside spots
Tarucus callinara.upperwing: Males are bright pale lilac-blue with a narrow black border, slender cell-end streak, and occasional faint dark discal spots; females are dark brown patched boldly with white and pale blue at the bases.
Tarucus callinara.underwing: Clean white marked with discrete, rounded dark brown to black spots across basal, discal, and postdiscal series rather than fused long streaks, a submarginal row broken into neat isolated dots, metallic green-dusted tornal specks, and a fine tail.
Tarucus callinara.similarSpecies: Differs from Rounded Pierrot (Tarucus nara) by broken submarginal spots instead of a solid line; closely resembles Pointed Pierrot (Tarucus indica) and often requires male genitalic verification where ranges overlap.
Tarucus callinara.habitat: Dry scrublands, thorny riverbanks, fallow fields, and dry deciduous foothills.
Tarucus callinara.behavior: Hovers briskly around low jujube bushes and visits tiny herbaceous blossoms or damp mud edges during sunny mornings.
Tarucus callinara.season: Recorded intermittently across dry and post-monsoon months from October to April.
Tarucus callinara.tnDistribution: Patchily distributed across drier plains and foothills of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Erode, Salem, Madurai, Tirunelveli, and Chengalpattu scrub.
Tarucus callinara.notes: Basu et al. (2019) clarified Indian Tarucus taxonomy showing that spotted forms like T. callinara overlap closely with T. indica in peninsular scrub habitats and share ant-tended Ziziphus larvae.

Tarucus indica.headline: Slightly sharp-winged translucent pierrot of dry thorn scrub
Tarucus indica.upperwing: Forewing apex slightly more pointed than Tarucus nara; males are pale, semi-translucent violet-blue showing faint shadows of underside spots through the membrane, with a thin border and cell-end dash; females are brown with white discal blotches.
Tarucus indica.underwing: Crisp white marked with sharp, well-spaced black dots, an oblique broken postdiscal series on the forewing, a broken submarginal row of neat round spots, subtle metallic green scaling on hindwing tornal spots, and a slender tail.
Tarucus indica.similarSpecies: Separated from Rounded Pierrot (Tarucus nara) by its slightly pointed forewing, translucent upperwing, and broken submarginal spots; differs from Spotted Pierrot (Tarucus callinara) reliably by male valva shape.
Tarucus indica.habitat: Semi-arid scrub jungles, thorny Ziziphus hedgerows, dry riverbeds, and open plains.
Tarucus indica.behavior: Flits nervously around thorny shrubs in open sun and settles on dry stems or small nectar flowers close to the ground.
Tarucus indica.season: Recorded predominantly in dry and post-monsoon seasons from October to April.
Tarucus indica.tnDistribution: Occurs across dry interior plains and foothills of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Erode, Dharmapuri, Salem, Madurai, and Tirunelveli.
Tarucus indica.notes: Originally treated as an Indian race of Tarucus theophrastus; caterpillars graze soft epidermis from Ziziphus leaves while attended by Crematogaster ants.

Tarucus ananda.headline: Woodland pierrot boldly banded in chocolate-black and tended by ants
Tarucus ananda.upperwing: Males are deep dark glossy purple-black with wide black margins, appearing nearly velvety black in the field; females are dark brown with small, restricted white discal patches and faint dark marginal lunules.
Tarucus ananda.underwing: Creamy white crossed by remarkably thick, heavy, solid chocolate-brown to black basal, median, and postdiscal bands, marginal dark lunules dusted near the tornus with metallic bluish-green flecks, and a thin white-tipped tail.
Tarucus ananda.similarSpecies: Immediately distinguished from all pale-spotted Tamil Nadu Tarucus species by its dark blackish male upperwing and broad, solid dark brown underside bands rather than fine dots or streaks.
Tarucus ananda.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous forests, shaded foothill paths, wooded streams, and hill scrub.
Tarucus ananda.behavior: Keeps closer to wooded hill clearings than plains Tarucus species; males mud-puddle on wet sand and perch on sunlit understory shrubs.
Tarucus ananda.season: Active most of the year in forest belts, peaking between August and February.
Tarucus ananda.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hill forests and wooded foothills including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Pachamalai.
Tarucus ananda.notes: Obligately myrmecophilous with Crematogaster ants, which even build carton shelters over feeding caterpillars and pupae on Ziziphus twigs; females also oviposit on Loranthus mistletoes hosting the same ants.

Zizeeria karsandra.headline: Tiny grassland blue flying inches above urban lawns and pastures
Zizeeria karsandra.upperwing: Dull violet-blue broadly edged in brown (males) or plain brown with blue sheen (females).
Zizeeria karsandra.underwing: Pale grey-brown marked with neat rows of black spots and two small dark spots inside the hindwing cell.
Zizeeria karsandra.similarSpecies: Unlike Lesser Grass Blue (Zizina otis) and Tiny Grass Blue (Zizula hylax), it retains clear black dots inside the base of the forewing underside.
Zizeeria karsandra.habitat: Short lawns, parks, roadside herbs, playgrounds, and dry grasslands.
Zizeeria karsandra.behavior: Weak fluttering flight barely above grass blades; suns with half-open wings.
Zizeeria karsandra.tnDistribution: Found throughout all districts of Tamil Nadu.
Zizeeria karsandra.notes: Among the smallest butterflies in Tamil Nadu wetlands and lawns, easily overlooked unless crouching close to clover and Amaranthus.

Zizina otis.headline: Lawnside grass blue lacking forewing cell spots and shifting spot 6 outward
Zizina otis.upperwing: Tailless; males are dull violet-blue bordered broadly in dark brown along the outer third of both wings, while females are plain dark brown with sparse dull blue scales restricted near the base.
Zizina otis.underwing: Pale buff-grey with faint blurry submarginal lunules, completely lacking dark spots inside the forewing cell and space 11, and showing the hindwing discal spot in space 6 shifted clearly outward out of line with spots 5 and 7.
Zizina otis.similarSpecies: Separated from Dark Grass Blue (Zizeeria karsandra) by lacking a spot inside the forewing cell, from Pale Grass Blue (Pseudozizeeria maha) by smaller size and outward-shifted hindwing spot 6, and from Tiny Grass Blue (Zizula hylax) by lacking two forewing costal spots.
Zizina otis.habitat: Short lawns, roadside verges, paddy bunds, coastal grasslands, and disturbed scrub.
Zizina otis.behavior: Weak, hovering flight inches above turf; settles frequently on prostrate clovers and Tridax blooms with wings half-open.
Zizina otis.tnDistribution: Common across every district of Tamil Nadu from coastal Chennai lawns to Nilgiri and Palani foothill pastures.
Zizina otis.notes: Indian subspecies Zizina otis decreta breeds steadily on creeping Fabaceae weeds in urban parks and agricultural bunds.

Pseudozizeeria maha.headline: Largest Tamil Nadu grass blue tied closely to creeping woodsorrel
Pseudozizeeria maha.upperwing: Tailless; males are pale silvery sky-blue (deeper purplish-blue in wet-season forms) with wide dusky brown margins, while females are dark brown with variable pale blue basal suffusion that expands widely in dry-season broods.
Pseudozizeeria maha.underwing: Pale chalky grey dotted with sharp black spots: lacks a spot inside the forewing cell, shows the uppermost forewing postdiscal spot (space 6) shifted abruptly inward, and bears a small black basal dot in hindwing space 7.
Pseudozizeeria maha.similarSpecies: Visibly larger with a chalky grey underside and inward-shifted top forewing discal spot compared to Lesser Grass Blue (Zizina otis) and Dark Grass Blue (Zizeeria karsandra).
Pseudozizeeria maha.habitat: Urban lawns, botanical gardens, moist fallow meadows, tea and coffee estate borders, and hill grasslands.
Pseudozizeeria maha.behavior: Flutters weakly just above shaded and sunny ground cover, basking flat on Oxalis mats and sipping nectar from tiny composite weeds.
Pseudozizeeria maha.season: Abundant year-round across Tamil Nadu, particularly conspicuous in hill stations and post-monsoon plains.
Pseudozizeeria maha.tnDistribution: Statewide across Tamil Nadu plains, cities, and high hills including Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Salem, Nilgiris, Kodaikanal, Valparai, and Yercaud.
Pseudozizeeria maha.notes: Subspecies Pseudozizeeria maha ossa shows pronounced seasonal dimorphism, with cool dry-season females gaining bright pale blue wings resembling males.

Zizula hylax.headline: Minute grass blue marked by twin black spots along the forewing costa
Zizula hylax.upperwing: Tailless and dainty; males are bright violet-blue edged in a moderate dark brown border, while females are dull smoky brown with faint blue scales confined near the wing bases.
Zizula hylax.underwing: Pale silvery-grey neatly dotted with crisp black spots: lacks a spot inside the forewing cell, carries two distinct black spots along the forewing costa (spaces 11 and 12), and shows an evenly curved hindwing discal spot row.
Zizula hylax.similarSpecies: Smaller and more delicate than Lesser Grass Blue (Zizina otis), and separated from both Z. otis and Dark Grass Blue (Zizeeria karsandra) by the two clear black spots along the forewing costa.
Zizula hylax.habitat: Roadside weeds, gardens, wetland margins, open scrub, and sunlit forest edges.
Zizula hylax.behavior: Weak, dancing flight inches over low herbs and marsh edges; perches delicately on grass stems and Acanthaceae flowers.
Zizula hylax.tnDistribution: Widespread across all districts of Tamil Nadu from coastal scrub and urban parks to Western and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Zizula hylax.notes: Among the smallest butterflies in India; unlike typical legume-feeding grass blues, its caterpillars feed largely on Acanthaceae buds and Lantana florets.

Everes lacturnus.headline: Dainty tailed blue bearing twin black spots framed in bright orange
Everes lacturnus.upperwing: Males are bright violet-blue with narrow dark outer borders and two small dark marginal dots near the hindwing tornus; females are dark brown with pale blue basal dusting and orange-capped dark tornal spots on the hindwing.
Everes lacturnus.underwing: Silky greyish-white marked with pale grey-brown discal dashes, two conspicuous black sub-basal dots on the hindwing, two jet-black tornal eyespots crowned together by a vivid orange-red patch in spaces 2 and 3, and a tiny hair-like tail at vein 2.
Everes lacturnus.similarSpecies: Separated from Plains Cupid (Chilades pandava) and Small Cupid (Chilades parrhassius) by its silky whiter underside with faint grey discal dashes, two bold black sub-basal hindwing dots, and a single shared bright orange tornal patch.
Everes lacturnus.habitat: Open grasslands, forest clearings, wetland margins, fallow fields, and mid-elevation hill meadows.
Everes lacturnus.behavior: Weak low flight over creeping pasture legumes; pauses with wings closed on grass stalks and puddles occasionally on wet mud.
Everes lacturnus.season: Recorded year-round, most common from October to March.
Everes lacturnus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu grasslands, foothills, and hill ranges including Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Salem, Nilgiris, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Everes lacturnus.notes: Represented in peninsular India by subspecies Everes lacturnus syntala; females tuck eggs deep inside tiny flower heads of creeping Fabaceae.

Talicada nyseus.headline: Garden lycaenid prized for its black-and-white wings with orange rim
Talicada nyseus.upperwing: Velvety dark black-brown with a bright scarlet-orange patch along the lower half of the hindwing.
Talicada nyseus.underwing: Crisp snow-white checked with black spots on the outer forewing and a broad bright orange hindwing border.
Talicada nyseus.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in southern India, no other small lycaenid pairs a snow-white-and-black underside with a vivid orange hindwing border.
Talicada nyseus.habitat: Urban gardens, balconies, rocky outcrops, dry scrub, and wooded hillsides wherever Kalanchoe grows.
Talicada nyseus.behavior: Weak, low flight right around succulent host plants; caterpillars mine inside fleshy Kalanchoe leaves.
Talicada nyseus.tnDistribution: Abundant across cities, rocky hills, and gardens throughout Tamil Nadu.
Talicada nyseus.notes: Tiny caterpillars bore directly inside succulent Kalanchoe leaf tissue and pupate on the outer surface.

Azanus ubaldus.headline: Tailless acacia blue carrying a dark velvety scent patch on the forewing
Azanus ubaldus.upperwing: Males are dark lilac-purple with narrow dark borders and a distinct velvety patch of dark scent scales covering the middle of the forewing; females are dull greyish-brown with light blue basal dusting.
Azanus ubaldus.underwing: Pale brownish-grey patterned with white-edged dark bands, a prominent elongated black streak inside the forewing cell, crisp black sub-basal dots on the hindwing, and two small black tornal dots dusted faintly with metallic green without orange crowns; tailless.
Azanus ubaldus.similarSpecies: Separated from African Babul Blue (Azanus jesous) by the dark velvety forewing scent patch in males and the dark brown streak inside the forewing cell rather than four sharp black sub-basal hindwing spots.
Azanus ubaldus.habitat: Arid thorn scrub, dry deciduous savannahs, babul groves, and rocky hillocks.
Azanus ubaldus.behavior: Very fast, erratic flight darting high around flowering thorny Acacia crowns; settles rapidly on dry twigs and mud edges.
Azanus ubaldus.season: Active throughout warm and dry months, peaking from October to April.
Azanus ubaldus.tnDistribution: Common in dry interior and rainshadow districts of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Thoothukudi, Ramanathapuram, Salem, and Sathyamangalam.
Azanus ubaldus.notes: Larvae feed inside yellow Acacia flower heads and are tended closely by Camponotus and Crematogaster ants.

Azanus jesous.headline: Rosy-lilac babul blue marked by four jet-black sub-basal hindwing dots
Azanus jesous.upperwing: Tailless; males are bright rosy lilac-blue without any velvety dark scent patch on the forewing and bear thin black borders, while females are pale brown with white-rimmed dark discal spots and soft blue basal scales.
Azanus jesous.underwing: Pale creamy-grey marked with a chestnut-brown streak along the forewing cell-base, four prominent jet-black sub-basal dots across the hindwing base, crisp dark discal bars, and dark tornal specks accented with metallic green scales.
Azanus jesous.similarSpecies: Told from Bright Babul Blue (Azanus ubaldus) by the lack of a dark forewing scent patch in males, brighter rosy-lilac dorsal tone, and four crisp black sub-basal hindwing dots below; differs from Small Cupid (Chilades parrhassius) by lacking tails and orange caps.
Azanus jesous.habitat: Open thorn scrub, dry plains, rocky scrub hills, and Acacia hedgerows.
Azanus jesous.behavior: Brisk low-to-mid-height flight around thorny scrub canopies; visits Mimosa and Tridax blossoms and puddles at sunlit wet patches.
Azanus jesous.season: Recorded year-round in dry regions, peaking between September and March.
Azanus jesous.tnDistribution: Widespread across dry scrublands and plains of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Ramanathapuram, Erode, Salem, Villupuram, and Chengalpattu.
Azanus jesous.notes: Females oviposit directly onto unopened Acacia flower buds, where caterpillars camouflage neatly among yellow stamens while tended by ants.

Neopithecops zalmora.headline: Shaded understory black-and-white blue with one bold subapical hindwing spot
Neopithecops zalmora.upperwing: Tailless and rounded; both sexes are smoky dark brown usually bearing a neat oval white discal patch on the forewing (sometimes reduced or absent in wet-season form dharma) and checkered wing fringes.
Neopithecops zalmora.underwing: Clean chalk-white displaying a large, unmistakable jet-black round spot near the hindwing apex (space 7), a small black dot near the inner margin (space 1a), faint broken grey postdiscal lines, and no series of black spots along the forewing costa.
Neopithecops zalmora.similarSpecies: Separated instantly from Malayan (Megisba malaya) by its clean chalk-white underside lacking a row of four forewing costal spots and three hindwing sub-basal dots, leaving the bold black subapical hindwing spot isolated.
Neopithecops zalmora.habitat: Shaded tropical dry evergreen groves, dense forest understories, bamboo thickets, and shaded orchards.
Neopithecops zalmora.behavior: Weak, slow, moth-like flutter just feet above shaded leaf litter beneath Glycosmis bushes; rarely leaves forest shade.
Neopithecops zalmora.season: Active year-round in shaded woodlands, peaking from September to March.
Neopithecops zalmora.tnDistribution: Occurs in shaded Western and Eastern Ghats forests plus coastal tropical dry evergreen groves in Tamil Nadu, including Guindy, Vandalur, Marakkanam, Point Calimere, Siruvani, Kallar, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Neopithecops zalmora.notes: Subspecies Neopithecops zalmora dharma shows seasonal variation where monsoon individuals turn almost completely smoky brown dorsally, losing the white forewing patch.

Megisba malaya.headline: White-patched woodland blue sporting four dark spots along the forewing costa
Megisba malaya.upperwing: South Indian subspecies thwaitesi is tailless; dark blackish-brown in both sexes with an oblique white central patch across the forewing (often extending onto the hindwing in dry-season broods) and no blue sheen.
Megisba malaya.underwing: Dull greyish-white peppered with fine dark lines, bearing a diagnostic row of four small black spots along the forewing costa, three distinct black sub-basal spots across the hindwing base plus a dark cell-end bar, and two black subtornal spots.
Megisba malaya.similarSpecies: Differs from Quaker (Neopithecops zalmora) by its four neat black spots along the forewing underside costa and three sub-basal spots across the hindwing base; southern race lacks the tail seen in northeastern Megisba populations.
Megisba malaya.habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous forest edges, shaded streams, and wooded plains.
Megisba malaya.behavior: Flies weakly in dappled shade along forest paths and gathers readily on damp sand, wet rocks, and bird droppings.
Megisba malaya.season: Recorded year-round in wooded hills, peaking between August and February.
Megisba malaya.tnDistribution: Found across Western and Eastern Ghats forests and moist wooded foothills of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, Kolli Hills, and Pachamalai.
Megisba malaya.notes: South Indian and Sri Lankan subspecies Megisba malaya thwaitesi is consistently tailless, making ventral costal-spot inspection essential in the field.

Acytolepis puspa.headline: Commonest Tamil Nadu hedge blue showing a basal black spot in space 7
Acytolepis puspa.upperwing: Tailless; males are bright glossy pale silvery-blue (often showing subtle whitish discal lightening) bordered by a black outer edge widening at the forewing apex; females are dark brown with bright iridescent blue inside the disc and a small white central smudge.
Acytolepis puspa.underwing: Bluish-white to chalky greyish-white marked with sharp black spots, an irregular stepped forewing postdiscal spot row, a crisp black spot at the extreme base of hindwing space 7, and a zigzag submarginal line enclosing neat marginal spots.
Acytolepis puspa.similarSpecies: Separated from Plain Hedge Blue (Celastrina lavendularis) by pale silvery-blue (not dark lavender) male colour and broader apical black borders; differs from Hampson's Hedge Blue (Acytolepis lilacea) by more pointed forewings and staggered forewing postdiscal spots.
Acytolepis puspa.habitat: Evergreen and deciduous hill forests, coastal dry evergreen parks, wooded gardens, and shaded streams.
Acytolepis puspa.behavior: Swift flier around flowering tree crowns; males puddle persistently on damp river sand and animal dung in sunny forest openings.
Acytolepis puspa.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills and wooded plains including Guindy, Vandalur, Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Nilgiris, Anamalai, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Shevaroys, and Pachamalai.
Acytolepis puspa.notes: Polyphagous larvae of subspecies Acytolepis puspa felderi feed on young flush and flower buds across several plant families and are regularly attended by ants.

Acytolepis lilacea.headline: Scarcer rounded-wing hedge blue breeding on wild mountain cycads
Acytolepis lilacea.upperwing: Tailless with rounder forewing apex and termen than Acytolepis puspa; males are uniform bright violet-blue without pale whitish discal patches in southern subspecies lilacea and carry a narrow dark outer margin; females are dark brown with restricted bright blue basal areas.
Acytolepis lilacea.underwing: Pale bluish-grey marked with dark postdiscal dashes arranged in a smoother, more regular arc on the forewing than in Acytolepis puspa, retaining the small black spot at the extreme base of hindwing space 7 and dentate submarginal crescents.
Acytolepis lilacea.similarSpecies: Very close to Common Hedge Blue (Acytolepis puspa) in the field, separated by its more rounded forewing shape, lack of whitish male discal patches, and more uniform forewing postdiscal spot line (confirmed conclusively by male genitalia).
Acytolepis lilacea.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests and riparian valleys.
Acytolepis lilacea.behavior: Flies swiftly along sunny canopy gaps and puddles along forest stream gravel beside commoner Acytolepis puspa.
Acytolepis lilacea.season: Uncommon; mostly encountered from September to April in hill forests.
Acytolepis lilacea.tnDistribution: Localized in Western Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including the Nilgiris, Anamalai, Siruvani, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Acytolepis lilacea.notes: Field life-history studies in the southern Western Ghats revealed that subspecies Acytolepis lilacea lilacea breeds on wild Cycas circinalis flush, unlike polyphagous Acytolepis puspa.

Celastrina lavendularis.headline: Rich lavender-blue montane hedge blue edged with a razor-thin border
Celastrina lavendularis.upperwing: Tailless; males are deep dark lavender-blue bordered only by a hairline black margin without white discal patches, while females are paler lavender framed by broad black-brown forewing costal and outer borders and dark hindwing submarginal spots.
Celastrina lavendularis.underwing: Greyish-white marked with neat, fine dark postdiscal dashes aligned smoothly on the forewing, a black sub-basal spot in hindwing space 7, and marginal spots enclosed by a sharp zigzag line.
Celastrina lavendularis.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Hedge Blue (Acytolepis puspa) by its deep uniform lavender-blue male upperwing and thread-thin margin, and from White-disc Hedge Blue (Celatoxia albidisca) by lacking crisp white discal patches.
Celastrina lavendularis.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation wet evergreen, shola, and moist deciduous hill forests above 600 m.
hostPlants: Fabaceae forest climbers such as Millettia and Callerya species (South Indian host awaiting formal confirmation)
Celastrina lavendularis.behavior: Strong, rapid flight along montane stream corridors and forest edges; males gather in puddling patches on wet soil and elephant dung.
Celastrina lavendularis.season: Recorded nearly year-round in hill ranges, peaking from October to March.
Celastrina lavendularis.tnDistribution: Common in higher Tamil Nadu hills including the Nilgiris, Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Anamalais, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Megamalai, Shevaroys, and Kalvarayan Hills.
Celastrina lavendularis.notes: Represented in South India and Sri Lanka by subspecies Celastrina lavendularis lavenduris; detailed larval host confirmation in Tamil Nadu hills remains a worthwhile field study.

Udara akasa.headline: Chalk-white shola hedge blue fluttering along high mountain streams
Udara akasa.upperwing: Tailless; males are extensively chalky white across both wings with wide black forewing apical-costal borders and soft bright blue iridescence restricted strictly to wing bases; females are overwhelmingly white with broad black borders and almost no blue.
Udara akasa.underwing: Pure crisp white sparsely etched with tiny black postdiscal dots, thin cell-end bars, and faint marginal dots, lacking prominent dark submarginal zigzag crescents.
Udara akasa.similarSpecies: Separated immediately from White-disc Hedge Blue (Celatoxia albidisca) by its extensive chalk-white upperwing across most of both wings and pure white, delicately dotted underside.
Udara akasa.habitat: High-elevation shola-grassland margins, montane streams, and wet evergreen paths above 1,200 m.
Udara akasa.behavior: Gentle fluttering flight at low to middle height around stream-side Persicaria thickets; males puddle steadily on sunlit wet sand.
Udara akasa.season: Active year-round in high hills, peaking from September to April.
Udara akasa.tnDistribution: High-elevation Western Ghats peaks of Tamil Nadu including the Nilgiris (Ooty, Avalanche, Kotagiri), Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Valparai, Anamalai, Megamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Udara akasa.notes: Represented in the southern Indian hills by endemic subspecies Udara akasa mavisa; its association with Persicaria chinensis keeps adults anchored near cool shola streams.

Celatoxia albidisca.headline: Western Ghats endemic hedge blue bearing crisp white discal windows
Celatoxia albidisca.upperwing: Tailless; males are deep dull indigo-blue with narrow black margins, a small sharply defined pure white patch in forewing spaces 2 and 3 outside the cell, and a neat white discal spot at the base of hindwing space 6; females are darker brown with broader white patches and faint blue bases.
Celatoxia albidisca.underwing: Pale whitish-grey patterned with fine crisp dark spots, bisinuate forewing postdiscal dashes, a small black basal spot in hindwing space 7, and neat dark marginal dots.
Celatoxia albidisca.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Plain Hedge Blue (Celastrina lavendularis) and Common Hedge Blue (Acytolepis puspa) by crisp pure white discal spots above, and from White Hedge Blue (Udara akasa) by deep indigo-blue wings rather than mostly white upperwings.
Celatoxia albidisca.habitat: Montane evergreen and shola-border forests generally above 900 m.
Celatoxia albidisca.behavior: Swift flier along shaded hill roads and canopy openings; males descend regularly to mud-puddle on damp gravel alongside Udara akasa.
Celatoxia albidisca.season: Recorded intermittently between September and April across high Western Ghats ridges.
Celatoxia albidisca.tnDistribution: Western Ghats endemic found in higher Tamil Nadu ranges including Nilgiris, Palani Hills, Anamalais, Megamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Celatoxia albidisca.notes: Endemic to the Western Ghats; even a brief basking glance showing the compact white discal windows on deep indigo wings confirms field identity.

Euchrysops cnejus.headline: WPA-protected pulse blue flashing twin orange-capped tornal eyespots
Euchrysops cnejus.upperwing: Males are pale violet-lilac blue with narrow dark borders and two prominent black marginal spots in hindwing spaces 1b and 2; females are dark brown with bright blue basal suffusion and orange-crowned black hindwing marginal spots.
Euchrysops cnejus.underwing: Pale buff-grey patterned with crisp white-rimmed brown bands, a small black costal spot near the forewing mid-costa, two jet-black sub-basal spots on the hindwing, two bright orange-crowned black tornal eyespots flecked with metallic green, and a short thread-like tail.
Euchrysops cnejus.similarSpecies: Separated from Forget-me-not (Catochrysops strabo) by two black basal hindwing dots and two equal orange-crowned tornal eyespots rather than one main eyespot in space 2, and from Plains Cupid (Chilades pandava) by larger size and buff-grey tone.
Euchrysops cnejus.habitat: Pulse farmlands, fallow scrub, urban gardens, dry grasslands, and hill foothills.
Euchrysops cnejus.behavior: Brisk low flight over flowering gram fields and open weeds; perches frequently on legume pods and visits damp soil.
Euchrysops cnejus.season: Common year-round statewide, peaking during post-monsoon cropping seasons.
Euchrysops cnejus.tnDistribution: Abundant across every district of Tamil Nadu from coastal plains and delta croplands to Nilgiri and Eastern Ghats foothills.
Euchrysops cnejus.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Euchrysops cnejus.notes: Despite legal protection under India's Wildlife (Protection) Act, it thrives across agricultural landscapes; caterpillars bore inside pulse pods guarded by Camponotus and Crematogaster ants.

Freyeria putli.headline: Minute brown grass jewel dotted below with metallic green-scaled black spots
Freyeria putli.upperwing: Tailless and completely lacking blue sheen; both sexes are plain dark earthy brown above with a row of small black submarginal spots along the hindwing edge lacking bright orange inner crowns.
Freyeria putli.underwing: Silky pale grey-brown dotted with crisp white-ringed dark brown spots across cell and disc, and a hindwing marginal row of jet-black spots speckled with glittering metallic green-blue scales where orange inner crescents are absent or reduced to faint buff traces.
Freyeria putli.similarSpecies: Separated from all tiny grass blues (Zizina, Zizeeria, Zizula) by the metallic green-scaled black marginal spots below and brown males; differs from Grass Jewel (Freyeria trochylus) by lacking vivid orange crowns inward of the black hindwing spots.
Freyeria putli.habitat: Dry open scrub, short dry lawns, coastal dunes, stony footpaths, and fallow fields.
Freyeria putli.behavior: Flutters weakly barely an inch over bare soil and prostrate herbs; rests on tiny pebbles or Heliotropium twigs with wings closed.
Freyeria putli.season: Abundant year-round statewide, especially in warm dry months.
Freyeria putli.tnDistribution: Found throughout all Tamil Nadu districts from coastal sands and urban parks to dry foothills.
Freyeria putli.notes: One of the smallest butterflies in the world; larvae feed on prostrate Heliotropium and Indigofera shoots attended by small ants such as Tapinoma and Pheidole.

Freyeria trochylus.headline: Localized miniature jewel carrying bright orange-crowned hindwing spots
Freyeria trochylus.upperwing: Tailless; both sexes are dark smoky brown lacking blue scaling, with the hindwing submarginal black spots distinctly capped inwardly by warm orange-ochreous crescents (brightest in females and fresh individuals).
Freyeria trochylus.underwing: Pale brownish-grey marked with white-ringed dark brown basal and discal spots, and a hindwing marginal series of metallic green-speckled black spots crowned conspicuously on the inner side by vivid orange lunules.
Freyeria trochylus.similarSpecies: Closely mirrors Small Grass Jewel (Freyeria putli) in size and ground pattern, but distinguished by prominent bright orange inner crowns bordering the metallic-flecked black hindwing spots on both surfaces.
Freyeria trochylus.habitat: Semi-arid stony scrublands, dry grassy fallows, and rainshadow foothills.
Freyeria trochylus.behavior: Hovers slowly inches above sun-baked ground and tiny prostrate herbs, basking briefly with half-parted wings during calm mornings.
Freyeria trochylus.season: Patchy and localized, recorded mainly in dry and post-monsoon seasons from October to April.
Freyeria trochylus.tnDistribution: Scarce and localized in drier western and southern parts of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Erode, Tiruppur, Madurai, and dry Western Ghats rainshadow foothills.
Freyeria trochylus.notes: Long lumped under Freyeria putli in regional checklists; larvae secrete sweet exudates attracting tending ants on low dry-zone herbs.

Chilades pandava.headline: Garden cycad blue whose caterpillars feed on sprouting sago-palm fronds
Chilades pandava.upperwing: Males are bright lavender-blue with narrow dark outer borders and a small dark tornal spot on the hindwing; females are dark brown with bright blue basal sheen and orange-crowned black marginal spots near the hindwing tornus.
Chilades pandava.underwing: Pale buff-brown to grey-brown with crisp white-edged darker bands, four small black sub-basal spots across the hindwing, two prominent black subtornal eyespots in spaces 1b and 2 capped brightly in orange, and a tiny short tail at vein 2.
Chilades pandava.similarSpecies: Separated from Lime Blue (Chilades lajus) by its fine tail and orange-capped tornal spots, and from Small Cupid (Chilades parrhassius) by larger size, wider seasonal variation, and close fidelity to Cycas plants.
Chilades pandava.habitat: Urban gardens, parks, institutional campuses with ornamental cycads, and wild Cycas hill slopes.
Chilades pandava.behavior: Weak, busy flight circling ornamental cycad crowns; females lay dozens of eggs on tender uncurling fronds and adults visit small garden flowers.
Chilades pandava.season: Abundant year-round wherever cycad shoots flush, especially post-monsoon.
Chilades pandava.tnDistribution: Statewide across cities, towns, and forested Cycas hills of Tamil Nadu from Chennai and Coimbatore to Eastern and Western Ghats slopes.
Chilades pandava.notes: Obligately ant-associated on cycad flush, where Crematogaster, Camponotus, and Tapinoma ants aggressively defend feeding caterpillars against predators.

Chilades parrhassius.headline: Compact tailed acacia cupid with clean pale grey-white undersides
Chilades parrhassius.upperwing: Males are dark lilac-blue with a relatively wide dusky brown forewing outer border and dark hindwing marginal spots capped with orange; females are brown with faint pale blue basal dusting and clearer orange-ringed hindwing spots.
Chilades parrhassius.underwing: Pale whitish-grey marked cleanly with white-edged dark brown postdiscal spots and bars, four jet-black sub-basal spots across the hindwing, two black subtornal eyespots crowned in bright orange and speckled with metallic scales, and a short white-tipped tail.
Chilades parrhassius.similarSpecies: Smaller with cleaner whitish-grey underside and wider male dark border than Plains Cupid (Chilades pandava); distinguished from Babul Blues (Azanus) by possessing a fine tail and bright orange tornal crowns.
Chilades parrhassius.habitat: Arid thorn scrub, Acacia grasslands, dry foothill pastures, and open sandy scrub.
Chilades parrhassius.behavior: Flits rapidly close to low thorny scrub and dry grass clumps; settles on tiny dry-zone herbs and damp soil margins.
Chilades parrhassius.season: Active throughout dry and post-monsoon months, peaking from October to March.
Chilades parrhassius.tnDistribution: Found across drier plains and foothills of Tamil Nadu including Coimbatore, Erode, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Ramanathapuram, Sathyamangalam, and Chengalpattu scrub.
Chilades parrhassius.notes: Often confused with tiny Chilades pandava in dry scrub, yet strictly tied to Mimosoideae thorn shrubs rather than cycads and tended by ants.

Chilades lajus.headline: Tailless citrus blue showing a dark hindwing blotch in dry winter broods
Chilades lajus.upperwing: Tailless; males are deep purple-blue with a slender dark marginal border and dusky hindwing marginal spots, while females are dark brown with vivid metallic blue confined to the basal half of both wings and pale-ringed dark hindwing spots.
Chilades lajus.underwing: Dull brownish-grey densely speckled with white-ringed black spots and bars (developing a large diffuse dark chocolate cloud across the hindwing disc in dry-season forms), small dark subtornal dots flecked faintly with metallic scales, and no orange crowns.
Chilades lajus.similarSpecies: Separated from Plains Cupid (Chilades pandava) and Gram Blue (Euchrysops cnejus) by lacking tails and orange tornal crowns, and from Grass Blues by its larger size, dense dark spots, and dry-season hindwing blotch.
Chilades lajus.habitat: Citrus orchards, backyard kitchen gardens, dry scrub, and woodland edges.
Chilades lajus.behavior: Flutters persistently around tender shoots of lime and curry-leaf relatives; basks with spread wings on sunny foliage and sips nectar at garden blooms.
Chilades lajus.season: Common year-round statewide, with dry-season clouded forms appearing from December to April.
Chilades lajus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu orchards, home gardens, and foothills including Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli, Salem, Dindigul, and Nilgiri slopes.
Chilades lajus.notes: Larvae feed on tender Rutaceae shoots and are regularly tended by Camponotus and Crematogaster ants; seasonal dry-winter forms display a dramatic dark discal cloud below.

Arhopala centaurus.headline: Large woodland oakblue with silvery-green edged cell spots beneath
Arhopala centaurus.upperwing: Males are rich dark purple-blue bordered by a thread-fine black line along the margins; females are lighter shining violet-blue over the inner half of both wings with broad dark brown costal and outer margins.
Arhopala centaurus.underwing: Warm grey-brown to purplish-brown crossed by large chocolate-brown bands and cell spots neatly edged in pale buff, with diagnostic metallic silvery-green lines outlining the forewing cell spots and an orange-free metallic green-dusted tornal lobe beside a stout white-tipped tail.
Arhopala centaurus.similarSpecies: Separated cleanly from Large Oakblue (Arhopala amantes) by the shining silvery-green outlines around the forewing underside cell spots and narrower dark borders on the female; lacks the frosty forewing apex of Tamil Oakblue (Arhopala bazaloides).
Arhopala centaurus.habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous hill forests, shaded stream corridors, and wooded plantations.
Arhopala centaurus.behavior: Strong, rapid canopy flyer that rests in shaded undergrowth during midday heat, occasionally basking with wings half-open on sunlit tree-trunk foliage or puddling on damp sand.
Arhopala centaurus.season: Recorded nearly year-round in wet hill forests, peaking from August to February.
Arhopala centaurus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, KMTR) and wooded Eastern Ghats hills (Shervaroys, Pachamalai, Kolli Hills).
Arhopala centaurus.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Arhopala centaurus pirama; caterpillars shelter inside folded leaves guarded fiercely by weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina).

Arhopala amantes.headline: Giant metallic-blue oakblue living in weaver-ant territories
Arhopala amantes.upperwing: Males flash brilliant deep metallic violet-blue bordered only by a hairline black margin; females show bright sky-to-purple blue restricted to basal wing discs framed by very broad dark black-brown margins.
Arhopala amantes.underwing: Silvery lilac-grey to pale pinkish-brown marked with bold chocolate-brown spots and angled discal bands edged in pale grey, a neat pair of square spots at right angles in spaces 4 and 5 of the hindwing, bright metallic green scales at the tornus, and a stout white-tipped tail.
Arhopala amantes.similarSpecies: Larger and brighter blue dorsally than Centaur Oakblue (Arhopala centaurus), with paler pinkish-grey undersides lacking metallic green rims inside the forewing cell; much larger and cleaner-marked than Kanara Oakblue (Arhopala alea).
Arhopala amantes.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous forests, riverine gallery woodland, shaded hill valleys, and wooded avenues.
Arhopala amantes.behavior: High-perching forest canopy flyer that descends to lower twigs in morning sun, basks briefly with partially spread wings, and feeds on tree sap or damp mineral patches.
Arhopala amantes.season: Active across most of the year with strong post-monsoon numbers from September to March.
Arhopala amantes.tnDistribution: Common in Western Ghats foothills (Kallar, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, KMTR) and recorded across Eastern Ghats ranges including Kalvarayan, Shervarayan (700-800 m), Pachamalai, and Sirumalai.
Arhopala amantes.notes: Subspecies Arhopala amantes amantes maintains an obligate partnership with Asian weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina), whose aggressive patrols shield larvae on host foliage.

Arhopala bazaloides.headline: Dusted oakblue listed among TNBS’s 4 target species awaiting validation
Arhopala bazaloides.upperwing: Males are deep lustrous purplish-blue; females are dark brown with purple wing bases.
Arhopala bazaloides.underwing: Pale lilac-brown marked with darker brown outlined bands and dusted with pale frosted scales toward the forewing apex.
Arhopala bazaloides.similarSpecies: Frosty pale dusting near the forewing apex underside helps distinguish Tamil Oakblue from other brown-banded Arhopala oakblues.
Arhopala bazaloides.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen foothill forests.
Arhopala bazaloides.behavior: Skulks in shaded understorey and settles with wings closed.
Arhopala bazaloides.tnDistribution: Listed among the 4 checklist species awaiting validated TNBS sighting confirmation in Tamil Nadu.
Arhopala bazaloides.notes: Look closely at frosted forewing apices beneath high evergreen canopies; dated photos help validate its Tamil Nadu status.

Arhopala alea.headline: Western Ghats endemic oakblue washed with rosy lilac beneath
Arhopala alea.upperwing: Males are deep glossy violet-blue with noticeably broad black costal and outer borders on both forewing and hindwing; females are dark greyish-black with muted pale bluish scaling confined to the basal wing centers and a more rounded forewing apex.
Arhopala alea.underwing: Warm brown overlaid with a soft rosy or pale lilac sheen, crossed by a long narrow slightly curved forewing discal band, a broken hindwing discal band, white-dusted scaling around the anal angle, and a slender white-tipped tail at vein 2.
Arhopala alea.similarSpecies: Smaller than Large Oakblue (Arhopala amantes) and Centaur Oakblue (Arhopala centaurus), lacking silvery-green cell outlines; separated from Tamil Oakblue (Arhopala bazaloides) by its rosy-lilac underside tone and lack of frosty pale apical forewing dusting.
Arhopala alea.habitat: Dense wet evergreen and moist semi-evergreen forest canopies and shaded hill streams in the southern Western Ghats.
Arhopala alea.behavior: Shade-loving forest dweller that keeps close to evergreen undergrowth and mid-storey branches, settling motionless with closed wings on leaf undersides.
Arhopala alea.season: Observed mainly during post-monsoon and cool winter months from October to March.
Arhopala alea.tnDistribution: Endemic to the Western Ghats, occurring locally in Tamil Nadu wet forests across the Nilgiris, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Arhopala alea.notes: Also called Sahyadri Rosy Oakblue; its restricted Western Ghats distribution and dependence on intact evergreen canopy trees make it a key bioindicator of forest continuity.

Arhopala abseus.headline: Triple-tailed forest oakblue bearing a stark white costal spot
Arhopala abseus.upperwing: Males show brilliant lustrous metallic blue with darkened veins and a broad black forewing border widening toward the apex; females are more rounded-winged with duller violet-blue central areas enclosed within wider blackish-brown margins.
Arhopala abseus.underwing: Glossy chocolate-brown suffused with pinkish-lilac sheen and heavily banded with pale-edged dark markings, diagnosed instantly by a crisp solid white costal spot in space 7 of the hindwing, metallic blue-green tornal scales, and three white-tipped tails at veins 1b, 2, and 3.
Arhopala abseus.similarSpecies: Easily separated from all other Tamil Nadu Arhopala oakblues by its smaller size, triple-tailed hindwing, and bright white mid-costal spot on the hindwing underside; Many-tailed Oakblue (Thaduka multicaudata) also has three tails but lacks the white costal spot and shows broken square spots.
Arhopala abseus.habitat: Shaded evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, moist ravines, and dense riparian undergrowth.
Arhopala abseus.behavior: Low-to-mid-storey forest skulker that flies swiftly between shaded perches, settles on fern fronds with wings tightly shut, and visits bird droppings or damp forest mud.
Arhopala abseus.season: Recorded mainly from September to April in humid hill tracts.
Arhopala abseus.tnDistribution: Moist evergreen Western Ghats pockets of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Arhopala abseus.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Arhopala abseus indicus; its short forewing vein 9 and triple-tailed hindwing set it apart anatomically from typical oakblues.

Thaduka multicaudata.headline: Unmistakable Sahyadri oakblue sporting three bold tails and scalloped wings
Thaduka multicaudata.upperwing: Both wings are black with a bright silvery-smalt blue basal and discal field, slightly broader and paler blue in females, framed by deeply scalloped hindwing margins and three black tails.
Thaduka multicaudata.underwing: Dark vinous-brown to purplish-grey crossed by square dark discal spots and angled submarginal lines on the forewing, irregular broken wavy dark bands on the hindwing, and three tails at veins 1b, 2, and 3 with the middle tail longest.
Thaduka multicaudata.similarSpecies: Distinct from all true Arhopala species by its scalloped wing outline, silver-blue dorsal sheen inside wide black margins, and three prominent tails lacking the white costal spot of Aberrant Bushblue (Arhopala abseus).
Thaduka multicaudata.habitat: Wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, wooded river gorges, and shaded forest tracks.
Thaduka multicaudata.behavior: Fast, erratic flyer that perches high on shaded subcanopy branches and drops down briefly to damp sand or sunlit forest paths during morning hours.
Thaduka multicaudata.season: Scarce and localized, seen mostly between October and April.
Thaduka multicaudata.tnDistribution: Southern and central Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Anamalais, Siruvani, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Thaduka multicaudata.notes: Only species in the genus Thaduka; southern Indian populations belong to the Western Ghats subspecies Thaduka multicaudata kanara.

Surendra quercetorum.headline: Wood-brown underside blue whose females lack dorsal blue and carry two tails
Surendra quercetorum.upperwing: Males are deep glossy violet-purple framed by broad dark brown costal and outer borders; females are uniform dull smoky-brown without any blue scaling, showing a paler brown central sheen in bright sun.
Surendra quercetorum.underwing: Bark-like pale ochreous-brown to greyish-brown crossed by fine, irregular dark wavy lines, minute submarginal black dots, and a tiny silver-ringed tornal spot; males bear one short tail at vein 2 while females carry two tails at veins 2 and 3.
Surendra quercetorum.similarSpecies: Separated from Silver-streaked Acacia Blue (Zinaspa todara) by lacking crisp silvery-white underside streak edges and by the female's completely brown upperside without blue.
Surendra quercetorum.habitat: Acacia-rich thorny scrub, deciduous foothills, forest clearings, and woodland edges.
Surendra quercetorum.behavior: Flies rapidly around thorny Acacia climbers, rests closely appressed against dry twigs and foliage where its bark-brown underside camouflages it, and feeds on small white flowers.
Surendra quercetorum.season: Active almost year-round, peaking from October to March.
Surendra quercetorum.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills and foothills including Coimbatore, Kallar, Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Anamalais, KMTR, Pachamalai, and Shervaroys.
Surendra quercetorum.notes: Represented in peninsular India by subspecies Surendra quercetorum biplagiata; larvae are tended by Crematogaster and Anoplolepis ants on young Acacia shoots.

Zinaspa todara.headline: Acacia-feeding hill blue adorned with fine silver-edged ventral lines
Zinaspa todara.upperwing: Males are black with a brilliant shining violet-blue discal patch across the cell and lower half of both wings; females retain duller, paler purple-blue over the inner forewing and variable basal areas of the hindwing.
Zinaspa todara.underwing: Warm pinkish-brown to purplish-grey cleanly traced with fine brown discal and submarginal lines neatly edged on the outer side with glistening silvery-white streaks, a small orange-capped black tornal spot, and a single fine white-tipped tail at vein 2.
Zinaspa todara.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Common Acacia Blue (Surendra quercetorum) by the crisp silver-white edges lining its underside brown bands, single fine tail in both sexes, and purple-blue scaling present on the female upperside.
Zinaspa todara.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen hill forests, bamboo edges, and Acacia-draped stream valleys.
Zinaspa todara.behavior: Brisk flyer around thorny lianas and mid-storey canopies; perches on sunlit edge leaves with wings held closed or half-open in early morning.
Zinaspa todara.season: Recorded mainly from September to April in hill forests.
Zinaspa todara.tnDistribution: Western Ghats and higher Eastern Ghats tracts of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Shervaroys.
Zinaspa todara.notes: Named after the Toda people of the Nilgiris by Frederic Moore in 1883; the nominate subspecies Zinaspa todara todara is characteristic of the southern Western Ghats.

Zesius chrysomallus.headline: Coppery-red male hairstreak whose caterpillars shelter inside weaver-ant nests
Zesius chrysomallus.upperwing: Strongly dimorphic: males are glowing pale coppery-red finely veined and narrowly edged in dark brown with silver-blue rimmed black anal spots, whereas females are dull rufous-brown richly glossed with pale metallic violet-blue over the basal and discal areas.
Zesius chrysomallus.underwing: Silvery grey-white marked with pale cinnamon-red to ochreous spots and wavy bands finely rimmed in dark brown and white, highlighted by a bold reddish spot near the forewing base and orange-crowned black tornal spots; males have two equal tails while females carry an extra third short tail at vein 3.
Zesius chrysomallus.similarSpecies: Males cannot be confused with Indian Red Flash (Rapala iarbus) or Cornelian (Deudorix epijarbas) once the pale grey underside spotted with dark-rimmed red-brown bars and two tails are seen; females differ from Arhopala oakblues by their silvery-grey spotted underside.
Zesius chrysomallus.habitat: Wooded plains, dry and moist deciduous forests, coastal groves, and orchards holding weaver-ant colonies.
Zesius chrysomallus.behavior: Swift, dashing flight around canopy trees; males perch aggressively on sunlit outer branches and females search closely for weaver-ant nests before laying eggs.
Zesius chrysomallus.season: Flies nearly year-round across plains and foothills, peaking from August to February.
Zesius chrysomallus.tnDistribution: Widespread in Tamil Nadu across Chennai coastal groves, Coimbatore, Kallar, Mudumalai, Erode, Pachamalai, Sirumalai, and Tirunelveli plains.
Zesius chrysomallus.notes: Exhibits one of India's tightest butterfly-ant symbioses: larvae often rest inside silken leaf-nests built by weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina), which aggressively guard them.

Amblypodia anita.headline: Hooked-tip purple hairstreak that closes into a dead brown leaf
Amblypodia anita.upperwing: Males are deep rich royal purple bordered narrowly in black along the forewing outer margin and broadly along the hindwing costa with a dull red anal lobe; females are duller brown with bright purplish-blue patches confined to the forewing cell and disc.
Amblypodia anita.underwing: Coppery rufous-brown to purplish-ochreous crossed cleanly from forewing apex to hindwing inner margin by a dark midrib-like discal line, giving resting individuals uncanny resemblance to a fallen dry leaf, with a blunt single tail and short tornal lobe.
Amblypodia anita.similarSpecies: Its strongly hooked forewing apex, single broad blunt tail, and dry-leaf underside with a continuous midrib line separate it easily from all Arhopala oakblues and Yamfly (Loxura atymnus).
Amblypodia anita.habitat: Dry evergreen forests, thorny scrub woodlands, coastal sacred groves, and moist deciduous foothills.
Amblypodia anita.behavior: Rapid, erratic flyer that settles suddenly on twigs or dry foliage with wings tightly shut, turning sideways to hide its silhouette like a withered leaf; also mud-puddles on damp sand.
Amblypodia anita.season: Present across most of the year, especially common from September to March.
Amblypodia anita.tnDistribution: Wide range from coastal Tamil Nadu scrub (Chennai, Guindy, Point Calimere) through interior plains to Western and Eastern Ghats foothills (Kallar, Sathyamangalam, Pachamalai, Sirumalai).
Amblypodia anita.notes: Subspecies Amblypodia anita dina breeds on climbing Olax shrubs; caterpillars secrete honeydew attracting attending ants along thorny stems.

Iraota timoleon.headline: Fig-feeding canopy hairstreak hiding glittering silver streaks beneath
Iraota timoleon.upperwing: Males gleam brilliant metallic azure-blue across the basal two-thirds of both wings framed by wide velvety black margins; females are plain dark purplish-brown above with at most a faint blue basal sheen and carry two tails plus a third tooth-like projection.
Iraota timoleon.underwing: Deep reddish chocolate-brown embellished with a prominent silvery-white club-shaped streak inside the forewing cell, a round silver cell-end spot, a bold forked silvery costal band on the hindwing, and pale lilac-dusted marginal areas; males have one tail and females two.
Iraota timoleon.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu: no other medium-large hairstreak pairs a metallic blue male upperside with a rich chocolate underside bearing bold silvery-white cell and costal streaks.
Iraota timoleon.habitat: Banyan and fig avenues, semi-evergreen and deciduous forests, village groves, and wooded hill foothills.
Iraota timoleon.behavior: Strong, fast flyer that stays high around fig tree canopies, basking with wings open in early morning sun and occasionally visiting damp mud or overripe fruit.
Iraota timoleon.season: Seen year-round where Ficus trees fruit, peaking post-monsoon from October to February.
Iraota timoleon.tnDistribution: Recorded statewide in Tamil Nadu from Chennai, Tiruchirappalli, and Coimbatore banyan groves to Kallar, Nilgiris, Anamalais, Sirumalai, and Pachamalai.
Iraota timoleon.notes: Subspecies Iraota timoleon arsaces feeds inside young Ficus syconia (figs) and tender shoots, sometimes attended by ants; pupates in bark crevices.

Pratapa deva.headline: Mistletoe royal whose males conceal a long black hair tuft beneath the forewing
Pratapa deva.upperwing: Males are shining pale mauve-blue with broad jet-black apical and outer borders on the forewing and a rounded glandular costal patch on the hindwing; females are paler blue with dark-marked veins, narrower borders, and no costal patch.
Pratapa deva.underwing: Creamy-white to pale greyish-white marked only by a broken series of thin dark postdiscal dashes, two orange-crowned black tornal spots with metallic blue scaling, and two delicate white-tipped tails; males carry a long black hair tuft along the bowed forewing inner margin.
Pratapa deva.similarSpecies: Separated from Peacock Royal (Tajuria cippus) and Plains Blue Royal (Tajuria jehana) by its paler mauve-blue male upperside with huge black apical area, broken underside dash line, and the male's prominent black forewing hair tuft.
Pratapa deva.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen hill forests, wooded valleys, and mistletoe-draped canopy trees.
Pratapa deva.behavior: Rapid canopy flyer that perches high on sunlit mistletoe clumps and outer tree branches, occasionally descending to hilltops or flowering shrubs in morning hours.
Pratapa deva.season: Recorded across most months in hill forests, peaking between September and March.
Pratapa deva.tnDistribution: Western Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and KMTR, plus wooded Eastern Ghats hills like Shervaroys and Pachamalai.
Pratapa deva.notes: Represented in southern India by Pratapa deva deva; caterpillars mimic mistletoe buds and shoots while feeding unobtrusively high in host crowns.

Tajuria jehana.headline: Lowland mistletoe royal breeding quietly across gardens and scrub plains
Tajuria jehana.upperwing: Males are duller slaty-blue than Peacock Royal with broad black forewing costal and apical borders; females are paler greyish-blue with a small whitish patch beyond the forewing cell, broader hindwing margins, and a darker discal lunular band.
