Tajuria jehana.underwing: Creamy greyish-white crossed by a fine continuous wavy brown discal line, two faint submarginal lunular rows, two prominent black tornal spots capped in dull orange-red, and two white-tipped black tails at veins 1b and 2.
Tajuria jehana.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Peacock Royal (Tajuria cippus) by its duller slaty-blue male upperside, continuous fine brown underside discal line rather than disjoint black dashes, and duller orange-red tornal caps; lacks the male hair tuft of Tufted White Royal (Pratapa deva).
Tajuria jehana.habitat: Open plains, urban gardens, dry scrub, roadside avenue trees, and dry deciduous foothills supporting Dendrophthoe mistletoes.
Tajuria jehana.behavior: Less strictly tied to high forest canopy than other royals; flies quickly around mistletoe clumps on roadside neem, mango, or tamarind trees and perches at medium height.
Tajuria jehana.season: Active throughout the year across plains and foothills, common from October to March.
Tajuria jehana.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains and foothills including Chennai, Coimbatore, Tiruchirappalli, Madurai, Sathyamangalam, and eastern Western Ghats fringes.
Tajuria jehana.notes: Early stages on Loranthaceae mistletoes in Coimbatore were documented in detail by TNBS member Ramanasaran Hari in Pattampoochi Magazine.

Tajuria cippus.headline: Electric cerulean-blue royal with twin vivid orange-crowned tornal spots
Tajuria cippus.upperwing: Males flash brilliant glowing royal-blue framed by broad black apical and costal borders on the forewing; females are paler greyish-blue with dark veins, a prominent curved discal band of dark lunules on the hindwing, and wider blackish margins.
Tajuria cippus.underwing: Uniform soft dove-grey crossed by an interrupted postdiscal row of fine black dashes (often very faint on the forewing) and marked on the hindwing by two large jet-black tornal spots brightly crowned with vivid orange and two long white-tipped black tails.
Tajuria cippus.similarSpecies: Males are brighter, richer blue than Plains Blue Royal (Tajuria jehana) and lack the forewing sex brand of Branded Royal (Tajuria melastigma); underside differs from Banded Royal (Rachana jalindra) by uniform dove-grey ground rather than half golden-brown and half white.
Tajuria cippus.habitat: Wooded plains, riverine forests, deciduous hills, orchards, and canopy trees hosting heavy mistletoe growth.
Tajuria cippus.behavior: Swift, high-perching butterfly that circles sunlit tree crowns and hilltops in morning hours, occasionally descending to nectar on Lantana or wet sand.
Tajuria cippus.season: Seen year-round in wooded tracts, peaking between September and February.
Tajuria cippus.tnDistribution: Occurs widely across Tamil Nadu from Chennai, Coimbatore, and Trichy wooded campuses to Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalais, KMTR, Pachamalai, and Shervaroys.
Tajuria cippus.notes: Subspecies Tajuria cippus cippus shows striking pupal camouflage resembling a bird dropping or knotted mistletoe twig.

Tajuria maculata.headline: Rare protected forest royal spotted boldly across snow-white undersides
Tajuria maculata.upperwing: Males show a shining sky-blue central field heavily suffused with white toward the outer edge inside broad black forewing borders; females have the blue largely replaced by a crisp white central patch dusted with lilac-blue only near the wing bases.
Tajuria maculata.underwing: Pure chalky-white scattered conspicuously with bold irregular jet-black spots across both wings, paired with two large black tornal spots and twin delicate black white-tipped tails.
Tajuria maculata.similarSpecies: Totally distinct from every other Tamil Nadu royal by its bold black-spotted snow-white underside and extensive dorsal white patches.
Tajuria maculata.habitat: Dense wet evergreen and moist semi-evergreen mid-elevation hill forests rich in tree-canopy mistletoes.
Tajuria maculata.behavior: Elusive canopy dweller that rarely descends to ground level, darting between sunlit high-forest foliage and mistletoe clusters in morning gaps.
Tajuria maculata.season: Extremely scarce; recorded sporadically during post-monsoon and early summer months (November to April).
Tajuria maculata.tnDistribution: Historically known from the Nilgiris in the Tamil Nadu Western Ghats, with rare verified sightings in high-rainfall Nilgiri-Wayanad and southern Western Ghats forests.
Tajuria maculata.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Tajuria maculata.notes: Rediscovered in the southern Western Ghats after more than a century without confirmed regional records following historical Nilgiri specimens; strictly protected under Indian wildlife law.

Tajuria melastigma.headline: Protected cerulean royal carrying a large velvety square brand on the forewing
Tajuria melastigma.upperwing: Males gleam bright cerulean-blue and are immediately recognized by a large, squarish velvety-dark sexual brand at the end of the forewing cell encircled by a curved black costal band; females are duller pale blue lacking the brand and carrying broader black borders.
Tajuria melastigma.underwing: Dull pinkish-grey to pale vinaceous-brown crossed by faint, delicate red-brown postdiscal linear dashes edged thinly in whitish, two orange-capped black tornal spots, and two delicate white-tipped tails.
Tajuria melastigma.similarSpecies: Male's large square coppery-dark forewing sex brand separates it cleanly from Peacock Royal (Tajuria cippus), while its pinkish-grey underside lacks the crisp white discal line of Broadtail Royal (Creon cleobis).
Tajuria melastigma.habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist hill forests, coffee estates, and mistletoe-infested hill canopies.
Tajuria melastigma.behavior: High-flying forest canopy hairstreak that perches briefly on sunlit outer foliage along ridge trails and forest streams.
Tajuria melastigma.season: Uncommon; seen mainly from October to April across moist hill ranges.
Tajuria melastigma.tnDistribution: Recorded locally in Tamil Nadu Western Ghats including Nilgiris, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Tajuria melastigma.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Tajuria melastigma.notes: Legally protected in India; males use the prominent quadrate forewing scent brand to disperse courtship pheromones while perched high in canopy gaps.

Creon cleobis.headline: Cream-brown underside royal bearing a fine sinuous red-brown discal line
Creon cleobis.upperwing: Males are deep glossy royal-blue with wide black apical and outer borders on the forewing; females are paler sky-blue with narrower, smoothly curved dark brown apical borders and dark marginal spots along the hindwing.
Creon cleobis.underwing: Warm creamy-brown crossed on both wings by a crisp, narrow red-brown discal line that turns sharply angular toward the hindwing inner margin, accompanied by two orange-crowned black tornal spots dusted in blue-grey scales and two white-tipped tails including a broadened inner tail.
Creon cleobis.similarSpecies: Warm creamy-brown underside with a crisp red-brown discal line distinguishes it cleanly from the dove-grey Peacock Royal (Tajuria cippus) and the boldly two-toned white-and-brown Banded Royal (Rachana jalindra).
Creon cleobis.habitat: Moist deciduous, semi-evergreen, and evergreen hill forests, shola edges, and wooded valleys.
Creon cleobis.behavior: Fast canopy flyer that frequently hill-tops on wooded peaks and visits sunlit blossom clusters or damp forest-stream sand.
Creon cleobis.season: Flies mostly from September to March across mid-to-high elevations.
Creon cleobis.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, and KMTR.
Creon cleobis.notes: Males possess a specialized vein fold and hair tuft near space 1a on the hindwing; caterpillars feed on mistletoe flowers and tender leaves high in forest trees.

Rachana jalindra.headline: Fast-flying mistletoe hairstreak highlighted in the Dec 2024 Pachamalai survey
Rachana jalindra.upperwing: Males are deep glossy violet-blue bordered in black; females are dark brown with bright white lower hindwing patches and twin delicate tails.
Rachana jalindra.underwing: Crisp pearly-white outer wing contrasting sharply against rich golden-brown inner wing halves separated by a clean straight dark line.
Rachana jalindra.similarSpecies: Two-toned golden-brown and snow-white underside with long white-tipped tails distinguishes Banded Royal cleanly from Broadtail Royal.
Rachana jalindra.habitat: Dense hill forests and forested slopes rich in parasitic mistletoe shrubs.
Rachana jalindra.behavior: Fast canopy flyer that settles briefly on high foliage and flower clusters.
Rachana jalindra.season: Peaks during post-monsoon and winter months.
Rachana jalindra.tnDistribution: Western Ghats (Kallar, Mudumalai, Siruvani) and a notable Eastern Ghats population recorded at Pachamalai Hills in December 2024.
Rachana jalindra.wpaStatus: Legally protected in India under Schedule II of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Rachana jalindra.notes: Recorded in healthy numbers in thick deciduous-evergreen Pachamalai forest during the December 2024 Trichy Forest Division survey.
sources: Pattampoochi Issue 27, Pachamalai Survey & Picture Story (pp. 21–22)

Hypolycaena nilgirica.headline: Endemic dark-brown hill tit breeding on ground-dwelling Eulophia orchids
Hypolycaena nilgirica.upperwing: Unlike blue royals, both sexes are dark brown above: males are plain dark reddish-brown with a subtle purple-brown sheen and white-rimmed black tornal spots crowned faintly in dull orange, while females are slightly paler brown with prominent white lunules above the hindwing tornal spots.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.underwing: Creamy-white to pale silvery-grey delicately marked with fine dull orange-brown cell-end bars, thin ring-like discal lines, faint submarginal lunules, two small black tornal spots near the lobe, and two white-ciliated black tails.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.similarSpecies: Instantly separated from Orchid Tit (Hypolycaena othona) by lacking blue uppersides in males and lacking the prominent black costal spot near the base of the hindwing underside.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.habitat: Foothill stream edges, grassy rocky slopes, open moist deciduous woods, and seasonal orchid habitats.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.behavior: Weak, fluttering low flyer compared to canopy royals; stays close to ground orchids and stream banks, perching on low herbs and grass stems with gentle hindwing movements.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.season: Seasonal and localized; most records fall between October and April around orchid flowering.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills of Tamil Nadu including the Nilgiris, Amaidhi Solai near Kombai Dam in the eastern Palani foothills, Anamalais, and KMTR.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Hypolycaena nilgirica.notes: Endemic to the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka; its Indian larval host plant, the terrestrial orchid Eulophia epidendraea, was confirmed only recently in southern Western Ghats foothills.

Hypolycaena othona.headline: Protected orchid-feeding hairstreak bearing a bold black subcostal spot beneath
Hypolycaena othona.upperwing: Males glow silky deep blue across the inner wings with the outer half of the forewing broadly black; females are plain dull dark brown with a small whitish tornal patch and dark submarginal spots on the hindwing.
Hypolycaena othona.underwing: Crisp chalky-white crossed by neat orange-yellow to ochreous-brown discal bands edged in dark brown, a diagnostic bold jet-black spot near the base of the hindwing costa, orange-ringed black tornal spots, and two pairs of delicate white-tipped tails.
Hypolycaena othona.similarSpecies: Distinct black subbasal spot near the hindwing costa and orange-brown bands on a pure white underside separate it cleanly from Nilgiri Tit (Hypolycaena nilgirica) and the long-tailed Fluffy Tit (Zeltus amasa).
Hypolycaena othona.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, riverine gorges, and epiphyte-rich forest trees.
Hypolycaena othona.behavior: Brisk flyer around mossy orchid-laden tree trunks and forest clearings; males mud-puddle on damp creek sand and females inspect epiphytic orchid inflorescences.
Hypolycaena othona.season: Seen mostly from October to April, coinciding with epiphytic orchid blooming.
Hypolycaena othona.tnDistribution: Moist Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Hypolycaena othona.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Hypolycaena othona.notes: Formerly placed in genus Chliaria; larvae bore into flower buds and capsules of epiphytic forest orchids and receive protection from attending ants.

Zeltus amasa.headline: Pale-blue forest tit trailing extraordinarily long, billowing white tails
Zeltus amasa.upperwing: Males have mostly blackish forewings with a pale azure-blue basal area and pale azure hindwings bordered by a large black apical patch and pure white anal margin; females are uniform brown with white-spotted hindwing tornal margins.
Zeltus amasa.underwing: Snow-white shaded softly with warm ochreous-brown across the outer half of both wings, crossed by thin brown postdiscal lines, carrying a small black basal spot in space 7 and two black tornal spots, and trailing two pairs of remarkably long fluffy white tails up to 13 mm long.
Zeltus amasa.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu once perched: its fluttering plume-like white tails are far longer and fluffier than those of Orchid Tit (Hypolycaena othona) and paired with an ochreous-tipped white underside rather than the orange-brown bands of Common Imperial (Cheritra freja).
Zeltus amasa.habitat: Shaded evergreen and moist semi-evergreen forests, wooded hill streams, and damp ravine undergrowth.
Zeltus amasa.behavior: Weak, bobbing flight through dappled forest shade; on landing on stream-side foliage its long fluffy white tails quiver in the slightest breeze, distracting birds from its body.
Zeltus amasa.season: Observed across moist hill forests mainly from September to March.
Zeltus amasa.tnDistribution: Tamil Nadu Western Ghats ranges including Nilgiris, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Zeltus amasa.notes: Subspecies Zeltus amasa amasa; the two extraordinarily long tails at veins 1b and 2 flutter like floating cotton threads when perched beside forest streams.

Ancema blanka.headline: Iridescent blue-rayed royal with silvery-sheen undersides in damp hill ravines
Ancema blanka.upperwing: Males are brilliant shining metallic blue radiating in fine blue streaks into broad jet-black apical and outer borders; females are slightly paler, clearer blue with wider black margins and rounder wing tips.
Ancema blanka.underwing: Pearly silvery-white to pale silvery-grey in males and greyish-buff in females, crossed by delicate broken dark postdiscal dashes, large orange-crowned black tornal spots dusted with silver-blue scales, and two slender white-tipped black tails at veins 1b and 2.
Ancema blanka.similarSpecies: Smaller and sleeker than Peacock Royal (Tajuria cippus), separated by the male's radiating blue streaks entering the black forewing margin and silvery-sheen underside.
Ancema blanka.habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded streams, and wooded hill peaks.
Ancema blanka.behavior: Very fast flyer that perches high in sunlit gaps, hill-tops around noon, and descends eagerly to damp sandy creek banks to mud-puddle.
Ancema blanka.season: Most records fall between September and April across wet hills.
Ancema blanka.tnDistribution: Recorded in Tamil Nadu Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, KMTR) as well as Eastern Ghats hills including Sirumalai.
Ancema blanka.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Ancema blanka argentea; its silvery ventral sheen catches light strikingly when males mud-puddle on wet rocks.

Loxura atymnus.headline: Bright orange-winged butterfly bobbing above wild yams with a long white-tipped tail
Loxura atymnus.upperwing: Both sexes are rich fiery orange-red with a sweeping black border along the forewing apex and outer margin and slightly paler orange hindwings ending in a single long orange-based tail tipped with black and white.
Loxura atymnus.underwing: Uniform warm ochreous-yellow crossed by very faint, fine wavy brown discal lines and dark marginal dots near the single long broad tail; prominent elongated palpi project forward like a snout.
Loxura atymnus.similarSpecies: Unlike Indian Red Flash (Rapala iarbus) or Cornelian (Deudorix epijarbas), both sexes are orange above, carry a long tapering tail and protruding palpi, and show an ochreous-yellow rather than grey-brown underside.
Loxura atymnus.habitat: Moist forest edges, bamboo thickets, shaded gardens, stream banks, and woodland trails where yam vines climb.
Loxura atymnus.behavior: Bouncy, unhurried low flight through undergrowth; rests sideways on shaded leaves where its yellow underside and long tail mimic a curled dry leaf.
Loxura atymnus.season: Active year-round in humid foothill and hill habitats, peaking from August to January.
Loxura atymnus.tnDistribution: Widespread in Tamil Nadu hills and wooded foothills including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Anamalais, Palani foothills (Amaidhi Solai), KMTR, Pachamalai, and Shervaroys.
Loxura atymnus.notes: Subspecies Loxura atymnus atymnus; caterpillars feed on tender shoots and stems of Dioscorea yams and are frequently tended by small ants.

Horaga onyx.headline: Three-tailed blue-and-white forest gem showing a crisp white ventral band
Horaga onyx.upperwing: Bright shining sky-to-royal blue over the inner wings broadly bordered in black across the forewing outer half and costa, punctuated by a clean white central patch on the forewing; females are duller blue with a larger white discal patch.
Horaga onyx.underwing: Warm ochreous-brown crossed cleanly across both wings by a straight, dark-edged snow-white discal band that continues to vein 1a on the hindwing, complemented by metallic green-blue tornal scales and three white-tipped black tails at veins 1b, 2, and 3.
Horaga onyx.similarSpecies: Unmistakable in Tamil Nadu by the stark white forewing discal spot above combined with three tails and a crisp straight white band across a cinnamon-ochreous underside.
Horaga onyx.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, wooded clearings, and shaded stream corridors.
Horaga onyx.behavior: Quick, erratic flier that perches high on sunlit tree-edge leaves and drops briefly to damp sand or low shrubs during morning sun.
Horaga onyx.season: Observed mainly from September to March in moist hill ranges.
Horaga onyx.tnDistribution: Tamil Nadu Western Ghats ranges including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, plus moist Eastern Ghats tracts.
Horaga onyx.notes: Represented in southern India and Sri Lanka by subspecies Horaga onyx cingalensis; its three tails and white band create an effective false-head decoy.

Rathinda amor.headline: Intricately patterned three-tailed hairstreak famous for twitching its false head
Rathinda amor.upperwing: Dull dark brown with an orange-white forewing spot and bright orange-brown lower hindwing bands.
Rathinda amor.underwing: Warm creamy-white intricately patterned with dark red-brown geometric blotches and carrying three delicate tails at the hindwing angle.
Rathinda amor.similarSpecies: Three filamentous tails paired with the geometric red-brown and cream underside make Monkey Puzzle unmistakable.
Rathinda amor.habitat: Scrub jungles, gardens, woodland trails, and coastal thickets.
Rathinda amor.behavior: Lands and instantly turns around while walking its hindwings up and down so its false head and tails fool predators.
Rathinda amor.tnDistribution: Common across coastal scrub, Chennai, Coimbatore, Pachamalai, and foothills.
Rathinda amor.notes: Dances backwards slowly after landing to keep predators focused on its waving three-tailed false head.

Cheritra freja.headline: Long-tailed forest hairstreak streaming two ribbon-like white tails
Cheritra freja.upperwing: Males are rich dark purple-brown across both wings with two white-barred black tornal spots; females are plain dark brown with larger white tornal patches above the long tails.
Cheritra freja.underwing: Creamy-white shaded warmly with orange-ochreous toward the forewing apex and outer margin, crossed by fine black discal dashes, black tornal spots crowned with metallic silver-green scales, and two pure white tails at veins 1b and 2 with vein 2 reaching up to 25 mm.
Cheritra freja.similarSpecies: Much larger and warmer-tinted beneath than Fluffy Tit (Zeltus amasa), with a plain brown-purple upperside and dramatically long ribbon-like tails reaching 20-25 mm.
Cheritra freja.habitat: Wet evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous hill forests, shaded trails, and forest-stream openings.
Cheritra freja.behavior: Graceful, swooping flight along shaded forest edges; perches with wings closed on sunlit shrubs where its long white ribbon tails sway gently in air currents.
Cheritra freja.season: Present across most of the year in wet forests, most abundant from September to March.
Cheritra freja.tnDistribution: Western Ghats stretches of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and KMTR.
Cheritra freja.notes: Southern Indian subspecies Cheritra freja butleri is a classic Western Ghats forest highlight; those colossal tails break easily when birds strike the false head, sparing the body.

Catapaecilma major.headline: Three-tailed miniature jewel spangled in metallic silver and black beneath
Catapaecilma major.upperwing: Males are deep rich violet-blue with narrow black wing margins; females are paler mauve-blue bordered broadly in dark brown along the costa and termen.
Catapaecilma major.underwing: Pale ochreous-buff richly covered with glittering metallic silver bands bordered neatly in black and orange-ochreous lines across both wings, ending in three fine white-tipped tails per hindwing at veins 1b, 2, and 3.
Catapaecilma major.similarSpecies: Unlike Cigaritis silverlines, its underside silver marks form ornate fragmented chain-like spangles across the entire wing rather than neat parallel transverse bars, and it bears three tails instead of two.
Catapaecilma major.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen hill forests, wooded river valleys, and bamboo-lined streams.
Catapaecilma major.behavior: Brisk, darting flier around mid-storey Terminalia branches; perches on sunlit edge twigs and occasionally visits damp mineral patches.
Catapaecilma major.season: Uncommon; recorded primarily between October and April.
Catapaecilma major.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill forests of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Anamalais, Siruvani, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Catapaecilma major.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Catapaecilma major callone; larvae feed on young Terminalia leaves while attended by Crematogaster ants.

Virachola isocrates.headline: Pomegranate and guava fruit-borer showing a pale orange patch in females
Virachola isocrates.upperwing: Males are dark smoky brown glossed brilliantly with deep violet-blue in angled light and show at most a faint diffuse orange spot beyond the forewing cell; females are brown with a conspicuous bright ochreous-orange discal patch beyond the cell.
Virachola isocrates.underwing: Vinous grey-brown crossed by faint dark cell-end bars and an irregular pale-edged darker discal band, a large black tornal spot ringed in orange beside metallic blue scales on the anal lobe, and a fine white-tipped tail at vein 2.
Virachola isocrates.similarSpecies: Smaller than Large Guava Blue (Virachola perse), lacking the large black subbasal spot near the hindwing costa underside and lacking sky-blue patches on the female upperside.
Virachola isocrates.habitat: Orchards, home gardens, scrub plains, dry deciduous woodlands, and foothill farms.
Virachola isocrates.behavior: Strong, fast flier; adults nectar on garden flowers in morning sun while females hover intently around developing guava and pomegranate fruits to oviposit.
Virachola isocrates.season: Active year-round statewide, peaking from August to March.
Virachola isocrates.tnDistribution: Common throughout Tamil Nadu plains, orchards, and hills from Chennai, Salem, Coimbatore, and Madurai to Sirumalai, Pachamalai, and Western Ghats foothills.
Virachola isocrates.notes: Caterpillars bore inside ripening fruits and plug the entry hole with their hardened anal shield to keep out predators while tying the fruit stalk with silk so it does not drop prematurely.

Virachola perse.headline: Bold-spotted forest fruit-borer flashing bright sky-blue on both sexes
Virachola perse.upperwing: Males are shining bright sky-blue over the inner wings inside broad black costal and outer margins (sometimes tinged faintly orange beyond the cell); females are duller blue with a whitish patch beyond the forewing cell and dark submarginal hindwing spots.
Virachola perse.underwing: Vinous grey-brown overlaid with a lilac sheen in fresh males, marked with dark pale-edged cell-end twin bars, broad chain-like discal spots, a diagnostic round black subbasal spot near the hindwing costa, orange-ringed tornal ocelli with metallic blue scales, and a slender white-tipped tail.
Virachola perse.similarSpecies: Larger and brighter sky-blue above than Guava Blue (Virachola isocrates), cleanly separated beneath by the bold black spot near the upper base of the hindwing and broader linked discal spots.
Virachola perse.habitat: Deciduous and semi-evergreen hill forests, foothill scrub woodlands, and wooded ridges where wild Catunaregam grows.
Virachola perse.behavior: Powerful, fast flyer that hill-tops on sunlit ridges during late morning and perches high on deciduous tree canopies.
Virachola perse.season: Recorded across most months, peaking between October and March.
Virachola perse.tnDistribution: Occurs across Western Ghats foothills (Kallar, Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Anamalais, KMTR) and Eastern Ghats ranges including Sirumalai, Pachamalai, and Shervaroys.
Virachola perse.notes: Like Virachola isocrates, larvae hollow out tough Catunaregam (Randia) fruits internally and secure the stem to the branch with silk before pupating inside the dried shell.

Deudorix epijarbas.headline: Fiery scarlet male hairstreak whose larvae bore inside forest seed pods
Deudorix epijarbas.upperwing: Strongly dimorphic: males are glowing scarlet-red to fiery orange-red framed by broad black forewing costal and outer margins and a black-veined red hindwing, whereas females are uniform dull coppery-brown without red patches.
Deudorix epijarbas.underwing: Uniform wood-brown to greyish-ochreous crossed by crisp double white-edged dark discal and submarginal lines, a prominent black tornal spot crowned with orange and edged in metallic green-blue scales, and a fine white-tipped tail at vein 2.
Deudorix epijarbas.similarSpecies: Male's bright scarlet upperside resembles Indian Red Flash (Rapala iarbus) but Cornelian is larger, lacks the dark trident mark at forewing vein bases, and shows clean double white-edged underside lines; female lacks the orange forewing patch of female Guava Blue.
Deudorix epijarbas.habitat: Moist deciduous, semi-evergreen, and dry evergreen hill forests, orchards, and wooded foothills.
Deudorix epijarbas.behavior: Extremely fast, direct flyer that patrols high canopy clearings, hill-tops vigorously in midday sun, and visits damp sand and hilltop shrubs.
Deudorix epijarbas.season: Active year-round in hill forests, common from September to March.
Deudorix epijarbas.tnDistribution: Widespread in Tamil Nadu hill ranges including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, KMTR, Pachamalai, Sirumalai, and Shervaroys.
Deudorix epijarbas.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Deudorix epijarbas epijarbas; caterpillars tunnel inside tough Sapindus and Connarus fruits and pods.

Bindahara moorei.headline: Protected forest hairstreak streaming sword-like tails behind a spotted white underside
Bindahara moorei.upperwing: Males are velvety jet-black above with a luminous metallic azure-blue band bordering the lower outer margin of the hindwing; females are warm dark brown with a clean white hindwing tornal patch and dark marginal spots.
Bindahara moorei.underwing: Creamy-white in females and warm buff-white in males, boldly barred with large dark-ringed brown basal spots, an angled brown discal band, metallic blue-green tornal dusting, and an extraordinarily long tail at vein 2 over twice body length.
Bindahara moorei.similarSpecies: Totally unmistakable in Tamil Nadu by its combination of velvet-black male with glowing blue hindwing rim, bold chocolate-blotched white underside, and huge trailing sword-like tails.
Bindahara moorei.habitat: Wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded ravines, and Salacia-draped forest interiors.
Bindahara moorei.behavior: Elusive canopy-to-understorey flyer that rests motionless on shaded lianas and leaf tips, gently swaying its extraordinarily long tails and large false-head lobe.
Bindahara moorei.season: Scarce; recorded mainly between October and March in wet forest tracts.
Bindahara moorei.tnDistribution: Tamil Nadu Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, KMTR) and documented in the Eastern Ghats at Sirumalai Hills during the October 2022 census.
Bindahara moorei.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Bindahara moorei.notes: Taxonomically treated by some authors as Bindahara phocides moorei; the October 2022 Sirumalai survey established the first confirmed Eastern Ghats record for Tamil Nadu.

Rapala iarbus.headline: Fiery red-and-black flash common across sunlit hedges and foothill gardens
Rapala iarbus.upperwing: Males are vivid scarlet-red with broad blackish-brown forewing costal and outer margins and a diagnostic dark trident-shaped mark along the bases of veins 2, 3, and 4; females are uniform dull coppery-brown.
Rapala iarbus.underwing: Warm pale ochreous-buff to greyish-stone crossed by narrow cell-end bars, a fine white-edged brown postdiscal line angled neatly above the tornus, a bright orange-crowned black tornal spot, and a white-tipped tail at vein 2.
Rapala iarbus.similarSpecies: Smaller and brighter orange-red than Cornelian (Deudorix epijarbas), separated by the dark basal vein trident on the male forewing and single-edged rather than double-edged white discal line beneath; female lacks the orange forewing spot of Guava Blue.
Rapala iarbus.habitat: Open scrub, home gardens, urban hedges, forest edges, and deciduous foothills.
Rapala iarbus.behavior: Very swift darting flight; perches aggressively on sunlit outer leaves, visits Lantana and Tridax flowers, and twists its hindwings slowly upon landing.
Rapala iarbus.season: Common year-round across plains and hills of Tamil Nadu.
Rapala iarbus.tnDistribution: Statewide across Tamil Nadu from Chennai, Coimbatore, Trichy, and Madurai to Kallar, Mudumalai, Pachamalai, Sirumalai, and Yercaud.
Rapala iarbus.notes: Subspecies Rapala iarbus sorya is the commonest red flash in Tamil Nadu; black-and-white banded legs and neat false-head tornal eyespots readily distinguish settled adults.

Rapala manea.headline: Slaty-purple flash of woodland edges and flowering garden shrubs
Rapala manea.upperwing: Males are dark slate-brown glossed richly with deep purple-blue in side light, carrying a hidden dark scent brand near the hindwing costa; females are uniform dull slate-brown lacking blue gloss.
Rapala manea.underwing: Pale slaty-grey to brownish-buff marked with double cell-end bars, a crisp narrow dark brown postdiscal line edged cleanly white on the outer side, a prominent orange-crowned black tornal spot with metallic bluish scales, and a fine white-tipped tail.
Rapala manea.similarSpecies: Smaller and duller slate-purple above than Indigo Flash (Rapala varuna), separated beneath by its narrower continuous postdiscal line kept well apart from the cell-end bar rather than broad conjoined dark spots.
Rapala manea.habitat: Scrub jungles, forest edges, village groves, gardens, and deciduous-to-evergreen hill tracks.
Rapala manea.behavior: Fast, erratic flier that returns repeatedly to favored sunlit bush perches, nectars avidly on Lantana and Leea, and rubs its hindwings at rest.
Rapala manea.season: Active year-round across Tamil Nadu, most numerous between September and March.
Rapala manea.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu from Chennai and Coimbatore gardens to Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalais, KMTR, Pachamalai, and Shervaroys.
Rapala manea.notes: Southern Indian subspecies Rapala manea schistacea is extraordinarily polyphagous on flower buds and young shoots across at least five plant families.

Rapala varuna.headline: Rich indigo-glossed flash marked beneath by broad white-edged bands
Rapala varuna.upperwing: Males show deep, rich indigo-blue gloss across both wings framed by narrow dark borders and a dark brown costal sex brand on the hindwing; females are paler steel-blue to purplish-grey with wider dark borders.
Rapala varuna.underwing: Dark brownish-grey crossed by unusually broad dark brown postdiscal bands (formed of fused squarish spots on the hindwing) crisply rimmed in white, with the hindwing cell-end bar sitting very close to or touching the discal band above a bright orange-crowned tornal spot.
Rapala varuna.similarSpecies: Separated cleanly from Slate Flash (Rapala manea) by its deeper indigo male gloss, bluish female upperside, and much wider underside postdiscal band touching or nearly touching the hindwing cell-end bar; lacks the rusty-ferruginous underside of Malabar Flash (Rapala lankana).
Rapala varuna.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forests, wooded stream valleys, and forest-edge gardens.
Rapala varuna.behavior: Swift canopy-edge flyer that basks with wings closed or slightly parted on sunlit foliage and visits forest-edge flowers and damp mud.
Rapala varuna.season: Seen across most months in wooded hills, peaking between September and February.
Rapala varuna.tnDistribution: Tamil Nadu Western Ghats ranges (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, KMTR) and moist Eastern Ghats hills like Shervaroys and Pachamalai.
Rapala varuna.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Rapala varuna lazulina; caterpillars feed on tender flower buds of Combretum vines and are sometimes tended by ants.

Rapala lankana.headline: Deep-purple hill flash carrying a warm rusty-brown underside
Rapala lankana.upperwing: Males appear nearly velvety black unless angled in sunlight, when the lower forewing and entire hindwing glow deep rich purple with a rusty spot on the anal lobe; females are pale violet-brown with a thin black margin and rusty anal lobe.
Rapala lankana.underwing: Warm pale ferruginous (rusty-brown) darkening toward the wing margins, crossed cleanly by a straight deep ferruginous discal band edged with white speckles only near the curved hindwing anal portion, plus a black tornal spot and white-tipped black tail.
Rapala lankana.similarSpecies: Instantly told apart from Slate Flash (Rapala manea) and Indigo Flash (Rapala varuna) by its warm rusty-ferruginous underside lacking broad white-rimmed dark grey bands, and separated from Cornelian (Deudorix epijarbas) female by its rusty rather than grey-brown underside.
Rapala lankana.habitat: Wet evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous hill forests along wooded stream valleys.
Rapala lankana.behavior: Uncommon, fast-flying forest-edge butterfly that perches on sunlit mid-storey twigs, visits damp forest paths, and feeds briefly at hill-forest blossoms.
Rapala lankana.season: Recorded sporadically between October and April in moist hill tracts.
Rapala lankana.tnDistribution: Southern and central Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Anamalais, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Rapala lankana.notes: Restricted to the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka; its deep purple male sheen and rusty-ferruginous underside make it one of southern India's most distinctive Flashes.

Abisara echerius.headline: Shaded woodland metalmark common across Western and Eastern Ghats
Abisara echerius.upperwing: Velvety maroon-brown wings crossed by pale greyish-white subapical bands and bearing dark twin spots near the hindwing margin.
Abisara echerius.underwing: Warm purplish-brown displaying crisp white diagonal median bands and black white-ringed submarginal eyespots.
Abisara echerius.similarSpecies: Closely resembles Plum Judy (Abisara bifasciata); Straight Plum Judy typically shows narrower, straighter median bands and habitat preference across peninsular hills.
Abisara echerius.habitat: Shaded forest trails, bamboo groves, overgrown estates, and stream sides.
Abisara echerius.behavior: Bobs jerkily through forest shade, settling with half-open wings on upper leaf surfaces and pivoting smoothly right after landing.
Abisara echerius.tnDistribution: Widespread in Tamil Nadu hill forests and foothills.
Abisara echerius.notes: Abrupt quarter-turn upon landing is a reliable behavioral clue along shaded forest undergrowth.

Abisara bifasciata.headline: Double-banded metalmark of dense moist forests in Tamil Nadu
Abisara bifasciata.upperwing: Rich dark plum-brown crossed by two broader pale whitish bands towards the forewing tip.
Abisara bifasciata.underwing: Deep purplish-brown with crisp contrasting median and post-discal white bands and twin black hindwing eyespots.
Abisara bifasciata.similarSpecies: Often treated alongside Abisara echerius; TNBS lists both species separately across Tamil Nadu forest surveys (including Mudumalai & Pachamalai).
Abisara bifasciata.habitat: Moist evergreen and deciduous hill forests and bamboo undergrowth.
Abisara bifasciata.behavior: Restless shaded flier turning abruptly after landing on leaves at eye level.
Abisara bifasciata.tnDistribution: Recorded in Western Ghats reserves (Mudumalai) and Eastern Ghats (Pachamalai).
Abisara bifasciata.notes: Represented regularly in TNBS Mudumalai and Pachamalai Eastern-Western Ghats joint surveys.

Badamia exclamationis.headline: Pointed-wing swift awl known for sudden mass arrivals
Badamia exclamationis.upperwing: Elongated, narrow-pointed chocolate-brown wings marked on the forewing with fine translucent white exclamation-mark spots.
Badamia exclamationis.underwing: Pale greyish-brown with a dark spot edged white near the hindwing inner corner.
Badamia exclamationis.similarSpecies: Extremely narrow pointed forewings and slender exclamation-like translucent streaks separate it immediately from Hasora awls.
Badamia exclamationis.habitat: Wooded foothills, parks, avenues, coastal forests, and dry hill trails.
Badamia exclamationis.behavior: Lightning-fast flight; rests under leaves in shade and is often active early morning and late afternoon.
Badamia exclamationis.season: Year-round with sudden seasonal population surges.
Badamia exclamationis.tnDistribution: Recorded across plains, foothills, and hill forests throughout Tamil Nadu.
Badamia exclamationis.notes: Capable of long-distance migratory flights across peninsular India during monsoon shifts.

Bibasis sena.headline: Chocolate-brown awl crowned by a fiery orange abdomen tip and red hindwing fringe
Bibasis sena.upperwing: Unspotted velvety dark chocolate-brown across both wings, accented by a bright carmine-orange hindwing tornal fringe (cilia) and a vivid orange abdominal tip.
Bibasis sena.underwing: Warm brown with a large buff-white patch along the inner forewing margin and a broad pure-white discal band with a soft outer edge across the hindwing; third palpal segment is slender and erect.
Bibasis sena.similarSpecies: Differs from Common Banded Awl (Hasora chromus) and White Banded Awl (Hasora taminatus) by its bright orange-tipped abdomen, carmine-red hindwing cilia, and wide buff-white inner forewing patch underneath.
Bibasis sena.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen foothill forests, wooded stream corridors, and bamboo-shaded ravines.
Bibasis sena.behavior: Darts rapidly along shaded trails at dawn, dusk, and in overcast weather, settling upright with closed wings beneath broad leaves and visiting bird droppings or forest flowers.
Bibasis sena.season: Recorded mostly during monsoon and post-monsoon months from June to December, with occasional dry-season sightings.
Bibasis sena.tnDistribution: Western Ghats tracts of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Bibasis sena.notes: Often placed in the genus Bibasis on Indian checklists; the bright orange abdominal tip shows clearly even when the butterfly perches with closed wings.

Burara jaina.headline: Large vinaceous-brown twilight awlet with an orange forewing costal streak
Burara jaina.upperwing: Deep purplish-brown marked by a bright orange costal streak from the forewing base toward mid-wing, bluish-grey basal hairs, and glowing orange-red hindwing cilia.
Burara jaina.underwing: Rich reddish-brown with pale orange-ochre streaks radiating along the hindwing veins, a large pale ochreous cell spot, and bright orange-tinged palpi and thorax front.
Burara jaina.similarSpecies: Separated from Pale Green Awlet (Burara gomata) by its orange forewing costal streak above and orange-ochre vein streaks below rather than pale greyish-green interspace stripes; larger and broader-winged than Bibasis sena.
Burara jaina.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, shaded stream valleys, and dense woody climber tangles.
Burara jaina.behavior: Strictly crepuscular, launching fast powerful flights at first light and dusk to nectar at tall forest trees, then hiding upright beneath leaves with closed wings by midday.
Burara jaina.season: Active primarily from June to January around monsoon and winter rains.
Burara jaina.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Anamalai Hills, Siruvani, Kallar, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai in the Western Ghats.
Burara jaina.notes: South Indian populations belong to subspecies Burara jaina fergusonii; adults sometimes feed on damp sand or bird droppings at dawn.

Burara gomata.headline: Elusive green-streaked awlet active at dawn and dusk in wet hill forests
Burara gomata.upperwing: Males are pale vinaceous-brown with yellowish interspace streaks and cilia; females are glossy bronzy-green shading to indigo-blue toward the apex, with yellow-banded black abdomens.
Burara gomata.underwing: Dark brown densely patterned with pale greyish-green streaks between every vein, broad pale inner forewing border, and bright orange-yellow underside thorax, palpi, and legs.
Burara gomata.similarSpecies: Unmistakable underside pattern of pale greenish interspace rays cleanly separates it from Orange Striped Awlet (Burara jaina) and from the black-veined green underside of Indian Awlking (Choaspes benjaminii).
Burara gomata.habitat: Dense wet evergreen forests, shola borders, and epiphytic climber canopies at mid- to high elevations.
Burara gomata.behavior: Strong, swift crepuscular flier emerging briefly at dawn and twilight to visit canopy blossoms or damp streamside rocks, resting closed-winged in deep shade by day.
Burara gomata.season: Recorded mainly between June and December during wet monsoon conditions.
Burara gomata.tnDistribution: Localized in high-rainfall Western Ghats pockets of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Valparai, Anamalai, and Tirunelveli hills.
Burara gomata.notes: Represented in southern India by subspecies Burara gomata kanara, whose larvae shelter inside rolled leaves of Schefflera vines.

Hasora chromus.headline: Fast twilight-loving awl with a crisp white hindwing underside band
Hasora chromus.upperwing: Plain dark glossy brown with an orange-brown sheen at wing bases; females show two pale yellow translucent forewing spots.
Hasora chromus.underwing: Deep purplish-brown crossed cleanly on the hindwing by a narrow pure-white straight band ending at a dark tornal patch.
Hasora chromus.similarSpecies: Narrow, clean straight white hindwing band (without metallic green tint) separates it from White Banded Awl (Hasora taminatus).
Hasora chromus.habitat: Avenues, wooded gardens, foothills, and forest clearings.
Hasora chromus.behavior: Most active at dawn, dusk, and in overcast weather; settles under leaves during bright midday sun.
Hasora chromus.tnDistribution: Widespread from Chennai and Coimbatore avenues to Mudumalai and Pachamalai.
Hasora chromus.notes: Life cycle documented by TNBS contributors on Pongamia pinnata street trees in urban Tamil Nadu.

Hasora taminatus.headline: Glossy brown awl flashing a metallic blue-green underside base and white band
Hasora taminatus.upperwing: Plain dark brown in males lacking any forewing sex brand and bathed in greenish hairs at the wing base; females carry two small pale yellowish hyaline spots on the forewing.
Hasora taminatus.underwing: Deep brown richly glossed with iridescent metallic blue-green across the basal half, cut sharply by a clean white straight hindwing band and a dark tornal patch; palpi are dull ochreous-brown.
Hasora taminatus.similarSpecies: Metallic blue-green basal sheen on the underside and broader sharply edged white band distinguish it cleanly from Common Banded Awl (Hasora chromus) and Plain Banded Awl (Hasora vitta).
Hasora taminatus.habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous forest edges, shaded gardens, and foothills.
Hasora taminatus.behavior: Flies swiftly at dawn, dusk, and under overcast canopy shade, nectaring eagerly at Clerodendrum and Leea flowers before snapping wings shut underneath foliage.
Hasora taminatus.season: Seen nearly year-round in hill forests, peaking from August to January.
Hasora taminatus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, KMTR) and Eastern Ghats (Yercaud, Kolli Hills, Pachamalai).
Hasora taminatus.notes: Nominate subspecies Hasora taminatus taminatus inhabits peninsular India and shares Pongamia and Derris climber hosts with Hasora chromus.

Hasora badra.headline: Large brown awl awaiting validated photographic record in Tamil Nadu
Hasora badra.upperwing: Plain dark brown in males; females bear large pale yellow hyaline spots in the forewing.
Hasora badra.underwing: Warm purplish-brown lacking the crisp white hindwing band of Common or White Banded Awl, showing instead a small dark-ringed white spot at the cell end and dark tornal lobe.
Hasora badra.similarSpecies: Lacks the continuous pale hindwing underside band seen in Hasora chromus and Hasora taminatus.
Hasora badra.habitat: Shaded evergreen forests and wooded hill ravines.
Hasora badra.behavior: Crepuscular flier sheltering beneath leaves during midday.
Hasora badra.tnDistribution: One of 4 checklist species awaiting validated TNBS sighting confirmation in Tamil Nadu.
Hasora badra.notes: Check crepuscular Derris vine thickets in wet Western Ghats valleys for the stark white underside hindwing cell spot.

Hasora vitta.headline: Purplish-glossed forest awl with an outwardly blurred white hindwing band
Hasora vitta.upperwing: Dark bronzy-brown showing at least one tiny pale subapical dot in males (without a discal sex brand) and two larger yellowish discal spots plus subapical dots in females.
Hasora vitta.underwing: Rich dark purplish-brown crossed by a broad creamy-white hindwing band whose inner edge is crisp while its outer margin blurs diffusely into the ground colour above a dark tornal lobe.
Hasora vitta.similarSpecies: Diffused outer edge of the white hindwing band and presence of a subapical forewing dot in both sexes separate it from Hasora chromus and Hasora taminatus.
Hasora vitta.habitat: Wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, stream corridors, and tall woody climber thickets.
Hasora vitta.behavior: Fast, darting twilight flier that visits sunlit forest clearings in early morning, settles closed-winged beneath leaves, and occasionally takes moisture from damp sand or bird droppings.
Hasora vitta.season: Mainly June to December during southwest and northeast monsoons.
Hasora vitta.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hills of Tamil Nadu including Anamalai, Valparai, Nilgiris, Siruvani, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Hasora vitta.notes: Southern Indian populations belong to subspecies Hasora vitta indica; far scarcer in Tamil Nadu than the ubiquitous Hasora chromus.

Choaspes benjaminii.headline: Jewel-like indigo-blue and emerald awlking with blazing orange tornal tails
Choaspes benjaminii.upperwing: Males gleam metallic indigo-blue with broad ochre-orange hindwing tornal lobe and cilia; females are shining dark olive-green with a copper-brown inner forewing margin and bright orange tornal patch.
Choaspes benjaminii.underwing: Striking glossy emerald-green veined heavily in black, highlighted by a bold black-spotted orange-red tornal patch on the hindwing and bright orange-red palpi and underside thorax.
Choaspes benjaminii.similarSpecies: Unmistakable among Tamil Nadu skippers; the bright black-veined green underside and vivid orange-red hindwing lobe separate it immediately from Burara gomata and all Hasora awls.
Choaspes benjaminii.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation evergreen hill forests, shola margins, and wooded mountain streams.
Choaspes benjaminii.behavior: Boisterous, rapid flier active even in bright morning sun along hill streams; perches upright with closed wings on wet pebbles, bird droppings, and wild flowers.
Choaspes benjaminii.season: Recorded almost year-round in high hills, with peaks in March-May and September-December.
Choaspes benjaminii.tnDistribution: Nilgiris (Coonoor, Kotagiri, Naduvattam), Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Anamalai, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Choaspes benjaminii.notes: Unlike strictly twilight awls, the Indian Awlking patrols sunny mountain streams by day and has brightly banded yellow-and-black larvae inside curled Meliosma leaves.

Tapena thwaitesi.headline: Dark purple-brown flat with scalloped outer wing margins and flat under-leaf rest
Tapena thwaitesi.upperwing: Males are deep purple-brown with blackish outer borders, faint dark discal bands, and two tiny white subapical dots; females are paler grey-brown with clear dark bands and white hyaline cell, discal, and subapical spots.
Tapena thwaitesi.underwing: Uniform dark purple-brown in males and lavender-grey in females with repeated dark bands; hindwing outer margin is conspicuously angled at vein 7 and scalloped.
Tapena thwaitesi.similarSpecies: Distinguished from Celaenorrhinus and Sarangesa flats by its distinctly excavated forewing margin below the apex and sharply angled, scalloped hindwing outline.
Tapena thwaitesi.habitat: Moist deciduous, semi-evergreen, and evergreen forests along shaded clearings and stream banks.
Tapena thwaitesi.behavior: Darts low and rapidly in forest shade before snapping abruptly underneath a broad leaf to rest completely flat with wings outspread.
Tapena thwaitesi.season: Post-monsoon and winter months from August to February, also seen during summer showers.
Tapena thwaitesi.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills and hills of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Anamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Tapena thwaitesi.notes: Even in flight, its dark silhouette and abruptly disappearing landing habit under leaves set it apart from open-perching Angles.

Coladenia indrani.headline: Golden-yellow and black pied flat studded with crisp black-rimmed white spots
Coladenia indrani.upperwing: Warm golden-ochre ground crossed by black borders, a clear black sub-basal spot below the forewing cell, and crisp black-edged semi-translucent white cell, discal, and subapical spots; cilia are black-and-white chequered.
Coladenia indrani.underwing: Dark blackish-brown richly suffused with bright golden-yellow scales, throwing the crisp white hyaline spots into sharp relief; antennae are yellow with black clubs.
Coladenia indrani.similarSpecies: Much brighter golden-yellow than Fulvous Pied Flat (Pseudocoladenia dan) and bears a prominent solid black spot near the base below the forewing cell.
Coladenia indrani.habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forests, foothills, bamboo brakes, and shaded wooded gardens.
Coladenia indrani.behavior: Flies fast near ground shrubs and rests flat on both upper and lower surfaces of sunlit or dappled leaves; visits bird droppings and low wildflowers.
Coladenia indrani.season: Active nearly year-round, most frequent from July to February.
Coladenia indrani.tnDistribution: Mudumalai, Kallar, Siruvani, Coimbatore foothills, Anamalai, Pachamalai, Kolli Hills, Yercaud, and Tirunelveli foothills.
Coladenia indrani.notes: Represented in South India by subspecies Coladenia indrani indra; dry-season broods tend to be noticeably brighter orange-yellow than wet-season individuals.

Gerosis bhagava.headline: White-banded olive-brown flat glowing orange-yellow beneath the thorax
Gerosis bhagava.upperwing: Dark olive-brown forewing with three triangular hyaline white discal spots and a curved subapical arc; hindwing displays a broad creamy-white sub-basal band edged by a semicircle of black spots, paired with a white abdominal belt.
Gerosis bhagava.underwing: Mirrors the crisp upperwing markings on a paler brown ground, contrasting strikingly with bright orange-yellow palpi and undersides of thorax and legs.
Gerosis bhagava.similarSpecies: White sub-basal hindwing band, white-belted abdomen, and vivid orange-yellow breast separate it instantly from Tagiades snow flats and Celaenorrhinus spotted flats.
Gerosis bhagava.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forests, wooded ravines, and shaded stream-side trails.
Gerosis bhagava.behavior: Swift, low shaded flight; settles flat underneath leaves with wings fully pressed open and occasionally visits bird droppings and damp soil.
Gerosis bhagava.season: Recorded chiefly from August to March during monsoon and cooler winter months.
Gerosis bhagava.tnDistribution: Western Ghats and foothills of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, Palani foothills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Gerosis bhagava.notes: Its diagnostic orange-yellow breast is visible when the butterfly perches upside down beneath high leaves or feeds on vertical stems.

Tagiades japetus.headline: Dusky brown snow flat lacking a pure white upper hindwing patch
Tagiades japetus.upperwing: Dark chocolate-brown forewings dotted with crisp tiny hyaline white spots (cell, discal spaces, and subapical arc); hindwings stay entirely brown above with only faint darker post-discal spots and pale cilia near the tornus.
Tagiades japetus.underwing: Buff-brown forewing repeating the white dots; hindwing heavily washed with chalky greyish-white over the lower two-thirds and dotted with a curved arc of dark brown spots.
Tagiades japetus.similarSpecies: Unlike Water Snow Flat (Tagiades litigiosa) and Suffused Snow Flat (Tagiades gana), the South Indian subspecies lacks a stark white patch on the upper hindwing.
Tagiades japetus.habitat: Evergreen, moist deciduous, and bamboo forests, shaded estate edges, and secondary woodlands.
Tagiades japetus.behavior: Darts briskly along sunlit gaps before snapping flat beneath a broad leaf with wings held horizontally; males patrol fixed leaf perches and visit bird droppings.
Tagiades japetus.season: Common year-round across wet hills and foothills.
Tagiades japetus.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Valparai, Kodaikanal slopes, Meghamalai, and Eastern Ghats (Yercaud, Kolli Hills, Pachamalai).
Tagiades japetus.notes: Represented in Tamil Nadu by subspecies Tagiades japetus obscurus, whose dark brown upper hindwing makes the chalky white underside flash unexpectedly in flight.

Tagiades gana.headline: Broad snow-white tornal flat with black marginal spots and reduced forewing dots
Tagiades gana.upperwing: Dark brown forewing bearing only three minute subapical white hyaline dots (lacking cell spots); hindwing shows a crisp snow-white lower third studded with black marginal spots along veins 1b to 4 and two dark anterior spots.
Tagiades gana.underwing: Paler brown with forewing apical dots repeated and the snow-white hindwing area expanding further toward the base and costa, dusted lightly with brown along the upper edge.
Tagiades gana.similarSpecies: Separated from Water Snow Flat (Tagiades litigiosa) by lacking forewing cell spots and having two dark spots along the upper margin of the white hindwing zone; far whiter above than Tagiades japetus.
Tagiades gana.habitat: Wet evergreen and semi-evergreen hill forests, shaded stream corridors, and wild yam thickets.
Tagiades gana.behavior: Flies swiftly at waist height along shaded trails, resting completely flat on undersides of leaves and occasionally nectaring at wild gingers or visiting bird droppings.
Tagiades gana.season: Present throughout the year in wet hills, peaking June to December.
Tagiades gana.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hills of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Nilgiris, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Tagiades gana.notes: South Indian populations correspond to subspecies Tagiades gana silvia; larvae build triangular leaf-flap shelters on forest Dioscorea climbers.

Tagiades litigiosa.headline: Bold black-and-snow-white flat resting openly with spread wings
Tagiades litigiosa.upperwing: Dark brown-black forewings specked with tiny white spots paired with hindwings whose lower half is snow-white with crisp black marginal dots.
Tagiades litigiosa.underwing: Almost pure snow-white across the hindwing.
Tagiades litigiosa.similarSpecies: Cleaner snow-white lower half of the hindwing upper surface with discrete black marginal dots separates it from Common Snow Flat (Tagiades japetus).
Tagiades litigiosa.habitat: Moist hill forests, wooded streams, and shaded foothills.
Tagiades litigiosa.behavior: Darts swiftly along shaded forest trails and settles flat underneath or atop broad leaves with wings spread.
Tagiades litigiosa.tnDistribution: Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Pachamalai, and Western/Eastern Ghats.
Tagiades litigiosa.notes: Contrasting snow-white hindwing margin makes it flash brightly against dark shaded forest trails.

Odontoptilum angulatum.headline: Warm chestnut-brown skipper with wavy wing edges and chalky white under-hindwings
Odontoptilum angulatum.upperwing: Rich chestnut-brown crossed by darker discal bands, pale crescentic hyaline forewing marks, and fine wavy whitish striae across an angled, tooth-edged hindwing.
Odontoptilum angulatum.underwing: Forewing mottled brown with pale violet-grey suffusion; hindwing starkly chalky white washed thinly with pale brown bands and dark outer specks, flashing bright white in flight.
Odontoptilum angulatum.similarSpecies: Rich chestnut upperside, deeply angled hindwing margin at vein 7, and chalky white under-hindwing separate it from Caprona angles and Tapena thwaitesi.
Odontoptilum angulatum.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous forests, foothills, bamboo-lined paths, and riparian scrub.
Odontoptilum angulatum.behavior: Basks completely flat on sunny upper leaf surfaces or rocky stream beds, often sipping damp mineral water and bird droppings before darting into shade.
Odontoptilum angulatum.season: Recorded year-round, peaking from July to January.
Odontoptilum angulatum.tnDistribution: Widespread in Western and Eastern Ghats foothills including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Anamalai, Pachamalai, Kolli Hills, and Yercaud.
Odontoptilum angulatum.notes: Males carry a prominent white hair-tuft on the forelegs while females bear a thick anal hair tuft used to cloak freshly laid eggs.

Caprona ransonnetti.headline: Dry-zone spotted flat breeding openly on Urena lobata foliage
Caprona ransonnetti.upperwing: Warm golden-brown wings dappled with translucent white forewing spots and pale scalloped outer margins.
Caprona ransonnetti.underwing: Chalky pale creamy-white speckled with small brown dots on the outer half, strongly contrasting with its brown upperside.
Caprona ransonnetti.similarSpecies: Bright chalky-white underside with crisp brown marginal spots separates Golden Angle from Spotted Angle (Caprona agama).
Caprona ransonnetti.habitat: Scrub forests, dry deciduous foothills, open sunny trails, and roadside Urena thickets.
Caprona ransonnetti.behavior: Rests flat with wings wide open on sunlit leaves or underneath leaf blades; caterpillars cut and fold neat leaf shelters.
Caprona ransonnetti.tnDistribution: Widespread across plains, scrub hills, and Western/Eastern Ghats foothills.
Caprona ransonnetti.notes: Pale yellow-green caterpillars feed openly during bright sunshine on Urena lobata shrubs, documented by TNBS photographers.
sources: Pattampoochi Issue 27, Picture Story: Golden Angle (p. 23)

Caprona agama.headline: Blackish-grey and white dappled angle marked below with crisp round black spots
Caprona agama.upperwing: Dark blackish-grey heavily checkered with semi-translucent white cell, discal, subapical, and submarginal spots across both wings; cilia are sharply checkered white and brown.
Caprona agama.underwing: Forewing white clouded with blackish-grey outer shading; hindwing clean white studded with well-defined round black dots including a twin basal spot, cell-end dot, and discal and submarginal rows.
Caprona agama.similarSpecies: Separated from Golden Angle (Caprona ransonnetti) and Pale Spotted Angle (Caprona alida) by its colder grey-black upperside and clean white under-hindwing dotted with sharp round black spots.
Caprona agama.habitat: Dry deciduous forests, scrub foothills, rocky hill trails, and open woodland edges.
Caprona agama.behavior: Low rapid flight over sunlit undergrowth; settles flat on upper leaf surfaces, twigs, or bare soil and visits Tridax and Lantana blooms.
Caprona agama.season: Mainly dry and post-monsoon seasons from September to April, with wet-season broods darker.
Caprona agama.tnDistribution: Scattered across dry foothills and Western/Eastern Ghats slopes including Mudumalai, Coimbatore foothills, Salem, Pachamalai, and Tirunelveli.
Caprona agama.notes: Exhibits marked seasonal polyphenism in India, with dry-season forms showing broader white marbling and cleaner underside markings.

Caprona alida.headline: Ochreous-brown angle heavily frosted white across the underside
Caprona alida.upperwing: Warm ochreous-brown (duller in females) bearing excavated white hyaline cell spots, median dots, a straight oblique line of three subapical spots, and faint scalloped brown lines on the hindwing; cilia white checkered brown.
Caprona alida.underwing: Pale brown uniformly smeared and frosted with chalky white scales across both wings, marked softly by brown outer marginal lines and lacking stark isolated black spots.
Caprona alida.similarSpecies: Differs from Spotted Angle (Caprona agama) by its warmer ochreous-brown upperside and uniformly white-frosted underside without bold round black dots; lacks the crisp outer black-spot row of Caprona ransonnetti.
Caprona alida.habitat: Dry deciduous jungles, foothill scrub, stony hill slopes, and open forest clearings.
hostPlants: Malvaceae shrubs (larval host unconfirmed in South India; related Caprona feed on Microcos and Helicteres)
Caprona alida.behavior: Restless low flyer patrolling sunny paths and boulders; perches flat on exposed twigs and leaves and visits small dry-zone wildflowers.
Caprona alida.season: Most often encountered from October to March across dry hill tracts.
Caprona alida.tnDistribution: Local and scarce across Tamil Nadu dry hills and foothills including Coimbatore, Mudumalai fringe, Javadi Hills, Pachamalai, and southern Eastern Ghats.
Caprona alida.notes: Peninsular Indian populations represent subspecies Caprona alida vespa; one of the less frequently photographed skippers in Tamil Nadu.

Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.headline: Endemic Western Ghats spotted flat dusted olive-gold with separated forewing spots
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.upperwing: Dark olive-brown richly dusted with golden-olive scales; forewing spots are pale creamy-yellow and separated rather than fused, while the hindwing carries irregular rows of dull yellow spots and chequered cilia.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.underwing: Warm brown with golden-yellow scaling at wing bases, repeating the well-separated pale forewing spots and distinct orange-yellow hindwing spot rows; antennal shaft dark and chequered.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Spotted Flat (Celaenorrhinus leucocera) and Bengal Spotted Flat (Celaenorrhinus putra) by its heavy olive-yellow dusting, well-separated discal spots, and spotted upper hindwing.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.habitat: Moist deciduous, semi-evergreen, and evergreen forests, shaded hill roads, and Strobilanthes undergrowth.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.behavior: Fast shaded flier that rests flat with outspread wings beneath leaves, on mossy rocks, or inside culverts, emerging in morning sun to feed at Impatiens and Strobilanthes.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.season: Active most of the year in wet hills, peaking July to December.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.tnDistribution: Western Ghats ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Celaenorrhinus ambareesa.notes: A Western Ghats and peninsular Indian endemic often found resting in cool stone culverts and rock overhangs during hot afternoons.

Celaenorrhinus leucocera.headline: Familiar forest spotted flat with snow-white male antennae and fused discal band
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown forewing crossed by a broad oblique white hyaline discal band where the cell and space 2 spots fuse cleanly, plus tiny subapical dots; hindwing carries dull orange-yellow spots and chequered cilia.
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.underwing: Dark brown repeating the crisp white forewing band and dull ochreous hindwing spots; males display wholly white antennal shafts while females show brown shafts with white clubs.
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.similarSpecies: Connected white discal band and chequered margins separate it from Malabar Spotted Flat (C. ambareesa) and Tamil Spotted Flat (C. fusca); distinct yellow hindwing spots separate it from Bengal Spotted Flat (C. putra).
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, shaded estate roads, and forest understorey.
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.behavior: Darts rapidly through dappled understorey before tucking flat beneath broad leaves; visits forest flowers early in the morning and mud-puddles along damp trails.
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.season: Common year-round in hill tracts, especially abundant from June to January.
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.tnDistribution: Common across Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Palani Hills, KMTR) and higher Eastern Ghats (Yercaud, Kolli Hills, Pachamalai).
Celaenorrhinus leucocera.notes: The gleaming white male antennal shafts are a reliable field clue even in dim forest light when resting beneath foliage.

Celaenorrhinus putra.headline: Pitch-dark spotted flat with unchequered cilia and an almost unmarked hindwing
Celaenorrhinus putra.upperwing: Deep sooty blackish-brown with narrower fused white discal spots on the forewing, a separated small spot in space 1b, almost unmarked dark hindwings, and dull brownish-white unchequered cilia.
Celaenorrhinus putra.underwing: Uniform blackish-brown echoing the clean white forewing spots with scarcely any yellow hindwing mottling; antennal club is white while the shaft remains dark brown in males.
Celaenorrhinus putra.similarSpecies: Darker sooty ground colour, unchequered hindwing cilia, dark male antennal shaft, and nearly plain upper hindwing separate it from Common Spotted Flat (Celaenorrhinus leucocera).
Celaenorrhinus putra.habitat: Dense wet evergreen forests, shaded hill streams, and deep understorey ravines.
Celaenorrhinus putra.behavior: Skulks in dark forest undergrowth, resting flat beneath broad leaves or damp rocks and briefly visiting blossoms in dappled sunbeams.
Celaenorrhinus putra.season: Mainly monsoon and post-monsoon months from June to December.
Celaenorrhinus putra.tnDistribution: Restricted to wet Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Nilgiris, Valparai, Anamalai, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Celaenorrhinus putra.notes: Subspecies Celaenorrhinus putra sanda occurs in southern India and prefers deeper, damper evergreen shade than C. leucocera.

Celaenorrhinus fusca.headline: Olive-brown flat with separated forewing spots and white-ringed antennal clubs
Celaenorrhinus fusca.upperwing: Dark olive-brown forewing where the hyaline white cell spot and space 2 discal spot stand clearly apart; hindwing is nearly plain dark brown above with crisp black-and-white chequered cilia.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.underwing: Dusky brown repeating the well-separated forewing hyaline spots and faint dull markings on the hindwing; antennae are sharply chequered white along the shaft with white clubs.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.similarSpecies: Clearly separated forewing cell and space 2 spots distinguish it from Celaenorrhinus leucocera and C. putra, while its plain dark upper hindwing and chequered white antennae separate it from C. ambareesa.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.habitat: Moist evergreen and shola-edge hill forests, bamboo-lined streams, and shaded undergrowth.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.behavior: Rapid erratic flier along shaded paths that settles flat beneath leaves and occasionally basks briefly with wide-open wings in morning sunflecks.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.season: Recorded chiefly from July to January in higher hill ranges.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Anamalai Hills, Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Meghamalai, and southern Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu.
Celaenorrhinus fusca.notes: Often listed under Celaenorrhinus ruficornis fusca; originally described from the Nilgiris and closely tied to montane Strobilanthes thickets.

Pseudocoladenia dan.headline: Warm rufous-brown flat common along sunlit forest paths and damp mud
Pseudocoladenia dan.upperwing: Rich tawny rufous-brown marked with pale yellow-white semi-hyaline forewing spots (paired conjoined spots at cell end, discal spots, and three subapical dots) and wavy dark spot rows across the hindwing.
Pseudocoladenia dan.underwing: Warm orange-brown repeating the dark hindwing bands and translucent forewing spots without crisp golden-black contrast; palpi are warm brown above and paler ochre beneath.
Pseudocoladenia dan.similarSpecies: Smaller and uniformly rufous-brown rather than bright black-and-golden-yellow like Tricoloured Pied Flat (Coladenia indrani), and lacks the bold black sub-basal forewing spot.
Pseudocoladenia dan.habitat: Forest edges, moist deciduous foothills, shaded gardens, coffee estates, and stream trails.
Pseudocoladenia dan.behavior: Darts briskly at low height and perches flat on upper leaf surfaces, twigs, and damp mud; visits Lantana, Bidens, and bird droppings.
Pseudocoladenia dan.season: Common throughout the year across hills and foothills.
Pseudocoladenia dan.tnDistribution: Abundant across Western Ghats (Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, Palani Hills, KMTR) and Eastern Ghats (Yercaud, Kolli Hills, Pachamalai).
Pseudocoladenia dan.notes: Nominate subspecies Pseudocoladenia dan dan flies in peninsular India; very accommodating to photographers when feeding at mineral-rich mud or flowers.

Sarangesa purendra.headline: Ash-brown small flat patterned with crisp hyaline dots and sharp pale underside spots
Sarangesa purendra.upperwing: Dull olive-greyish brown bearing distinct white semi-hyaline spots across the forewing (two cell marks, discal spots in spaces 2 and 3, a lower dot, and subapical dots) and faint dark mottled bands on the hindwing.
Sarangesa purendra.underwing: Paler grey-brown showing sharper pale spots, a clear white streak below the forewing cell base, and a well-defined curved arc of whitish discal spots plus a central cell spot on the hindwing.
Sarangesa purendra.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Small Flat (Sarangesa dasahara) by stronger, cleaner hyaline forewing spotting above and sharper pale discal spots (not blurred dark blotches) beneath.
Sarangesa purendra.habitat: Dry deciduous scrub, thorny foothills, rocky hill slopes, and open forest edges.
Sarangesa purendra.behavior: Flies close to dry stony ground and low shrubs, resting flat on sun-warmed rocks, dry twigs, or undersides of leaves and nectaring at Tridax and Justicia.
Sarangesa purendra.season: Seen nearly year-round in dry hills, peaking October to March.
Sarangesa purendra.tnDistribution: Coimbatore foothills, Mudumalai, Moyar valley, Salem, Dharmapuri, Pachamalai, and drier Eastern Ghats slopes.
Sarangesa purendra.notes: South Indian populations correspond to subspecies Sarangesa purendra hopkinsi, favouring drier, more open scrub than S. dasahara.

Sarangesa dasahara.headline: Dusky small flat with blurred dark underside blotches common in shaded lanes
Sarangesa dasahara.upperwing: Dark smoky grey-brown with tiny pin-point white hyaline subapical and upper cell dots on the forewing, faint darker discal bands, and brownish-grey chequered cilia.
Sarangesa dasahara.underwing: Paler grey-brown marked with large, soft-edged blackish-brown blotches across the forewing and faint greyish suffusion with obscure dark spot rows on the hindwing.
Sarangesa dasahara.similarSpecies: Tiny forewing white dots and blurred dark underside blotches distinguish it from Spotted Small Flat (Sarangesa purendra), which has sharper white spots above and below.
Sarangesa dasahara.habitat: Wooded gardens, moist and dry deciduous forest paths, bamboo brakes, and shaded road banks.
Sarangesa dasahara.behavior: Patrols low shaded earth banks and path edges, darting erratically before settling flat on soil, dry leaves, or beneath foliage; drinks from damp mud and small herbs.
Sarangesa dasahara.season: Common year-round statewide, peaking post-monsoon from September to February.
Sarangesa dasahara.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu hills and foothills from Mudumalai, Siruvani, and Anamalai to Pachamalai, Yercaud, Kolli Hills, and wooded plains.
Sarangesa dasahara.notes: Often rests pressed against shaded mud cuttings and tree trunks where its smoky grey-brown wings provide effective camouflage.

Gomalia elma.headline: Compact olive-and-white marbled skipper of dry scrub and Abutilon thickets
Gomalia elma.upperwing: Olive-brown marbled with blackish-brown bands, a square dark costal patch framed by white hyaline cell and subapical dots on the forewing, and a broad pale creamy median band across the hindwing.
Gomalia elma.underwing: Paler greyish-olive repeating the crisp white median hindwing band and forewing cell markings, with white-ringed dark palpi and rounded, non-hooked antennal clubs.
Gomalia elma.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Grizzled Skipper (Spialia galba) by its olive-marbled pattern, broad continuous white hindwing band, and lack of neat black-and-white checkered wing borders.
Gomalia elma.habitat: Arid scrub jungles, coastal dune thickets, fallow fields, rocky hillocks, and dry plains.
Gomalia elma.behavior: Darts rapidly inches above sun-baked ground around Abutilon bushes, perching flat on bare soil, stones, or tiny wildflowers with wings open.
Gomalia elma.season: Active throughout the year in dry plains and scrublands, peaking November to March.
Gomalia elma.tnDistribution: Widespread across Chennai, Chengalpattu, Madurai, Ramanathapuram, Coimbatore plains, Moyar scrub, and dry Eastern Ghats foothills.
Gomalia elma.notes: South Asian populations represent subspecies Gomalia elma albofasciata; a classic dry-zone skipper shared between Africa and peninsular India.

Spialia galba.headline: Tiny checkered black-and-white skipper basking flat on sunlit ground
Spialia galba.upperwing: Charcoal-black checkered neatly with crisp white spots across both forewings and hindwings.
Spialia galba.underwing: Olive-grey crossed by clean broken white bands.
Spialia galba.similarSpecies: Smaller and evenly checkered with black-and-white bars across the margins compared to African Marbled Skipper (Gomalia elma).
Spialia galba.habitat: Sunny lawns, dry scrub, rocky paths, fallow fields, and open plains.
Spialia galba.behavior: Darts rapidly inches above sunlit ground and perches with wings wide open.
Spialia galba.tnDistribution: Common across Tamil Nadu plains and open foothills.
Spialia galba.notes: Tucked neatly under dry grass heads at dusk, resembling a small checkered moth until sunlight hits its spread wings.

Baracus subditus.headline: Montane Western Ghats grass skipper bearing pale longitudinal streaks below
Baracus subditus.upperwing: Dark olive-brown with diffuse pale yellowish streaks and small spots in the forewing disc and apex (stronger in females) and pale-edged greyish-ochre cilia.
Baracus subditus.underwing: Ochreous-brown crossed lengthwise on the hindwing by prominent continuous pale creamy-yellow streaks through the cell and interspaces, bordered cleanly by dark vein lines.
Baracus subditus.similarSpecies: Separated from Hampson's Hedge Hopper (Baracus hampsoni) by continuous longitudinal pale streaks across the under-hindwing rather than broken rows of discrete spots.
Baracus subditus.habitat: High-elevation montane grasslands, shola margins, marshy stream banks, and grassy hill slopes above 1,200 m.
Baracus subditus.behavior: Weak, low bouncing flight weaving just above wet tussock grass; settles with wings closed or half-open in jet-plane posture and feeds at tiny highland daisies and clover.
Baracus subditus.season: Mainly February to May and September to December around highland clearings.
Baracus subditus.tnDistribution: High ranges of Tamil Nadu Western Ghats including Nilgiris (Avalanche, Mukurthi, Ooty), Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), and high Anamalais.
Baracus subditus.notes: A strictly montane Western Ghats endemic generally replacing B. hampsoni above 1,200 m elevation south of the Palakkad Gap.

Baracus hampsoni.headline: Foothill Western Ghats hedge hopper marked with broken pale spots underneath
Baracus hampsoni.upperwing: Dark umber-brown dusted olive at the wing base, displaying small discrete pale yellowish discal and subapical forewing spots (brighter in females) and plain dark hindwings.
Baracus hampsoni.underwing: Warm ochreous-brown on the hindwing broken into distinct rows of separated pale creamy-yellow spots and dark-edged blotches rather than unbroken longitudinal stripes.
Baracus hampsoni.similarSpecies: Spot-broken under-hindwing pattern separates it from the cleanly striped Hedge Hopper (Baracus subditus), and it lacks the bright yellow underside of Bush Hopper (Ampittia dioscorides).
Baracus hampsoni.habitat: Mid-elevation forest grasslands, bamboo clearings, moist deciduous edges, and grassy stream banks from 300 to 1,200 m.
Baracus hampsoni.behavior: Hops low through damp grass blades, basking in jet-plane posture in morning sun and nectaring at small ground herbs such as Justicia and Ageratum.
Baracus hampsoni.season: Recorded chiefly from August to January during monsoon and post-monsoon grass growth.
Baracus hampsoni.tnDistribution: Mid-elevation Western Ghats slopes of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Anamalai foothills, Mudumalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
