Baracus hampsoni.notes: An intermediate population described from the Anamalai Hills as form gotha bridges variation between B. hampsoni and B. subditus.

Ampittia dioscorides.headline: Tiny black-and-golden marsh skipper thriving around paddy fields and wet reeds
Ampittia dioscorides.upperwing: Males are dark brown emblazoned with bright golden-yellow patches across the forewing disc, costa, and hindwing centre; females are darker brown with tiny yellow forewing spots and a small hindwing bar.
Ampittia dioscorides.underwing: Bright golden-yellow densely speckled with crisp black dots across the hindwing and outer margins; antennal clubs are black above and tipped yellow beneath.
Ampittia dioscorides.similarSpecies: Black-spotted golden-yellow underside and bright yellow male upperside patches separate it instantly from grass darts (Taractrocera, Potanthus) and Baracus hedge hoppers.
Ampittia dioscorides.habitat: Paddy bunds, freshwater marshes, wet grassy ditches, irrigated gardens, and stream-side reeds.
Ampittia dioscorides.behavior: Bobs weakly among emergent rice and sedge stems just above water, basking in classic jet-plane posture and visiting Lindernia, Tridax, and Lantana flowers.
Ampittia dioscorides.season: Active throughout the year, peaking during monsoon and paddy cropping months.
Ampittia dioscorides.tnDistribution: Widespread across coastal wetlands, Cauvery delta, Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, and hill valleys throughout Tamil Nadu.
Ampittia dioscorides.notes: One of the easiest skippers to recognise in Tamil Nadu wetlands; males hold tiny sunny grass-tip territories over flooded paddy borders.

Aeromachus dubius.headline: Minute olive-brown grass skipper with ochreous-dusted undersides and hooked antennae
Aeromachus dubius.upperwing: Uniform dark olive-brown with greyish-white cilia; forewing spots are obsolete or faintly hinted, and males carry a tiny raised scale-fold brand along vein 1a.
Aeromachus dubius.underwing: Forewing umber-brown with a pale upper cell-end dot and faint post-medial spot arc; hindwing densely dusted yellow-ochreous without crisp white scaling; antennal club bears a short pointed apiculus.
Aeromachus dubius.similarSpecies: Slightly larger than Pygmy Scrub Hopper (Aeromachus pygmaeus), showing ochreous-yellow rather than frosted white hindwing scaling and a distinct pointed tip (apiculus) on the antennal club.
Aeromachus dubius.habitat: Shaded forest trails, grassy hill clearings, scrub edges, and moist deciduous understorey.
Aeromachus dubius.behavior: Flies close to shaded grass tufts with rapid buzzing wingbeats, resting upright with closed wings or jet-plane basking and sipping tiny Acanthaceae flowers.
Aeromachus dubius.season: Recorded almost year-round in hills, peaking July to December.
Aeromachus dubius.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, Pachamalai, Kolli Hills, and Yercaud.
Aeromachus dubius.notes: Nominate subspecies Aeromachus dubius dubius occurs across southern India; easily overlooked because of its tiny size and low shaded flight.

Aeromachus pygmaeus.headline: Smallest Tamil Nadu skipper recognized by blunt antennal clubs and frosted undersides
Aeromachus pygmaeus.upperwing: Plain dark olive-brown in both sexes without distinct discal spots and no male forewing brand, edged by pale greyish-brown cilia.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.underwing: Paler brown dusted heavily with minute frosty white scales over the hindwing and forewing apex, showing a tiny white cell-end dot and faint curved discal band; antennal club is blunt without a hooked apiculus.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.similarSpecies: Blunt club-tipped antennae lacking an apiculus and heavy frosty-white hindwing scaling separate it from Dingy Scrub Hopper (Aeromachus dubius) and dark bobs.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.habitat: Sunlit grassy forest edges, open lawns near scrub, foothill paths, and dry-to-moist grassland pockets.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.behavior: Flutters weakly only centimetres above short grass, perching on grass blades with wings closed or slightly parted to feed at tiny Desmodium and Tridax blossoms.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.season: Mostly July to February following monsoon rains, though lingering year-round in moist pockets.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats foothills, Coimbatore, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kanyakumari, and coastal wooded parks.
Aeromachus pygmaeus.notes: At barely 20 mm across, this minute skipper holds the record as one of the smallest butterflies in southern India.

Halpemorpha hyrtacus.headline: Western Ghats endemic ace contrasting dark forewings with a pure white hindwing band
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.upperwing: Shining dark hair-brown with colourless hyaline forewing spots (two oblique cell dots, two discal spots, three subapical dots) and a shining black oblique male brand; hindwing unmarked dark brown.
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.underwing: Dull dark grey-brown on the forewing; hindwing starkly bicoloured with a broad pure-white discal band widest toward the inner margin (stopping short of the costa) and obscure ochreous outer spots.
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.similarSpecies: Broad pure-white inner band stopping below the costa on the under-hindwing and glossy black male brand separate it from Moore's Ace (Halpe porus) and Southern Spotted Ace (Thoressa astigmata).
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.habitat: Wet evergreen and bamboo-reed hill forests, shaded forest streams, and Ochlandra reed brakes.
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.behavior: Swift, bounding flight along shaded stream clearings; rests upright on bamboo leaves or basks briefly in morning sunspots and visits damp sand and forest flowers.
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.season: Mainly August to January during and after southwest and northeast monsoons.
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Anamalai, Valparai, Siruvani, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Halpemorpha hyrtacus.notes: Widely known as Sovia hyrtacus in older Indian guides and now placed in Halpemorpha; strictly tied to endemic Ochlandra reed-bamboos.

Thoressa honorei.headline: Endemic bright orange-patched ace lighting up southern Western Ghats bamboo hills
Thoressa honorei.upperwing: Dark dusky brown with golden-yellow basal hair streaks, a large rhomboidal cell spot, elongated median and subapical spots on the forewing, and a vivid large orange-yellow discal patch enclosing a dark dot on the hindwing.
Thoressa honorei.underwing: Forewing blackish with broad ochre-yellow apex and outer margin; hindwing bright warm ochre-yellow throughout, dotted neatly with a black cell-end spot and curved postdiscal dark dots.
Thoressa honorei.similarSpecies: Large bright orange-yellow discal patch on the upper hindwing and bright yellow dotted under-hindwing distinguish it instantly from all other Tamil Nadu Thoressa and Halpe aces.
Thoressa honorei.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests with thick bamboo and reed undergrowth.
Thoressa honorei.behavior: Strong darting flier that perches prominently on sunlit bamboo tips in jet-plane posture, visits Lantana and Strobilanthes blooms, and puddles on wet forest roads.
Thoressa honorei.season: Recorded nearly year-round in wet hills, peaking May-June and September-December.
Thoressa honorei.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kovai Kutralam, Anamalai, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Thoressa honorei.notes: First described from the Palani and Nilgiri region in the nineteenth century; the most brightly coloured member of the endemic South Indian Thoressa group.

Thoressa astigmata.headline: Unbranded endemic ace bearing a neat arc of seven white dots beneath
Thoressa astigmata.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown lacking any male forewing brand, bearing seven crisp semi-hyaline white spots (two conjoined cell spots, two quadrate discal spots, three subapical dots) and dull ochre hairs over an unmarked hindwing.
Thoressa astigmata.underwing: Rich dark chocolate-brown marked on the hindwing by an elegant curved row of six or seven discrete pure-white spots and a twin white tornal mark; antennal clubs are white beneath with red tips.
Thoressa astigmata.similarSpecies: Curved row of discrete white spots (not a solid white band) on a dark chocolate under-hindwing separates it cleanly from Halpe porus and Halpemorpha hyrtacus, and it lacks a male sex brand.
Thoressa astigmata.habitat: Moist evergreen forests, shaded valleys, and reed-bamboo thickets along hill streams.
Thoressa astigmata.behavior: Fast, wary forest skipper that basks in sunflecks on bamboo leaves and drops down to damp stream-side sand or bird droppings in morning light.
Thoressa astigmata.season: Active primarily from August to December and March to May.
Thoressa astigmata.tnDistribution: Western Ghats tracts of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Anamalai, Valparai, Meghamalai, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Thoressa astigmata.notes: Its species name astigmata highlights the absence of the male forewing stigma (brand) present in many related bamboo aces.

Thoressa sitala.headline: Rare high-elevation Nilgiri and Palani ace clothed in rusty ochre undersides
Thoressa sitala.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown forewing with two small cell spots, two well-separated discal spots, and two subapical white dots; hindwing unmarked dark brown draped in long ochreous hairs, with ochreous hindwing cilia.
Thoressa sitala.underwing: Forewing apex and costal half washed rusty ferruginous-ochreous; hindwing uniformly rusty ochre-brown marked faintly with two obscure whitish median dots and faint tornal marks; forewing cilia spotted brown.
Thoressa sitala.similarSpecies: Very close to Evershed's Ace (Thoressa evershedi), separated by uniformly ochreous (non-grey) hindwing cilia and a uniformly rusty-ochre under-hindwing without a distinct brown marginal band.
Thoressa sitala.habitat: High-elevation shola-grassland margins, montane evergreen forest edges, and highland bamboo breaks above 1,200 m.
Thoressa sitala.behavior: Darts swiftly along sunlit shola edges and stream clearings, basking in jet-plane posture on bamboo culms and feeding at highland Impatiens and Strobilanthes flowers.
Thoressa sitala.season: Mainly March to May and September to November.
Thoressa sitala.tnDistribution: High Western Ghats plateaus of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris (Coonoor, Ooty slopes), Anamalai, and Palani Hills.
Thoressa sitala.notes: A localized Western Ghats highland endemic first described from Ooty in the Nilgiris and much prized during mountain butterfly surveys.

Thoressa evershedi.headline: Palani and southern hills endemic ace with orange-tipped clubs and plain grey cilia
Thoressa evershedi.upperwing: Deep blackish-brown bearing slightly smaller ochre-white hyaline spots than Thoressa sitala; forewing cilia are grey checkered brown while hindwing cilia are plain uniform grey without brown spots.
Thoressa evershedi.underwing: Forewing costal and apical areas and entire hindwing washed ochreous-red, with brown suffusion along the hindwing inner margin and a distinct brownish outer-marginal spot band; antennal club is bright orange-red distally.
Thoressa evershedi.similarSpecies: Separated from Sitala Ace (Thoressa sitala) by its plain unspotted grey hindwing cilia, brown-suffused inner under-hindwing, brownish outer-marginal band, and bright orange-red apical half of the antennal club.
Thoressa evershedi.habitat: High-altitude shola forests, montane evergreen streams, and dense Ochlandra reed-bamboo brakes.
Thoressa evershedi.behavior: Flies swiftly along sunny forest gaps and stream corridors at mid-morning, settling on low shrubs or reed tips in jet-plane posture and visiting damp earth.
Thoressa evershedi.season: Recorded chiefly between March and May and September to December.
Thoressa evershedi.tnDistribution: Palani Hills (Kodaikanal slopes), High Wavys / Meghamalai, Anamalai, and Tirunelveli-Agasthyamalai hills of Tamil Nadu.
Thoressa evershedi.notes: Originally discovered in the Palani Hills by astronomer and naturalist John Evershed and formally described by W. H. Evans in 1910.

Halpe porus.headline: Dark brown bamboo ace crossed below by a bold vein-cut white band
Halpe porus.upperwing: Velvety dark brown bearing paired (upper and lower) semi-hyaline white cell spots, two discal spots in spaces 2 and 3, and three subapical dots on the forewing, with chequered cilia.
Halpe porus.underwing: Dull dark brown on the forewing; hindwing crossed cleanly by an outwardly curved pure-white discal band cut sharply into elongated bars by dark veins, plus submarginal white spots and a cell-end dot.
Halpe porus.similarSpecies: Two distinct forewing cell spots and crisp pure-white dark-veined discal band plus submarginal spots beneath separate it cleanly from South Indian Ace (Halpe hindu) and Bicolour Ace (Halpemorpha hyrtacus).
Halpe porus.habitat: Bamboo forests, wooded hill trails, shaded gardens near bamboo clumps, and moist deciduous valleys.
Halpe porus.behavior: Fast, darting bamboo-edge flier that perches in jet-plane posture on sunlit bamboo foliage and feeds readily on Lantana, Stachytarpheta, and damp sand.
Halpe porus.season: Active most of the year, peaking from July to January.
Halpe porus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu Western Ghats (Mudumalai, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalai, KMTR) and Eastern Ghats (Pachamalai, Kolli Hills, Yercaud).
Halpe porus.notes: Named Bispot Banded Ace for the twin hyaline dots in its forewing cell; also one of the few Halpe aces that reaches wooded foothill bamboo plantations.

Halpe hindu.headline: Endemic Western Ghats banded ace with single cell spot and ochre-dusted underside
Halpe hindu.upperwing: Blackish-brown forewing bearing an oblique male sex brand, usually a single small hyaline spot in the upper cell end, two discal spots, and two to three tiny subapical dots; hindwing plain dark brown.
Halpe hindu.underwing: Paler ochre-tinted brown dusted basally with dull greyish-ochreous scales on the hindwing and crossed by a curved series of obscure ochreous-white discal spots and faint submarginal dots.
Halpe hindu.similarSpecies: Single (or absent) forewing cell spot, oblique male brand, and dull ochreous-smeared under-hindwing with broken pale spots separate it from the crisp white-banded Moore's Ace (Halpe porus).
Halpe hindu.habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous hill forests, bamboo groves, and shaded stream banks.
Halpe hindu.behavior: Bounds swiftly among mid-storey bamboo leaves, basking in jet-plane posture on sunlit foliage and visiting damp stream gravel and wild flowers.
Halpe hindu.season: Recorded chiefly from June to December around monsoon seasons.
Halpe hindu.tnDistribution: Western Ghats tracts of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Anamalai, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Halpe hindu.notes: Elevated to full species status from the Halpe homolea complex; strictly endemic to the Western Ghats hills.

Arnetta mercara.headline: Endemic Western Ghats forest hopper awaiting validated TN confirmation
Arnetta mercara.upperwing: Dark brown bearing small pale translucent spots toward the outer forewing.
Arnetta mercara.underwing: Rich dark chocolate-brown dusted with golden-ochre scales toward the outer half of the hindwing and dotted with tiny pale specks.
Arnetta mercara.similarSpecies: Dark chocolate underside suffused golden-ochre distally separates it from Vindhyan Bob (Arnetta vindhiana).
Arnetta mercara.habitat: Undergrowth of moist evergreen forests in the Western Ghats.
Arnetta mercara.behavior: Low, brisk flier along shaded evergreen trails.
Arnetta mercara.tnDistribution: One of 4 checklist species awaiting validated TNBS sighting confirmation in Tamil Nadu.
Arnetta mercara.notes: Shaded Ochlandra reed brakes along high Western Ghats slopes offer the best habitat to confirm photographic records.

Arnetta vindhiana.headline: Ashy-fringed olive-brown hill bob common in dry bamboo and jungle slopes
Arnetta vindhiana.upperwing: Dark olive-brown forewing marked with an upper cell-end dot, three conjoined subapical dots, two discal spots, and an oval dot above vein 1b, bordered by pale ashy-grey cilia.
Arnetta vindhiana.underwing: Warm dusky ochreous-brown with broadly black lower forewing area; hindwing displays a small yellow crescent at the cell end, an upper costal dot, and five small pale discal specks.
Arnetta vindhiana.similarSpecies: Dusky ochreous under-hindwing with yellow cell crescent and pale specks separates it from Coorg Forest Hopper (Arnetta mercara), which shows a rich dark chocolate underside suffused golden-ochre distally.
Arnetta vindhiana.habitat: Dry bamboo tracts, moist deciduous hill slopes, scrub-forest edges, and grassy clearings.
Arnetta vindhiana.behavior: Flies low and rapidly between grass tussocks and shaded paths, settling in jet-plane posture on dry twigs or grass tips and visiting tiny wildflowers.
Arnetta vindhiana.season: Seen nearly year-round in hills, peaking post-monsoon from September to February.
Arnetta vindhiana.tnDistribution: Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Palani Hills, Meghamalai, Anamalai, and Eastern Ghats ranges such as Yercaud, Kolli Hills, and Pachamalai.
Arnetta vindhiana.notes: Unlike the strictly evergreen Coorg Forest Hopper (Arnetta mercara), Vindhyan Bob readily tolerates drier bamboo slopes and deciduous scrub.

Iambrix salsala.headline: Small rusty-brown grass bob dotted below with crisp silver-white pinpricks
Iambrix salsala.upperwing: Dark brown with a warm olive sheen; males bear a short oblique row of two or three blurred rusty-orange discal spots on the forewing, whereas females carry a curved chain of tiny white hyaline spots.
Iambrix salsala.underwing: Rich chestnut-brown washed black on the inner forewing and studded on the hindwing with tiny black-ringed silver-white pinprick spots (usually one in the cell and several discal dots).
Iambrix salsala.similarSpecies: Rich warm chestnut underside dotted with sharp silver-white pinpricks separates it from Dingy Scrub Hopper (Aeromachus dubius), Vindhyan Bob (Arnetta vindhiana), and Indian Palm Bob (Suastus gremius).
Iambrix salsala.habitat: Shaded forest edges, grassy garden lanes, bamboo thickets, coconut-shaded undergrowth, and foothill streams.
Iambrix salsala.behavior: Weak, bobbing low flight around shaded grass banks; rests upright with closed wings when feeding at Lantana, Tridax, and Asystasia, or opens half-way in morning sunflecks.
Iambrix salsala.season: Abundant year-round across wet and wooded regions.
Iambrix salsala.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, Coimbatore, Kanyakumari, and shaded coastal gardens of Tamil Nadu.
Iambrix salsala.notes: Southern Indian populations belong to subspecies Iambrix salsala luteipalpis, named for the bright yellowish palpi underneath its head.

Psolos fuligo.headline: Plain dark shade-loving skipper that rests with diverged forewing tips
Psolos fuligo.upperwing: Uniform unmarked dark chocolate-brown across both forewing and hindwing in both sexes; males carry an oval black sex-brand only on the underside of the forewing rather than dorsally.
Psolos fuligo.underwing: Slightly paler dark brown overlaid with a dull greyish-purple sheen toward the forewing apex and across the hindwing, marked with faint pale spots in forewing spaces 4-9 and obscure dark-ringed spots in hindwing spaces 2-7 and end-cell.
Psolos fuligo.similarSpecies: Total lack of upperwing spots separates Coon from Common Banded Demon (Notocrypta paralysos) and Restricted Demon (Notocrypta curvifascia), while the dull purplish-grey spotted hindwing underside separates it from smaller dark forest hoppers like Vindhyan Bob (Arnetta vindhiana) and Chestnut Bob (Iambrix salsala).
Psolos fuligo.habitat: Deeply shaded evergreen and semi-evergreen forest understorey, bamboo-lined hill streams, and cardamom or coffee shade groves.
Psolos fuligo.behavior: Weak-looking, low erratic flier that hugs cool shaded undergrowth; settles on broad leaves with forewing tips noticeably diverged outward rather than pressed tight, and visits damp stream soil and shaded ginger blooms.
Psolos fuligo.season: Active year-round in humid hill tracts, peaking from June to December during monsoon and post-monsoon months.
Psolos fuligo.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Anamalais (Top Slip and Valparai), Mudumalai, Nilgiri slopes, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Psolos fuligo.notes: Unlike sun-loving grass skippers that adopt a tight jet-plane stance, this Marantaceae feeder keeps to dim forest floors and holds its forewing apices angled outward at rest.

Notocrypta paralysos.headline: Jet-black forest skipper crossed by a broad white forewing band without subapical dots
Notocrypta paralysos.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown forewing crossed by a broad, slightly curved translucent white discal band across the cell end and spaces 1b-3 plus one small isolated white dot in space 4; subapical dots are normally absent and the hindwing is unmarked.
Notocrypta paralysos.underwing: Dark blackish-brown lightly dusted with lilac-grey scales along the forewing apex and outer hindwing margin; the white forewing band repeats cleanly without continuing into pale streaks along the costal margin.
Notocrypta paralysos.similarSpecies: Separated from Restricted Demon (Notocrypta curvifascia) by lacking crisp white subapical dots in spaces 6-8 and costal extensions above the band below; distinguished from Grass Demon (Udaspes folus) by its plain unmarked dark hindwing.
Notocrypta paralysos.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen hill forests, shaded stream banks, bamboo gullies, and overgrown plantation edges.
Notocrypta paralysos.behavior: Darts swiftly along shaded woodland paths and lands abruptly on ginger leaves or damp sand in a half-open basking posture; probes tubular forest flowers and feeds on bird droppings and wet gravel.
Notocrypta paralysos.season: Recorded throughout the year in wet hills, peaking between May and December.
Notocrypta paralysos.tnDistribution: Western Ghats ranges including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Kanyakumari, plus moist Eastern Ghats pockets such as Kolli Hills.
Notocrypta paralysos.notes: Females carry slightly wider white forewing bands than males and frequently lay single eggs on unfurling Zingiberaceae shoots in shaded ravines.

Notocrypta curvifascia.headline: Larger forest demon bearing subapical white spots beyond a stepped discal band
Notocrypta curvifascia.upperwing: Velvety blackish-brown forewing crossed by a narrower, stepped translucent white discal band spanning the cell and spaces 2-3, accompanied by three sharp white subapical dots in spaces 6-8 and an outer dot in space 4; hindwing uniformly dark.
Notocrypta curvifascia.underwing: Dark brown washed with purplish-grey along the outer margins; the forewing white band continues upward into pale streaks in spaces 10 and 11 toward the costa, while the hindwing shows faint dark discal shading.
Notocrypta curvifascia.similarSpecies: Larger than Common Banded Demon (Notocrypta paralysos) and separated cleanly by the three white subapical dots in spaces 6-8 and white costal streaks above the band on the forewing underside; lacks the large central white hindwing patch of Grass Demon (Udaspes folus).
Notocrypta curvifascia.habitat: Evergreen and semi-evergreen forest clearings, shaded cardamom estates, riparian undergrowth, and wild ginger patches.
Notocrypta curvifascia.behavior: Swift, low flight through shaded forest openings; basks briefly in sunflecks in a two-angle jet-plane stance, probes deep nectar corollas, and puddles at wet stream gravel and bird droppings.
Notocrypta curvifascia.season: Active year-round in humid hill forests, most abundant from June to November.
Notocrypta curvifascia.tnDistribution: Western Ghats stretches of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Valparai, Palani Hills, and Meghamalai.
Notocrypta curvifascia.notes: Caterpillars roll neat cylindrical tubes out of ginger and turmeric leaf edges tied with silk, emerging mainly around dusk and early morning to feed.

Udaspes folus.headline: Bold black-and-white skipper of ginger and turmeric patches
Udaspes folus.upperwing: Jet-black wings boldly marked with semi-translucent pure white forewing spots and a single large irregular white patch covering the hindwing centre.
Udaspes folus.underwing: Dark brown dusted pale along outer margins, highlighting the huge white central hindwing patch.
Udaspes folus.similarSpecies: The huge pure-white central patch on the hindwing separates Grass Demon cleanly from Common Banded Demon (Notocrypta paralysos), which has plain dark hindwings.
Udaspes folus.habitat: Moist gardens, ginger/turmeric plots, forest clearings, and shaded stream edges.
Udaspes folus.behavior: Fast-darting flyer that hovers at Lantana, Clerodendrum, and Ixora flowers and suns with half-open wings.
Udaspes folus.season: Common during and after monsoon rains.
Udaspes folus.tnDistribution: Widespread across gardens, farms, and hill forests of Tamil Nadu.
Udaspes folus.notes: Beneficial garden visitor when ginger and turmeric patches are tolerated for occasional rolled-leaf larval shelters.

Suastus gremius.headline: Sturdy brown bob patterned with bold black spots on a grey underside
Suastus gremius.upperwing: Warm dark brown forewing carrying square pale-yellow spots.
Suastus gremius.underwing: Smooth pale purplish-grey speckled prominently with sharp black dots across the hindwing.
Suastus gremius.similarSpecies: Distinctive sharp jet-black spots dotted across a smooth pale grey hindwing underside make Indian Palm Bob straightforward to identify.
Suastus gremius.habitat: Coconut plantations, urban palm avenues, coastal parks, and scrub.
Suastus gremius.behavior: Quick darting flight around palm shoots; visits Lantana and Ixora flowers in gardens.
Suastus gremius.tnDistribution: Common statewide across coastal towns, plains, and foothills.
Suastus gremius.notes: Commonly encountered across urban coconut avenues as well as rural palmyra groves.

Suastus minutus.headline: Rattan-dwelling palm bob with sparse black dots on a blue-grey hindwing below
Suastus minutus.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown; males of the southern subspecies are nearly plain above or retain only obscure pale specks on the forewing, while females bear small white spots in the cell and spaces 2-3; hindwing plain dark brown.
Suastus minutus.underwing: Forewing brown with faint pale marks at the cell end and space 1b; hindwing dusted smoothly in pale bluish-grey and marked with just three or four small black dots (a cell-end dot, an inner-space spot, and a tornal spot).
Suastus minutus.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Palm Bob (Suastus gremius) by smaller size, plain or weakly spotted male upperwings, and far fewer black spots on a distinctly bluer-grey hindwing underside; separated from Vindhyan Bob (Arnetta vindhiana) and Maculate Lancer (Salanoemia sala) by sharp black dots lacking a ring-circle pattern.
Suastus minutus.habitat: Primary evergreen forest understorey, cane brakes, shaded palm and rattan gullies, and wet foothill streams.
Suastus minutus.behavior: Quick, jerky flight low among forest rattan shoots; settles on sunlit fern blades or stream rocks in a half-open basking stance and feeds on bird droppings and small forest blossoms.
Suastus minutus.season: Recorded chiefly from July to January across wet Western Ghats slopes, with scattered dry-season sightings.
Suastus minutus.tnDistribution: Southern and central Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Anamalais, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kanyakumari forests.
Suastus minutus.notes: Represented in southern India by the Western Ghats subspecies Suastus minutus bipunctus, closely associated with wild Calamus rattans in undisturbed hill forests.

Cupitha purreea.headline: Golden-banded skipper flashing a sulphur-yellow underside with bold black wedges
Cupitha purreea.upperwing: Dark chocolate-brown forewing marked with a bright golden-yellow oblique discal band from space 1b to space 4, costal streaking, and subapical dots; hindwing carries a short yellow median band, and males have an oval waxy cushion brand in the cell covered by a dark hair tuft.
Cupitha purreea.underwing: Vivid sulphur-yellow across both wings, sharply broken on the forewing by a jet-black basal wedge and large black tornal patch, and on the hindwing by a dark brown inner-marginal band widening toward the tornal angle.
Cupitha purreea.similarSpecies: Bright sulphur-yellow underside framed by bold black basal and tornal wedges distinguishes Wax Dart cleanly from all Oriens, Potanthus, and Telicota darts as well as Bush Hopper (Ampittia dioscorides).
Cupitha purreea.habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen foothill forests, wooded stream corridors, and sunlit woodland clearings.
Cupitha purreea.behavior: Energetic darting flier that defends sunny shrub tips in the two-angle jet-plane posture; avidly puddles on damp forest paths and feeds at bird droppings and small woodland flowers.
Cupitha purreea.season: Most frequent post-monsoon from September to March, with occasional sightings after pre-monsoon showers.
Cupitha purreea.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills and moist forests including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Top Slip, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, plus scattered Eastern Ghats tracts.
Cupitha purreea.notes: One of the few Indian Hesperiinae feeding on woody Combretaceae and Boraginaceae trees and lianas rather than monocots; named for the male's oval waxy scent gland on the dorsal hindwing.

Zographetus ogygia.headline: Warm rufous-ochre flitter dotted with small purple-brown spots beneath
Zographetus ogygia.upperwing: Dark chocolate-brown dusted basally with golden-ochre hair scales; forewing carries four or five small semi-translucent pale yellow spots (paired cell spots, larger spots in spaces 2 and 3, and minute subapical dots), while the hindwing is unmarked brown.
Zographetus ogygia.underwing: Rich ferruginous-ochre to warm rufous-brown across the hindwing and outer forewing, patterned on the hindwing with small dark purplish-brown spots (two basal spots and a curved discal arc) that appear subdued in dry forms.
Zographetus ogygia.similarSpecies: Separated from Tree Flitter (Hyarotis adrastus) by warm rufous-ochre hindwing scaling with small dark purple-brown spots rather than white lunules; separated from Maculate Lancer (Salanoemia sala) and Moore's Ace (Halpe porus) by lacking a lilac-grey spot ring or pale submarginal band.
Zographetus ogygia.habitat: Shaded evergreen and moist deciduous forest trails, bamboo-lined stream valleys, and woodland-edge clearings.
Zographetus ogygia.behavior: Brisk, low flier inside shaded gaps; perches abruptly on sunlit twigs or leaf margins in a tight jet-plane posture and visits damp stream sand, bird droppings, and Stachytarpheta blooms.
Zographetus ogygia.season: Recorded primarily during monsoon and post-monsoon months from June to December.
Zographetus ogygia.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forest belts of Tamil Nadu including Anamalais, Siruvani, Nilgiris, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Zographetus ogygia.notes: Recent taxonomic revisions separated Western Ghats populations historically recorded as Zographetus ogygia into the endemic Sahyadri Spotted Flitter (Zographetus mathewi), making detailed field documentation valuable across Tamil Nadu.

Hyarotis adrastus.headline: Dark palm-feeding flitter with bold white forewing spots and white-banded hindwings below
Hyarotis adrastus.upperwing: Deep chocolate-brown forewing marked with crisp semi-translucent pure white spots comprising a quadrate cell spot, prominent discal spots in spaces 2 and 3, and three neat subapical spots in spaces 6-8; hindwing plain dark brown with checkered fringes.
Hyarotis adrastus.underwing: Warm dark brown basally and paler along the margins; hindwing crossed by a striking double series of pure white, dark-edged lunules and discal spots, while the antennae display a bright white sub-apical band.
Hyarotis adrastus.similarSpecies: Larger white forewing spots, checkered wing fringes, and bold white-lunulate hindwing underside separate Tree Flitter cleanly from Brush Flitter (Hyarotis coorga) and Purple Spotted Flitter (Zographetus ogygia), as well as from Thoressa and Halpe aces.
Hyarotis adrastus.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forests, palm and rattan groves, shaded wooded gardens, and foothill stream valleys.
Hyarotis adrastus.behavior: Rapid, erratic flight along shaded forest tracks and late-afternoon sunflecks; rests beneath leaves or suns briefly on palm fronds in jet-plane posture and visits damp mud and bird droppings.
Hyarotis adrastus.season: Active throughout the year in humid foothill forests, peaking from August to January.
Hyarotis adrastus.tnDistribution: Western Ghats foothills and valleys including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Top Slip, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, plus moist Eastern Ghats pockets.
Hyarotis adrastus.notes: Its bright white band just below the hooked antennal apiculus stands out sharply in close photographs even when the butterfly perches in dim shade.

Hyarotis coorga.headline: Rare Western Ghats endemic flitter with dark unbanded hindwings below
Hyarotis coorga.upperwing: Deep blackish-brown forewing bearing small, discrete semi-translucent white spots (a narrow cell spot, small spots in spaces 2 and 3 separated by dark-scaled veins, and minute subapical dots); hindwing uniformly dark brown with uncheckered fringes.
Hyarotis coorga.underwing: Dark purplish-brown washed subtly paler toward the outer margins, lacking crisp white lunular bands; hindwing carries only faint dark post-discal shadows, while males possess a dark hair brush on the hind tibia.
Hyarotis coorga.similarSpecies: Separated from Tree Flitter (Hyarotis adrastus) by smaller vein-separated forewing spots, uncheckered dark fringes, and an unmarked dark brown hindwing underside; separated from Golden Flitter (Quedara basiflava) by lacking a bright yellow basal hindwing patch below.
Hyarotis coorga.habitat: Primary wet evergreen hill forests, shaded cane brakes, and mid-elevation stream gorges of the Western Ghats.
Hyarotis coorga.behavior: Elusive shade-lover that darts rapidly down dim stream corridors and rests under broad leaves or on damp twigs; adults visit Leea indica flowers and occasionally puddle at wet soil.
Hyarotis coorga.season: Rare and localized, recorded mainly between September and April across post-monsoon and early dry months.
Hyarotis coorga.tnDistribution: Restricted Western Ghats evergreen belts of Tamil Nadu, notably Anamalais (Valparai and Top Slip), Nilgiri slopes, and southern hill tracts.
Hyarotis coorga.notes: Originally described from Kodagu and long treated as a subspecies of Hyarotis microstictum, this Western Ghats endemic is now recognized as a full species.

Quedara basiflava.headline: Endemic evergreen flitter hiding a bright golden-yellow hindwing base beneath
Quedara basiflava.upperwing: Glossy blackish-brown forewing crossed by a broad, conspicuous creamy-white translucent oblique band formed by conjoined spots across the cell end and spaces 2-3 (females adding a small spot in space 1b and minute subapical specks); hindwing completely plain dark.
Quedara basiflava.underwing: Forewing dark brown repeating the broad white median band; hindwing immediately diagnostic with a bright chrome-yellow basal patch covering the inner third of the wing against glossy dark brown outer scaling.
Quedara basiflava.similarSpecies: The vivid golden-yellow basal patch on the dark hindwing underside separates Golden Flitter instantly from Common Banded Demon (Notocrypta paralysos), Tree Flitter (Hyarotis adrastus), and Brush Flitter (Hyarotis coorga).
Quedara basiflava.habitat: Wet evergreen hill forests, dense rattan gullies, shaded stream valleys, and humid reed-cane undergrowth.
Quedara basiflava.behavior: Fast, shadow-hugging flight low along shaded cane thickets; settles with wings closed over the back displaying the golden hindwing base, or suns briefly in weak forest light and feeds at Strobilanthes and Leea flowers.
Quedara basiflava.season: Recorded primarily from August to February across humid evergreen valleys.
Quedara basiflava.tnDistribution: Endemic to the Western Ghats; known in Tamil Nadu from Anamalais, Siruvani, Nilgiri slopes, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Quedara basiflava.notes: A Western Ghats endemic whose cryptic closed-wing profile flashes sudden golden-yellow when the skipper shifts posture in dim evergreen ravines.

Salanoemia sala.headline: Lancer patterned beneath with a neat circular ring of dark spots around a central dot
Salanoemia sala.upperwing: Dark velvety brown forewing marked with four small translucent white spots (two minute dots in the cell and small spots in spaces 2 and 3, plus occasional faint subapical specks); hindwing completely plain dark brown.
Salanoemia sala.underwing: Pale lilac-grey to vinaceous-buff across the hindwing and forewing apex, bearing a highly distinctive rosette of six small dark brown spots arranged in a neat ring encircling a single central dark dot on the hindwing disc.
Salanoemia sala.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Palm Bob (Suastus gremius) and Small Palm Bob (Suastus minutus) by the lilac-buff underside bearing a delicate rosette ring around a central spot; separated from Purple Spotted Flitter (Zographetus ogygia) by lacking rufous-ochre ground scaling.
Salanoemia sala.habitat: Low- to mid-elevation moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, bamboo-rattan gullies, and shaded stream banks.
Salanoemia sala.behavior: Flies swiftly low through shaded forest undergrowth and perches abruptly on overhanging cane tips or wet rocks in a jet-plane basking stance; visits damp stream sand and bird droppings.
Salanoemia sala.season: Uncommon; observed chiefly from August to March along humid forested valleys.
Salanoemia sala.tnDistribution: Western Ghats forests of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Anamalais, Nilgiri foothills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Salanoemia sala.notes: Caterpillars stitch sections of thorny Calamus rattan leaflets into tight shelters hidden inside damp evergreen ravines.

Gangara thyrsis.headline: Huge twilight skipper with crimson eyes feeding on palm fronds
Gangara thyrsis.upperwing: Massive dark chocolate-brown skipper bearing large square semi-translucent golden-yellow spots on the forewing.
Gangara thyrsis.underwing: Brown dusted lightly with pale greyish-blue scales across the hindwing.
Gangara thyrsis.similarSpecies: Much larger than Rounded Palm-redeye (Erionota torus) and wears square golden forewing spots plus crimson-red eyes.
Gangara thyrsis.habitat: Palm groves, wooded urban gardens, coconut plantations, and damp foothills.
Gangara thyrsis.behavior: Crepuscular, hides under leaves during daylight and darts rapidly among palm flowers at dawn and dusk; caterpillars coat themselves in fluffy white wax filaments.
Gangara thyrsis.tnDistribution: Cities, coastal palm belts, Coimbatore, and moist hill foothills.
Gangara thyrsis.notes: Nocturnal and crepuscular giant skipper whose woolly white-waxed caterpillars roll heavy palm fronds.

Erionota torus.headline: Huge twilight banana skipper with rounded forewings and bright crimson eyes
Erionota torus.upperwing: Very large dark chocolate-brown skipper with markedly rounded forewing outer margins and three broad, well-separated semi-translucent yellow-ochre spots on the forewing (one quadrate cell spot and two large discal spots in spaces 2 and 3); hindwing unmarked with pale tornal fringes.
Erionota torus.underwing: Smooth pale greyish-brown across the hindwing and outer forewing, repeating the three large yellow forewing spots without bands or dots on the hindwing; compound eyes glow ruby-red in life.
Erionota torus.similarSpecies: Slightly smaller than Giant Redeye (Gangara thyrsis) and distinguished by rounded forewing termen and smooth unmarked greyish-brown hindwing underside lacking pale blue-grey scaling; vastly larger than Common Redeye (Matapa aria).
Erionota torus.habitat: Banana plantations, homestead gardens, moist forest edges, foothill farms, and shaded palm-rich valleys.
Erionota torus.behavior: Strongly crepuscular, sheltering motionless beneath banana fronds by day and flying powerfully at dawn and dusk to nectar at banana flowers, Lantana, and Ixora; occasionally suns briefly in early morning.
Erionota torus.season: Active year-round across banana-growing belts and foothills, peaking during monsoon and post-monsoon months.
Erionota torus.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu banana zones and hills including Coimbatore, Kallar, Pollachi, Nilgiri slopes, Madurai, and Kanyakumari.
Erionota torus.notes: Larvae cut and roll thick tubular shelters from Musa leaf margins and dust themselves with powdery white wax; the convex forewing termen separates it from the Southeast Asian Erionota thrax.

Matapa aria.headline: Unspotted bamboo skipper flashing vivid crimson eyes and golden wing fringes
Matapa aria.upperwing: Uniform warm olive-brown without hyaline spots on either wing; males carry a narrow, slightly curved dark grey sex-brand across the forewing disc, while both sexes feature pale golden-yellow fringes and bright red eyes.
Matapa aria.underwing: Smooth ferruginous to ochreous-brown lacking any spots or bands, paler along the forewing inner margin and brightened at the golden-yellow cilia.
Matapa aria.similarSpecies: Instantly separated from Blank Swift (Caltoris kumara), Pelopidas swifts, and Common Redeye lookalikes by complete absence of forewing white spots paired with ruby-red eyes and golden-yellow hindwing fringes; far smaller than Rounded Palm-redeye (Erionota torus).
Matapa aria.habitat: Bamboo clumps inside moist deciduous and evergreen forests, riparian bamboo thickets, botanical gardens, and shaded plantations.
Matapa aria.behavior: Largely crepuscular and shade-loving, hiding inside dense bamboo clumps at midday and darting briskly around bamboo shoots at dawn, dusk, and overcast hours; visits Clerodendrum and Lantana flowers.
Matapa aria.season: Present year-round wherever bamboo clumps thrive, most frequently seen from July to January.
Matapa aria.tnDistribution: Bamboo-bearing forests and gardens across Tamil Nadu including Kallar, Siruvani, Mudumalai, Top Slip, Yercaud, Kolli Hills, and Kanyakumari.
Matapa aria.notes: Larvae fold stout bamboo leaves into wax-lined cylinders before pupating inside the sheltered blade.

Parnara bada.headline: Common wetland swift showing small scattered white dots across the hindwing disc
Parnara bada.upperwing: Dark olive-brown forewing lacking cell spots (rarely a minute dot in females), bearing small white discal spots in spaces 2-4 with spot 3 midway between 2 and 4, and usually only two tiny subapical dots; hindwing carries an irregular arc of 2-4 tiny white dots.
Parnara bada.underwing: Dull ochreous-brown on the hindwing, repeating an uneven, well-separated series of tiny white discal dots across spaces 2-5 (sometimes also space 6) with no cell spot.
Parnara bada.similarSpecies: Separated from Rice Swift (Borbo cinnara) and Bevan's Swift (Borbo bevani) by lacking forewing cell spots and aligning its hindwing spots across spaces 2-5; separated from Continental Swift (Parnara ganga) by smaller, irregular, separated hindwing dots.
Parnara bada.habitat: Irrigated paddy fields, grassy marsh edges, roadside ditches, lowland wetlands, and open forest clearings.
Parnara bada.behavior: Fast, buzzing flight low above rice bunds and wetland grasses; basks in the two-angle jet-plane posture on grass blades and feeds eagerly at Tridax, Lantana, and Wedelia blossoms.
Parnara bada.season: Common throughout the year in irrigated wetlands, peaking from August to February.
Parnara bada.tnDistribution: Statewide across Tamil Nadu plains, Cauvery delta paddies, Chennai wetlands, Coimbatore, and lower Western and Eastern Ghats valleys.
Parnara bada.notes: Frequently flies alongside Borbo cinnara in South Indian paddy landscapes, where larvae stitch rice leaf blades into narrow feeding shelters.

Parnara ganga.headline: Swift marked by a tight straight bar of four white spots across the hindwing
Parnara ganga.upperwing: Dark brown forewing bearing chalky-white spots in spaces 2-4 (with spot 3 set closer to spot 2 than to 4) and subapical dots in spaces 6-8 (occasionally a minute lower cell dot); hindwing displays a straight central row of four clear white spots in spaces 2-5.
Parnara ganga.underwing: Olive-ochreous brown on the hindwing, marked by a prominent, closely aligned and nearly conjoined straight line of four white discal spots in spaces 2-5, with space 6 almost always unmarked and no cell spot.
Parnara ganga.similarSpecies: Separated from Oriental Straight Swift (Parnara bada) by larger, tidy, closely aligned hindwing spots in spaces 2-5 lacking spot 6; separated from Pelopidas branded swifts by lacking both a hindwing cell spot and male forewing brand.
Parnara ganga.habitat: Open grassy wetlands, paddy bunds, moist grasslands, scrub clearings, and mid-elevation grassy hill slopes.
Parnara ganga.behavior: Rapid, direct flight low through tall marsh grasses; suns in sunny glades with forewings raised at 45 degrees and hindwings flat in jet-plane basking posture, visiting wild Asteraceae blooms and damp mud.
Parnara ganga.season: Recorded chiefly from July to January across monsoon-fed grasslands and wetlands.
Parnara ganga.tnDistribution: Scattered across Tamil Nadu hills and plains, recorded from Coimbatore, Nilgiri foothills, Anamalai grasslands, and northern wetlands.
Parnara ganga.notes: Much scarcer than Parnara bada in Tamil Nadu and reliably confirmed in the field only from sharp underside views showing the straight four-spot hindwing row.

Borbo cinnara.headline: Common grassland swift spotted across paddy fields and lawns
Borbo cinnara.upperwing: Olive-brown wings bearing neat pale semi-translucent white spots in a curved forewing arc.
Borbo cinnara.underwing: Olive-greenish brown with three neat separated white discal spots across the hindwing.
Borbo cinnara.similarSpecies: Three well-separated white spots in spaces 2, 3, and 6 on the underside hindwing distinguish Rice Swift from Pelopidas branded swifts.
Borbo cinnara.habitat: Paddy fields, lawns, gardens, wetlands, and hill clearings.
Borbo cinnara.behavior: Fast low flight from grass flower to flower; basks in jet-plane posture.
Borbo cinnara.tnDistribution: Statewide across wetlands, plains, and hills.
Borbo cinnara.notes: One of the few rice-feeding skippers equally at home on coastal sandbars, paddy bunds, and mountain clearings.

Borbo bevani.headline: Slender olive-grey swift carrying up to five tiny hindwing dots below
Borbo bevani.upperwing: Dull olive-brown forewing bearing narrow pale yellowish-white translucent spots comprising one small upper cell spot (lower cell spot usually absent), three small discal spots in spaces 2-4, two or three subapical dots, and no spot in space 1b; hindwing unmarked.
Borbo bevani.underwing: Pale greyish-ochreous brown across the hindwing, showing a faint curved arc of four or five tiny white discal dots across spaces 2-6 and no white cell spot.
Borbo bevani.similarSpecies: Separated from Rice Swift (Borbo cinnara) by duller greyish-ochreous hindwing underside with up to five faint evenly spaced dots (including space 4) instead of three bold spots in spaces 2, 3, and 6, plus a single upper cell spot; separated from Pelopidas swifts by lacking a hindwing cell spot.
Borbo bevani.habitat: Dry grasslands, upland meadows, paddy field edges, scrub foothills, and sunny woodland clearings.
Borbo bevani.behavior: Darts swiftly between low grass stalks and perches in full sun in a two-angle jet-plane stance; visits Tridax procumbens, Lantana, and Chromolaena flowers and puddles on damp soil.
Borbo bevani.season: Active throughout the year across grassy plains and foothills, peaking from August to February.
Borbo bevani.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains and hills including Coimbatore, Chennai, Salem, Nilgiris, Palani Hills, and Tirunelveli scrub.
Borbo bevani.notes: Treated in some references as Pseudoborbo bevani; often feeds alongside Rice Swifts on roadside flowers across dry interior districts.

Pelopidas agna.headline: Uniform greyish-ochre branded swift whose cell-spot axis misses the male brand
Pelopidas agna.upperwing: Dark olive-brown forewing with narrow translucent white spots (two small cell spots, slender discal spots in spaces 2-4, and three subapical dots); males carry an oblique dark sex-brand in space 1b positioned so a line through the two cell spots passes behind or touches only its lower end; hindwing plain.
Pelopidas agna.underwing: Uniform dull greyish-ochreous brown across the hindwing, marked with a small white spot at the upper end of the cell and a neat curved post-discal series of tiny white dots in spaces 2-6.
Pelopidas agna.similarSpecies: Males separate from Small Branded Swift (Pelopidas mathias) by smaller forewing spots and the cell-spot line missing the middle of the brand; separated from Borbo swifts by the presence of a white hindwing cell spot underneath.
Pelopidas agna.habitat: Paddy fields, moist grassy clearings, stream margins, lowland gardens, and woodland borders.
Pelopidas agna.behavior: Extremely brisk flight low over grass beds; basks on exposed blades with hindwings flat and forewings angled upward, and feeds avidly at flowers, wet sand, and bird droppings.
Pelopidas agna.season: Seen year-round across Tamil Nadu, peaking between August and January.
Pelopidas agna.tnDistribution: Statewide across plains, coastal scrub, Cauvery wetlands, Coimbatore, Eastern Ghats, and Western Ghats foothills.
Pelopidas agna.notes: Females closely mirror female Pelopidas mathias, making male sex-brand geometry and uniform vs mottled hindwing scaling essential field cues.

Pelopidas subochracea.headline: Golden-dusted branded swift marked by a large square white spot in space 6 below
Pelopidas subochracea.upperwing: Warm olive-brown heavily dusted with golden-ochre scales basally; forewing bears well-developed translucent pale yellowish-white spots (two large cell spots, broad spots in spaces 2-4, three subapical dots, plus a space 1b spot in females) and a narrow white-edged male brand; hindwing often carries 2-3 faint pale spots.
Pelopidas subochracea.underwing: Golden-ochreous brown on the hindwing with a crisp white upper cell spot (often with a tiny dot above it) and a prominent post-discal series in spaces 2-7 in which the white spot in space 6 is noticeably large and quadrate.
Pelopidas subochracea.similarSpecies: Larger and warmer golden-ochreous than Small Branded Swift (Pelopidas mathias) and Little Branded Swift (Pelopidas agna), separated cleanly by the large quadrate spot in space 6 on the hindwing underside; smaller and branded in males unlike Conjoined Swift (Pelopidas conjuncta).
Pelopidas subochracea.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forest margins, bamboo-lined clearings, marshy valleys, and hill meadows.
Pelopidas subochracea.behavior: Powerful, swift flier patrolling sunny forest tracks and bamboo fringes; perches alertly on tall grass tips in jet-plane posture and visits Lantana, Chromolaena, and damp mud patches.
Pelopidas subochracea.season: Most abundant from July to January across post-monsoon hill forests.
Pelopidas subochracea.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kolli Hills, and Yercaud.
Pelopidas subochracea.notes: Represented in southern India by Pelopidas subochracea subochracea; sharp lateral photographs clearly reveal the diagnostic square spot in space 6 on the hindwing underside.

Pelopidas mathias.headline: Ubiquitous branded swift whose cell-spot axis bisects the male forewing brand
Pelopidas mathias.upperwing: Olive-brown forewing with sharp translucent white spots (two clear cell spots, quadrate spot in space 2, smaller spots in 3-4, three subapical dots, and an extra space 1b spot in females); males bear an oblique dark-bordered brand cut cleanly across its middle by an imaginary line through the two cell spots; hindwing mostly unmarked.
Pelopidas mathias.underwing: Mottled greyish-ochreous brown across the hindwing with uneven pale grey shading and dark smudges encircling a crisp white upper cell spot and a curved row of small white spots in spaces 2-6.
Pelopidas mathias.similarSpecies: Males separate from Little Branded Swift (Pelopidas agna) by the cell-spot axis cutting the middle of the brand and broader forewing spots; separated from Rice Swift (Borbo cinnara) by the white hindwing cell spot below.
Pelopidas mathias.habitat: Agricultural lands, coastal scrub, urban lawns, grasslands, wetlands, and open hill slopes.
Pelopidas mathias.behavior: Fast, brisk flier commonly seen basking in jet-plane posture on sunlit grass stalks and nectaring across Tridax, Lantana, and garden flowers; participates in seasonal local flights.
Pelopidas mathias.season: Abundant year-round across plains and hills, peaking between September and January.
Pelopidas mathias.tnDistribution: Ubiquitous statewide from Chennai coast and interior districts to Western and Eastern Ghats foothills and mid-elevations.
Pelopidas mathias.notes: One of Tamil Nadu's commonest skippers and a familiar leaf-folding caterpillar on rice, millet, and garden lawn grasses.

Pelopidas conjuncta.headline: Large unbranded swift marked with creamy-yellow spots and a crisp hindwing arc
Pelopidas conjuncta.upperwing: Large dark brown skipper dusted basally with golden-ochre hairs; forewing bears prominent pale yellowish-white translucent spots (two separate cell spots, a big quadrate spot in space 2, smaller spots in 3-4, three subapical dots, and a spot in space 1b in both sexes), and males lack any sex-brand; hindwing shows 2-4 faint pale dots.
Pelopidas conjuncta.underwing: Rich ochreous-brown on the hindwing, displaying a neat white spot near the upper cell end and a clean, curved post-discal arc of uniform dark-edged white spots across spaces 2-5 (often extending faintly to space 6).
Pelopidas conjuncta.similarSpecies: Separated from all branded Tamil Nadu Pelopidas swifts (P. mathias, P. agna, P. subochracea) by larger size, yellowish-white spots, presence of a space 1b spot in both sexes, and lack of a male forewing brand; separated from Caltoris swifts by the white spotted hindwing underside with cell spot.
Pelopidas conjuncta.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forest edges, bamboo clumps, tall marsh reeds, and shaded hill streams.
Pelopidas conjuncta.behavior: Swift, heavy-bodied flier patrolling sunny forest clearings and bamboo margins; perches on tall blades in two-angle jet-plane posture and visits Chromolaena, Mussaenda, wet sand, and bird droppings.
Pelopidas conjuncta.season: Recorded throughout the year in humid hill tracts, peaking from August to December.
Pelopidas conjuncta.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Siruvani, Kallar, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Kolli Hills, and Yercaud.
Pelopidas conjuncta.notes: Represented in South India by Pelopidas conjuncta narooa, whose caterpillars roll broad leaf-tubes on coarse bamboos and tall grasses.

Polytremis lubricans.headline: Ochre-tinted swift recognized by fused pale yellow forewing cell spots
Polytremis lubricans.upperwing: Dark golden-olive brown clothed basally in warm ochreous hairs; forewing carries pale yellow translucent spots featuring two elongated cell spots closely fused together, staggered discal spots in spaces 1b-4, and three subapical spots; hindwing shows 2-3 small pale yellow discal dots.
Polytremis lubricans.underwing: Warm rusty ochreous-brown washed evenly across the hindwing, carrying a neat curved row of 3-4 tiny pale yellow dark-ringed discal dots in spaces 2-5 with no white cell spot; forewing repeats the conjoined cell marks.
Polytremis lubricans.similarSpecies: Fused pale yellow forewing cell spots and warm rusty-ochre hindwing underside lacking a cell spot separate Contiguous Swift cleanly from Pelopidas branded swifts and Caltoris swifts.
Polytremis lubricans.habitat: Forest clearings, bamboo borders, grassy hill tracks, overgrown estate edges, and stream-side meadows.
Polytremis lubricans.behavior: Fast, agile flier patrolling sunlit openings near woodland borders; basks in two-angle jet-plane posture on ferns and grass heads and feeds at Lantana, Ageratum, and damp mineral mud.
Polytremis lubricans.season: Common from June to January in hills and foothills, scarcer during dry summer months.
Polytremis lubricans.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hills and foothills (Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Kanyakumari) as well as Kolli Hills and Shevaroys.
Polytremis lubricans.notes: Unlike Pelopidas and Borbo whose cell spots stay neatly separated, the fused hourglass-shaped forewing cell spot gives this species its vernacular name.

Baoris farri.headline: Protected bamboo swift sporting a black erectile hair-brush on the male hindwing
Baoris farri.upperwing: Dark brown forewing marked with crisp translucent white spots (two distinct cell spots, discal spots in spaces 2-4, and three subapical dots in spaces 6-8, plus an opaque pale spot in space 1b in females); hindwing unspotted, with males bearing a bold black erectile hair-brush inside a dorsal cell pouch.
Baoris farri.underwing: Smooth dark rufous-ochreous brown across the hindwing and outer forewing, normally completely unspotted on the hindwing (rarely 1-2 minute specks) and lacking any cell spot.
Baoris farri.similarSpecies: Separated from Blank Swift (Caltoris kumara) and Philippine Swift (Caltoris philippina) by having two clear forewing cell spots; separated from Kanara Swift (Caltoris canaraica) and Pelopidas swifts by its unmarked dark hindwing underside and male dorsal hindwing hair-brush.
Baoris farri.habitat: Bamboo-rich moist deciduous and evergreen forests, riparian bamboo corridors, and shaded hill trails.
Baoris farri.behavior: Swift, powerful flier operating in sunlit gaps along bamboo groves; rests in jet-plane basking posture on bamboo fronds, puddles on damp stream gravel, and visits bird droppings and Lantana.
Baoris farri.season: Recorded primarily from July to February across bamboo-rich hill ranges.
Baoris farri.tnDistribution: Western Ghats and moist Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Siruvani, Kallar, Mudumalai, Top Slip, Palani Hills, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, and Kolli Hills.
Baoris farri.wpaStatus: Protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Baoris farri.notes: Named for the male's prominent black paintbrush tuft covering a scent gland on the dorsal hindwing; legally protected in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.

Caltoris canaraica.headline: Peninsular swift with ochre-dusted hindwings dotted in four or five white spots below
Caltoris canaraica.upperwing: Dark olive-brown clothed basally in pale olive hairs; forewing bears translucent white spots including two oval cell spots, three subapical dots in spaces 6-8, and three discal spots in spaces 2-4 (females adding a dot in space 1b); females often show faint discal spots on the hindwing.
Caltoris canaraica.underwing: Brown heavily speckled with ochreous-yellow scales across the forewing apex and entire hindwing, which displays four or five neat white discal spots across spaces 2-6 and lacks a cell spot.
Caltoris canaraica.similarSpecies: Separated from Blank Swift (Caltoris kumara) and Philippine Swift (Caltoris philippina) by having two forewing cell spots and distinct white discal spots on an ochre-dusted hindwing underside; separated from Paintbrush Swift (Baoris farri) by its spotted ochre hindwing below and absence of a male hair-brush.
Caltoris canaraica.habitat: Wet evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, montane bamboo brakes, and shaded reed-lined hill streams.
Caltoris canaraica.behavior: Brisk, darting flier frequenting sunny gaps along bamboo-lined streams; basks in two-angle jet-plane posture on foliage and feeds at wet gravel, bird droppings, and Strobilanthes blooms.
Caltoris canaraica.season: Uncommon; mainly recorded during monsoon and post-monsoon months from July to January.
Caltoris canaraica.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Anamalais, Valparai, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
Caltoris canaraica.notes: A peninsular Indian specialty closely tied to native hill bamboos including Pseudoxytenanthera monadelpha in wet Western Ghats valleys.

Caltoris kumara.headline: Large bamboo swift lacking forewing cell spots and carrying plain ochre hindwings below
Caltoris kumara.upperwing: Rich dark olive-brown forewing completely lacking cell spots, crossed by a stepped series of narrow pale yellowish translucent spots in spaces 2-4 and tiny subapical dots in spaces 6-7 (females adding an opaque yellow spot in space 1b); hindwing entirely plain dark brown.
Caltoris kumara.underwing: Deep warm ochreous-brown across the hindwing and forewing apex, characteristically unmarked without discal arcs, dark borders, or cell spots (rarely showing a single faint dot).
Caltoris kumara.similarSpecies: Larger than Philippine Swift (Caltoris philippina) with a straighter forewing outer margin and warm ochre-brown rather than bright olive-green hindwing underside; separated from Kanara Swift (Caltoris canaraica) and Paintbrush Swift (Baoris farri) by lacking forewing cell spots.
Caltoris kumara.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forests, bamboo brakes, reed-fringed hill streams, and coffee or tea shade estates.
Caltoris kumara.behavior: Strong, rapid flier active along sunlit forest openings and bamboo edges; perches prominently in jet-plane posture on tall leaves and visits Lantana, Chromolaena, damp sand, and bird droppings.
Caltoris kumara.season: Recorded through most of the year in wet hills, peaking from August to January.
Caltoris kumara.tnDistribution: Western Ghats and moist hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Siruvani, Anamalais, Palani Hills, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, plus Kolli Hills.
Caltoris kumara.notes: Represented in southern India by Caltoris kumara kumara, where the combination of spotless forewing cell and clean ochre-brown hindwing below provides a reliable field clue.

Caltoris philippina.headline: Compact swift with a pinched forewing margin and bright olive-green hindwing below
Caltoris philippina.upperwing: Dark brown forewing with a noticeably concave outer margin at vein 2, lacking cell spots and marked with small pale translucent spots in spaces 2-4 and 6-7 plus a small spot in space 1b in both sexes; hindwing plain dark brown.
Caltoris philippina.underwing: Dark brown heavily washed with bright golden-olive to greenish scaling across the hindwing and forewing apex; hindwing normally unmarked or showing at most one or two minute pale specks.
Caltoris philippina.similarSpecies: Separated from Blank Swift (Caltoris kumara) by smaller size, concave forewing outer margin at vein 2, spot in space 1b, and striking olive-green hindwing underside; separated from Paintbrush Swift (Baoris farri) and Kanara Swift (Caltoris canaraica) by lacking forewing cell spots.
Caltoris philippina.habitat: Bamboo clumps in moist forests, coastal and riverine reedbeds, foothill gardens, and humid scrub clearings.
Caltoris philippina.behavior: Swift, low darting flight near bamboo and tall reeds; suns in a crisp two-angle jet-plane posture on leaf tips and feeds at small blossoms, damp sand, and bird droppings.
Caltoris philippina.season: Seen mainly from June to February across humid lowland and foothill tracts.
Caltoris philippina.tnDistribution: Scattered across coastal and foothill Tamil Nadu as well as Western Ghats valleys including Siruvani, Kallar, Pollachi, Chennai fringes, and Tirunelveli.
Caltoris philippina.notes: Represented in peninsular India by Caltoris philippina philippina; the fresh olive-green sheen beneath fades with wear, making the pinched forewing margin helpful on older individuals.

Taractrocera maevius.headline: Tiny white-spotted lawn dart with pale grey-outlined veins across the hindwing below
Taractrocera maevius.upperwing: Small dark olive-brown skipper dotted with crisp white to yellowish-white spots; forewing carries a short cell streak, broken discal series in spaces 1b-5, and subapical dots, while the hindwing bears an irregular pale discal row and cell spot; antennal clubs are blunt without a hooked apiculus.
Taractrocera maevius.underwing: Olive-brown dusted pale greyish-ochreous with all hindwing veins prominently outlined in whitish-grey, framing crisp white spots in the cell and curved discal series.
Taractrocera maevius.similarSpecies: White spots and starkly grey-veined hindwing underside distinguish it immediately from Tamil Grass Dart (Taractrocera ceramas) and all tawny-orange Oriens and Potanthus darts, while blunt unhooked antennal clubs separate it from tiny Borbo swifts.
Taractrocera maevius.habitat: Open lawns, dry grasslands, paddy field bunds, coastal scrub meadows, and fallow agricultural plots.
Taractrocera maevius.behavior: Low, fluttering zigzag flight barely above short grass blades (often mistaken for a Grass Blue lycaenid); rests close to the ground in two-angle basking posture and feeds at tiny lawn blooms like Tridax and Evolvulus.
Taractrocera maevius.season: Active year-round across Tamil Nadu plains, surging from August to January.
Taractrocera maevius.tnDistribution: Widespread statewide from Chennai coastal lawns, Point Calimere, and Coimbatore plains to lower hill grasslands of Nilgiris and Palani Hills.
Taractrocera maevius.notes: Like other Taractrocera grass darts, its flattened spoon-shaped antennal club lacks the slender terminal apiculus hook seen in nearly all other skippers.

Taractrocera ceramas.headline: Montane grass dart bearing rounded separated tawny-orange spots and blunt antennae
Taractrocera ceramas.upperwing: Dark rufous-brown patterned with small, well-separated bright tawny-orange spots; forewing displays a small orange dash in the cell, rounded separated discal spots in spaces 1b-5 (with 4-5 shifted outward), and subapical dots; hindwing carries a neat curved row of small orange spots and a cell spot.
Taractrocera ceramas.underwing: Warm ochreous-brown along the forewing costa and across the hindwing, repeating the rounded tawny-orange spots on dark-veined ochre ground alongside a bright orange costal streak and blunt apiculus-free antennal clubs.
Taractrocera ceramas.similarSpecies: Separated from Common Grass Dart (Taractrocera maevius) by bright tawny-orange rather than white spots and unlined hindwing veins; separated from Oriens dartlets and Potanthus darts by discrete rounded spots instead of solid orange bands and blunt unhooked antennae.
Taractrocera ceramas.habitat: Montane grasslands, grassy forest clearings, roadside hill banks, and plateau meadows of the Western Ghats.
Taractrocera ceramas.behavior: Flits briskly close to grass tufts in sunlit clearings; basks in two-angle jet-plane posture on low blades and nectars at Bidens, Ageratum, and Stachytarpheta flowers.
Taractrocera ceramas.season: Active across most months in the hills, peaking between August and February.
Taractrocera ceramas.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Anamalais, Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Meghamalai, and Siruvani.
Taractrocera ceramas.notes: Represented in the Nilgiris and Palani Hills by the nominate Western Ghats subspecies Taractrocera ceramas ceramas, characterized by smaller, cleaner-separated tawny spots than northern races.

Oriens concinna.headline: Western Ghats hill dartlet with isolated forewing cell spot and dusky hindwing below
Oriens concinna.upperwing: Deep blackish-brown crossed by rich dark orange-ochreous bands; on the forewing, the orange cell spot is clearly isolated and disconnected from the oblique discal band, and the subapical patch sits separate near the costa; hindwing bears a compact orange discal band.
Oriens concinna.underwing: Dark smoky ochre-brown across the hindwing where the orange discal band appears noticeably dull, obscured, and washed out against dark shading rather than sharply golden-contrasted.
Oriens concinna.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Dartlet (Oriens goloides) by slightly larger size, isolated forewing cell spot separated from the discal band, and obscure dull-banded hindwing underside; separated from Potanthus darts by solid dark-bordered orange bands and dark underside shading.
Oriens concinna.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation evergreen forest clearings, shola edges, grassy glades, and shaded hill trails of the Western Ghats.
Oriens concinna.behavior: Swift, low darting flier patrolling sunlit shola-forest gaps; perches in two-angle jet-plane basking posture on fern fronds and grass stems, visiting Impatiens, Lantana, and damp stream sand.
Oriens concinna.season: Localized and uncommon; recorded mainly from August to March across montane hills.
Oriens concinna.tnDistribution: Endemic to the southern Western Ghats; recorded from the Nilgiris, Palani Hills (Kodaikanal), Anamalais, and Meghamalai in Tamil Nadu.
Oriens concinna.notes: A Western Ghats endemic named for Tamil Nadu's hill ranges, favoring cooler, wetter shola-grassland edges above the range of most lowland dartlets.

Oriens goloides.headline: Tiny garden dartlet whose forewing cell spot merges directly into the golden band
Oriens goloides.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown crossed by bright golden-orange bands; on the forewing, the orange cell-end marking joins directly onto the oblique discal band across spaces 1b-5 with only faint vein cuts, accompanied by a subapical bar; hindwing bears a solid golden-orange discal band.
Oriens goloides.underwing: Golden-ochreous scaling washes across the forewing costa and hindwing, clearly outlining the sinuous golden-orange hindwing discal band edged thinly in dark brown.
Oriens goloides.similarSpecies: Separated from Tamil Dartlet (Oriens concinna) by smaller size, conjoined forewing cell and discal bands, and brighter golden-ochre hindwing underside; separated from Potanthus darts by tiny wingspan and unbroken orange band running continuously from cell into spaces 2-3.
Oriens goloides.habitat: Grassy forest paths, shaded gardens, moist deciduous clearings, paddy margins, and overgrown scrub edges.
Oriens goloides.behavior: Fast, buzzing flight low among shaded and sunlit grass tufts; suns in two-angle jet-plane posture on broad leaves and feeds regularly at Tridax, Lantana, and Stachytarpheta blooms.
Oriens goloides.season: Common throughout the year in foothills and humid gardens, peaking from September to January.
Oriens goloides.tnDistribution: Widespread across Western and Eastern Ghats foothills, Coimbatore, Nilgiris, Siruvani, Palani Hills, Yercaud, Kolli Hills, and Kanyakumari.
Oriens goloides.notes: One of the smallest orange-banded skippers in Tamil Nadu gardens, often sharing sunlit Lantana edges with Indian Darts.

Potanthus pseudomaesa.headline: Common orange-and-black dart whose hindwing band projects outward at space 6
Potanthus pseudomaesa.upperwing: Dark brown heavily banded in bright orange-yellow; forewing displays an orange cell bar, subapical band in spaces 6-8, and stepped discal band where spots in spaces 4-5 slightly overlap spots 2-3 below and 6-8 above across faintly darkened veins; hindwing bears an orange discal band and cell spot.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.underwing: Warm golden-ochreous across the hindwing and forewing apex, with the pale orange hindwing discal band cleanly outlined by dark borders and spots and its upper apical spot in space 6 projected noticeably outward.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.similarSpecies: Separated from Pallid Dart (Potanthus pallidus) by richer orange bands with spots 4-5 overlapping rather than widely detached; separated from Chinese Dart (Potanthus confucius) by dark-dusted veins crossing the band and outward-projected spot 6 below; much smaller than Telicota palm-darts.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.habitat: Open grasslands, scrub jungles, garden borders, agricultural hedges, and dry-to-moist woodland clearings.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.behavior: Brisk, darting flier defending grassy perches in full sun; adopts the two-angle jet-plane basking posture and visits Tridax, Lantana, and damp soil.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.season: Common year-round, peaking from August to February.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.tnDistribution: Widespread across Tamil Nadu plains, scrublands, Coimbatore, Chennai outskirts, Eastern Ghats, and lower Western Ghats slopes.
Potanthus pseudomaesa.notes: The commonest Potanthus across peninsular India, though worn specimens overlapping with rarer montane congeners require careful underside or genital verification.

Potanthus confucius.headline: Clean-veined golden dart with continuous overlap across forewing spaces 4 and 5
Potanthus confucius.upperwing: Rich dark brown banded in deep golden-orange; forewing features a smooth, continuous discal band in which spots 4 and 5 clearly overlap both spots 2-3 below and subapical spots 6-8 above, with veins across the band remaining clean orange; hindwing shows an orange discal band and cell spot.
Potanthus confucius.underwing: Bright ochreous-orange across the hindwing, highlighting a clean golden discal band neatly edged with fine dark lines and uncrossed by darkened veins; abdominal tip marked orange-yellow above.
Potanthus confucius.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Dart (Potanthus pseudomaesa) and Pallid Dart (Potanthus pallidus) by clean undarkened veins crossing the orange band and continuous overlap across spaces 4-5; separated from Palni Dart (Potanthus palnia) by bright ochreous underside without greenish shading.
Potanthus confucius.habitat: Moist forest clearings, bamboo-lined trails, hill gardens, and grassy riparian openings.
Potanthus confucius.behavior: Fast, darting flier patrolling sunlit bamboo and forest edges; perches with forewings angled at 45 degrees and hindwings flat, feeding at Lantana, Chromolaena, and wet gravel.
Potanthus confucius.season: Recorded primarily during monsoon and post-monsoon months from July to January.
Potanthus confucius.tnDistribution: Western and Eastern Ghats hill ranges of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Anamalais, Palani Hills, Siruvani, and Kolli Hills.
Potanthus confucius.notes: Represented in India by Potanthus confucius dushta; crisp photographs showing clean un-blackened veins across the orange bands help separate it from co-occurring darts.

Potanthus palnia.headline: Montane dart named for the Palni Hills with greenish-shaded hindwings below
Potanthus palnia.upperwing: Dark brown marked with rich deep orange-tawny bands; forewing spots in spaces 4 and 5 show minimal overlap with spot 3 below, spot 5 is noticeably smaller than spot 4, and veins are faintly dark-dusted across the band; hindwing bears a short orange discal band and black abdominal tip.
Potanthus palnia.underwing: Hindwing heavily suffused with dark greenish-ochreous scales, subduing the orange discal band and edging it in faint dark spots rather than bright clean yellow.
Potanthus palnia.similarSpecies: Separated from Chinese Dart (Potanthus confucius) and Indian Dart (Potanthus pseudomaesa) by its dark greenish-shaded hindwing underside, smaller forewing spot 5, weak overlap below space 4, and black-tipped abdomen; deeper orange than Pallid Dart (Potanthus pallidus).
Potanthus palnia.habitat: Mid- to high-elevation evergreen forest borders, shola-grassland margins, bamboo clearings, and hill stream banks.
Potanthus palnia.behavior: Rapid, energetic flier patrolling sunny openings at hill elevations; basks in jet-plane posture on bracken or grass stems and feeds at Bidens, Lantana, and damp stream sand.
Potanthus palnia.season: Principally recorded from August to February across montane forest tracts.
Potanthus palnia.tnDistribution: Montane Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu, especially Palani Hills (type locality), Nilgiris, Anamalais, and Meghamalai.
Potanthus palnia.notes: Described and named directly after Tamil Nadu's Palni (Palani) Hills by W.H. Evans in 1914 from South Indian montane specimens.

Potanthus pallidus.headline: Scarce hill dart with pale yellowish bands split sharply by dark veins
Potanthus pallidus.upperwing: Dark blackish-brown patterned with distinctly paler, dull yellowish-orange bands sharply segmented into blocks by dark-dusted veins; forewing spots in spaces 4 and 5 sit widely detached from spots 2-3 below and subapical spots 6-8 above; hindwing discal band narrow and vein-divided.
Potanthus pallidus.underwing: Dull pale greenish-ochreous across the hindwing, with the narrow pale yellow discal band conspicuously cut by darkened veins and bordered by fine blackish spots.
Potanthus pallidus.similarSpecies: Separated from Indian Dart (Potanthus pseudomaesa), Palni Dart (Potanthus palnia), and Chinese Dart (Potanthus confucius) by paler yellowish-cream markings, strongly dark-dusted veins bisecting the bands, and widely detached forewing spots in spaces 4 and 5.
Potanthus pallidus.habitat: Higher-elevation grassy slopes, montane forest clearings, bamboo-fringed streams, and wooded hill paths.
Potanthus pallidus.behavior: Brisk, low flier favoring sunny gaps inside hill forests; suns on exposed blades in two-angle jet-plane stance and visits wild hillside blooms and damp gravel.
Potanthus pallidus.season: Scarce and seasonal, recorded chiefly during post-monsoon and winter months from September to February.
Potanthus pallidus.tnDistribution: High-elevation Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Palani Hills, and Anamalais.
Potanthus pallidus.notes: Much less frequent in South India than Potanthus pseudomaesa, best spotted by its pale straw-tinted bands and widely detached forewing spots 4 and 5.

Potanthus pava.headline: Large long-winged forest dart with clean golden bands and orange space 3 base
Potanthus pava.upperwing: Larger, longer-winged dark brown dart with bright golden-orange bands; forewing displays a nearly continuous orange discal band with spots 4-5 overlapping above and below, an orange-filled base in space 3 in males, and clean orange veins; hindwing bears a broad orange band and orange-tipped abdomen.
Potanthus pava.underwing: Bright golden-ochre across the hindwing, displaying a broad clean golden discal band edged by dark brown speckles and clean undarkened veins; forewing dark basal shading ends cleanly before the bright discal band.
Potanthus pava.similarSpecies: Larger and longer-winged than Indian Dart (Potanthus pseudomaesa) and Palni Dart (Potanthus palnia), separated from Chinese Dart (Potanthus confucius) by the male's orange base in forewing space 3 and broader bright ochreous hindwing underside; smaller than Pale Palm-Dart (Telicota colon) and lacking a brand.
Potanthus pava.habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forest margins, shaded bamboo corridors, and hill stream valleys.
Potanthus pava.behavior: Strong, rapid flier patrolling tall grass and bamboo edges; perches alertly in jet-plane posture on sunlit shrubs and visits Lantana, Chromolaena, and wet sand.
Potanthus pava.season: Uncommon; recorded mainly from July to January across humid forest valleys.
Potanthus pava.tnDistribution: Western Ghats hills and moist valleys of Tamil Nadu including Nilgiris, Anamalais, Siruvani, and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai.
